Amino acids: the building blocks

L1LearningHigh yield
What four groups are attached to an amino acid's α-carbon?
  1. A. Amino group
    Carboxyl group
    Hydrogen
    Side chain (R group)
  2. B. Amino group
    Hydroxyl group
    Hydrogen
    Side chain (R group)
  3. C. Imino group
    Carboxyl group
    Methyl group
    Side chain (R group)
AnswerA. Amino group
Carboxyl group
Hydrogen
Side chain (R group)
WhyThe α-carbon carries an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a side chain (R); only the R group differs between amino acids.
Explanation

Every amino acid has the same core: a central α-carbon bonded to an α-amino group (–NH2, –NH3+ at pH 7.4), an α-carboxyl group (–COOH, –COO− at pH 7.4), a hydrogen atom and a variable side chain. The side chain gives each amino acid its size, charge and polarity, and so decides its class.

  • Hydroxyl instead of carboxyl: an –OH alone is not an acid; without the carboxyl there is nothing to form the peptide bond.
  • Imino + methyl: the methyl is alanine's R group, not a fixed fourth substituent; 'imino' describes proline only.
Slides (3)

Side-chain classes

L2LearningHigh yield
Which amino acids does the lecture class as hydrophobic and aliphatic?
  1. A. Gly (G), Ala (A), Ser (S), Val (V), Leu (L), Ile (I), Met (M)
  2. B. Gly (G), Ala (A), Cys (C), Val (V), Leu (L), Ile (I), Phe (F)
  3. C. Gly (G), Ala (A), Cys (C), Val (V), Leu (L), Ile (I), Met (M)
AnswerC. Gly (G), Ala (A), Cys (C), Val (V), Leu (L), Ile (I), Met (M)
WhyHydrophobic aliphatic (lecture): Gly, Ala, Cys, Val, Leu, Ile, Met; aliphatic means a non-ring carbon chain.
Explanation
Hydrophobic, aliphaticG A C V L I M
Hydrophobic, aromaticF Y W
IminoP
Polar, unchargedS T N Q
Acidic (−)D E
Basic (+)K R H
  • Ser carries an –OH and is polar uncharged.
  • Phe has a benzene ring, so it is aromatic, not aliphatic.

This primer places cysteine with the aliphatic group; many textbooks list it as polar uncharged.

Slides (1)
L3LearningHigh yield
What is histidine's main charge state at pH 7.4?
  1. A. Fully positive, because it is a strong base
  2. B. Mostly negative, because it is a weak acid
  3. C. Mostly uncharged, because it is only a weak base
AnswerC. Mostly uncharged, because it is only a weak base
WhyHistidine's imidazole (pKa ~6) is weakly basic, so at pH 7.4 most histidine side chains are uncharged.
Explanation

At a pH above a group's pKa, the deprotonated form dominates. With pKa ~6 and pH 7.4, only a small fraction of imidazole rings carry the extra proton. Because its pKa is so close to physiological pH, histidine easily gains or loses a proton, which makes it the key buffering and catalytic residue (enzyme active sites, haemoglobin).

  • Fully positive fits lysine and arginine, whose pKas are far above 7.4.
  • Negative: imidazole accepts a proton; it never carries a negative charge in proteins.

The slide still files His under 'net positive' with the basic group, and review keys mark it '+' at physiological pH: when a question asks which amino acids are basic or positively charged, include histidine.

Slides (2)

Side chains decide where a residue sits

L4LearningHigh yield
Where do a soluble protein and a membrane protein put their nonpolar side chains?
  1. A. Soluble: turned outward to the water
    Membrane: buried inside the protein
  2. B. Soluble: buried inside
    Membrane: buried inside, away from the lipid
  3. C. Soluble: buried inside
    Membrane: turned outward into the lipid bilayer
AnswerC. Soluble: buried inside
Membrane: turned outward into the lipid bilayer
WhyNonpolar side chains go where water is absent: the core of a soluble protein, and the lipid-facing surface of a membrane-spanning segment.
Explanation

The hydrophobic effect pushes nonpolar side chains away from water. In a cytosolic or plasma protein that means the interior, with charged and polar residues on the surface. In the lipid bilayer the surroundings are themselves hydrophobic, so a membrane-spanning segment shows its nonpolar residues outward to the fatty-acid tails.

  • Soluble outward would expose nonpolar groups to water and destabilise the fold.
  • Membrane inward, away from lipid would leave polar groups facing the lipid, which is unfavourable.
Slides (1)

Charge vs pH: zwitterion and pI

L5LearningHigh yield
At pH 7.4, in what form are an amino acid's α-carboxyl and α-amino groups?
  1. A. –COOH and –NH3+
  2. B. –COOH and –NH2
  3. C. –COO− and –NH3+
AnswerC. –COO− and –NH3+
WhyAt pH 7.4 the α-carboxyl is deprotonated (COO−) and the α-amino is protonated (NH3+).
Explanation

pH 7.4 is far above the carboxyl pKa (~2.2), so it has lost its proton; it is far below the amino pKa (~9.4), so the amino group keeps an extra proton. One + and one − give a net charge of zero for an amino acid with an uncharged side chain: a zwitterion.

  • –COOH and –NH3+ is the form below pH ~2 (net +1).
  • –COOH and –NH2 never predominates: it would need the carboxyl protonated and the amine deprotonated at the same time.
Slides (2)
L6LearningHigh yield
What is the net charge of an amino acid or protein below its pI, and above it?
  1. A. Below pI: net positive
    Above pI: net negative
  2. B. Below pI: net negative
    Above pI: net positive
  3. C. Below pI: net zero
    Above pI: net negative
AnswerA. Below pI: net positive
Above pI: net negative
WhyBelow the pI (more H+) the net charge is positive; above the pI it is negative.
Explanation

Lowering the pH adds protons: carboxylates become neutral –COOH while amino groups stay –NH3+, so + wins. Raising the pH strips protons: amino groups become neutral –NH2 while carboxylates stay –COO−, so − wins.

  • The reversed pairing is the common slip.
  • Net zero below pI: net zero happens only at the pI itself.

The lecture slide calls the negatively charged form 'cationic'; the correct word is anionic (an anion is negative). Hook: 'below the pI, protons pile on → positive'.

Slides (2)

Calculating pI and peptide charge

L7LearningHigh yield
How do you calculate the pI of an amino acid with an ionisable side chain?
  1. A. Average the two nearest pKas
  2. B. Use the side-chain pKa alone
  3. C. Average all three pKas
AnswerA. Average the two nearest pKas
WhyWith three ionisable groups, the pI is the average of the two nearest pKas: the two that flank the neutral form.
Explanation

Write out the forms from low to high pH and find the one with net charge 0; the pI is the average of the pKas on either side of it.

  • Acidic amino acids (Asp, Glu): the neutral form lies between the two low pKas → average pK1 and pKR.
  • Basic amino acids (Lys, Arg): the neutral form lies between the two high pKas → average pK2 and pKR.

Averaging all three, or using pKR alone, does not land at the point of zero charge.

Slides (2)

The peptide bond and reading a sequence

L8LearningHigh yield
Why can't the peptide bond rotate freely?
  1. A. It has partial double-bond character from resonance
  2. B. Neighbouring side chains clash across it
  3. C. It is a full C=N double bond
AnswerA. It has partial double-bond character from resonance
WhyResonance gives the C–N peptide bond partial double-bond character, so it is rigid and planar.
Explanation

The lone pair on the amide nitrogen delocalises toward the carbonyl oxygen. The C–N bond is therefore shorter than a single bond and behaves like ~40% double bond: it cannot twist, and the six atoms around it lie in one plane (the peptide unit).

  • Side-chain clash explains why the R groups prefer trans, not why the bond cannot rotate.
  • Full double bond overstates it: the bond is intermediate between single and double, and the C=O keeps partial double-bond character too.
Slides (2)
L9LearningHigh yield
In which direction is a peptide sequence written and read?
  1. A. C-terminus (left) → N-terminus (right)
  2. B. N-terminus (left) → C-terminus (right)
  3. C. N-terminus (right) → C-terminus (left)
AnswerB. N-terminus (left) → C-terminus (right)
WhySequences are written and read from the N-terminal (free amino end, left) to the C-terminal (free carboxyl end, right).
Explanation

This matches the direction of synthesis on the ribosome, which adds each new amino acid to the free carboxyl end. The name follows the same order: all residues but the last end in '-yl', so Tyr-Gly-Gly-Phe-Leu (Leu-enkephalin) is tyrosylglycylglycylphenylalanylleucine.

  • C → N is backwards.
  • N on the right puts the ends on the wrong sides.
Slides (1)

Four levels of structure

L10LearningHigh yield
What is tertiary structure, and what holds it together?
  1. A. The 3-D fold of one chain, held by side-chain interactions (non-covalent and covalent)
  2. B. The local folding of the backbone, held by side-chain interactions (covalent only)
  3. C. The arrangement of several chains, held by side-chain interactions (non-covalent and covalent)
AnswerA. The 3-D fold of one chain, held by side-chain interactions (non-covalent and covalent)
WhyTertiary structure is the overall 3-D fold of a single chain, held by R-group interactions, both non-covalent and covalent (disulfide).
Explanation

Secondary elements pack together into motifs and domains. The fold is stabilised by hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, metal ions and covalent disulfide bonds between side chains.

  • Covalent only is wrong twice: that is the local (secondary) level, and most tertiary forces are non-covalent.
  • Several chains is quaternary structure.

Common trap: 'tertiary structure involves only non-covalent interactions' is false.

Slides (3)

α-helix, β-sheet and random coil

L11LearningHigh yield
How are the hydrogen bonds arranged in an α-helix?
  1. A. Each side chain bonds the backbone four residues along; bonds run inside, parallel to the axis
  2. B. Each C=O bonds an N–H on a neighbouring chain; bonds run outside, perpendicular to the axis
  3. C. Each C=O bonds the N–H four residues along the same chain; bonds run inside, parallel to the axis
AnswerC. Each C=O bonds the N–H four residues along the same chain; bonds run inside, parallel to the axis
WhyIn an α-helix the C=O of residue n bonds the N–H of residue n + 4 in the same chain (intrachain); the bonds lie inside, parallel to the axis.
Explanation

Every backbone C=O and N–H inside the helix is paired, which is what makes the helix stable. Because each bond links residues one turn apart, the bonds point along the helix axis, and the peptide-unit planes are parallel to that axis.

  • Side chain to backbone: helix hydrogen bonds are backbone-to-backbone only.
  • Neighbouring chain, perpendicular: that describes a β-sheet, where bonds run between strands.
Slides (2)
L12Learning
What two orientations can the strands of a β-sheet have?
  1. A. Coiled (wound together)
    Antiparallel (opposite directions)
  2. B. Parallel (same direction)
    Antiparallel (opposite directions)
  3. C. Left-handed (same direction)
    Right-handed (opposite directions)
AnswerB. Parallel (same direction)
Antiparallel (opposite directions)
Whyβ-sheets are parallel (neighbouring strands run the same N → C direction) or antiparallel (opposite directions).
Explanation

Direction is judged from N- to C-terminus of each strand. Antiparallel sheets, often formed by a chain folding back on itself through a β-turn, have straighter, slightly stronger hydrogen bonds; parallel sheets need a longer crossover connection between strands.

  • Coiled describes coiled coils of α-helices, not sheet strands.
  • Left/right-handed describes helices; sheet strands are classed by direction only.
Slides (1)

Which residues build helices, sheets and turns

L13LearningHigh yield
Which amino acid is called the 'helix breaker', and why?
  1. A. Glycine, because its bulky ring blocks hydrogen bonding
  2. B. Proline, because its rigid ring kinks the chain
  3. C. Proline, because its charged side chain repels the backbone
AnswerB. Proline, because its rigid ring kinks the chain
WhyProline is the helix breaker: its rigid ring locks the N–Cα bond, kinks the chain and leaves no N–H for the helix hydrogen bond.
Explanation

In a helix every residue's N–H donates a hydrogen bond to the C=O four back. Proline's nitrogen is bonded to its own side chain, so it has no hydrogen to donate, and its ring fixes Φ at an angle that does not fit the helix. Proline is therefore never found inside an α-helix, only at its ends and in bends.

  • Glycine has no ring at all (R = H); it is a weak helix former because it is too flexible.
  • Charged: proline's side chain is nonpolar and uncharged.
Slides (2)

Tertiary and quaternary interactions

L14LearningHigh yield
Which five interactions stabilise tertiary structure?
  1. A. Hydrophobic interactions
    Phosphodiester bonds
    Ionic bonds
    Disulfide bonds
    Metal ions
  2. B. Hydrophobic interactions
    Hydrogen bonds
    Ionic bonds
    Peptide bonds
    Glycosidic bonds
  3. C. Hydrophobic interactions
    Hydrogen bonds
    Ionic bonds
    Disulfide bonds
    Metal ions
AnswerC. Hydrophobic interactions
Hydrogen bonds
Ionic bonds
Disulfide bonds
Metal ions
WhyTertiary structure is held by hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and metal-ion complexes, all between R groups.
Explanation

Four are non-covalent; the disulfide bond is the one covalent cross-link. Mnemonic 'HHIDM': Hydrophobic, Hydrogen, Ionic, Disulfide, Metal.

  • Phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides in DNA/RNA.
  • Peptide and glycosidic bonds: peptide bonds make primary structure; glycosidic bonds join sugars.

Quaternary structure uses the same forces minus the disulfide bond (non-covalent only).

Slides (2)

Folding, chaperones and misfolding

L15LearningHigh yield
What is the main driving force of protein folding?
  1. A. Hydrogen bonding, gathering polar side chains in the core away from water
  2. B. The hydrophobic effect, gathering nonpolar side chains on the surface toward water
  3. C. The hydrophobic effect, gathering nonpolar side chains in the core away from water
AnswerC. The hydrophobic effect, gathering nonpolar side chains in the core away from water
WhyThe hydrophobic effect drives folding: nonpolar side chains collapse into the core, away from water, an entropy-driven process.
Explanation

Water forms ordered 'cages' around exposed nonpolar groups. Burying those groups releases the water, raising the entropy of the solvent; that gain outweighs the loss of chain flexibility, so folding is favourable. The folded protein settles at its lowest free energy. Hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and van der Waals forces then fine-tune the fold.

  • Hydrogen bonding stabilises the fold but is not the main driver; polar side chains mostly stay on the surface.
  • Nonpolar on the surface is the reverse of what happens in a soluble protein.
Slides (1)
L16Learning
What does Hsp70 do?
  1. A. Cleaves exposed hydrophobic stretches that would aggregate
  2. B. Encloses the folding chain in a chamber and acts as a template
  3. C. Binds and stabilises exposed hydrophobic stretches that would aggregate
AnswerC. Binds and stabilises exposed hydrophobic stretches that would aggregate
WhyHsp70 binds and stabilises hydrophobic regions of a new or unfolded chain that would otherwise aggregate or misfold.
Explanation

A newly made chain leaving the ribosome exposes hydrophobic stretches before the rest of the protein exists to bury them. Hsp70 clamps onto those stretches (with Hsp40 helping), using ATP, and releases them in cycles so the chain can fold.

  • Cleaves: chaperones do not cut proteins; proteases do.
  • Encloses as a template is Hsp60 (the barrel-shaped chaperonin).

Hook: Hsp70 = holds the chain (binds); Hsp60 = a 'chamber' around it.

Slides (2)
L17LearningHigh yield
What secondary structure do amyloid-forming proteins adopt, and what do they form?
  1. A. β-sheet, forming insoluble amyloid fibrils
  2. B. β-sheet, forming only soluble monomers
  3. C. α-helix, forming insoluble amyloid fibrils
AnswerA. β-sheet, forming insoluble amyloid fibrils
WhyMisfolded amyloid proteins adopt mainly β-sheet structure, oligomerise and form insoluble amyloid fibrils.
Explanation

In amyloid, β-strands from many molecules stack into long, protease-resistant fibrils, held by inter-strand hydrogen bonds. Amyloid β, α-synuclein, TDP-43, polyglutamine proteins and prions all follow this pattern.

  • Soluble monomers only: fibrils are insoluble aggregates; that is why they deposit as plaques.
  • α-Helix: the disease change is helix → sheet; a drug that pushes the protein back to α-helix is the therapeutic idea.
Slides (2)
L18Learning
How does the disease-causing prion protein PrPSc differ from normal PrPC?
  1. A. Same amino acid sequence, extra disulfide bonds
  2. B. Different amino acid sequence, same conformation
  3. C. Same amino acid sequence, different conformation
AnswerC. Same amino acid sequence, different conformation
WhyPrPSc has the same amino acid sequence as normal PrPC but a different 3-D conformation (β-sheet-rich).
Explanation

The prion protein gene is a normal part of the genome. Disease comes from a change of shape alone: α-helical PrPC refolds into β-sheet-rich PrPSc. Prions are proteinaceous infectious agents that cause the transmissible spongiform encephalopathies.

  • Extra disulfide bonds: the difference is conformation, not covalent change.
  • Different sequence: sporadic and acquired cases have the normal sequence.
Slides (2)

Fibrous vs globular proteins

How do fibrous and globular proteins differ in shape and role?
  1. A. Fibrous: long and narrow, structural
    Globular: rounded, functional (catalysis, transport)
  2. B. Fibrous: rounded, functional (catalysis, transport)
    Globular: long and narrow, structural
  3. C. Fibrous: long and narrow, functional (catalysis, transport)
    Globular: rounded, structural
AnswerA. Fibrous: long and narrow, structural
Globular: rounded, functional (catalysis, transport)
WhyFibrous proteins are long, narrow and structural (strength, support); globular proteins are rounded and functional (catalysis, transport).
Explanation
FibrousGlobular

In waterGenerally insolubleGenerally soluble
