Tier 2The next layer across every concept+18 questions

Amino acids: the building blocks

L20LearningHigh yield
Which stereoisomer is found in mammalian proteins?
  1. A. L isomers only
  2. B. A racemic mix of D and L isomers
  3. C. D isomers only
AnswerA. L isomers only
WhyAll amino acids that occur in mammalian proteins are L isomers.
Explanation

An amino acid with an asymmetric α-carbon has two stereoisomers, mirror images labelled L and D by the arrangement around the α-carbon. Ribosomes and tRNA charging use only L amino acids, so every residue in a human protein (except achiral glycine) is L.

  • D isomers occur in bacterial cell walls and some antibiotics, not in mammalian proteins.
  • A racemic mix (50:50 D and L) is what a non-enzymatic chemical synthesis gives; biology is stereospecific.
Slides (2)
L21Learning
What are the one-letter codes for glutamine, glutamate, asparagine and aspartate?
  1. A. E, Q, D, N
  2. B. Q, E, N, D
  3. C. G, E, A, D
AnswerB. Q, E, N, D
WhyGlutamine = Q, glutamate = E, asparagine = N, aspartate = D.
Explanation

These four are the classic code traps because the obvious first letters are taken (G = glycine, A = alanine). The amides (glutamine, asparagine) carry the 'odd' letters Q and N; the acids carry E and D.

  • E, Q, D, N swaps each amide with its acid.
  • G, E, A, D uses glycine's and alanine's letters.

Asx (B) and Glx (Z) mean 'Asn or Asp' and 'Gln or Glu' when the amide is not known. Hook: 'Q-tamine' (glutamine), 'asparagi-N-e'. The Q in 'polyQ' diseases is glutamine.

Slides (3)

Side-chain classes

L22LearningHigh yield
Which amino acids are hydrophobic and aromatic?
  1. A. Phe (F), Tyr (Y), Pro (P)
  2. B. Phe (F), His (H), Trp (W)
  3. C. Phe (F), Tyr (Y), Trp (W)
AnswerC. Phe (F), Tyr (Y), Trp (W)
WhyThe aromatic (ring-containing) hydrophobic amino acids are phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan.
Explanation

All three carry a large flat aromatic ring: benzene (Phe), phenol (Tyr) and indole (Trp). Their bulky rings make them more common in β-sheets than in α-helices.

  • Proline has a ring, but it is a saturated (non-aromatic) pyrrolidine ring; it is the separate 'imino' class.
  • Histidine's imidazole ring is aromatic, but it is a weak base and is classed as hydrophilic, basic.
Slides (1)
L23LearningHigh yield
Which amino acids are polar and uncharged?
  1. A. Ser (S), Thr (T), Asp (D), Glu (E)
  2. B. Ser (S), Thr (T), Asn (N), Gln (Q)
  3. C. Ser (S), Cys (C), Asn (N), His (H)
AnswerB. Ser (S), Thr (T), Asn (N), Gln (Q)
WhyHydrophilic uncharged: serine, threonine (–OH) and asparagine, glutamine (amide); they form hydrogen bonds.
Explanation

These side chains carry hydroxyl or amide groups that hydrogen-bond with water and with other side chains, but none ionises at physiological pH. Serine and threonine hydroxyls are also sites of phosphorylation and O-linked glycosylation.

  • Asp and Glu are the acids of Asn and Gln: their carboxylates are negatively charged at pH 7.4.
  • His is basic; Cys is placed with the aliphatic hydrophobics in this primer.
Slides (1)

Side chains decide where a residue sits

L24LearningHigh yield
In sickle cell disease, glutamate 6 of the β-globin chain is replaced by valine. How does the side chain change?
  1. A. Basic → hydrophobic
  2. B. Acidic → hydrophobic
  3. C. Acidic → polar uncharged
AnswerB. Acidic → hydrophobic
WhyGlutamate (acidic, negative) → valine (hydrophobic aliphatic): a charged surface residue becomes a sticky nonpolar patch.
Explanation

Glu6 sits on the surface of the β chain. Valine's nonpolar side chain there creates a hydrophobic patch that, in deoxy-HbS, fits into a pocket on a neighbouring tetramer, so HbS polymerises into long fibres and the red cells sickle.

  • Basic → hydrophobic: glutamate is acidic; the basic residues are Lys, Arg and His. (HbC is Glu6 → Lys: acidic → basic.)
  • Acidic → polar uncharged: valine has no polar group; Glu → Gln would be that change.
Slides (1)

Charge vs pH: zwitterion and pI

L25LearningHigh yield
What is the isoelectric point (pI)?
  1. A. The pH at which the net charge is greatest
  2. B. The pH at which the net charge is zero
  3. C. The pH at which the side chain first becomes charged
AnswerB. The pH at which the net charge is zero
WhyThe pI is the pH at which an amino acid (or protein) exists as a zwitterion: net charge zero.
Explanation

At the pI the positive and negative charges balance exactly. Below it the molecule carries extra protons (net +); above it it has lost them (net −). Because the net charge is zero, a molecule at its pI does not move in an electric field and is least soluble.

  • Greatest net charge is reached at the extremes of pH, far from the pI.
  • Side chain becomes charged describes the side-chain pKR, not the pI.
Slides (2)

Calculating pI and peptide charge

L26LearningHigh yield
What is the net charge at pH 7.4 of the peptide NH3+-Ala-Phe-Glu-Lys-Asp-Pro-Asp-COO−?
  1. A. −1
  2. B. −2
  3. C. +1
AnswerB. −2
WhyTermini cancel (+1, −1); Glu, Asp, Asp give −3, Lys gives +1: net −2.
Explanation

Method for any peptide at pH 7.4:

  • Free N-terminus +1, free C-terminus −1 (they cancel).
  • Each Asp or Glu −1; each Lys or Arg +1.
  • His: the course lists it with the positive (basic) residues and review keys count it +1, although with a pKa ~6 most His side chains are uncharged at 7.4. Cys and Tyr are uncharged.
  • All other residues 0.

Here: −1 (Glu) +1 (Lys) −1 (Asp) −1 (Asp) = −2. −1 forgets one acidic residue; +1 reverses the signs.

Slides (1)

The peptide bond and reading a sequence

L27LearningHigh yield
What is released when a peptide bond forms, and what is needed to break it?
  1. A. Forming releases ATP (condensation)
    Breaking needs ATP (phosphorolysis)
  2. B. Forming releases water (condensation)
    Breaking needs water (hydrolysis)
  3. C. Forming releases CO2 (decarboxylation)
    Breaking needs water (hydrolysis)
AnswerB. Forming releases water (condensation)
Breaking needs water (hydrolysis)
WhyPeptide bonds form by condensation (H2O released) and break by hydrolysis (H2O added).
Explanation

The –OH of one carboxyl and an –H of the next amino group leave as a water molecule, joining the two residues. Putting the water back cleaves the bond, which is what proteases and gastric/pancreatic digestion do. Hydrolysis is thermodynamically favourable but very slow without an enzyme, so proteins are kinetically stable.

  • ATP: ATP pays for amino acid activation (tRNA charging) but is not a product of the bond itself.
  • CO2: no carbon is lost; decarboxylation makes amines (e.g. histamine), not peptides.
Slides (2)

Four levels of structure

L28LearningHigh yield
What is secondary structure, and what holds it together?
  1. A. Local folding of the backbone, held by peptide bonds between neighbouring residues
  2. B. Local folding of the backbone, held by hydrogen bonds between side chains
  3. C. Local folding of the backbone, held by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H
AnswerC. Local folding of the backbone, held by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H
WhySecondary structure (α-helix, β-sheet) is local backbone folding held by hydrogen bonds between main-chain C=O and N–H groups.
Explanation

The carbonyl oxygen of one peptide unit accepts a hydrogen bond from the amide N–H of another. In an α-helix these bonds lie within one stretch of chain; in a β-sheet they link neighbouring strands. Both the helix and the sheet are held by hydrogen bonds.

  • Peptide bonds make the chain itself (primary).
  • Side-chain hydrogen bonds are a tertiary interaction; secondary structure uses backbone atoms only.
Slides (3)

α-helix, β-sheet and random coil

L29Learning
What handedness and how many residues per turn does an α-helix have?
  1. A. Right-handed; 3.6 residues per turn
  2. B. Left-handed; 3.6 residues per turn
  3. C. Right-handed; 5.0 residues per turn
AnswerA. Right-handed; 3.6 residues per turn
WhyThe α-helix is a right-handed spiral with 3.6 residues per turn.
Explanation

It is a rigid, rod-like structure that forms spontaneously and looks like a spiral staircase turning clockwise as it moves away from the viewer. 3.6 residues per turn means residue n sits almost directly below residue n + 4, the partner it hydrogen-bonds with.

  • Left-handed helices are strained for L amino acids and almost never occur in proteins (collagen's individual chains are a special left-handed polyproline-type helix).
  • 5.0 per turn does not match the α-helix geometry.
Slides (1)

Which residues build helices, sheets and turns

L30Learning
On the lecture's helix-propensity scale, which two amino acids are the least compatible with an α-helix?
  1. A. Alanine and leucine
  2. B. Tryptophan and tyrosine
  3. C. Glycine and proline
AnswerC. Glycine and proline
WhyGlycine (1.00 kcal/mol) and proline (3.16 kcal/mol) carry the largest penalties for being in an α-helix.
Explanation

The scale lists the energy cost of placing each residue in a helix, relative to alanine (0). Proline cannot fit (rigid ring, no N–H); glycine is so flexible that pinning it into a helix costs entropy. The same two residues are what build β-turns.

  • Alanine and leucine are at the top of the table (0.00 and 0.21): strong helix formers.
  • Tryptophan and tyrosine sit in the middle (~0.5); the slide notes they are more often found in β-sheets.
Slides (2)

Tertiary and quaternary interactions

L31LearningHigh yield
Which tertiary interaction is covalent, which residues form it, and which protein is the lecture example?
  1. A. Disulfide bond, between methionines; e.g. insulin
  2. B. Disulfide bond, between cysteines; e.g. insulin
  3. C. Disulfide bond, between serines; e.g. myoglobin
AnswerB. Disulfide bond, between cysteines; e.g. insulin
WhyThe disulfide bond (–S–S–) is the covalent tertiary link, formed by oxidising two cysteine –SH groups; insulin's A and B chains are joined this way.
Explanation

Two cysteine sulfhydryls are oxidised to a disulfide (the paired residue is sometimes called cystine). Disulfides are common in secreted and extracellular proteins (insulin, immunoglobulins), where they lock the fold against denaturation. Insulin has two interchain disulfides between its A and B chains and one within the A chain.

  • Methionine contains sulfur, but as a thioether with no free –SH, so it cannot form disulfides.
  • Serine has –OH, not –SH; myoglobin has no disulfide bonds.
Slides (1)
L32Learning
How can the subunits of a quaternary protein behave relative to one another?
  1. A. Only independently, never cooperatively
  2. B. Independently, or cooperatively as in haemoglobin
  3. C. Independently, or cooperatively as in myoglobin
AnswerB. Independently, or cooperatively as in haemoglobin
WhySubunits may act independently or cooperatively; haemoglobin's four subunits bind O2 cooperatively.
Explanation

In cooperative binding, O2 binding to one haemoglobin subunit shifts the tetramer from the T (tense) to the R (relaxed) state and raises the affinity of the remaining subunits. That produces the sigmoidal O2-dissociation curve, which lets haemoglobin load O2 in the lungs and unload it in tissues.

  • Only independently ignores cooperativity, the main reason haemoglobin is a tetramer.
  • Myoglobin is a monomer; its O2 curve is hyperbolic, not cooperative.
Slides (1)

Folding, chaperones and misfolding

L33Learning
According to the lecture, what determines a protein's tertiary structure?
  1. A. Its primary sequence
  2. B. The chaperones that fold it
  3. C. The order in which its disulfide bonds form
AnswerA. Its primary sequence
WhyThe tertiary structure is determined by the primary sequence: the side chains' chemistry decides how the chain folds.
Explanation

The amino acid sequence encodes the fold: which residues are hydrophobic (to be buried), which are charged or polar (to face water), where prolines and glycines put turns. A denatured protein can often refold on its own when the denaturant is removed (Anfinsen's experiment).

  • Chaperones help a chain reach its native fold faster and avoid aggregation, but they do not encode the final shape.
  • Disulfide bonds stabilise the fold once it forms; which cysteines pair is itself set by the sequence.
Slides (1)
L34Learning
Which protein forms the amyloid in Alzheimer disease?
  1. A. Amyloid β (Aβ)
  2. B. TDP-43
  3. C. α-Synuclein
AnswerA. Amyloid β (Aβ)
WhyAlzheimer disease → amyloid β (Aβ), deposited as extracellular amyloid plaques.
Explanation

Aβ is a 40- or 42-residue fragment cut from amyloid precursor protein (APP). It spontaneously adopts β-sheet structure and aggregates into fibrils that accumulate as plaques between neurons.

DiseaseProtein
AlzheimerAmyloid β
Parkinsonα-Synuclein
ALSTDP-43
HuntingtonPolyglutamine (huntingtin)
Slides (3)
L35Learning
How is Aβ produced in Alzheimer disease?
  1. A. Amyloid precursor protein (APP) cut by α- and β-secretase → Aβ 40/42 → neurofibrillary tangles
  2. B. Amyloid precursor protein (APP) cut by α- and γ-secretase → Aβ 40/42 → amyloid plaques
  3. C. Amyloid precursor protein (APP) cut by β- and γ-secretase → Aβ 40/42 → amyloid plaques
AnswerC. Amyloid precursor protein (APP) cut by β- and γ-secretase → Aβ 40/42 → amyloid plaques
Whyβ- then γ-secretase cut APP to release Aβ 40/42, a neurotoxic peptide that aggregates into plaques.
Explanation

APP is a membrane protein. In the amyloidogenic pathway β-secretase cuts outside the membrane and γ-secretase cuts within it, releasing Aβ; the 42-residue form is the most aggregation-prone. Aβ adopts β-sheet structure and forms extracellular fibrils and plaques.

  • α + β, ending in tangles: tangles are intracellular tau, not Aβ.
  • α + γ: α-secretase cuts inside the Aβ region, so it prevents Aβ forming.
Slides (2)
L36Learning
What two properties make PrPSc pathogenic?
  1. A. It forms protease-resistant fibrils
    It carries its own nucleic acid genome
  2. B. It forms protease-resistant fibrils
    It templates PrPC into more PrPSc
  3. C. It forms soluble α-helical monomers
    It templates PrPSc back into PrPC
AnswerB. It forms protease-resistant fibrils
It templates PrPC into more PrPSc
WhyPrPSc forms insoluble, protease-resistant fibrils and acts as a template that converts normal PrPC into PrPSc.
Explanation

Each PrPSc molecule recruits PrPC and refolds it, so the abnormal form multiplies exponentially without any genetic material. The aggregates resist proteolysis (like other amyloid fibrils), accumulate and destroy neurons, giving the spongy brain.

  • Own nucleic acid: prions have none; that is what makes them unique among infectious agents.
  • Soluble α-helical, templating back to PrPC reverses the direction of the disease.
Slides (1)
L37Learning
What are the three origins of prion disease, with examples?
  1. A. Acquired (most cases)
    Inherited: familial Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (X-linked)
    Sporadic: mad cow disease, cadaveric growth hormone, kuru
  2. B. Sporadic (most cases)
    Inherited: familial Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (autosomal dominant)
    Acquired: mad cow disease, cadaveric growth hormone, kuru
  3. C. Inherited (most cases)
    Sporadic: familial Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (autosomal recessive)
    Acquired: mad cow disease, cadaveric growth hormone, kuru
AnswerB. Sporadic (most cases)
Inherited: familial Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (autosomal dominant)
Acquired: mad cow disease, cadaveric growth hormone, kuru
WhyPrion disease is mostly sporadic; it can be inherited (familial CJD, autosomal dominant) or acquired by infection (mad cow, cadaveric growth hormone, iatrogenic CJD, kuru).
Explanation
  • Sporadic: most cases; PrPC converts spontaneously.
  • Inherited: a point mutation lowers the energy barrier for folding into PrPSc; autosomal dominant.
  • Acquired: eating infected beef (variant CJD from bovine spongiform encephalopathy), cadaver-derived human growth hormone, contaminated instruments or grafts, ritual cannibalism (kuru).

The wrong options misplace 'most cases' and give the wrong inheritance pattern.

Slides (2)
Tier 3The rest of the section+16 questions

Amino acids: the building blocks

L38LearningHigh yield
What property sets an amino acid's class?
  1. A. Its side chain: hydrophobic side chains avoid water, hydrophilic ones face it
  2. B. Its carboxyl group: acidic ones face water, basic ones avoid it
  3. C. Its α-amino group: charged ones face water, neutral ones avoid it
AnswerA. Its side chain: hydrophobic side chains avoid water, hydrophilic ones face it
WhyAmino acids are classed by the chemistry of their side chain (R group): hydrophobic (nonpolar) vs hydrophilic (polar).
Explanation

The α-amino and α-carboxyl groups are the same in every amino acid, so they cannot tell amino acids apart. The R group does. The course scheme:

  • Hydrophobic (nonpolar): aliphatic, aromatic, imino (proline).
  • Hydrophilic (polar): uncharged; charged → acidic or basic.

The carboxyl and α-amino options fail because those groups are shared by all 20 and are both ionised at pH 7.4.

Slides (2)

Side-chain classes

L39Learning
Which two amino acids does the amino acid primer class as hydrophobic, although many textbooks list them as polar uncharged?
  1. A. Serine and threonine
  2. B. Cysteine and tyrosine
  3. C. Glycine and proline
AnswerB. Cysteine and tyrosine
WhyThe primer puts cysteine (aliphatic) and tyrosine (aromatic) with the hydrophobics; many textbook charts list both as polar uncharged.
Explanation

Cysteine (–SH) and tyrosine (phenol –OH) are borderline: each has a weakly polar group that can hydrogen-bond and can ionise at high pH (Cys pKa ~8.3, Tyr ~10), but each is largely nonpolar. The primer files them as hydrophobic; the review slides' nonpolar list (Gly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Met, Phe, Trp, Pro) leaves them out. Know both views.

  • Serine and threonine are polar uncharged in every scheme.
  • Glycine and proline are nonpolar in every scheme.
Slides (3)
L40LearningHigh yield
Which amino acids are acidic, and what is their charge at pH 7.4?
  1. A. Asp (D), Glu (E): negative
  2. B. Asp (D), Glu (E): positive
  3. C. Asn (N), Gln (Q): negative
AnswerA. Asp (D), Glu (E): negative
WhyAspartate and glutamate have side-chain carboxyl groups that are deprotonated (–COO−) at pH 7.4: net negative.
Explanation

The side-chain carboxyls of Asp and Glu have pKas near 4. At any pH well above the pKa a group gives up its proton, so at 7.4 both carry −1. They form ionic bonds (salt bridges) with lysine and arginine.

  • Positive: a carboxylate cannot be positive; positive charge comes from amino, guanidinium or imidazole groups.
  • Asn and Gln are the amides of Asp and Glu: polar but uncharged.
Slides (2)

Side chains decide where a residue sits

L41Learning
When related proteins are compared across species, which feature is the most highly conserved?
  1. A. The DNA sequence of the gene
  2. B. The three-dimensional structure (fold)
  3. C. The amino acid sequence
AnswerB. The three-dimensional structure (fold)
WhyProtein structure is more highly conserved than the DNA or amino acid sequence: function depends on the fold, and many different sequences can produce the same fold.
Explanation

Natural selection acts on what a protein does, and what it does depends on its 3-D fold. Because many different sequences can fold into the same shape, related proteins from distant species often keep nearly the same fold while their sequences have drifted apart. This is why structural elements, and the chemistry of the residues that build them, can be used to predict function: seven hydrophobic transmembrane α-helices mark a G-protein-coupled receptor.

  • DNA sequence is the least conserved: silent (synonymous) codon changes alter the gene without changing the protein at all.
  • Amino acid sequence changes more than structure: conservative substitutions (e.g. leucine → isoleucine in the core) keep the fold while changing the sequence.
Slides (1)
L42LearningHigh yield
A receptor for thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) has seven α-helical segments, each ~20 residues, rich in valine, leucine and isoleucine. What do these segments do?
  1. A. Bind TSH on the outside of the cell
  2. B. Span the cell membrane
  3. C. Phosphorylate tyrosine residues
AnswerB. Span the cell membrane
Why~20-residue helices of Val, Leu, Ile are transmembrane segments: the TSH receptor is a 7-helix GPCR.
Explanation

About 20 residues in an α-helix (1.5 Å rise per residue) give ~30 Å, the thickness of the bilayer's hydrophobic core. Val, Leu and Ile are hydrophobic aliphatic, so a run of them is happiest inside the lipid. Seven such helices is the GPCR signature.

  • Binding TSH is the job of the extracellular N-terminal domain, which is polar and faces water.
  • Phosphorylating tyrosines is kinase activity (receptor tyrosine kinases), not a property of hydrophobic helices.
Slides (2)

Charge vs pH: zwitterion and pI

L43Learning
Where on alanine's titration curve is its buffering capacity greatest?
  1. A. Near pH 5.7, its pI
  2. B. Near pH 2.3 and 9.1, its pKas
  3. C. Near pH 7.4, physiological pH
AnswerB. Near pH 2.3 and 9.1, its pKas
WhyAn amino acid buffers best near each pKa, where protonated and deprotonated forms are equal.
Explanation

A buffer resists pH change when it holds plenty of both the proton donor and the proton acceptor. That happens at pH = pKa (± ~1 unit), the flat 'regions of buffering' shaded on the alanine curve at 2.3 and 9.1. At the pI only one form (the zwitterion) dominates, so the curve is steep and buffering is poorest there.

  • pI (5.7) is the worst buffering region.
  • pH 7.4 is far from both of alanine's pKas; only histidine's side chain (pKa ~6) buffers near there.
Slides (2)

Calculating pI and peptide charge

L44Learning
What is the pI of aspartate (pKas 2.0, 4.0, 9.5)?
  1. A. 6.75 = (4.0 + 9.5) / 2
  2. B. 5.75 = (2.0 + 9.5) / 2
  3. C. 3.0 = (2.0 + 4.0) / 2
AnswerC. 3.0 = (2.0 + 4.0) / 2
WhyAspartate is acidic, so its neutral form sits between the two low pKas: pI = (2.0 + 4.0) / 2 = 3.0.
Explanation

Going up in pH, aspartate passes through net +1 (all protonated), 0 (α-carboxyl lost its proton at 2.0), −1 (side-chain carboxyl lost its proton at 4.0) and −2 (amino group deprotonated at 9.5). The zero-charge form lies between 2.0 and 4.0, so the pI is 3.0. An acidic amino acid always has a low pI.

  • 5.75 averages the two α-groups and ignores the side chain.
  • 6.75 averages the wrong pair: between 4.0 and 9.5 aspartate is already net −1.
Slides (2)

The peptide bond and reading a sequence

L45LearningHigh yield
Around which bonds can a polypeptide backbone rotate, and what are the angles called?
  1. A. N–Cα (Φ, phi)
    Cα–C (Ψ, psi)
  2. B. N–Cα (Ψ, psi)
    Cα–C (Φ, phi)
  3. C. C–N peptide bond (Φ, phi)
    Cα–C (Ψ, psi)
AnswerA. N–Cα (Φ, phi)
Cα–C (Ψ, psi)
WhyRotation occurs at each α-carbon: around N–Cα (Φ, phi) and Cα–C (Ψ, psi). This gives the chain its flexibility.
Explanation

Each peptide unit is a rigid plane; the planes meet at the α-carbons, which act as swivels. The pair of angles (Φ, Ψ) at every residue determines the local backbone shape, and particular pairs give the α-helix or β-sheet. Proline's ring fixes its Φ, which is part of why it breaks helices.

  • Φ and Ψ swapped mislabels the bonds: Φ is the N–Cα bond.
  • C–N peptide bond cannot rotate (partial double bond).
Slides (2)

Four levels of structure

L46LearningHigh yield
What is quaternary structure, and what holds it together?
  1. A. The arrangement of several polypeptide chains, held by non-covalent interactions
  2. B. The 3-D fold of one chain, held by non-covalent interactions
  3. C. The arrangement of several polypeptide chains, held by peptide bonds
AnswerA. The arrangement of several polypeptide chains, held by non-covalent interactions
WhyQuaternary structure is the assembly of two or more subunits, held (per the lecture) by non-covalent forces.
Explanation

The subunits are separate folded chains that associate through hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic contacts and metal ions. Haemoglobin (2α + 2β) is the standard example; myoglobin, a single chain, has none.

  • One chain is tertiary.
  • Peptide bonds join residues within a chain, never separate subunits.

Textbook note: a few multi-chain proteins (e.g. antibodies) also have inter-chain disulfide bonds; for this exam answer 'non-covalent'.

Slides (3)

α-helix, β-sheet and random coil

L47Learning
Which way do the R groups point in an α-helix?
  1. A. Outward from the helix
  2. B. Along the helix axis
  3. C. Inward to the helix core
AnswerA. Outward from the helix
WhyIn an α-helix the R groups point outward, while the hydrogen bonds are inside.
Explanation

The tightly wound backbone fills the centre of the helix, leaving no room inside; the side chains project out like the steps of a spiral staircase. Their chemistry then decides how the helix packs: a membrane helix shows hydrophobic R groups to the lipid; an amphipathic helix has a polar face and a nonpolar face.

  • Inward is the classic trap; the core is occupied by backbone atoms.
  • Along the axis describes the hydrogen bonds, not the side chains.
Slides (1)
L48Learning
What is the flexible, irregular structure found between helices and sheets called?
  1. A. β-turn
  2. B. Random coil
  3. C. Domain
AnswerB. Random coil
WhyIrregular, flexible stretches of polypeptide that are neither helix nor sheet are called random coil.
Explanation

'Random' does not mean disordered or useless: these loops have a defined structure in a given protein, often form the active or binding site, and link the regular elements. They simply lack a repeating hydrogen-bond pattern.

  • β-turn is a regular, tight four-residue U-turn with a specific hydrogen bond (C=O of residue 1 to N–H of residue 4).
  • Domain is a large, independently folded tertiary unit, not a local backbone shape.
Slides (2)

Which residues build helices, sheets and turns

L49Learning
Why are tryptophan, tyrosine and phenylalanine often found in β-sheets rather than α-helices?
  1. A. Their rings form the hydrogen bonds between strands
  2. B. The extended sheet gives their large ring side chains room
  3. C. Their rings form covalent cross-links between strands
AnswerB. The extended sheet gives their large ring side chains room
WhyLarge-ring residues (Trp, Tyr, Phe) fit β-sheets because the extended sheet, with side chains above and below, gives them space.
Explanation

In a helix the side chains crowd together around the tight spiral; bulky rings clash. In a β-sheet the chain is extended and successive side chains alternate above and below the sheet, so there is more room.

  • Rings form the inter-strand hydrogen bonds: sheet hydrogen bonds are backbone C=O to N–H.
  • Covalent cross-links: only cysteine disulfides cross-link chains covalently.

Note: the same lecture also says 'small amino acids are common, large amino acids destabilise β-sheets' (true for very tightly stacked sheets such as silk). The point tested is the slide's: aromatic residues favour sheets over helices.

Slides (2)

Tertiary and quaternary interactions

L50Learning
In a folded protein, a serine hydroxyl interacts with a glutamate side-chain carboxylate. What type of interaction is this?
  1. A. Ionic bond
  2. B. Disulfide bond
  3. C. Hydrogen bond
AnswerC. Hydrogen bond
WhySerine's –OH donates a hydrogen bond to glutamate's carboxylate oxygen.
Explanation

A hydrogen bond forms when an H on an electronegative atom (O or N) is attracted to a lone pair on another O or N. Serine is polar uncharged, so it cannot form a salt bridge, but its hydroxyl readily hydrogen-bonds with charged or polar partners.

  • Ionic bond needs two opposite full charges, e.g. aspartate with lysine; serine is uncharged.
  • Disulfide bond needs two cysteines.
Slides (1)

Folding, chaperones and misfolding

L51Learning
What usually happens to a misfolded protein?
  1. A. It is secreted from the cell
  2. B. It is stored as amyloid plaque
  3. C. It is degraded
AnswerC. It is degraded
WhyMisfolded proteins are usually degraded (ubiquitin–proteasome or autophagy–lysosome); only some escape to form aggregates.
Explanation

Chaperones first try to refold a misfolded chain. If they fail, it is tagged with ubiquitin and destroyed by the proteasome, or aggregates are removed by autophagy. Disease arises when misfolded proteins resist this clearance and form insoluble aggregates or toxic fibrils.

  • Secreted: quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum holds back misfolded secretory proteins rather than exporting them.
  • Amyloid plaque is the pathological exception, not the usual fate.
Slides (1)
L52Learning
Which gene is linked to sporadic Alzheimer disease?
  1. A. SNCA
  2. B. APP
  3. C. APOE
AnswerC. APOE
WhySporadic (late-onset) Alzheimer disease is linked to the APOE gene (apolipoprotein E, ε4 allele).
Explanation

The review slide splits Alzheimer disease into sporadic (ApoE gene) and familial (the 'amyloid hypothesis': APP and its processing). The ε4 allele of apolipoprotein E raises risk and lowers age of onset.

  • APP mutations (with presenilins) cause familial early-onset disease.
  • SNCA encodes α-synuclein (Parkinson disease).
Slides (1)

Fibrous vs globular proteins

L53Learning
How do fibrous and globular proteins differ in amino acid sequence?
  1. A. Fibrous: repetitive
    Globular: repetitive
  2. B. Fibrous: irregular
    Globular: repetitive
  3. C. Fibrous: repetitive
    Globular: irregular
AnswerC. Fibrous: repetitive
Globular: irregular
WhyFibrous proteins have a repetitive sequence; globular proteins have an irregular one.
Explanation

A repeating sequence builds a repeating structure, ideal for a long cable (collagen's Gly-X-Y repeat makes the triple helix). A globular protein needs a unique, irregular sequence to fold into a specific shape with a binding or active site.

The wrong options swap the pairing or make both repetitive.

Slides (2)

BIO-P9 Primer: acids & bases

Tier 1: 8 of 24
Learning questions 24
Tier 1Every concept once8 questions

pH, acids and bases

L1LearningHigh yield
How much does [H+] change for a one-unit change in pH, and which way?
  1. A. Tenfold; lower pH = less H+
  2. B. Twofold; lower pH = more H+
  3. C. Tenfold; lower pH = more H+
AnswerC. Tenfold; lower pH = more H+
WhypH is a log scale: each unit is a tenfold change in [H+], and because of the minus sign a lower pH means more H+.
Explanation

Because pH = −log[H+], moving one pH unit multiplies or divides [H+] by 10, two units by 100, three by 1000. The minus sign reverses the direction: high [H+] = low pH = more acidic; low [H+] = high pH = more basic.

  • Lower pH = less H+ has the direction backwards; this is the commonest trap (the school asks "which is NOT true: a low pH means a low [H+]").
  • Twofold is the change for about 0.3 pH units (log 2 ≈ 0.3), not for one whole unit.
Slides (2)
L2LearningHigh yield
What makes an acid or base weak?
  1. A. It dissociates completely, in one direction (HA → H+ + A−)
  2. B. It dissociates only partly, reaching an equilibrium (HA ⇌ H+ + A−)
  3. C. It does not dissociate in water at all
AnswerB. It dissociates only partly, reaching an equilibrium (HA ⇌ H+ + A−)
WhyA weak acid or base dissociates incompletely: it sets up a dynamic equilibrium between HA and A−, whose position is set by its pKa.
Explanation

Weak acids (acetic, lactic, carbonic acid) and weak bases (NH3) exist as a mixture of protonated and deprotonated forms. Because both forms are present, the ratio between them can be described by the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, and the pair can act as a buffer.

  • Complete, one-way dissociation defines a strong acid (HCl).
  • No dissociation at all would not make it an acid; a weak acid does release some H+.
Slides (2)

Henderson–Hasselbalch and buffers

L3Learning
State the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for a weak acid.
  1. A. pH = pKa + log([HA]/[A−])
  2. B. pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA])
  3. C. pKa = pH + log([A−]/[HA])
AnswerB. pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA])
WhypH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]): deprotonated (base) form on top, protonated (acid) form below.
Explanation

The Henderson–Hasselbalch (HH) equation links the pH of a solution to the ratio of the two forms of a weak acid. For a weak base it reads pH = pKa + log([B]/[BH+]): again the deprotonated form on top.

  • log([HA]/[A−]) inverts the ratio; it would make pH fall as the base form rises.
  • pKa = pH + log([A−]/[HA]) puts the log term on the wrong side: rearranged correctly, pKa = pH − log([A−]/[HA]).

Hook: "base over acid", as in A over HA.

Slides (2)
L4LearningHigh yield
Aspirin is a weak acid (pKa 3.5). Stomach pH ≈ 2, duodenum pH ≈ 6, blood pH ≈ 7.4. Which best describes its initial transport?
  1. A. Stomach → blood
  2. B. Duodenum → blood
  3. C. Blood → stomach
AnswerA. Stomach → blood
WhyIn the stomach pH 2 < pKa 3.5, so aspirin is mostly uncharged HA and diffuses across the gastric lining into the blood.
Explanation

Uncharged drugs cross membranes; charged ones do not. Compare pH with pKa in each place:

  • Stomach (pH 2, below 3.5): mostly HA, uncharged → absorbed. This is the first site the drug meets, so it is the initial transport.
  • Duodenum → blood: at pH 6 (2.5 units above the pKa) aspirin is >99% charged A−, so passive absorption there is poor.
  • Blood → stomach: in blood (pH 7.4) aspirin is charged and trapped; it does not diffuse back into the stomach.

A weak acid with a higher pKa still follows the same rule: compare stomach pH with the pKa.

Slides (2)
L5Learning
At what pH does a buffer resist pH change best, and why?
  1. A. At pH = 7, where H+ and OH− are equal
  2. B. At pH = pKa + 1, where the base form is ten times greater
  3. C. At pH = pKa, where acid and base forms are equal
AnswerC. At pH = pKa, where acid and base forms are equal
WhyBuffering capacity is highest at pH = pKa: there are equal amounts of acid and base, ready for either added base or added acid.
Explanation

On the titration curve of acetic acid (pKa 4.8), the flattest part, where adding OH− changes pH least, is centred on pH 4.8, where [HA] = [A−]. Moving away from the pKa, one form runs short and the curve steepens.

  • pH 7 is the neutrality of pure water; it has nothing to do with a buffer’s best pH unless its pKa happens to be 7.
  • pKa + 1 is the edge of the useful range: only one-eleventh of the buffer is left as acid to neutralise added base.
Slides (2)

The body's buffers

L6LearningHigh yield
What is the main buffer in blood, and what is its pKa?
  1. A. Bicarbonate/CO2, pKa 6.8
  2. B. Bicarbonate/CO2, pKa 6.1
  3. C. Haemoglobin, pKa 7.8
AnswerB. Bicarbonate/CO2, pKa 6.1
WhyThe most important blood buffer is bicarbonate/CO2, pKa 6.1; phosphate (6.8) works inside cells and haemoglobin (7.8) also buffers in blood.
Explanation
BufferWherepKa
Bicarbonate/CO2Blood6.1
PhosphateInside cells6.8
HaemoglobinBlood (red cells)7.8

Plasma pH 7.4; intracellular pH 6.9.

  • 6.8 is phosphate’s pKa, not bicarbonate’s.
  • Haemoglobin buffers in blood too, but it is not the main blood buffer system the lecture names.
Slides (2)
L7Learning
In CO2 + H2O ⇌ H+ + HCO3−, what happens when the reaction is pushed to the right (for example by adding CO2)?
  1. A. H+ is consumed, so pH rises
  2. B. More H+ is generated, so pH falls
  3. C. No change in pH, because bicarbonate also rises
AnswerB. More H+ is generated, so pH falls
WhyPushing right turns CO2 into H+ + HCO3−: acid is generated and pH falls; pulling left consumes H+.
Explanation

This is the core of acid–base physiology: retain CO2 (hypoventilation) → reaction driven right → more H+ → respiratory acidosis. Blow off CO2 (hyperventilation) → reaction pulled left → H+ used up → respiratory alkalosis. Adding acid from elsewhere drives it left, using up HCO3− and producing CO2 for the lungs to exhale.

  • H+ consumed is what happens when the reaction runs left.
  • No change: HCO3− does rise slightly, but [H+] rises too; the ratio HCO3−/CO2 falls, so pH falls.
Slides (2)
L8LearningHigh yield
Why is the bicarbonate buffer called an open buffer system?
  1. A. Both halves are controlled: kidneys → CO2; lungs → HCO3−
  2. B. Both halves are controlled: lungs → CO2; kidneys → HCO3−
  3. C. Its pKa equals blood pH, so it is never saturated
AnswerB. Both halves are controlled: lungs → CO2; kidneys → HCO3−
WhyCO2 levels are controlled by the lungs and bicarbonate levels by the kidneys, so neither half is fixed: the system is open to the outside.
Explanation

In a closed beaker, buffering uses up the base form for good. In the body the acid half (CO2) is exhaled or retained by the lungs, and the base half (HCO3−) is reabsorbed, regenerated or excreted by the kidneys. This is the framework for naming disorders: CO2 problems are respiratory, HCO3− problems are metabolic.

  • Kidneys → CO2, lungs → HCO3− swaps the organs (the school’s favourite distractor: "flip the organ systems").
  • pKa equals blood pH is false: 6.1 is 1.3 units below 7.4.
Slides (3)
Tier 2The next layer across every concept+9 questions

pH, acids and bases

L9Learning
How does [H+] at blood pH 7.1 compare with [H+] at the normal pH of 7.4?
  1. A. About half as much
  2. B. About ten times as much
  3. C. About twice as much
AnswerC. About twice as much
WhyA fall of 0.3 pH units is a factor of 100.3 ≈ 2: [H+] at 7.1 is about double normal (+99%).
Explanation

The primer’s "Goldilocks zone" table: normal [H+] at pH 7.4 is 4.0 × 10−8 M; at 7.1 it is 7.9 × 10−8 M (+99%); at 7.0 it is 1.0 × 10−7 M (+151%); at 7.7 it is −50%. So the narrow-looking blood pH window hides large swings in [H+].

  • About half is the direction for a pH rise of 0.3 (pH 7.7).
  • Ten times would need a full pH unit (7.4 → 6.4).
Slides (2)
L10Learning
What does a lower pKa tell you about an acid?
  1. A. It is a weaker acid (holds its proton more tightly)
  2. B. It is a stronger base
  3. C. It is a stronger acid (dissociates more readily)
AnswerC. It is a stronger acid (dissociates more readily)
WhypKa = −log Ka, so a lower pKa means a larger dissociation constant: the acid gives up its proton more readily, a stronger acid.
Explanation

Ka is the dissociation constant: high Ka = more H+ released = stronger acid. Taking −log flips the scale, so high Ka = low pKa. The pKa is also the pH at which the acid is exactly half dissociated: an acid with a low pKa is already half dissociated at a very acidic pH.

  • Weaker acid goes with a high pKa (low Ka).
  • Stronger base: a low pKa describes the acid; its conjugate base is actually a weaker base.
Slides (3)

Henderson–Hasselbalch and buffers

L11Learning
A solute with pKa 9 is dissolved at pH 7. Which form predominates?
  1. A. [A−] is about 100 times [HA]
  2. B. [HA] equals [A−]
  3. C. [HA] is about 100 times [A−]
AnswerC. [HA] is about 100 times [A−]
WhypH is 2 units below the pKa: log([A−]/[HA]) = −2, so HA is ~100 times A−, the protonated form wins.
Explanation

Rule of thumb from the primer: pH < pKa → more HA than A−; pH > pKa → more A−; pH = pKa → equal. Here 7 − 9 = −2, ratio 10−2.

  • A− 100 times HA is the answer for pH two units above the pKa (pH 11).
  • Equal needs pH = pKa.
Slides (2)
L12Learning
A drug is a weak base with pKa 7.0. At pH 9.0, which form predominates?
  1. A. Charged BH+ (about 99%), which is trapped
  2. B. Uncharged B (about 99%), which crosses membranes
  3. C. Equal amounts of B and BH+
AnswerB. Uncharged B (about 99%), which crosses membranes
WhyFor a base, pH = pKa + log([B]/[BH+]); at pH 9 the ratio is 102, so ~99% is uncharged B and can cross membranes.
Explanation

A weak base is protonated (charged, BH+) in acid and deprotonated (uncharged, B) in alkali: the mirror of a weak acid. Above its pKa a base is mostly uncharged and lipid-soluble; below its pKa it is mostly charged.

  • Charged BH+ dominates below the pKa (for example in the acidic stomach).
  • Equal amounts occurs only at pH = pKa = 7.0.

Tip: for an acid, charged = above pKa; for a base, charged = below pKa.

Slides (2)
L13Learning
What is a buffer?
  1. A. A strong acid mixed with its conjugate base
  2. B. A strong acid mixed with a strong base
  3. C. A weak acid mixed with its conjugate base
AnswerC. A weak acid mixed with its conjugate base
WhyA buffer is a solution that resists pH change: a weak acid (protonated) plus its conjugate base (deprotonated).
Explanation

Both halves must be present in useful amounts: the acid half neutralises added base and the base half neutralises added acid. Examples: acetic acid/acetate, carbonic acid (CO2)/bicarbonate, H2PO4−/HPO42−.

  • A strong acid dissociates completely, so its "conjugate base" (for example Cl−) cannot take protons back: no buffering.
  • Strong acid + strong base simply neutralise each other to salt and water.
Slides (2)

The body's buffers

L14Learning
Which half of the bicarbonate system can be adjusted faster, and why?
  1. A. HCO3−: the kidneys act within minutes; the lungs need hours to days for CO2
  2. B. Both equally fast: lungs and kidneys respond within seconds
  3. C. CO2: the lungs change ventilation within minutes; the kidneys need hours to days for HCO3−
AnswerC. CO2: the lungs change ventilation within minutes; the kidneys need hours to days for HCO3−
WhyBreathing changes PCO2 within minutes; the kidneys need hours to days to reabsorb or make enough HCO3−.
Explanation

This timing explains the pattern of compensation: metabolic disorders are compensated by the lungs (fast), respiratory disorders by the kidneys (slow), which is why a respiratory disorder has an acute (uncompensated) and a chronic (renally compensated) phase.

  • Kidneys within minutes reverses the speeds.
  • Both within seconds: renal acid–base adjustment requires changes in tubular transport and ammonium production that take hours to days.
Slides (2)
L15LearningHigh yield
Write the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for blood (bicarbonate system).
  1. A. pH = 6.8 + log([HCO3−] / (0.03 × PCO2))
  2. B. pH = 6.1 + log((0.03 × PCO2) / [HCO3−])
  3. C. pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−] / (0.03 × PCO2))
AnswerC. pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−] / (0.03 × PCO2))
WhypH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−] / (0.03 × PCO2)): bicarbonate (base) on top, dissolved CO2 (acid) below, pKa 6.1.
Explanation

This is the general HH equation (pH = pKa + log[base]/[acid]) applied to blood. Dissolved CO2 stands in for carbonic acid and is calculated from the partial pressure: [CO2] = 0.03 × PCO2 (mm Hg) in mmol/L. The equation shows at a glance why HCO3− (kidneys, metabolic) and PCO2 (lungs, respiratory) push pH in opposite directions.

  • 6.8 is the pKa of phosphate.
  • PCO2 on top inverts the ratio: acid must go in the denominator.
Slides (1)
L16LearningHigh yield
In which three ways do the kidneys contribute to acid–base balance?
  1. A. Reabsorb filtered HCO3−
    Produce new HCO3−
    Excrete H+ as ammonium (NH4+)
  2. B. Reabsorb filtered H+
    Produce new HCO3−
    Excrete HCO3− as ammonium (NH4+)
  3. C. Reabsorb filtered HCO3−
    Produce new H+
    Excrete H+ as glutamine
AnswerA. Reabsorb filtered HCO3−
Produce new HCO3−
Excrete H+ as ammonium (NH4+)
WhyKidneys reabsorb filtered HCO3−, make new HCO3− and excrete H+ as NH4+.
Explanation

Bicarbonate is freely filtered; the tubules reclaim almost all of it (otherwise it would be lost in urine) and also generate new HCO3− to replace what was used up buffering metabolic acids. The H+ secreted to do this leaves in the urine, largely bound to NH3 as NH4+ (the NH3 comes from glutamine).

  • Reabsorb H+: the kidney secretes and excretes H+; it does not reclaim it. Bicarbonate is not excreted as ammonium.
  • Produce new H+ and excrete H+ as glutamine: glutamine is the source of NH3, not the carrier excreted.
Slides (2)
L17Learning
In red cells in tissue capillaries, CO2 from metabolism is converted to HCO3−. What happens next?
  1. A. Cl− leaves the red cell in exchange for HCO3−; H+ is exhaled
  2. B. HCO3− leaves the red cell in exchange for Cl− (chloride shift); H+ binds haemoglobin
  3. C. HCO3− stays inside the red cell; H+ is released into plasma
AnswerB. HCO3− leaves the red cell in exchange for Cl− (chloride shift); H+ binds haemoglobin
WhyHCO3− leaves the red cell in exchange for Cl− (chloride shift), while the H+ formed with it is buffered by deoxyhaemoglobin (HbH).
Explanation

Tissue capillary: CO2 + H2O → (carbonic anhydrase) H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3−. The H+ binds haemoglobin, which helps it unload O2 (Bohr effect). HCO3− is carried to the lungs in plasma. In the lungs everything reverses (reverse chloride shift): HCO3− re-enters the red cell, combines with H+ released from Hb as it binds O2, and the CO2 formed is exhaled.

  • Cl− leaving the cell is the reverse chloride shift, which happens in the lungs.
  • HCO3− staying in, H+ released: the H+ is held by haemoglobin, otherwise venous blood would become strongly acidic.
Slides (3)
Tier 3The rest of the section+7 questions

pH, acids and bases

L18Learning
Why is the pH of pure water 7?
  1. A. In pure water [H+] = [OH−] = 10−14 M
  2. B. In pure water [H+] = [OH−] = 107 M
  3. C. In pure water [H+] = [OH−] = 10−7 M
AnswerC. In pure water [H+] = [OH−] = 10−7 M
WhyWater dissociates so that [H+][OH−] = 10−14; with equal amounts each is 10−7 M, and −log 10−7 = 7.
Explanation

H2O ⇌ H+ + OH−. The product [H+][OH−] is fixed at 1 × 10−14 (the ion product of water). In pure water the two ions are made in equal amounts, so each is the square root, 1 × 10−7 M, and pH = −log(10−7) = 7, neutral.

  • 10−14 M is the product of the two concentrations, not each one.
  • 107 M drops the minus sign of the exponent: that would be an impossibly huge concentration.
Slides (1)
L19Learning
What is an acid, by the proton (Brønsted) definition?
  1. A. A proton acceptor: HA + H+ → H2A+
  2. B. A proton donor: HA → H+ + A−
  3. C. An electron donor: HA → H + A
AnswerB. A proton donor: HA → H+ + A−
WhyAn acid donates a proton (H+); what is left, A−, is its conjugate base.
Explanation

HA ⇌ H+ + A−. The acid (protonated form) gives up H+; the deprotonated form A− can take a proton back, so it is a base, the conjugate base of HA (acetic acid → acetate, lactic acid → lactate, carbonic acid → bicarbonate).

  • Proton acceptor is the definition of a base.
  • Electron donor belongs to redox chemistry (and the Lewis definition of a base), not to the proton definition used here.
Slides (2)

Henderson–Hasselbalch and buffers

L20LearningHigh yield
Over what range of pH is a buffer useful?
  1. A. Within about ±0.1 pH unit of its pKa
  2. B. Within about ±3 pH units of its pKa
  3. C. Within about ±1 pH unit of its pKa
AnswerC. Within about ±1 pH unit of its pKa
WhyBuffering capacity is high within ±1 pH unit of the pKa, where both forms are present at ratios between 1 : 10 and 10 : 1.
Explanation

Outside that window one form makes up more than about 90% of the pair, so there is too little of the other form to neutralise further additions and pH changes quickly. For acetic acid (pKa 4.8) the buffer region is about 3.8–5.8.

  • ±0.1 is far too narrow; buffering is still good half a unit away from the pKa.
  • ±3 units is far too wide: three units away the ratio is 1000 : 1 and one form is essentially gone.
Slides (2)
L21Learning
You need a buffer to hold a solution at pH 5.0. Which weak acid would serve best?
  1. A. Lactic acid (pKa 3.9)
  2. B. Carbonic acid (pKa 6.4)
  3. C. Acetic acid (pKa 4.8)
AnswerC. Acetic acid (pKa 4.8)
WhyA buffer works best when its pKa is close to the pH to be held: acetic acid (4.8) is only 0.2 units from 5.0.
Explanation

Choose the buffer whose pKa sits nearest the target pH, and at least within one unit of it. At pH 5.0 the acetate/acetic acid ratio is about 1.6 : 1, both forms are plentiful.

  • Lactic acid (pKa 3.9) is 1.1 units away: at pH 5.0 it is >90% lactate, outside its useful range.
  • Carbonic acid (pKa 6.4) is 1.4 units away: at pH 5.0 it is mostly undissociated.
Slides (1)

The body's buffers

L22Learning
Why is bicarbonate the main blood buffer even though its pKa (6.1) is more than one unit below blood pH (7.4)?
  1. A. It is the only buffer present in plasma
  2. B. Carbonic anhydrase raises its effective pKa to 7.4
  3. C. The lungs and the kidneys keep resetting both of its halves
AnswerC. The lungs and the kidneys keep resetting both of its halves
WhyBicarbonate is an open system: the lungs adjust CO2 and the kidneys adjust HCO3−, so it never runs out; it is also plentiful (24 mEq/L).
Explanation

A closed buffer at pH 7.4 with pKa 6.1 would be poor (ratio 20 : 1). But the acid half, CO2, is a gas that the lungs can blow off or retain within minutes, and the base half, HCO3−, is reclaimed and regenerated by the kidneys. So both sides of the ratio are actively controlled.

  • Only buffer in plasma: plasma also contains phosphate and proteins, and red cells contain haemoglobin.
  • Carbonic anhydrase only speeds up CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3; an enzyme does not change a pKa or an equilibrium.
Slides (2)
L23Learning
Calculate normal blood pH from HCO3− 24 mEq/L and PCO2 40 mm Hg.
  1. A. 24/(0.03 × 40) = 20 → log 20 = 1.3 → 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4
  2. B. 24/(0.03 × 40) = 20 → log 20 = 1.3 → 6.8 + 1.3 = 8.1
  3. C. (0.03 × 40)/24 = 0.05 → log 0.05 = −1.3 → 6.1 − 1.3 = 4.8
AnswerA. 24/(0.03 × 40) = 20 → log 20 = 1.3 → 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4
Why0.03 × 40 = 1.2; 24/1.2 = 20; log 20 = 1.3; 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4. A 20 : 1 ratio always means pH 7.4.
Explanation

Memorise the ratio: whenever [HCO3−]/(0.03 × PCO2) is 20, pH is 7.4, whatever the absolute values. A disorder changes one term; compensation moves the other term in the same direction to bring the ratio back towards 20. The acid–base map (figure) plots PCO2 against HCO3−; each line is one pH, and the orange ellipse marks the normal range around 24 and 40.

  • 6.8 + 1.3 uses phosphate’s pKa.
  • (0.03 × 40)/24 inverts the ratio (acid over base).
Slides (2)
L24Learning
Which enzyme in renal tubule cells is central to reabsorbing filtered bicarbonate and making new bicarbonate?
  1. A. Glutaminase
  2. B. Carbonic anhydrase
  3. C. Na+/K+-ATPase
AnswerB. Carbonic anhydrase
WhyCarbonic anhydrase interconverts CO2 + H2O and H2CO3, letting the tubule reclaim filtered HCO3− and generate new HCO3−.
Explanation

In the proximal tubule diagram: secreted H+ meets filtered HCO3− in the lumen → H2CO3 → (luminal carbonic anhydrase) CO2 + H2O; CO2 enters the cell, where intracellular carbonic anhydrase re-forms H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3−; the HCO3− goes to blood and the H+ is secreted again.

  • Glutaminase frees NH3 from glutamine for NH4+ excretion; it is not the bicarbonate-handling enzyme the lecture names.
  • Na+/K+-ATPase powers sodium gradients on the blood side; it does not convert CO2 and bicarbonate.
Slides (2)

BIO-P10 Primer: lipid structures

Tier 1: 12 of 33
Learning questions 33
Tier 1Every concept once12 questions

What a lipid is: polar, nonpolar, storage, membrane

L1LearningHigh yield
Which lipids are storage lipids, and what are their properties?
  1. A. Triacylglycerols and cholesteryl esters; neutral, kept in intracellular lipid droplets (above all adipose)
  2. B. Phospholipids and cholesterol; amphipathic, kept in cell membranes (above all myelin)
  3. C. Triacylglycerols and cholesteryl esters; amphipathic, kept in cell membranes (above all adipose)
AnswerA. Triacylglycerols and cholesteryl esters; neutral, kept in intracellular lipid droplets (above all adipose)
WhyStorage lipids (triacylglycerols, cholesteryl esters) are neutral and stored inside cells in lipid droplets, above all in adipose tissue.
Explanation

A storage lipid has every polar group masked: triacylglycerol is glycerol with all three hydroxyls esterified to fatty acids, and a cholesteryl ester is cholesterol with its single hydroxyl esterified. With nothing polar left, they cannot sit in a membrane; they coalesce into droplets (in a white adipocyte one droplet fills most of the cell).

  • Phospholipids and cholesterol are membrane lipids, not storage lipids.
  • Amphipathic, in membranes is the description of membrane lipids; TAG and cholesteryl esters are not amphipathic.
Slides (2)

Fatty acid structure and naming

L2Learning
What does the name 18:2Δ9,12 (linoleic acid) mean?
  1. A. 18 carbons; 2 double bonds, at C9 and C12 counted from the methyl (ω) carbon
  2. B. 18 carbons; 2 double bonds, at C9 and C12 counted from the carboxyl carbon
  3. C. 18 carbons; 2 branches, at C9 and C12 counted from the carboxyl carbon
AnswerB. 18 carbons; 2 double bonds, at C9 and C12 counted from the carboxyl carbon
WhyΔ numbers give where each double bond starts, counted from the carboxyl carbon (C1): linoleic acid has double bonds at C9–C10 and C12–C13.
Explanation

Δ (delta) notation follows the normal numbering, which starts at the carboxyl carbon. So 18:2Δ9,12 means 18 carbons, 2 double bonds, beginning at C9 and C12. Oleic acid is 18:1Δ9.

  • Counted from the methyl end is the ω (omega) system. From that end linoleic acid's first double bond is at ω-6 (18 − 12 = 6), which is why it is an omega-6 fatty acid; ω-9 would be wrong for it.
  • Branches: the number after the colon counts double bonds, and natural fatty acids are unbranched.
Slides (1)

Saturation, kinks and melting point

L3Learning
Which three fatty acids are polyunsaturated (PUFA)?
  1. A. Oleic, linoleic and arachidonic acid
  2. B. Linoleic, linolenic and arachidonic acid
  3. C. Palmitoleic, oleic and linolenic acid
AnswerB. Linoleic, linolenic and arachidonic acid
WhyPolyunsaturated = two or more double bonds: linoleic (18:2), linolenic (18:3) and arachidonic (20:4) acid.
Explanation
TypeDouble bondsExamples
Saturatednonepalmitic 16:0, stearic 18:0
Monounsaturatedonepalmitoleic 16:1, oleic 18:1
PUFAtwo or morelinoleic 18:2, linolenic 18:3, arachidonic 20:4

Both wrong options slip in a monounsaturated acid (oleic, palmitoleic). Linoleic and linolenic acid are the essential fatty acids; arachidonic acid (20:4) is made from linoleic acid.

Slides (2)
L4LearningHigh yield
How does a fatty acid's melting point change with chain length and with unsaturation?
  1. A. Rises with chain length; rises with unsaturation
  2. B. Falls with chain length; rises with unsaturation
  3. C. Rises with chain length; falls with unsaturation
AnswerC. Rises with chain length; falls with unsaturation
WhyMelting point rises with chain length (more van der Waals contact) and falls with unsaturation (cis kinks stop tight packing).
Explanation

Melting means pulling chains apart. Longer chains touch over a greater length, so they need more heat. Each cis double bond adds a kink that keeps chains apart, so less heat is needed. That is why fats rich in unsaturated fatty acids (vegetable oils) are liquid at room temperature and saturated animal fats are solid.

  • Rises with unsaturation is backwards: unsaturation lowers the melting point.
  • Falls with chain length is the classic true/false trap; it rises.
Slides (2)

Triacylglycerol: the storage fat

L5Learning
Why is fat a better energy store than glycogen?
  1. A. Same energy per gram as carbohydrate; stored dry, whereas glycogen carries water
  2. B. More than twice the energy per gram; stored with water, whereas glycogen is stored dry
  3. C. More than twice the energy per gram; stored dry, whereas glycogen carries water
AnswerC. More than twice the energy per gram; stored dry, whereas glycogen carries water
WhyFat gives about 9 kcal/g versus about 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate or protein, and it is stored without water, whereas glycogen is heavily hydrated.
Explanation

Fatty acid carbons are highly reduced (mostly CH2), so their oxidation releases more energy per gram. Being hydrophobic, TAG packs into droplets with almost no water, while each gram of glycogen holds roughly two grams of water. Gram for gram of stored tissue, fat therefore carries several times more usable energy.

  • Same energy per gram is wrong: fat gives more than twice as much.
  • Fat stored with water, glycogen dry reverses the hydration: glycogen is the hydrated one.
Slides (1)

Glycerophospholipids

L6Learning
How does a glycerophospholipid differ from a TAG?
  1. A. All three fatty acids are replaced by phosphate groups
  2. B. One fatty acid is replaced by a sugar head group
  3. C. One fatty acid is replaced by a phosphate-containing head group
AnswerC. One fatty acid is replaced by a phosphate-containing head group
WhyA glycerophospholipid keeps fatty acids on C1 and C2 of glycerol but carries a phosphate-linked polar head group on C3 instead of a third fatty acid.
Explanation

Swapping one fatty acid for a charged phosphate head turns a neutral storage lipid into an amphipathic membrane lipid: two nonpolar tails plus one polar head. That single change is why glycerophospholipids are the primary constituents of cell membranes.

  • All three replaced would leave no nonpolar tails, so the molecule could not form a membrane.
  • A sugar head group without phosphate describes a glycolipid.
Slides (2)

Cardiolipin, phosphatidylinositol and PAF

L7Learning
A 30-year-old woman has had two deep-vein thromboses and three miscarriages. Her serum contains antiphospholipid antibodies against the lipid also used as the antigen in syphilis screening. Which lipid is it?
  1. A. Phosphatidylinositol
  2. B. Sphingomyelin
  3. C. Cardiolipin
AnswerC. Cardiolipin
WhyThrombosis + recurrent miscarriage = antiphospholipid syndrome; the classic target is cardiolipin, the inner-mitochondrial-membrane lipid also used in syphilis tests.
Explanation

Cardiolipin (two phosphatidic acids joined through a glycerol) is the antigen of anti-cardiolipin antibodies, found in antiphospholipid syndrome, syphilis and lupus. Antiphospholipid antibodies make the blood prone to clot, causing venous and arterial thromboses and placental clotting that leads to pregnancy loss.

  • Phosphatidylinositol is a signalling membrane lipid; the lecture links no antibody disease to it.
  • Sphingomyelin is the myelin sphingophospholipid; it is not the antigen in these tests.
Slides (2)
L8LearningHigh yield
How does phosphatidylinositol take part in cell signalling?
  1. A. Its phosphorylated form, PIP2, is split by phospholipase C into IP3 and DAG (Gq pathway)
  2. B. Its phosphorylated form, PIP2, is split by adenylyl cyclase into cAMP and DAG (Gs pathway)
  3. C. Its phosphorylated form, PIP2, is split by phospholipase C into cAMP and ceramide (Gi pathway)
AnswerA. Its phosphorylated form, PIP2, is split by phospholipase C into IP3 and DAG (Gq pathway)
WhyPI is phosphorylated to PIP2, which Gq-activated phospholipase C splits into the second messengers IP3 and diacylglycerol (DAG).
Explanation

Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) sits in the inner leaflet. When a Gq-coupled receptor fires, phospholipase C cleaves it: IP3 diffuses to the endoplasmic reticulum and releases Ca2+, while DAG stays in the membrane and activates protein kinase C. PI's C2 is often esterified with arachidonic acid, linking it to eicosanoid production.

  • Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP from ATP (Gs), not from PIP2.
  • Ceramide comes from sphingolipids, and phospholipase C does not make cAMP.
Slides (1)
L9Learning
What is the structure of platelet-activating factor (PAF)?
  1. A. C1: ether-linked saturated chain
    C2: acetyl ester
    C3: phosphoinositol
  2. B. C1: ether-linked saturated chain
    C2: acetyl ester
    C3: phosphocholine
  3. C. C1: ester-linked saturated chain
    C2: acetyl ester
    C3: phosphocholine
AnswerB. C1: ether-linked saturated chain
C2: acetyl ester
C3: phosphocholine
WhyPAF = glycerol with an ether-linked saturated chain at C1, an acetyl ester at C2 and phosphocholine at C3.
Explanation

PAF is an unusual glycerophospholipid. At C1 the chain is attached through an ether bond (C–O–C), not the usual ester. At C2 there is only a two-carbon acetyl group instead of a long fatty acid. Its head group is the same phosphocholine found in PC.

  • Phosphoinositol at C3 is the head of phosphatidylinositol.
  • Ester-linked at C1 misses PAF's defining ether bond.

Hook: PAF is the ether lipid of the lesson; sphingolipids are the amide lipids.

Slides (2)

Sphingolipids and sphingomyelin

L10Learning
What is ceramide?
  1. A. Sphingosine + phosphocholine; the parent of every sphingolipid
  2. B. Sphingosine + a fatty acid (amide); the parent of every sphingolipid
  3. C. Glycerol + a fatty acid (amide); the parent of every glycerophospholipid
AnswerB. Sphingosine + a fatty acid (amide); the parent of every sphingolipid
WhyCeramide = sphingosine + one amide-linked fatty acid; all sphingolipids are derivatives of ceramide.
Explanation

Ceramide is the sphingolipid equivalent of diacylglycerol: two hydrophobic tails (sphingosine's own chain plus the fatty acid) and a free C1 hydroxyl waiting for a head group. Add phosphocholine → sphingomyelin; add a sugar → cerebroside; add an oligosaccharide with sialic acid → ganglioside.

  • Sphingosine + phosphocholine lacks the fatty acid (sphingosylphosphocholine); it is not ceramide.
  • Glycerol + fatty acid: glycerol takes fatty acids as esters, and the parent of glycerophospholipids is phosphatidic acid.
Slides (2)
L11Learning
What do sphingomyelin and lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) have in common, and how do they differ?
  1. A. Same phosphocholine head; sphingomyelin is built on ceramide (sphingosine), lecithin on glycerol
  2. B. Same glycerol backbone; sphingomyelin carries a phosphocholine head, lecithin a phosphoserine head
  3. C. Same phosphocholine head; sphingomyelin is built on glycerol, lecithin on ceramide (sphingosine)
AnswerA. Same phosphocholine head; sphingomyelin is built on ceramide (sphingosine), lecithin on glycerol
WhyBoth carry a phosphocholine head group (both are phospholipids), but sphingomyelin sits on ceramide while lecithin sits on glycerol.
Explanation

Same head, different backbone: lecithin is a glycerophospholipid (two ester-linked fatty acids on glycerol); sphingomyelin is a sphingophospholipid (sphingosine's own chain + one amide-linked fatty acid). Both are abundant in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane. The two are compared in the lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio of amniotic fluid, used to judge fetal lung maturity.

  • Same glycerol backbone is wrong for sphingomyelin, and a phosphoserine head belongs to PS, not lecithin.
  • The third option swaps the backbones, the classic mix-up.
Slides (1)

Cholesterol in membranes

L12Learning
What does cholesterol do in membranes?
  1. A. Forms the bilayer core on its own; has no effect on fluidity
  2. B. Wedges between phospholipids; buffers membrane fluidity
  3. C. Spans the membrane as a channel; regulates ion flow
AnswerB. Wedges between phospholipids; buffers membrane fluidity
WhyCholesterol wedges between phospholipids and acts as a fluidity buffer: less fluid when warm, stops the membrane stiffening when cold.
Explanation

The rigid rings restrain the movement of the neighbouring fatty acid chains, so at body temperature cholesterol reduces fluidity. At low temperatures it keeps the chains from packing into a rigid gel, so it prevents stiffening. It also clusters with sphingomyelin into ordered membrane patches.

  • Forms the core alone: cholesterol cannot form a bilayer by itself; it needs phospholipids.
  • Channel: cholesterol is a small lipid, not a pore-forming protein.
Slides (2)
Tier 2The next layer across every concept+11 questions

What a lipid is: polar, nonpolar, storage, membrane

L13LearningHigh yield
What property defines lipids as a group?
  1. A. Insoluble in water; soluble in nonpolar solvents (chloroform, ether)
  2. B. Soluble in water; insoluble in nonpolar solvents (chloroform, ether)
  3. C. Insoluble in both water and nonpolar solvents (chloroform, ether)
AnswerA. Insoluble in water; soluble in nonpolar solvents (chloroform, ether)
WhyLipids are a chemically heterogeneous group united by solubility: relatively insoluble in water, soluble in nonpolar solvents such as chloroform and ether.
Explanation

Fatty acids, triacylglycerols, phospholipids, sphingolipids and sterols share no single chemical skeleton. What they share is that they are mostly hydrocarbon: C–H bonds cannot hydrogen-bond with water, so lipids stay out of water and dissolve instead in nonpolar organic solvents (like dissolves like). That is why lipids are extracted from tissue with chloroform or ether.

  • Soluble in water, insoluble in nonpolar solvents describes sugars, amino acids and salts: the opposite of a lipid.
  • Insoluble in both is wrong: solubility in nonpolar solvents is the very definition of the group.
Slides (2)

Fatty acid structure and naming

L14LearningHigh yield
How are fatty acids classified by chain length?
  1. A. Short <4 C
    Medium 4–8
    Long 10–16
    Very long >16
  2. B. Short <6 C
    Medium 6–12
    Long 14–22
    Very long >36
  3. C. Short <6 C
    Medium 6–12
    Long 14–22
    Very long >22
AnswerC. Short <6 C
Medium 6–12
Long 14–22
Very long >22
WhyShort <6 carbons, medium 6–12, long 14–22, very long >22.
Explanation

The classes matter later: medium-chain fatty acids are handled differently from long-chain ones in digestion and in mitochondrial uptake, and very-long-chain ones start their breakdown in peroxisomes. Dietary fat and stored fat are mostly long-chain (palmitic 16, stearic 18, oleic 18).

  • The <4 / 4–8 / 10–16 scheme shifts every boundary down.
  • Very long >36 is impossible: 36 carbons is the upper limit of natural chains.

Some texts put the very-long cut-off at more than 20 carbons; this lecture uses more than 22.

Slides (3)

Saturation, kinks and melting point

L15Learning
How does replacing saturated fatty acid tails with cis-unsaturated ones change a membrane?
  1. A. Kinked tails pack loosely → membrane more fluid
  2. B. Kinked tails pack tightly → membrane more rigid
  3. C. Straight tails pack loosely → membrane more fluid
AnswerA. Kinked tails pack loosely → membrane more fluid
WhyCis double bonds kink the phospholipid tails, which cannot pack tightly, so the membrane becomes more fluid.
Explanation

The same packing logic that sets a fat's melting point sets a membrane's fluidity. Saturated tails are straight, pack tightly and make the bilayer more ordered and less fluid. Kinked unsaturated tails leave space between them, so lipids move more freely. This is also why the unsaturated fatty acid usually sits at C2 of membrane glycerophospholipids.

  • Kinked tails pack tightly is a contradiction: kinks prevent tight packing.
  • Straight tails belong to saturated fatty acids, and straight tails pack tightly.
Slides (2)
L16Learning
Which fats does the lecture list as risk factors for coronary artery disease?
  1. A. Monounsaturated and cis fats
  2. B. Omega-3 and omega-6 fats
  3. C. Saturated and trans fats
AnswerC. Saturated and trans fats
WhySaturated and trans fats are risk factors for coronary artery disease; both have straight chains that pack tightly.
Explanation

Diets high in saturated and trans fat raise blood LDL cholesterol and promote atherosclerosis. Trans fats are the worse of the two (they also lower HDL), which is why they have been largely removed from processed foods.

  • Monounsaturated cis fats (oleic acid, olive oil) are associated with lower coronary risk.
  • Omega-3 and omega-6 fats are polyunsaturated cis fats; they are not on the risk list.
Slides (2)

Triacylglycerol: the storage fat

L17LearningHigh yield
What is a triacylglycerol (TAG)?
  1. A. Three fatty acids on a sphingosine backbone
  2. B. Three fatty acids on a glycerol backbone
  3. C. Two fatty acids on a glycerol backbone
AnswerB. Three fatty acids on a glycerol backbone
WhyA triacylglycerol (triglyceride) is three fatty acids ester-linked to the three hydroxyl groups of glycerol.
Explanation

Glycerol is a three-carbon alcohol with one hydroxyl on each carbon; each hydroxyl forms an ester with one fatty acid. The three fatty acids are usually different (often an unsaturated one in the middle position). TAG is fat as you know it: the lipid of adipose tissue, butter and vegetable oil.

  • Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids, which carry only one amide-linked fatty acid.
  • Two fatty acids on glycerol is a diacylglycerol, or with a phosphate head on C3, a glycerophospholipid.
Slides (2)

Glycerophospholipids

L18Learning
What do phospholipids form in water, and how are they arranged?
  1. A. A micelle: tails outward, heads inward
  2. B. A bilayer: tails inward, heads outward
  3. C. A bilayer: heads inward, tails outward
AnswerB. A bilayer: tails inward, heads outward
WhyPhospholipids form a bilayer: polar heads face the water on both surfaces and nonpolar tails meet in the middle.
Explanation

Two tails per molecule make a phospholipid roughly cylindrical, which suits a flat double layer rather than a sphere. The heads line the extracellular and cytoplasmic faces; the tails form the hydrophobic core that blocks ions and polar molecules.

  • Micelle with tails outward: in water, tails always point away from water, and single-tailed lipids (fatty acids, bile salts) are the ones that form micelles.
  • Bilayer with heads inward, tails outward would expose the tails to water, which is unstable.
Slides (1)
L19Learning
What are the three most abundant phospholipids in humans?
  1. A. Phosphatidylcholine (PC)
    Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE)
    Phosphatidylserine (PS)
  2. B. Phosphatidylglycerol (PG)
    Phosphatidylserine (PS)
    Platelet-activating factor (PAF)
  3. C. Phosphatidylinositol (PI)
    Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE)
    Phosphatidic acid (PA)
AnswerA. Phosphatidylcholine (PC)
Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE)
Phosphatidylserine (PS)
WhyThe three most abundant human phospholipids are PC, PE and PS, each built on phosphatidic acid.
Explanation

PC (lecithin) is the most abundant; PE and PS follow. In the plasma membrane PC sits mainly in the outer leaflet, while PE and PS sit mainly in the inner leaflet.

  • PAF is a potent signalling lipid present in tiny amounts, and phosphatidylglycerol is a minor lipid (best known in lung surfactant).
  • PI is a minor membrane lipid valued for signalling, and phosphatidic acid is the precursor, kept at low levels.
Slides (2)

Cardiolipin, phosphatidylinositol and PAF

L20Learning
What does platelet-activating factor (PAF) do?
  1. A. Activates inflammatory cells
    Mediates surfactant secretion and lung expansion
    Platelets aggregate and release serotonin
  2. B. Inhibits inflammatory cells
    Mediates wound healing and tolerance
    Platelets disaggregate and take up serotonin
  3. C. Activates inflammatory cells
    Mediates hypersensitivity, acute inflammation, anaphylaxis
    Platelets aggregate and release serotonin
AnswerC. Activates inflammatory cells
Mediates hypersensitivity, acute inflammation, anaphylaxis
Platelets aggregate and release serotonin
WhyPAF activates inflammatory cells, mediates hypersensitivity, acute inflammatory and anaphylactic reactions, and makes platelets aggregate and release serotonin.
Explanation

PAF is a potent lipid mediator made by activated leucocytes, platelets and endothelium at very low concentrations. It recruits and activates neutrophils and other inflammatory cells, increases vascular permeability, constricts bronchi, and drives the hypotension and shock of anaphylaxis. It was named for its first-found action: aggregating platelets and making them release serotonin.

  • Surfactant secretion and lung expansion are the job of type II pneumocytes and their phosphatidylcholine-rich surfactant, not PAF.
  • Inhibits inflammation, platelets disaggregate is the opposite of what PAF does.
Slides (2)

Sphingolipids and sphingomyelin

L21LearningHigh yield
Which bond type marks each lipid family: glycerol lipids, sphingolipids and PAF's C1?
  1. A. Ester → glycerol (TAG, glycerophospholipids)
    Ether → sphingosine (ceramide, sphingolipids)
    Amide → C1 of PAF
  2. B. Ester → glycerol (TAG, glycerophospholipids)
    Amide → sphingosine (ceramide, sphingolipids)
    Ether → C1 of PAF
  3. C. Amide → glycerol (TAG, glycerophospholipids)
    Ester → sphingosine (ceramide, sphingolipids)
    Ether → C1 of PAF
AnswerB. Ester → glycerol (TAG, glycerophospholipids)
Amide → sphingosine (ceramide, sphingolipids)
Ether → C1 of PAF
WhyEster links fatty acids to glycerol; amide links the fatty acid to sphingosine; ether links PAF's C1 chain.
Explanation
BondFormed fromWhere
Ester (–CO–O–)acid + alcoholTAG, glycerophospholipids, cholesteryl esters, PAF C2 acetyl
Amide (–CO–NH–)acid + amineceramide and every sphingolipid
Ether (C–O–C)alcohol + alcoholPAF C1 (and plasmalogens)

The wrong options swap the amide with the ether or with the ester. Hook: sphingosine has the amino group, so it makes the amide.

Slides (1)
L22Learning
Where is sphingomyelin especially important, and with which lipid is it usually associated?
  1. A. Myelin sheath; alongside cholesterol in the membrane
  2. B. Lung surfactant; alongside phosphatidylglycerol
  3. C. Inner mitochondrial membrane; alongside cardiolipin
AnswerA. Myelin sheath; alongside cholesterol in the membrane
WhySphingomyelin is an important constituent of the myelin sheath, and in membranes it is usually associated with cholesterol.
Explanation

Myelin wraps axons in many layers of membrane that insulate and protect the fibres and speed conduction. Sphingomyelin's long, mostly saturated chains pack tightly with cholesterol into ordered membrane patches.

  • Lung surfactant is mainly phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) with phosphatidylglycerol; sphingomyelin is only a minor component.
  • The inner mitochondrial membrane is the home of cardiolipin, not sphingomyelin.

Cholesterol in membranes

L23LearningHigh yield
How does free cholesterol sit in a phospholipid bilayer?
  1. A. Fully nonpolar; buried entirely among the fatty acid tails
  2. B. Amphipathic; its hydroxyl by the polar heads, its rings among the fatty acid tails
  3. C. Fully polar; lying flat on the membrane surface in the water
AnswerB. Amphipathic; its hydroxyl by the polar heads, its rings among the fatty acid tails
WhyFree cholesterol is amphipathic: its single –OH sits next to the phospholipid heads while its rigid rings line up with the fatty acid tails.
Explanation

That one hydroxyl is enough to make cholesterol a membrane lipid (the lecture lists it with phospholipids and glycolipids). It anchors the molecule at the water interface while the ring system slots in between the acyl chains.

  • Fully nonpolar describes cholesteryl esters and TAG, not free cholesterol.
  • Fully polar is wrong: the ring system and side chain are hydrocarbon.

Of TAG, cholesteryl esters and cholesterol, only cholesterol is amphipathic.
