Tier 3The rest of the section+10 questions

What a lipid is: polar, nonpolar, storage, membrane

L24LearningHigh yield
Which lipids are membrane lipids, and what property do they share?
  1. A. Phospholipids, cholesterol, triacylglycerols; fully nonpolar
  2. B. Triacylglycerols, cholesteryl esters, glycolipids; neutral
  3. C. Phospholipids, cholesterol, glycolipids; amphipathic
AnswerC. Phospholipids, cholesterol, glycolipids; amphipathic
WhyMembrane lipids (phospholipids, cholesterol, glycolipids) are amphipathic: each has a polar part and a nonpolar part.
Explanation

To build a membrane a lipid must face water on one side and the oily interior on the other. Phospholipids have a charged phosphate head; glycolipids have a sugar head; cholesterol has a single hydroxyl group. All three also carry nonpolar hydrocarbon tails or rings.

  • Triacylglycerols are neutral storage lipids; they are not membrane components, and membrane lipids are not fully nonpolar.
  • Triacylglycerols and cholesteryl esters are the neutral storage lipids; glycolipids belong in the membrane list.
Slides (2)

Fatty acid structure and naming

L25Learning
What is the structure of a fatty acid?
  1. A. Long hydrocarbon chain + alcohol (hydroxyl) group at each end
  2. B. Short hydrocarbon chain + phosphate group at one end
  3. C. Long hydrocarbon chain + acid (carboxyl) group at one end
AnswerC. Long hydrocarbon chain + acid (carboxyl) group at one end
WhyA fatty acid is a carboxylic acid: a hydrocarbon chain ending in a carboxyl (–COOH) group at one end and a methyl group at the other.
Explanation

The general formula is CH3–(CH2)n–COOH. The chain is nonpolar; the carboxyl end is polar and, at body pH, mostly ionised to carboxylate (–COO–), so a free fatty acid is itself amphipathic. Almost every lipid in this lesson is built from fatty acids attached to a backbone (glycerol or sphingosine).

  • A hydroxyl at each end would make a diol (an alcohol), not an acid.
  • A phosphate group is what a phospholipid adds through its glycerol backbone; fatty acids themselves carry none.
Slides (2)
L26Learning
How long are natural fatty acid chains, and what two features do almost all share?
  1. A. 4–36 carbons; unbranched, even number of carbons
  2. B. 12–24 carbons; branched, even number of carbons
  3. C. 2–10 carbons; unbranched, odd number of carbons
AnswerA. 4–36 carbons; unbranched, even number of carbons
WhyNatural fatty acids have 4–36 carbons; almost all have an even number of carbons and are unbranched.
Explanation

The even number follows from how fatty acids are made and broken down: two carbons at a time (acetyl-CoA units in synthesis, acetyl-CoA released in β-oxidation). The straight, unbranched chain lets saturated fatty acids pack tightly.

  • 12–24, branched: the range is too narrow and branching is the exception (e.g. phytanic acid), not the rule.
  • 2–10, odd: too short, and odd-chain fatty acids are rare (their breakdown leaves propionyl-CoA).
Slides (1)
L27Learning
How are the carbons of a fatty acid numbered and named?
  1. A. C1 = carboxyl carbon
    C2 = β-carbon
    C3 = α-carbon
    Far methyl carbon = ω-carbon
  2. B. C1 = methyl carbon
    C2 = α-carbon
    C3 = β-carbon
    Far carboxyl carbon = ω-carbon
  3. C. C1 = carboxyl carbon
    C2 = α-carbon
    C3 = β-carbon
    Far methyl carbon = ω-carbon
AnswerC. C1 = carboxyl carbon
C2 = α-carbon
C3 = β-carbon
Far methyl carbon = ω-carbon
WhyNumbering starts at the carboxyl carbon (C1); C2 is the α-carbon, C3 the β-carbon, and the terminal methyl carbon is the ω-carbon.
Explanation

The carboxyl end is where most reactions of storage and energy release start, so it is C1. The Greek letters label the carbons next to it: α right beside the carboxyl, β after that; ω (the last Greek letter) is the methyl carbon at the far end. In palmitic acid the ω-carbon is C16.

  • β at C2, α at C3 swaps the two letters.
  • C1 = methyl carbon numbers from the wrong end; the methyl end is the ω end.

Hook: β-oxidation is named for the β-carbon (C3), the one oxidised in each cycle.

Slides (3)

Saturation, kinks and melting point

L28Learning
Which form of double bond is natural in fatty acids, and what does it do to the chain?
  1. A. Cis; keeps the chain straight
  2. B. Cis; puts a kink in the chain
  3. C. Trans; puts a kink in the chain
AnswerB. Cis; puts a kink in the chain
WhyNatural unsaturated fatty acids have cis double bonds, each of which puts a kink (about 30°) in the chain; more cis bonds = more kinks.
Explanation

In a cis double bond both chain segments sit on the same side of the C=C, so the chain bends there. Oleic acid (cis-18:1) has one bend; linoleic acid two; arachidonic acid four, making it strongly curved.

  • Cis, straight: a cis bond always bends the chain.
  • Trans, kinked: in a trans bond the segments sit on opposite sides, so the chain stays nearly straight.
Slides (2)

Triacylglycerol: the storage fat

L29LearningHigh yield
What is the body's main store of fuel?
  1. A. Glycogen in the liver
  2. B. Protein in skeletal muscle
  3. C. Triacylglycerol in adipose tissue
AnswerC. Triacylglycerol in adipose tissue
WhyTriacylglycerol in adipose tissue is the largest fuel reserve: roughly 15 kg in a lean adult, against only about 100 g of liver glycogen.
Explanation

TAG is the most important form of lipid storage in both white and brown adipocytes, and it holds by far the most energy (well over 80% of stored fuel energy in a typical adult).

  • Liver glycogen (about 100 g) supports blood glucose for less than a day of fasting; it is a buffer, not the main store.
  • Muscle protein is structural and functional; breaking it down for fuel is a last resort in prolonged starvation.
Slides (1)

Glycerophospholipids

L30Learning
What is phosphatidic acid?
  1. A. The simplest glycerophospholipid: phosphate with no further head group; precursor of the others
  2. B. A glycerophospholipid with a choline head group; precursor of the others
  3. C. A sphingolipid with no head group; precursor of the others
AnswerA. The simplest glycerophospholipid: phosphate with no further head group; precursor of the others
WhyPhosphatidic acid is diacylglycerol 3-phosphate with nothing attached to the phosphate: the precursor from which all glycerophospholipids derive.
Explanation

Attach a head group to its phosphate and you get the familiar phospholipids: serine → phosphatidylserine, ethanolamine → phosphatidylethanolamine, choline → phosphatidylcholine, inositol → phosphatidylinositol. Cardiolipin is two phosphatidic acids joined through a glycerol.

  • Choline head group describes phosphatidylcholine (lecithin), a derivative of phosphatidic acid, not the parent.
  • A sphingolipid: the parent of the sphingolipids is ceramide, built on sphingosine.
Slides (2)
L31Learning
What is lecithin?
  1. A. Phosphatidylcholine (PC)
  2. B. Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE)
  3. C. Phosphatidylserine (PS)
AnswerA. Phosphatidylcholine (PC)
WhyLecithin = phosphatidylcholine (PC): glycerol + two fatty acids + phosphocholine head.
Explanation

Lecithin is the most abundant phospholipid of human membranes and the main lipid of lung surfactant (as dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine). The lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio in amniotic fluid is used to judge fetal lung maturity.

  • PE (ethanolamine head) and PS (serine head) are the other two of the big three, but neither is lecithin.

Hook: leCithin = Choline.

Slides (1)

Sphingolipids and sphingomyelin

L32LearningHigh yield
What is the main feature that distinguishes glycerolipids from sphingolipids?
  1. A. The type of head group attached
  2. B. The backbone molecule
  3. C. The type of fatty acid present
AnswerB. The backbone molecule
WhyThe backbone decides the class: glycerol for glycerolipids, the amino alcohol sphingosine for sphingolipids.
Explanation

Everything else follows from the backbone. Glycerol carries fatty acids as esters on C1 and C2; sphingosine already has its own long hydrocarbon chain and takes one more fatty acid through an amide bond, forming ceramide.

  • Head group: both families can carry the same head (PC and sphingomyelin both have phosphocholine).
  • Fatty acid type: both can carry saturated or unsaturated fatty acids; it is not the distinguishing feature.
Slides (2)
L33Learning
How is a polar head group attached to sphingosine (ceramide)?
  1. A. By a glycosidic or amide bond
  2. B. By a glycosidic or phosphodiester bond
  3. C. By an amide or peptide bond
AnswerB. By a glycosidic or phosphodiester bond
WhyThe head group joins ceramide's C1 hydroxyl by a glycosidic bond (sugar heads: glycosphingolipids) or a phosphodiester bond (phosphate heads: sphingomyelin).
Explanation

The type of link splits the sphingolipids in two:

  • Phosphodiester → sphingophospholipid: sphingomyelin (phosphocholine head).
  • Glycosidic → glycosphingolipids: cerebrosides (one sugar), globosides and gangliosides (sugar chains).

The amide bond is used once, to attach the fatty acid, not the head group. Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins.

Myoglobin vs haemoglobin: structure and haem

L1LearningHigh yield
Myoglobin and haemoglobin differ at which level of protein structure?
  1. A. Tertiary
  2. B. Quaternary
  3. C. Secondary
AnswerB. Quaternary
WhyBoth fold the same way around a haem; they differ in quaternary structure: myoglobin is one chain, haemoglobin four.
Explanation

Quaternary structure is the arrangement of several separate polypeptide chains (subunits) into one molecule. Myoglobin is a single chain, so it has none; haemoglobin is a tetramer of four chains. That one difference is what lets haemoglobin's subunits signal to each other (cooperativity, allosteric control by H+, CO2 and 2,3-BPG).

  • Tertiary: both chains have the same 'globin fold', about eight α-helices wrapped around a haem pocket.
  • Secondary: both are mostly α-helix.

The lecture also calls their primary structures similar; strictly, their amino-acid sequences are only distantly related, but they fold the same way.

Slides (3)
L2Learning
What is haem?
  1. A. Ferrous iron (Fe2+) held in a protoporphyrin ring
  2. B. Magnesium held in a chlorin ring
  3. C. Cobalt held in a corrin ring
AnswerA. Ferrous iron (Fe2+) held in a protoporphyrin ring
WhyHaem is a ferrous iron (Fe2+) atom held at the centre of a protoporphyrin ring; the globin chain wraps around it.
Explanation

Haem is the prosthetic group of haemoglobin and myoglobin: a flat protoporphyrin ring (four linked pyrrole rings) whose four nitrogens grip one iron atom. The globin plus its haem is the working unit; the iron is where O2 binds.

  • Magnesium in a chlorin ring is chlorophyll.
  • Cobalt in a corrin ring is vitamin B12 (cobalamin).
Slides (1)

Cooperativity, the oxygen curve and P50

L3LearningHigh yield
What is cooperativity in haemoglobin?
  1. A. One subunit binds O2 → changes shape → the other subunits bind O2 more easily
  2. B. One subunit binds O2 → changes shape → the other subunits bind O2 less easily
  3. C. One subunit binds CO2 → changes shape → the other subunits bind O2 more easily
AnswerA. One subunit binds O2 → changes shape → the other subunits bind O2 more easily
WhyPositive cooperativity: O2 binding to one subunit changes the shape of the others and raises their O2 affinity.
Explanation

When the first O2 binds, its subunit shifts shape and loosens the bonds that hold the whole tetramer in the low-affinity T state. The remaining subunits flip toward the high-affinity R state, so each further O2 binds more easily. This positive cooperativity produces the sigmoid curve.

  • 'Less easily' would be negative cooperativity; haemoglobin does the opposite.
  • CO2 binding stabilises the T state, so it lowers, not raises, O2 affinity.

Cooperativity needs several subunits that touch each other, which is why the single-chain myoglobin cannot show it.

Slides (3)
L4LearningHigh yield
Why does haemoglobin's curve need to be sigmoid?
  1. A. It loads fully in the lungs (high PO2) and unloads readily in the tissues (lower PO2)
  2. B. It holds O2 tightly at all PO2 values so none is lost before the tissues
  3. C. It loads fully in the tissues (high PO2) and unloads readily in the lungs (lower PO2)
AnswerA. It loads fully in the lungs (high PO2) and unloads readily in the tissues (lower PO2)
WhyThe S-shape lets haemoglobin load almost fully in the lungs yet release a large share of its O2 over the lower PO2 of the tissues.
Explanation

The top of the S is flat across lung PO2 (about 100 mm Hg), so haemoglobin fills almost completely. The middle of the S is steep across tissue PO2 (about 20–40 mm Hg), so it gives up much of its load there. A transporter needs both properties.

  • Holding O2 tightly everywhere describes a high-affinity store such as myoglobin; it would deliver little.
  • Loading in the tissues and unloading in the lungs reverses where PO2 is high and low.
Slides (3)

T and R states: shifting the curve

L5Learning
How do the effectors H+, CO2, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG), O2 and CO change haemoglobin's grip on O2?
  1. A. By changing the oxidation state of the haem iron
  2. B. By shifting the T ⇌ R equilibrium
  3. C. By changing the number of globin chains
AnswerB. By shifting the T ⇌ R equilibrium
WhyEffectors bind haemoglobin and shift the T ⇌ R equilibrium: T-stabilisers lower O2 affinity, R-stabilisers raise it.
Explanation

Haemoglobin is always a mix of T and R molecules. An effector that binds T better (H+, CO2, 2,3-BPG) pulls the mix toward T: lower affinity, right shift, more O2 released. One that binds R better (O2, CO) pulls it toward R: higher affinity, left shift.

  • Oxidising the iron makes methaemoglobin, which cannot bind O2 at all; it is not how normal regulation works.
  • Changing the number of chains: the tetramer stays a tetramer in both states.
Slides (3)

The Bohr effect and CO2

L6LearningHigh yield
What is the Bohr effect?
  1. A. Acid and CO2 raising haemoglobin's O2 affinity
  2. B. Acid and CO2 lowering haemoglobin's O2 affinity
  3. C. O2 binding lowering haemoglobin's affinity for CO2
AnswerB. Acid and CO2 lowering haemoglobin's O2 affinity
WhyThe Bohr effect: H+ (low pH) and CO2 lower haemoglobin's O2 affinity, shifting the curve right and promoting O2 release.
Explanation

A fall in pH pushes the T ⇌ R equilibrium toward T, so the curve shifts right (in the lecture figure, P50 rises from about 20 at pH 7.6 to about 30 mm Hg at pH 7.2); a rise in pH shifts it left. CO2 acts mostly by producing H+ and partly by forming carbamino groups.

  • Raising affinity reverses the direction.
  • O2 lowering the affinity for CO2 is the reverse relationship, known as the Haldane effect; it is not the Bohr effect.
Slides (3)

2,3-BPG and altitude

L7LearningHigh yield
Where does 2,3-BPG bind haemoglobin, and with what effect?
  1. A. Positively charged pocket between the two β chains of deoxyhaemoglobin → stabilises T, lowers affinity
  2. B. Positively charged pocket between the two α chains of deoxyhaemoglobin → stabilises T, lowers affinity
  3. C. Negatively charged pocket between the two β chains of oxyhaemoglobin → stabilises R, raises affinity
AnswerA. Positively charged pocket between the two β chains of deoxyhaemoglobin → stabilises T, lowers affinity
WhyNegatively charged 2,3-BPG fits a positively charged pocket between the two β chains of deoxyhaemoglobin, stabilising T and lowering O2 affinity.
Explanation

One 2,3-BPG binds per tetramer, in the central cavity between the β chains, held by positively charged residues (such as β-lysine 82 and β-histidine 143). In the R state the cavity narrows and 2,3-BPG is squeezed out, so it can only bind T. Result: right shift, more O2 released at tissue PO2.

  • Between the α chains: the pocket is formed by the β chains.
  • Negative pocket in oxyhaemoglobin: a negatively charged molecule needs a positive pocket, and it binds the deoxy form.
Slides (2)
L8LearningHigh yield
Why does a right shift help at high altitude?
  1. A. A large loss in loading is offset by better unloading
  2. B. A small gain in loading buys a bigger gain in unloading
  3. C. A small loss in loading buys a bigger gain in unloading
AnswerC. A small loss in loading buys a bigger gain in unloading
WhyBecause the curve's top is flat and its middle steep, a right shift costs little loading in the lungs but gains much unloading in the tissues.
Explanation

On the lecture's numbers: loading falls by 10 points (90 → 80%) while unloading improves by 20 points (60 → 40%), so delivery rises from 30% to 40% of capacity. A patient who cannot make 2,3-BPG would therefore adapt poorly to altitude.

  • A large loss in loading: the loss is small, because it happens on the flat part of the curve.
  • A gain in loading: a right shift lowers affinity, so loading falls slightly; it never rises.
Slides (2)

Carbon monoxide; PO2, saturation and O2 content

L9LearningHigh yield
What do partial pressure of O2, O2 saturation and O2 content each measure?
  1. A. PO2: total O2 per unit of blood
    Saturation: fraction of Hb sites occupied
    Content: pressure of dissolved O2
  2. B. PO2: pressure of dissolved O2
    Saturation: total O2 per unit of blood
    Content: fraction of Hb sites occupied
  3. C. PO2: pressure of dissolved O2
    Saturation: fraction of Hb sites occupied
    Content: total O2 per unit of blood
AnswerC. PO2: pressure of dissolved O2
Saturation: fraction of Hb sites occupied
Content: total O2 per unit of blood
WhyPO2 is the pressure of O2 dissolved in plasma; saturation is the share of haem sites holding O2; content is the total O2 per volume of blood (bound + dissolved).
Explanation

PO2 is the 'push' that loads haemoglobin; it depends on the air and the lungs, not on haemoglobin. Saturation is read off the curve at that PO2. Content (about 20 mL O2 per 100 mL blood normally) is mostly haemoglobin-bound O2: roughly 1.34 × haemoglobin (g/dL) × saturation, plus a tiny dissolved part. Keeping the three apart is the key to the CO, methaemoglobin and anaemia questions.

  • 'PO2 = total O2, content = pressure' swaps the definitions of PO2 and content.
  • 'Saturation = total O2, content = fraction of sites' swaps the definitions of saturation and content.
Slides (2)
L10LearningHigh yield
Why does carbon monoxide cut O2 delivery in two ways at once?
  1. A. Takes haem sites from O2
    Pushes Hb into the R state (left shift) → the O2 still bound is not released
  2. B. Oxidises the haem iron to Fe3+
    Pushes Hb into the R state (left shift) → the O2 still bound is not released
  3. C. Takes haem sites from O2
    Pushes Hb into the T state (right shift) → O2 released too early, in the lungs
AnswerA. Takes haem sites from O2
Pushes Hb into the R state (left shift) → the O2 still bound is not released
WhyCO occupies haem sites (less O2 carried) and stabilises R (left shift), so the O2 on the remaining sites is held too tightly to be released.
Explanation

Hit one: each CO-bound haem is a site lost to O2, so content falls. Hit two: CO binding, like O2 binding, pushes the tetramer into the high-affinity R state; the remaining haems bind O2 more tightly, the curve shifts left and becomes more hyperbolic, and little O2 comes off at tissue PO2.

  • Oxidising the iron to Fe3+ is methaemoglobin, a different poisoning; CO binds Fe2+.
  • T state, right shift reverses CO's effect on the remaining sites; the classic exam trap is 'remaining sites bind with lower affinity'.
Slides (2)

Methaemoglobin

L11LearningHigh yield
What is methaemoglobin?
  1. A. Haemoglobin whose iron is oxidised to Fe3+: it cannot carry O2
  2. B. Haemoglobin with CO bound to its Fe2+: it cannot carry O2
  3. C. Haemoglobin whose iron is reduced to Fe+: it cannot carry O2
AnswerA. Haemoglobin whose iron is oxidised to Fe3+: it cannot carry O2
WhyMethaemoglobin is haemoglobin with its haem iron oxidised from Fe2+ to Fe3+; ferric haem cannot bind O2.
Explanation

A little methaemoglobin forms every day as the iron is oxidised by the O2 it carries and by reactive oxygen species; red-cell enzymes reduce it back. When oxidation outpaces repair, methaemoglobin builds up (methaemoglobinaemia) and the blood carries less O2. Partly oxidised tetramers also hold the O2 they still carry more tightly (left shift).

  • CO on Fe2+ is carboxyhaemoglobin.
  • Reduced to Fe+: methaemoglobin is an oxidation, not a reduction.
Slides (2)
L12Learning
How is methaemoglobinaemia treated?
  1. A. Sodium nitrite: drives Fe3+ back to Fe2+
  2. B. Methylene blue: drives Fe3+ back to Fe2+
  3. C. Hyperbaric O2: displaces CO from the haem iron
AnswerB. Methylene blue: drives Fe3+ back to Fe2+
WhyMethylene blue acts as an electron carrier that lets red-cell methaemoglobin reductase reduce Fe3+ back to Fe2+.
Explanation

The lecture says methylene blue works via methaemoglobin reductase. Strictly, it uses the red cell's NADPH-dependent reductase, so the NADPH supply from G6PD must be intact: in G6PD deficiency methylene blue works poorly and can trigger haemolysis.

  • Sodium nitrite does the opposite: it oxidises haemoglobin and is given deliberately to make methaemoglobin in cyanide poisoning.
  • Hyperbaric O2 treats CO poisoning; it cannot reduce Fe3+.
Slides (2)

Globin genes and switching by age

L13Learning
What chain make-up does every normal human haemoglobin share, from embryo to adult?
  1. A. Two α-like chains (α or ζ) + two β-like chains (ε, γ, δ or β)
  2. B. Two true α chains + two true β chains in every haemoglobin
  3. C. Four identical chains, all from one globin gene family
AnswerA. Two α-like chains (α or ζ) + two β-like chains (ε, γ, δ or β)
WhyA mature haemoglobin is always a tetramer of two α-like and two β-like chains; which members are used changes with age.
Explanation

The rule on the slides is "2 α-like + 2 β-like". The α-like slot is filled by ζ in the embryo and by α from about week 5 onwards; the β-like slot is filled by ε, then γ, then β (with a little δ). So Hb Gower 1 is ζ2ε2, HbF is α2γ2, HbA is α2β2 and HbA2 is α2δ2.

  • Two true α + two true β describes only HbA; HbF and the embryonic haemoglobins break it.
  • Four identical chains (β4 = HbH, γ4 = Hb Bart) appear only when α chains are missing in α-thalassaemia; they are abnormal, not normal haemoglobins.
Slides (2)

Fetal haemoglobin and the adult haemoglobins

L14LearningHigh yield
What does weak 2,3-BPG binding do to HbF's O2 affinity, and why does the fetus need it?
  1. A. Lower O2 affinity, so O2 is pushed back across the placenta to the mother
  2. B. Higher O2 affinity, so CO2 cannot cross the placenta to the mother
  3. C. Higher O2 affinity, so O2 is pulled across the placenta from maternal blood
AnswerC. Higher O2 affinity, so O2 is pulled across the placenta from maternal blood
WhyHbF's higher O2 affinity (left-shifted curve, lower P50) lets fetal blood take O2 from maternal HbA at the low PO2 of the placenta.
Explanation

In the placenta maternal and fetal blood exchange gases at the same low PO2. At that PO2 the left-shifted fetal curve sits above the maternal curve: HbF is more saturated, so O2 moves from maternal HbA to fetal HbF. HbF is therefore one of the classic causes of a left shift.

  • Lower affinity is the opposite of what weak 2,3-BPG binding produces, and would move O2 the wrong way.
  • HbF's affinity has nothing to do with blocking CO2; fetal CO2 must cross to the mother to be exhaled.
Slides (3)
L15LearningHigh yield
What are HbA's chains, and what share of normal adult haemoglobin is it?
  1. A. α2γ2, about 90%
  2. B. α2β2, about 90%
  3. C. α2β2, about 70%
AnswerB. α2β2, about 90%
WhyHbA = α2β2 and makes up about 90% of adult haemoglobin; the rest is HbA2, HbF and glycated HbA1c.
Explanation
FormChainsShare (adult)
HbAα2β2~90%
HbA2α2δ22–3%
HbFα2γ2<2%
HbA1cα2β2 + glucose4–6%
  • α2γ2 is HbF, the fetal form.
  • 70% is too low: HbA is by far the dominant adult haemoglobin.

The case-session table prints HbA2 as 2–5% and HbA1c as 3–9%; the lecture's values are the ones above.

Slides (2)

Disease types and β-thalassaemia

L16LearningHigh yield
What is a quantitative haemoglobinopathy, and what is the lecture's example?
  1. A. A normal amount of a structurally abnormal chain; the thalassaemias
  2. B. A structurally normal chain made in too small an amount; the thalassaemias
  3. C. A structurally normal chain made in too small an amount; sickle cell disease
AnswerB. A structurally normal chain made in too small an amount; the thalassaemias
WhyQuantitative = the globin chain is normal in structure but too little is made: the thalassaemias (α and β).
Explanation

In thalassaemia, deletions or mutations reduce or abolish synthesis of one chain type (β+ = reduced, β0 = none). What is made is normal; the damage comes from the imbalance, because the partner chain is left over and precipitates.

  • "Normal amount, abnormal structure" is a qualitative disorder.
  • Sickle cell disease is qualitative: HbS is made in normal amounts but has valine at β6.
Slides (2)
L17Learning
How many β-globin genes does a person have, and what do β+ and β0 alleles make?
  1. A. Four (two on each chromosome 11); β+ makes a reduced amount, β0 makes none
  2. B. Two (one on each chromosome 11); β+ makes none, β0 makes a reduced amount
  3. C. Two (one on each chromosome 11); β+ makes a reduced amount, β0 makes none
AnswerC. Two (one on each chromosome 11); β+ makes a reduced amount, β0 makes none
WhyEach chromosome 11 has one β gene (two in all). β+ = reduced β-chain synthesis; β0 = no functional β chain.
Explanation

The β-thalassaemia types depend on which two alleles a person has: β (normal), β+ (some β chain) or β0 (none). One abnormal allele gives minor, two mildly abnormal give intermedia, and β0/β0 gives major (Cooley anaemia).

  • Four genes, two per chromosome describes the α genes on chromosome 16.
  • The superscripts are easy to swap: think of 0 as "zero β made" and + as "some made".
Slides (1)

α-thalassaemia

L18Learning
How many α-globin genes does a person have, and what sets the severity of α-thalassaemia?
  1. A. Four (two on each chromosome 11); severity tracks how many are lost
  2. B. Two (one on each chromosome 16); severity tracks which one is lost
  3. C. Four (two on each chromosome 16); severity tracks how many are lost
AnswerC. Four (two on each chromosome 16); severity tracks how many are lost
WhyThere are four α genes (α1 and α2 on each chromosome 16); α-thalassaemia severity rises with the number of genes lost, from 1 to 4.
Explanation

Because α genes are duplicated, losing one or two leaves enough α chain for mild or no disease; losing three or four causes serious disease. Most α-thalassaemia is due to gene deletions (the HBA1 and HBA2 genes).

Genes lostTypePicture
1silent carrierno symptoms
2α-thalassaemia traitmild anaemia
3HbH diseaseβ4, Heinz bodies, variable anaemia
4Hb Bart (γ4)hydrops fetalis, fetal death
  • α genes are on chromosome 16; chromosome 11 holds the β family.
Slides (2)

Sickle cell disease: mutation and mechanism

L19LearningHigh yield
What is the sickle cell (HbS) mutation?
  1. A. Glutamate → lysine at position 6 of the β chain (E6K)
  2. B. Valine → glutamate at position 6 of the β chain (V6E)
  3. C. Glutamate → valine at position 6 of the β chain (E6V)
AnswerC. Glutamate → valine at position 6 of the β chain (E6V)
WhyHbS = E6V: the glutamate at position 6 of β-globin is replaced by valine, in both β chains of HbSS.
Explanation

A single base change in codon 6 of the β-globin gene (GAG → GTG) swaps negatively charged glutamate for nonpolar valine. Every HbS molecule carries the change on both of its β chains; α chains are normal.

  • Glutamate → lysine (E6K) is HbC, at the same position.
  • Valine → glutamate reverses the direction: in HbS valine is the new residue, glutamate the normal one.

Hook: "Sickle = V for valine, C = K for lysine".

Slides (2)
L20LearningHigh yield
What general rule follows from HbS polymerising only in the T (deoxy) state?
  1. A. Anything that favours the R (oxy) state favours sickling
  2. B. Anything that favours the T (deoxy) state favours sickling
  3. C. Anything that lowers 2,3-BPG favours sickling
AnswerB. Anything that favours the T (deoxy) state favours sickling
WhyBecause only deoxy-HbS polymerises, anything that favours the T state (hypoxia, acidosis, ↑CO2, ↑2,3-BPG, ↑temperature) promotes sickling.
Explanation

This one rule explains most crisis triggers. Low PO2 (altitude, exercise, lung disease) leaves more HbS deoxygenated; acidosis and CO2 stabilise the T state through the Bohr effect; 2,3-BPG binds and stabilises deoxy-HbS.

  • Favouring the R state keeps HbS oxygenated and soluble: it reduces sickling (this was the logic of voxelotor).
  • Lowering 2,3-BPG shifts haemoglobin towards R, so it would reduce sickling, not favour it.
Slides (2)

Sickle cell triggers and the Jasmine D. case

L21Learning
Besides favouring the T (deoxy) state, by what other routes can triggers provoke sickle crises?
  1. A. They raise the HbS concentration in the cell, blood viscosity or oxidative stress
  2. B. They lower the HbS concentration in the cell, blood viscosity or oxidative stress
  3. C. They raise blood O2 content, red-cell volume or 2,3-BPG breakdown
AnswerA. They raise the HbS concentration in the cell, blood viscosity or oxidative stress
WhyBeyond pushing HbS into the T state, triggers act by ↑[HbS] inside the cell (dehydration), ↑blood viscosity and ↑oxidative stress.
Explanation

Polymerisation depends strongly on HbS concentration: when a red cell loses water, HbS molecules crowd together and polymerise faster. Dehydration also thickens the blood and slows flow, giving sickled cells time to stick and occlude vessels. Oxidative stress damages the red-cell membrane (the target of L-glutamine therapy).

  • Lowering HbS concentration or viscosity is protective; that is the point of hydration.
  • Raising O2 content or cell volume, or removing 2,3-BPG, would all reduce sickling.
Slides (2)
L22LearningHigh yield
Jasmine D.'s labs: Na+ 147, Cl− 110, HCO3− 16 mEq/L; pH 7.36; PCO2 29 mmHg. What is her anion gap, and what acid–base disorder is it?
  1. A. 21; normal-anion-gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis
  2. B. 37; high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
  3. C. 21; high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
AnswerC. 21; high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
WhyAnion gap = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−) = 147 − (110 + 16) = 21 (normal 8–16): a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, from alcohol-driven lactic acid.
Explanation

pH 7.36 with HCO3− 16 (below 24) is a metabolic acidosis. The anion gap estimates unmeasured anions: when an acid such as lactic acid is added, its anion replaces the HCO3− it used up, so the gap widens. When HCO3− is simply lost (diarrhoea), Cl− replaces it and the gap stays normal.

  • 21 is above 8–16, so this is not a normal-gap (hyperchloraemic) acidosis.
  • 37 comes from forgetting to subtract HCO3− (147 − 110).
Slides (2)

Sickle cell treatment; HbC

L23LearningHigh yield
How does hydroxyurea help in sickle cell disease?
  1. A. It converts the β6 valine back to glutamate
  2. B. It raises fetal haemoglobin (HbF, γ-chain) production
  3. C. It raises 2,3-BPG so HbS unloads O2 faster
AnswerB. It raises fetal haemoglobin (HbF, γ-chain) production
WhyHydroxyurea (a chemotherapy drug) raises HbF (α2γ2) production; HbF dilutes HbS and does not join the polymer, so sickling and painful crises fall.
Explanation

Raising γ-chain synthesis means each red cell holds more HbF and less HbS. HbF molecules cannot fit into the HbS fibre, so they interrupt polymerisation; this is also why people who inherit persistently high HbF with HbS have milder disease. Hydroxyurea reduces the frequency of acute painful episodes.

  • No drug reverses the DNA mutation; gene therapy adds or edits genes rather than converting the residue.
  • More 2,3-BPG stabilises the deoxy T state and would increase sickling.
Slides (3)
L24LearningHigh yield
Why does HbC not polymerise into fibres the way HbS does?
  1. A. Its β6 lysine is charged and polar, so it creates no hydrophobic sticky patch
  2. B. Its β6 lysine is nonpolar, but the β chain lacks the matching hydrophobic pocket
  3. C. HbC carries its mutation on the α chain, away from the polymer contact site
AnswerA. Its β6 lysine is charged and polar, so it creates no hydrophobic sticky patch
WhyIn HbC, glutamate is replaced by lysine, which is charged and polar: no hydrophobic patch forms, so HbC does not polymerise or sickle.
Explanation

Sickling depends on a hydrophobic residue (valine) docking into a hydrophobic pocket on a neighbouring deoxy-HbS. Lysine stays charged and water-loving on the protein surface, so that contact never forms. HbC is less soluble than HbA, however, and tends to form crystals instead, which stiffen the red cell.

  • Lysine is not nonpolar; it carries a positive charge. The hydrophobic pocket exists in HbC as in HbA.
  • The HbC mutation is on the β chain, at the same position 6 as HbS.
Slides (1)
Tier 2The next layer across every concept+22 questions

Myoglobin vs haemoglobin: structure and haem

L25LearningHigh yield
Where is myoglobin found, and what does it do?
  1. A. Red blood cells: carries O2 from the lungs to the contracting muscles
  2. B. Cardiac and skeletal muscle: stores O2 for the muscle's own ATP production during contraction
  3. C. Cardiac and skeletal muscle: carries CO2 out of the muscle to the capillaries
AnswerB. Cardiac and skeletal muscle: stores O2 for the muscle's own ATP production during contraction
WhyMyoglobin sits in cardiac and skeletal muscle and stores O2 for the muscle's own oxidative ATP production during contraction.
Explanation

Myoglobin is the muscle's private O2 reservoir. Its very high affinity lets it take O2 from haemoglobin in the muscle capillaries and hold it until the muscle cell's PO2 drops during heavy contraction; then it releases O2 to the mitochondria. It is also why red, slow-twitch muscle and heart muscle look dark red.

  • Red blood cells, lungs to muscle: that is haemoglobin's job.
  • Carrying CO2 out of muscle: CO2 leaves as bicarbonate, dissolved CO2 and carbamino-haemoglobin, not on myoglobin.
Slides (2)

Cooperativity, the oxygen curve and P50

L26LearningHigh yield
What shape is each oxygen-binding curve?
  1. A. Haemoglobin: sigmoid (S-shaped)
    Myoglobin: sigmoid (S-shaped)
  2. B. Haemoglobin: hyperbola
    Myoglobin: sigmoid (S-shaped)
  3. C. Haemoglobin: sigmoid (S-shaped)
    Myoglobin: hyperbola
AnswerC. Haemoglobin: sigmoid (S-shaped)
Myoglobin: hyperbola
WhyHaemoglobin (cooperative) gives a sigmoid curve; myoglobin (one site) gives a hyperbola that rises steeply and flattens near 100%.
Explanation

On the graph, myoglobin's hyperbola lies above and to the left of haemoglobin's S-curve at every PO2 below the lungs: it is nearly saturated even at very low PO2 (P50 about 1 mm Hg), while haemoglobin is half-saturated at about 26 mm Hg.

  • Both sigmoid: a sigmoid curve needs cooperativity, which a single-site protein cannot have.
  • Swapped shapes is the classic trap: the four-site, cooperative protein is the S-shaped one.
Slides (3)
L27Learning
What are the P50s of myoglobin and haemoglobin?
  1. A. Myoglobin ~1 mm Hg
    Haemoglobin ~50 mm Hg
  2. B. Myoglobin ~26 mm Hg
    Haemoglobin ~1 mm Hg
  3. C. Myoglobin ~1 mm Hg
    Haemoglobin ~26 mm Hg
AnswerC. Myoglobin ~1 mm Hg
Haemoglobin ~26 mm Hg
WhyMyoglobin is half-saturated at about 1 mm Hg, haemoglobin at about 26 mm Hg.
Explanation

Both values are marked under the lecture's curve. Haemoglobin's P50 of 26 mm Hg sits inside the tissue PO2 range, which is why it unloads there; myoglobin's 1 mm Hg means it stays loaded until the muscle is almost anoxic. (One lecture graph labels myoglobin's P50 as 2.8 mm Hg instead of 1; either way it is a few mm Hg, far below haemoglobin's.)

  • Haemoglobin ~50 mm Hg would describe a strongly right-shifted curve, not normal adult blood.
  • Swapped values: the storage protein has the lower P50.
Slides (2)

T and R states: shifting the curve

L28LearningHigh yield
If the O2–haemoglobin curve shifts to the right, what happens to P50 and to O2 affinity?
  1. A. P50 falls; affinity rises; less O2 is released to the tissues
  2. B. P50 rises; affinity rises; less O2 is released to the tissues
  3. C. P50 rises; affinity falls; more O2 is released to the tissues
AnswerC. P50 rises; affinity falls; more O2 is released to the tissues
WhyA right shift means a higher PO2 is needed for 50% saturation: P50 rises, affinity falls and more O2 is unloaded.
Explanation

Moving the whole curve right means that at any given PO2 haemoglobin is less saturated, so it has given up more O2. In the lecture's example, lowering pH from 7.6 to 7.2 moves P50 from about 20 to about 30 mm Hg. A left shift is the reverse: lower P50, higher affinity, less unloading.

  • P50 falls, affinity rises describes a left shift.
  • P50 rises with affinity rising is impossible: a higher P50 is lower affinity by definition.

Hook: Right = Release.

Slides (3)

The Bohr effect and CO2

L29Learning
Why does the Bohr effect deliver O2 where it is needed most?
  1. A. The kidneys release erythropoietin when tissue O2 is low
  2. B. The busiest tissue makes the most CO2 and acid, which unload O2 right there
  3. C. Active tissue releases 2,3-BPG into the plasma for red cells to take up
AnswerB. The busiest tissue makes the most CO2 and acid, which unload O2 right there
WhyA tissue signals its own need with its own waste: the CO2 and acid it makes lower haemoglobin's affinity locally, so O2 is released right there.
Explanation

No hormone or nerve is needed: the more a tissue works, the more CO2 and H+ it produces, and the more O2 haemoglobin drops off in that tissue's capillaries.

  • Erythropoietin raises red-cell production over days to weeks; it does not steer O2 to one tissue.
  • 2,3-BPG is made inside red cells from glycolysis, not released by tissues, and it changes over hours to days, not capillary by capillary.
Slides (2)
L30LearningHigh yield
How does carbonic anhydrase drive the Bohr effect in the tissues?
  1. A. CO2 → carbonic acid → H+ binds the haem iron → stabilises R
  2. B. CO2 → carbonic acid → H+ binds ionisable side chains on the globin → stabilises R
  3. C. CO2 → carbonic acid → H+ binds ionisable side chains on the globin → stabilises T
AnswerC. CO2 → carbonic acid → H+ binds ionisable side chains on the globin → stabilises T
WhyCarbonic anhydrase turns tissue CO2 into carbonic acid; its H+ binds ionisable amino-acid side chains on haemoglobin and stabilises the deoxy T state.
Explanation

In red cells: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3− (carbonic anhydrase speeds the first step). The H+ protonates side chains (chiefly histidines) that then form T-state salt bridges, so O2 is released (HbO2 + H+ → HbH + O2). The bicarbonate leaves the cell for the plasma.

  • H+ on the haem iron: H+ binds the protein, not the iron.
  • Stabilises R reverses the effect; protonated haemoglobin is the T form.
Slides (3)

2,3-BPG and altitude

L31LearningHigh yield
Where does 2,3-BPG come from?
  1. A. The liver makes it from a glycolytic intermediate and releases it into the plasma
  2. B. Red cells make it from a glycolytic intermediate, and can change how fast they make or break it down
  3. C. Red cells make it from a Krebs-cycle intermediate, at a fixed rate they cannot change
AnswerB. Red cells make it from a glycolytic intermediate, and can change how fast they make or break it down
WhyRed cells make 2,3-BPG from the glycolytic intermediate 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and tune its level by changing its synthesis and breakdown.
Explanation

A side-branch of red-cell glycolysis converts 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate into 2,3-BPG. By speeding or slowing this branch and the enzyme that breaks 2,3-BPG down, red cells adjust their own O2 affinity. Like the Bohr effect it shifts the curve right, but it works over hours to days rather than capillary by capillary.

  • The liver: 2,3-BPG is made and kept inside red cells.
  • Krebs cycle, fixed rate: mature red cells have no mitochondria, so no Krebs cycle, and the whole point is that the level can change.
Slides (2)
L32LearningHigh yield
When does the red-cell 2,3-BPG level rise?
  1. A. Acidosis
    Hypothermia
  2. B. Long storage of donated blood
    Breathing 100% O2
  3. C. Chronic hypoxia (high altitude, anaemia, chronic lung disease)
    Exercise
AnswerC. Chronic hypoxia (high altitude, anaemia, chronic lung disease)
Exercise
Why2,3-BPG rises when O2 supply is low or demand is high: chronic hypoxia (altitude, anaemia, chronic lung disease) and exercise.
Explanation

The lecture lists chronic hypoxia, high altitude and exercise. Anaemia and chronic lung disease (e.g. COPD) are chronic hypoxia too. The extra 2,3-BPG shifts the curve right so a larger share of the available O2 is released in the tissues.

  • Acidosis slows 2,3-BPG production (this offsets the Bohr effect over hours); hypothermia does not raise it.
  • Stored blood loses 2,3-BPG, and extra O2 removes the hypoxic stimulus.
Slides (2)

Carbon monoxide; PO2, saturation and O2 content

L33LearningHigh yield
In carbon monoxide poisoning, what happens to arterial PO2, true O2 saturation and O2 content?
  1. A. PO2 low
    Saturation low
    Content low
  2. B. PO2 normal
    Saturation normal
    Content low
  3. C. PO2 normal
    Saturation low
    Content low
AnswerC. PO2 normal
Saturation low
Content low
WhyCO does not affect the O2 dissolved in plasma, so PO2 is normal; CO occupies haem sites, so O2 saturation and content fall.
Explanation

The lungs and the air are normal, so dissolved O2 and therefore PO2 are normal (e.g. PaO2 100 mm Hg with a measured O2 saturation of 60%). Haem sites taken by CO lower both the true saturation and the content. A standard pulse oximeter reads carboxyhaemoglobin as if it were oxyhaemoglobin and can show a falsely normal value; a co-oximeter on a blood sample shows the real fall.

  • PO2 low: CO does not block O2 from entering the blood.
  • Saturation normal: the share of haem sites holding O2 is what CO steals.
Slides (1)
L34LearningHigh yield
Why does 100% O2 (hyperbaric if severe) treat carbon monoxide poisoning?
  1. A. CO binding is irreversible, so extra O2 only raises the O2 dissolved in plasma
  2. B. O2 oxidises the bound CO to CO2, which is then breathed out
  3. C. CO binding is reversible and competitive, so a very high PO2 displaces CO from haem
AnswerC. CO binding is reversible and competitive, so a very high PO2 displaces CO from haem
WhyCO and O2 compete reversibly for the same haem iron; flooding the blood with O2 displaces CO and speeds its removal.
Explanation

Because the binding is reversible, the share of haem holding CO depends on the ratio of CO to O2. Raising inspired O2 to 100% shortens the half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin from roughly 4–6 hours on room air to about 1–1.5 hours; hyperbaric O2 shortens it further, to under half an hour. This is the immediate treatment in the clinic cases (closed tent with a propane lantern, forklift in a closed room).

  • Irreversible: the lecture stresses that CO binding is still reversible, which is why O2 works.
  • Oxidising CO to CO2 does not happen in blood; CO leaves unchanged through the lungs.
Slides (2)

Methaemoglobin

L35LearningHigh yield
Which group of agents oxidises haemoglobin to methaemoglobin?
  1. A. Ascorbic acid
    Glutathione
    NADH
  2. B. Nitrates and nitrites
    Local anaesthetics (benzocaine)
    Sodium nitroprusside
    NO2
  3. C. Carbon monoxide
    Carbon dioxide
    2,3-BPG
AnswerB. Nitrates and nitrites
Local anaesthetics (benzocaine)
Sodium nitroprusside
NO2
WhyOxidising drugs and chemicals, such as nitrates and nitrites, benzocaine, sodium nitroprusside and NO2, turn Fe2+ into Fe3+; the cell's own reactive oxygen species can too.
Explanation

Typical scenarios: nitrite exposure at work; nitrate drugs for angina; well water contaminated with nitrate from farm run-off; benzocaine teething gels or throat sprays.

  • Ascorbic acid, glutathione and NADH are reducing agents: they keep the iron as Fe2+ or return it there.
  • CO, CO2 and 2,3-BPG bind haemoglobin and change its O2 binding, but do not oxidise the iron.
Slides (3)

Globin genes and switching by age

L36Learning
Why do β-chain disorders such as sickle cell disease and β-thalassaemia major usually cause no symptoms until a few months after birth?
  1. A. Maternal HbA crossing the placenta protects the infant for the first months
  2. B. HbF (α2γ2), which has no β chains, carries most O2 until the γ → β switch
  3. C. α-chain synthesis does not begin until a few months after birth
AnswerB. HbF (α2γ2), which has no β chains, carries most O2 until the γ → β switch
WhyNewborns still carry mostly HbF (α2γ2); a faulty β gene only matters once β chains replace γ chains over the first months of life.
Explanation

A β-globin mutation can only harm haemoglobins that contain β chains. At birth most haemoglobin is still HbF, whose β-like chains are γ, so the mutant β chain is a minor product. As γ falls and β rises (the switch is largely complete by about 6 months), HbS or the β-chain shortfall becomes the dominant problem and symptoms appear.

  • Maternal haemoglobin stays inside maternal red cells; it does not cross the placenta.
  • α chains are made from about week 5 of development, so α-chain timing does not explain the delay (and α-thalassaemia, unlike β disease, can harm the fetus).

The same logic is why raising HbF (hydroxyurea, Casgevy) treats both diseases.

Slides (2)

Fetal haemoglobin and the adult haemoglobins

L37LearningHigh yield
Why does HbF bind 2,3-BPG more weakly than HbA?
  1. A. Its γ chains carry extra positive residues that repel 2,3-BPG
  2. B. Its γ chains lack some of the positive residues lining the 2,3-BPG pocket
  3. C. Its γ chains lack the negative residues lining the 2,3-BPG pocket
AnswerB. Its γ chains lack some of the positive residues lining the 2,3-BPG pocket
Why2,3-BPG is negatively charged and sits in a positively charged pocket between the two β-like chains; HbF's γ chains lack some of those positive residues.
Explanation

In HbA, 2,3-BPG binds in the central cavity between the two β chains of deoxy-haemoglobin, held by positively charged side chains (including His143). Binding stabilises the T state and lowers O2 affinity. The γ chains of HbF have serine in place of His143, so the pocket holds 2,3-BPG less well.

  • Extra positive residues would make 2,3-BPG bind more tightly, not repel it: opposite charges attract.
  • The pocket is lined by positive, not negative, residues; 2,3-BPG itself is the negative partner.
Slides (3)
L38LearningHigh yield
How does HbA1c form, and what does its level reflect?
  1. A. Enzymatic glycosylation of HbF; the fasting blood glucose on the day of testing
  2. B. Spontaneous glycation of HbA; average blood glucose over the previous 2–3 weeks
  3. C. Spontaneous glycation of HbA; average blood glucose over the previous 2–3 months
AnswerC. Spontaneous glycation of HbA; average blood glucose over the previous 2–3 months
WhyGlucose attaches to HbA without an enzyme (glycation), and red cells live about 120 days, so HbA1c reflects average glucose over the past 2–3 months.
Explanation

Glycation is a slow, non-enzymatic reaction between glucose and a free amino group (the N-terminal valine of the β chain). It is effectively irreversible for the life of the red cell. Because red cells survive about 120 days, the HbA1c fraction integrates glucose over the previous 8–12 weeks, which is why it is used to follow diabetic control.

  • Enzymatic glycosylation of HbF is wrong on both counts, and a single day's fasting glucose is what a fasting glucose test measures.
  • 2–3 weeks is too short: the window matches red-cell lifespan, measured in months.
Slides (2)

Disease types and β-thalassaemia

L39LearningHigh yield
In β-thalassaemia, which haemoglobins rise?
  1. A. HbA2 (α2δ2) and Hb Bart (γ4)
  2. B. HbA (α2β2) and HbH (β4)
  3. C. HbA2 (α2δ2) and HbF (α2γ2)
AnswerC. HbA2 (α2δ2) and HbF (α2γ2)
WhyIn β-thalassaemia the spare α chains pair with the other β-like chains, so HbA2 (α2δ2) and HbF (α2γ2) rise.
Explanation

HbA2 and HbF contain no β chain, so their synthesis is untouched by a β-gene defect, and the excess α chains are available to pair with δ and γ. A raised HbA2 (above about 3.5%) is the diagnostic marker of β-thalassaemia trait; in β-thalassaemia major HbF is the main haemoglobin and HbA may be absent.

  • Hb Bart (γ4) and HbH (β4) form only when α chains are lacking: α-thalassaemia.
  • HbA falls, not rises, when β chains are scarce.
Slides (2)
L40LearningHigh yield
β-thalassaemia major (Cooley anaemia): what is the genotype, and how does it present?
  1. A. β0/β0; severe anaemia, splenomegaly, bone deformities; regular transfusions
  2. B. β+/β0; severe anaemia, splenomegaly, bone deformities; regular transfusions
  3. C. β0/β; severe anaemia, splenomegaly, bone deformities; occasional transfusions
AnswerA. β0/β0; severe anaemia, splenomegaly, bone deformities; regular transfusions
WhyMajor (Cooley) = β0/β0, no β chain at all: severe anaemia, splenomegaly, bone deformities and regular transfusions.
Explanation

With no HbA, the child depends on HbF and becomes severely anaemic as γ synthesis falls in the first year. The marrow expands massively to compensate, deforming the skull and facial bones, and the spleen enlarges from red-cell destruction and blood formation outside the marrow. Lifelong transfusion is needed, which leads to iron overload.

  • β+/β0 is listed under intermedia on the slide (some β is still made).
  • β0/β has one normal allele: that is minor.
Slides (3)

α-thalassaemia

L41LearningHigh yield
α-thalassaemia with all four α genes lost: what forms, and with what result?
  1. A. HbH (β4); hydrops fetalis and fetal death
  2. B. Hb Bart (γ4); hydrops fetalis and fetal death
  3. C. Hb Bart (α4); hydrops fetalis and fetal death
AnswerB. Hb Bart (γ4); hydrops fetalis and fetal death
WhyWith no α genes, fetal γ chains form γ4 (Hb Bart), which cannot release O2 to tissues: hydrops fetalis and fetal death.
Explanation

The fetus normally relies on HbF (α2γ2). Without α chains, the γ chains pair with each other. γ4 binds O2 extremely tightly and without cooperativity, so tissues are starved of O2. Severe anaemia and hypoxia cause heart failure with massive oedema (hydrops fetalis), usually fatal before or soon after birth. Hb Bart syndrome is the most severe form of α-thalassaemia.

  • HbH (β4) is the three-gene picture, compatible with life.
  • Hb Bart is γ4, not α4: there are no α chains to form it.
Slides (2)

Sickle cell disease: mutation and mechanism

L42LearningHigh yield
Why does the glutamate → valine change make HbS molecules stick to each other?
  1. A. It adds a hydrophilic charged group that bonds ionically to a neighbouring molecule
  2. B. It removes a hydrophobic residue, so neighbouring molecules no longer repel
  3. C. It creates a hydrophobic protrusion that fits a hydrophobic pocket on a neighbouring molecule
AnswerC. It creates a hydrophobic protrusion that fits a hydrophobic pocket on a neighbouring molecule
WhyReplacing charged glutamate with nonpolar valine puts a hydrophobic patch on the β-chain surface that docks into a hydrophobic pocket of another HbS molecule.
Explanation

Glutamate is negatively charged and sits happily in water on the protein surface. Valine is nonpolar, so at β6 it forms a sticky hydrophobic knob. In deoxy-HbS a complementary hydrophobic pocket on the β chain of a neighbouring molecule is exposed, the knob fits into it, and molecules link into long chains.

  • Valine is nonpolar and uncharged; the change removes a charge rather than adding one.
  • The change adds a hydrophobic residue; it does not remove one.
Slides (2)
L43LearningHigh yield
What is a vaso-occlusive crisis in sickle cell disease?
  1. A. Rigid sickled cells block capillaries, causing ischaemia, microinfarction, tissue anoxia and severe pain
  2. B. Rigid sickled cells block large arteries, causing painless gangrene of whole limbs
  3. C. Sickled cells pool and haemolyse in the spleen, causing a sudden fall in haemoglobin and shock
AnswerA. Rigid sickled cells block capillaries, causing ischaemia, microinfarction, tissue anoxia and severe pain
WhyIn a vaso-occlusive crisis rigid sickled cells plug small vessels (capillaries), causing ischaemia, microinfarction and tissue anoxia, felt as severe pain.
Explanation

Sickled cells are stiff and sticky; they lodge in capillaries and small venules, slow the flow, deoxygenate further and recruit more sickling (a vicious cycle). The ischaemic tissue becomes inflamed and painful. Typical sites are bones, back, chest and abdomen, as in Jasmine D.'s back, abdominal and limb pain.

  • The occlusion is in the microcirculation, and it is intensely painful, not painless.
  • Sudden splenic pooling (splenic sequestration) is a different crisis, mostly in young children, defined by a falling haemoglobin and an enlarging spleen rather than pain.
Slides (2)

Sickle cell triggers and the Jasmine D. case

L44LearningHigh yield
What is the appropriate short-term treatment for an acute sickle cell vaso-occlusive pain episode like Jasmine D.'s?
  1. A. IV opioids · IV normal saline · O2 if saturation <95% · ambulation · heparin prophylaxis if admitted
  2. B. IV opioids · IV diuretics · O2 if saturation <95% · bed rest · warfarin to dissolve clots if admitted
  3. C. IV opioids · IV normal saline · hyperbaric O2 for every patient · bed rest · thrombolysis if admitted
AnswerA. IV opioids · IV normal saline · O2 if saturation <95% · ambulation · heparin prophylaxis if admitted
WhyAcute care: IV opioids (morphine, hydromorphone), rehydration with IV normal saline, O2 if saturation <95%, encourage ambulation, and heparin thromboprophylaxis if admitted.
Explanation

Each step reverses part of the cascade: opioids treat severe ischaemic pain; IV saline (then IV plus oral fluids) corrects dehydration, dilutes HbS and lowers viscosity; O2 when saturation is low reduces the deoxy-HbS fraction; walking and low-molecular-weight or unfractionated heparin lower the risk of venous thromboembolism in a hospitalised patient.

  • Diuretics would worsen dehydration; warfarin does not dissolve clots.
  • Hyperbaric O2 is for CO poisoning, and thrombolysis has no role: the occlusion is by sickled cells, not a fibrin clot.
Slides (2)

Sickle cell treatment; HbC

L45Learning
How does Casgevy (approved 2023) treat sickle cell disease?
  1. A. Lentiviral vector adding an anti-sickling β-globin gene, with a stem-cell transplant
  2. B. CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing that raises HbF, with a stem-cell transplant
  3. C. CRISPR/Cas9 editing that corrects the E6V mutation directly, with no transplant needed
AnswerB. CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing that raises HbF, with a stem-cell transplant
WhyCasgevy uses CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing of the patient's own blood stem cells to raise HbF; the cells are given back by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
Explanation

The edit disrupts BCL11A, a repressor that normally switches γ-globin off after birth. With BCL11A down, the edited cells keep making γ chains and therefore HbF, which does not sickle. The patient's marrow is cleared with chemotherapy before the edited cells are reinfused (autologous transplant).

  • A lentiviral anti-sickling gene is Lyfgenia.
  • Casgevy does not correct the E6V base itself, and it does require a stem-cell transplant.
Slides (2)
L46Learning
What is HbSC disease?
  1. A. A compound heterozygote (one HbS + one HbC allele) with a silent carrier state and no disease
  2. B. A compound heterozygote (one HbS + one HbC allele) with sickle-type disease that is usually milder
  3. C. A compound heterozygote (one HbS + one β-thalassaemia allele) with sickle-type disease that is usually milder
AnswerB. A compound heterozygote (one HbS + one HbC allele) with sickle-type disease that is usually milder
WhyHbSC disease = one HbS and one HbC allele (both β alleles abnormal); it causes the same kind of disease as sickle cell, usually milder.
Explanation

A person with HbSC makes no HbA. Their cells contain roughly equal HbS and HbC; HbC does not polymerise itself, but it does not dilute HbS the way HbA does, so sickling, vaso-occlusion and haemolysis still happen, generally less often and less severely than in HbSS.

  • It is not silent: with no normal β allele, sickling disease occurs.
  • HbS plus a β-thalassaemia allele is HbS/β-thalassaemia, a different compound state.
Slides (3)
Tier 3The rest of the section+20 questions

Myoglobin vs haemoglobin: structure and haem

L47Learning
Which amino acid bonds the haem iron from below in myoglobin and in each haemoglobin chain?
  1. A. Proximal histidine (F8)
  2. B. Distal histidine (E7)
  3. C. Proximal cysteine (F8)
AnswerA. Proximal histidine (F8)
WhyThe proximal histidine (F8) bonds the haem iron (fifth position); O2 binds on the other face (sixth position), next to the distal histidine (E7).
Explanation

Ferrous iron makes six bonds: four to the protoporphyrin nitrogens, one to the proximal histidine (the 8th residue of helix F) and one, on the opposite face, to O2. When O2 binds, the iron moves into the ring plane and pulls the proximal histidine and helix F with it; in haemoglobin this movement is what passes the T → R change to the other subunits.

  • Distal histidine (E7) sits on the O2 side without bonding the iron; it hydrogen-bonds the bound O2 and crowds out CO, which is why CO's advantage in haemoglobin is ~220× rather than the thousands-fold seen with free haem.
  • Cysteine is the iron ligand in cytochrome P450, not in the globins.
Slides (2)

Cooperativity, the oxygen curve and P50

L48LearningHigh yield
Alveolar PO2 is normally 104 mm Hg (saturation ~97%). While climbing a mountain it falls to 60 mm Hg. What happens to saturation?
  1. A. Falls to about 50%
  2. B. Falls only to about 89%
  3. C. Falls to about 75%
AnswerB. Falls only to about 89%
WhyOn the flat top of the curve, alveolar PO2 can fall from 104 to 60 mm Hg while saturation falls only from ~97% to ~89%.
Explanation

The plateau of the S-curve is a safety margin: a big drop in alveolar PO2 (altitude, mild lung disease) costs only a few percent of saturation. Below about 60 mm Hg the curve turns steep and saturation falls quickly.

  • About 50% happens only near the P50, about 26 mm Hg.
  • About 75% is the saturation of mixed venous blood at a PO2 of about 40 mm Hg.
Slides (1)

T and R states: shifting the curve

L49LearningHigh yield
Which state is deoxyhaemoglobin in, and what is its O2 affinity?
  1. A. T (taut): low affinity
  2. B. T (taut): high affinity
  3. C. R (relaxed): low affinity
AnswerA. T (taut): low affinity
WhyDeoxyhaemoglobin is the T (taut) state, held by extra bonds between its subunits, with low O2 affinity.
Explanation

In the T state the subunits are tied together by extra salt bridges and hydrogen bonds; that constraint ('taut') makes the haems harder to load. T = deoxy = low affinity is the anchor for every shift question: anything that stabilises T lowers affinity and shifts the curve right.

  • T with high affinity pairs the right name with the wrong property.
  • R (relaxed) is the oxygenated, high-affinity form.
Slides (2)
L50Learning
In haemoglobin Kansas, a β-chain asparagine that forms a bond stabilising the R state is replaced by threonine. What is the expected effect?
  1. A. Lower O2 affinity than HbA (curve shifted right)
  2. B. Higher O2 affinity than HbA (curve shifted left)
  3. C. Sickling of the red cells when deoxygenated
AnswerA. Lower O2 affinity than HbA (curve shifted right)
WhyLosing a bond that holds the R state tips the equilibrium toward T, so Hb Kansas has lower O2 affinity (right shift).
Explanation

Use the T ⇌ R rule for any variant: weaken R and the molecule spends more time in T (low affinity, right shift); weaken T or its 2,3-BPG binding and it spends more time in R (high affinity, left shift; e.g. Hb Helsinki, or HbF). Hb Kansas is a real low-affinity variant that causes mild cyanosis.

  • Higher affinity would follow from destabilising T, not R.
  • Sickling is specific to HbS, whose β6 valine makes deoxyhaemoglobin polymerise.
Slides (1)

The Bohr effect and CO2

L51Learning
What is carbaminohaemoglobin?
  1. A. CO2 bound in the 2,3-BPG pocket between the β chains: stabilises R
  2. B. CO2 bound to the terminal amino groups of the globin chains: stabilises T
  3. C. CO bound to the terminal amino groups of the globin chains: stabilises R
AnswerB. CO2 bound to the terminal amino groups of the globin chains: stabilises T
WhyCarbaminohaemoglobin forms when CO2 reacts with the terminal amino groups of the globin chains; this stabilises T and promotes O2 release.
Explanation

Hb–NH2 + CO2 ⇌ Hb–NH–COO− + H+. So CO2 lowers O2 affinity in two ways: as the source of carbonic acid (H+), and directly by forming these carbamino groups, which also release more H+. It is also one of the ways CO2 is carried back to the lungs.

  • The 2,3-BPG pocket binds 2,3-BPG, not CO2.
  • CO (carbon monoxide) binds the haem iron, not amino groups, and makes carboxyhaemoglobin.
Slides (2)
L52Learning
What happens to the Bohr-effect chemistry in the lungs?
  1. A. It runs backwards: CO2 breathed out → H+ leaves haemoglobin → O2 loads
  2. B. It runs backwards: CO2 breathed out → H+ binds haemoglobin → O2 unloads
  3. C. It runs the same way: CO2 taken up → H+ binds haemoglobin → O2 unloads
AnswerA. It runs backwards: CO2 breathed out → H+ leaves haemoglobin → O2 loads
WhyIn the lungs the high PO2 drives haemoglobin to R, which releases its H+; H+ + HCO3− re-form CO2, which is breathed out, and haemoglobin loads O2.
Explanation

Binding O2 and binding H+ oppose each other. In the tissues H+ wins and O2 leaves; in the lungs O2 wins and H+ leaves (HbH + O2 → HbO2 + H+). Carbonic anhydrase then converts H+ + HCO3− back to CO2 for exhalation. So oxygenation lowers haemoglobin's affinity for H+.

  • H+ binding and O2 unloading in the lungs would stop haemoglobin loading where it must.
  • CO2 taken up in the lungs: CO2 is lost in the lungs, not gained.
Slides (3)

2,3-BPG and altitude

L53LearningHigh yield
A 3-month-old girl has red-cell pyruvate kinase deficiency. What does her haemoglobin's oxygen-binding curve look like?
  1. A. Sigmoid, shifted to the left
  2. B. Sigmoid, shifted to the right
  3. C. Hyperbolic, shifted to the right
AnswerB. Sigmoid, shifted to the right
WhyThe block at pyruvate kinase backs up glycolytic intermediates, so red cells make more 2,3-BPG: the curve stays sigmoid but shifts right.
Explanation

Pyruvate kinase is the last step of glycolysis, and red cells depend entirely on glycolysis. When it is deficient, the intermediates above it, including 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, pile up and more is diverted to 2,3-BPG. More 2,3-BPG stabilises T: right shift, more O2 unloaded (partly offsetting the anaemia caused by haemolysis).

  • Shifted left would need less 2,3-BPG, as in a block above the 2,3-BPG branch (hexokinase deficiency).
  • Hyperbolic: her haemoglobin is normal, so cooperativity and the S-shape are intact.
Slides (2)

Carbon monoxide; PO2, saturation and O2 content

L54LearningHigh yield
How much more tightly than O2 does carbon monoxide (CO) bind haemoglobin?
  1. A. About 22×
  2. B. About 220×
  3. C. About 2,200×
AnswerB. About 220×
WhyHaemoglobin binds CO about 220 times more tightly than O2, although the binding is still reversible.
Explanation

CO binds the same ferrous iron as O2. With a ~220-fold advantage, even a small amount of CO in inspired air occupies a large share of haem sites over time (e.g. faulty heaters, car exhaust in a closed garage, propane equipment indoors). Other sources quote 200–250×.

  • 22× and 2,200× are tenfold off in each direction.
Slides (1)

Methaemoglobin

L55Learning
Which enzyme normally reduces methaemoglobin back to haemoglobin, and what happens when it is deficient?
  1. A. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) → carboxyhaemoglobin builds up
  2. B. NADH–cytochrome b5 reductase (NADH–methaemoglobin reductase) → carboxyhaemoglobin builds up
  3. C. NADH–cytochrome b5 reductase (NADH–methaemoglobin reductase) → methaemoglobin builds up
AnswerC. NADH–cytochrome b5 reductase (NADH–methaemoglobin reductase) → methaemoglobin builds up
WhyNADH–cytochrome b5 reductase uses NADH from glycolysis to return Fe3+ to Fe2+; when it is deficient, methaemoglobin builds up.
Explanation

This NADH-dependent enzyme does most of the daily repair of oxidised haem in red cells. An inherited deficiency causes lifelong cyanosis from birth (the blue-skinned patient whose relative had the same 'blood problem').

  • G6PD makes NADPH; its deficiency causes oxidative haemolysis (Heinz bodies), and carboxyhaemoglobin comes only from CO.
  • Right enzyme, carboxyhaemoglobin: the reductase acts on oxidised iron; it has nothing to do with CO.
Slides (3)
L56LearningHigh yield
What are the signs of methaemoglobinaemia?
  1. A. Cyanosis with chocolate-brown blood
    Anxiety, headache, dyspnoea (in proportion to the hypoxia)
  2. B. Pallor with cherry-red blood
    Anxiety, headache, dyspnoea (in proportion to the hypoxia)
  3. C. Jaundice with dark-red blood
    Itch, fatigue, dark urine (in proportion to the haemolysis)
AnswerA. Cyanosis with chocolate-brown blood
Anxiety, headache, dyspnoea (in proportion to the hypoxia)
WhyCyanosis with chocolate-brown blood, plus anxiety, headache and dyspnoea whose severity follows the degree of hypoxia.
Explanation

Methaemoglobin is dark brown, so blood looks chocolate-coloured and skin and lips look blue-grey, and the cyanosis does not improve with supplemental O2. The nickname 'blue baby syndrome' comes from infants given formula made with nitrate-contaminated well water: their reductase activity is still low.

  • Cherry-red blood is the classic (if unreliable) sign of CO poisoning.
  • Jaundice and dark urine are signs of haemolysis, not of oxidised haem.
Slides (2)

Globin genes and switching by age

L57Learning
Which chromosome carries the β-globin gene family, and which genes does it hold?
  1. A. Chromosome 11: ε (epsilon), α1 and α2, δ (delta), β
  2. B. Chromosome 16: ε (epsilon), Gγ and Aγ (gamma), δ (delta), β
  3. C. Chromosome 11: ε (epsilon), Gγ and Aγ (gamma), δ (delta), β
AnswerC. Chromosome 11: ε (epsilon), Gγ and Aγ (gamma), δ (delta), β
WhyThe β-globin family on chromosome 11 holds, in order of use, ε (embryo), Gγ and Aγ (fetus), and δ and β (adult).
Explanation

The β-like cluster on chromosome 11 contains five genes arranged roughly in the order they are switched on during development: ε (embryonic), the two γ genes Gγ and Aγ (fetal, differing by one amino acid), then δ and β (adult). There is only one β gene per chromosome 11, so a person has two β genes, which is why β-thalassaemia genotypes are written as pairs (β+/β, β0/β0…).

  • α1 and α2 belong to the α family on chromosome 16.
  • Chromosome 16 is the α-family chromosome; the γ, δ and β genes are not there.
Slides (2)
L58Learning
Which haemoglobin does the embryo make in the first month of development, and where?
  1. A. Hb Gower, made by the embryonic yolk sac
  2. B. Hb Gower, made by the fetal liver
  3. C. HbF, made by the embryonic yolk sac
AnswerA. Hb Gower, made by the embryonic yolk sac
WhyIn the first month the yolk sac makes embryonic Hb Gower (Gower 1 = ζ2ε2), built from the two embryonic chains ζ and ε.
Explanation

Blood formation starts in the yolk sac, and its red cells carry the embryonic haemoglobins. Hb Gower 1 (ζ2ε2) is the main one; on the graph ζ and ε are at their peak at −9 months and fall away by about −6 months as α and γ take over.

  • The fetal liver becomes the main site only from about week 5, when production switches to HbF.
  • HbF (α2γ2) is the product of the liver/marrow phase, not of the yolk sac.

Sequence to remember: yolk sac → Gower; liver/marrow → HbF; around birth → HbA.

Slides (2)

Disease types and β-thalassaemia

L59Learning
Why does under-producing one globin chain damage red cells?
  1. A. α and β are normally made 1:1, so the partner chain is left in excess
  2. B. α and β are normally made 2:1, so the partner chain is left in excess
  3. C. α and β are normally made 1:1, so the partner chain is degraded as well
AnswerA. α and β are normally made 1:1, so the partner chain is left in excess
Whyα and β chains are normally made in equal (1:1) amounts; a shortfall of one leaves the other in excess, and the spare chains precipitate.
Explanation

HbA needs two α and two β chains, so balanced 1:1 synthesis leaves no extras. If β synthesis falls, unpaired α chains aggregate and precipitate inside erythroid precursors and red cells, causing ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis; if α synthesis falls, spare β (or γ) chains form β4 (HbH) or γ4 (Hb Bart). The shortfall can come from point mutations, gene deletions or other defects.

  • The ratio is 1:1, not 2:1; each tetramer has two of each.
  • The partner chain is not efficiently removed; its accumulation is the problem.
Slides (2)
L60LearningHigh yield
β-thalassaemia minor: what is the genotype, and how does it present?
  1. A. β0/β0; mild microcytic anaemia
  2. B. β+/β or β0/β; mild microcytic anaemia
  3. C. β+/β+; no anaemia (silent carrier)
AnswerB. β+/β or β0/β; mild microcytic anaemia
WhyMinor = one abnormal allele with one normal (β+/β or β0/β); mild microcytic anaemia.
Explanation

One normal β gene makes enough β chain for near-normal haemoglobin, but the cells are small (microcytic) and HbA2 is raised. Patients are usually well; iron does not correct the anaemia, and the main importance is genetic counselling.

TypeGenotypePicture
Minorβ+/β, β0/βmild microcytic anaemia
Intermediaβ+/β+, β+/β0microcytic anaemia, occasional transfusions
Major (Cooley)β0/β0severe anaemia, splenomegaly, bone deformities, regular transfusions
  • β0/β0 is major; β+/β+ is intermedia, which is anaemic.
Slides (3)

α-thalassaemia

L61Learning
α-thalassaemia with three α genes lost: what is it called, and what forms?
  1. A. Hb Bart disease: spare γ chains form γ4, causing hydrops fetalis
  2. B. HbH disease: spare β chains form β4 (HbH), which precipitates as Heinz bodies; variable anaemia
  3. C. HbH disease: spare α chains form α4 (HbH), which precipitates as Heinz bodies; variable anaemia
AnswerB. HbH disease: spare β chains form β4 (HbH), which precipitates as Heinz bodies; variable anaemia
WhyWith three α genes lost, spare β chains form β4 tetramers (HbH), which precipitate as Heinz bodies; anaemia is variable.
Explanation

Only one α gene is left, so β chains greatly outnumber α chains. The unpaired β chains assemble into β4 (HbH). HbH has a very high O2 affinity and no cooperativity, so it is useless for O2 delivery, and it is unstable: it precipitates inside red cells as Heinz bodies, and the damaged cells are removed by the spleen (haemolytic anaemia, splenomegaly).

  • γ4 (Hb Bart) dominates when all four genes are lost, causing hydrops fetalis.
  • α4 cannot be the problem: α chains are the ones in short supply.
Slides (2)

Sickle cell disease: mutation and mechanism

L62LearningHigh yield
Why do patients with sickle cell disease have chronic anaemia and sometimes jaundice?
  1. A. Sickled cells are fragile, haemolyse and are removed by the spleen
  2. B. Sickled cells are rigid and are filtered by the kidney into the urine
  3. C. Sickled cells cannot leave the marrow, so too few are released
AnswerA. Sickled cells are fragile, haemolyse and are removed by the spleen
WhySickled cells are fragile: they haemolyse and are removed by the spleen, shortening red-cell life (chronic haemolytic anaemia); the bilirubin released causes jaundice.
Explanation

Red-cell survival in sickle cell disease is a fraction of the normal 120 days. Haemoglobin from destroyed cells is broken down to unconjugated bilirubin, which can exceed the liver's capacity and show as jaundice and scleral icterus. Jasmine D.'s Hb 9 g/dL, haematocrit 27% and pale nail beds show this chronic anaemia.

  • The kidney does not filter whole red cells; renal damage in sickle cell is from medullary infarction.
  • Marrow output is increased, not blocked; the problem is destruction, not production.
Slides (3)

Sickle cell triggers and the Jasmine D. case

L63LearningHigh yield
Why was Jasmine D. breathing fast (respiratory rate 24, PCO2 29 mmHg)?
  1. A. Respiratory compensation for a metabolic alkalosis
  2. B. Respiratory compensation for her metabolic acidosis
  3. C. A primary respiratory alkalosis from pain and anxiety
AnswerB. Respiratory compensation for her metabolic acidosis
WhyHer tachypnoea is respiratory compensation: hyperventilation blows off CO2 (PCO2 29) to limit the fall in pH from her metabolic acidosis.
Explanation

A metabolic acidosis is compensated quickly by the lungs: the fall in pH stimulates breathing, PCO2 drops, and pH is pulled back towards 7.4 (here 7.36). Compensation limits but does not fully correct the change. Her HCO3− fall of 8 predicts a PCO2 fall of about 10 (to ~30), close to the 29 measured.

  • A metabolic alkalosis would raise HCO3− and be compensated by hypoventilation.
  • A primary respiratory alkalosis would raise pH above 7.4; her pH is 7.36 with a low HCO3−, so the primary process is acidosis.
Slides (2)

Sickle cell treatment; HbC

L64Learning
What is crizanlizumab, and what does it do in sickle cell disease?
  1. A. A monoclonal antibody against E-selectin (2019); reduces vaso-occlusive crises
  2. B. A monoclonal antibody against P-selectin (2019); reduces vaso-occlusive crises
  3. C. A small molecule that blocks HbS polymerisation (2019); reduces haemolysis
AnswerB. A monoclonal antibody against P-selectin (2019); reduces vaso-occlusive crises
WhyCrizanlizumab (approved 2019) is a monoclonal antibody against P-selectin that reduces the frequency of vaso-occlusive crises.
Explanation

P-selectin is an adhesion molecule on activated endothelial cells and platelets. It helps sickled red cells, white cells and platelets stick to the vessel wall, which seeds vaso-occlusion. Blocking it lowers the number of painful crises.

  • E-selectin is a related endothelial adhesion molecule, but it is not crizanlizumab's target.
  • A small-molecule polymerisation inhibitor describes voxelotor, also first approved in 2019 and later withdrawn.
Slides (2)
L65Learning
In sickle cell disease, what does chronic red-cell transfusion aim for, and what is its main long-term cost?
  1. A. Keeping HbS below about 50% (for example to prevent stroke); cost: iron overload
  2. B. Keeping HbS below about 50% (for example to prevent stroke); cost: iron deficiency
  3. C. Keeping HbF above about 50% (for example to prevent pain crises); cost: iron overload
AnswerA. Keeping HbS below about 50% (for example to prevent stroke); cost: iron overload
WhyTransfusion dilutes the patient's own cells to keep HbS below about 50% (to treat anaemia, prepare for surgery, prevent stroke); the cost is transfusion reactions and iron overload.
Explanation

Transfused red cells contain HbA, so the HbS fraction falls and sickling decreases. Each unit also brings about 200–250 mg of iron that the body cannot excrete, so repeated transfusion causes iron overload (treated with iron chelation). For primary stroke prevention, many guidelines aim even lower, at HbS below 30%; the case slide gives 50% as its example.

  • Transfusion causes iron excess, not deficiency.
  • Transfusion lowers HbS; it does not raise HbF (that is hydroxyurea).
Slides (1)
L66Learning
What disease do HbC homozygotes and HbC carriers have?
  1. A. Homozygotes: mild chronic haemolytic anaemia without pain crises; carriers: silent
  2. B. Homozygotes: severe haemolytic anaemia with frequent pain crises; carriers: mild anaemia
  3. C. Homozygotes: no disease; carriers: mild chronic haemolytic anaemia
AnswerA. Homozygotes: mild chronic haemolytic anaemia without pain crises; carriers: silent
WhyHbC homozygotes have a mild, chronic haemolytic anaemia without the severe pain crises of sickle cell; carriers are "silent".
Explanation

Two HbC alleles mean all β chains are HbC, enough crystal formation to shorten red-cell life modestly. One HbC allele plus one normal β allele leaves mostly HbA, with no clinical disease.

  • Severe anaemia with frequent pain crises describes sickle cell disease (HbSS).
  • The pattern is not reversed: disease needs two HbC alleles (or HbC with HbS); one allele is silent.
Slides (2)

BIO-L23 Acid–base balance in health and disease (+ CV Acid–base disorder)

Tier 1: 16 of 46
Learning questions 46
Tier 1Every concept once16 questions

Naming the four disorders

L1Learning
In the blood Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, which change defines a primary metabolic acidosis?
  1. A. The denominator, 0.03 × PCO2, rises, so the ratio and pH fall
  2. B. The numerator, [HCO3−], falls, so the ratio and pH fall
  3. C. The pKa falls from 6.1, so the pH falls
AnswerB. The numerator, [HCO3−], falls, so the ratio and pH fall
WhyMetabolic disorders change the numerator (HCO3−); respiratory disorders change the denominator (PCO2). A falling numerator lowers the ratio: pH ↓.
Explanation

Write the four disorders into pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−] / (0.03 × PCO2)):

  • Metabolic acidosis: ↓[HCO3−] → ↓pH
  • Metabolic alkalosis: ↑[HCO3−] → ↑pH
  • Respiratory acidosis: ↑PCO2 → ↓pH
  • Respiratory alkalosis: ↓PCO2 → ↑pH

A rise in the denominator is respiratory acidosis. The pKa is a constant of the buffer pair; disease does not change it.

Slides (1)
L2LearningHigh yield
What is the difference between acidaemia and acidosis?
  1. A. Acidaemia = blood pH below 7.4
    Acidosis = the process pushing it there
  2. B. Acidosis = blood pH below 7.4
    Acidaemia = the process pushing it there
  3. C. Acidaemia = a respiratory acid excess
    Acidosis = a metabolic acid excess
AnswerA. Acidaemia = blood pH below 7.4
Acidosis = the process pushing it there
WhyAcidaemia is the state (blood pH < 7.4); acidosis is the physiological process responsible for it. Likewise alkalaemia (pH > 7.4) vs alkalosis.
Explanation

"-aemia" = in the blood (a measured value); "-osis" = a process or condition. They usually travel together, but not always: a patient can have an acidosis without an acidaemia if an alkalosis is running at the same time. On the acid–base map the red arc (acidaemia) and blue arc (alkalaemia) label pH values, not causes.

  • Acidosis = blood pH below 7.4 swaps the two words (the school’s trap).
  • Respiratory vs metabolic is a separate axis; both kinds of acidosis cause acidaemia.
Slides (1)

Causes of each disorder

L3LearningHigh yield
Which list gives causes of respiratory acidosis?
  1. A. Anxiety hyperventilation, salicylates, analeptics
    Hypoxaemia (via peripheral chemoreceptors)
    Pulmonary emboli; excessive mechanical ventilation
  2. B. Chronic lung disease (COPD), asthma, restrictive lung disease
    Central respiratory depression, myasthenia gravis
    Excess CO2 in inspired air; malignant hyperthermia
  3. C. Increased ketogenesis, lactic acidosis
    Diarrhoea, kidney failure
    Methanol, ethylene glycol
AnswerB. Chronic lung disease (COPD), asthma, restrictive lung disease
Central respiratory depression, myasthenia gravis
Excess CO2 in inspired air; malignant hyperthermia
WhyRespiratory acidosis = ↓alveolar ventilation (lung, airway, chest wall, nerve/muscle disease, central depression), excess inspired CO2 or ↑CO2 production.
Explanation
