The lecture’s list: excess CO2 in inspired air; decreased alveolar ventilation (central respiratory depression, e.g., opioids; nerve or muscle disorders, e.g., myasthenia gravis; lung or chest-wall defects, e.g., restrictive lung disease; airway disorders, e.g., asthma); increased CO2 production (hypercatabolic states such as malignant hyperthermia). Summary slide: "chronic lung disease".

  • The list starting anxiety hyperventilation is respiratory alkalosis (too much ventilation).
  • The list starting increased ketogenesis is metabolic acidosis.

Note on asthma: a severe or tiring attack retains CO2 (acidosis), but early in an attack patients often hyperventilate and show respiratory alkalosis; read the blood gas.

Slides (3)
L4LearningHigh yield
Which list gives causes of metabolic alkalosis?
  1. A. Diarrhoea, renal bicarbonate loss
    Ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis
    Kidney failure
  2. B. Anxiety hyperventilation, high altitude
    Pulmonary emboli
    Excessive mechanical ventilation
  3. C. Loss of H+ via the gut (vomiting) or kidneys (diuretics)
    Sodium bicarbonate infusion
    Metabolism of ketoanions and other salts of metabolic acids
AnswerC. Loss of H+ via the gut (vomiting) or kidneys (diuretics)
Sodium bicarbonate infusion
Metabolism of ketoanions and other salts of metabolic acids
WhyMetabolic alkalosis = H+ lost (vomiting, diuretics) or base gained, exogenous (NaHCO3 infusion) or endogenous (metabolism of ketoanions/organic-acid salts).
Explanation

From the lecture: loss of H+ via kidneys (diuretics) or gut (vomiting); gain of alkali from an exogenous source (NaHCO3 infusion) or an endogenous source (metabolism of ketoanions); summary slide: "administration of salts of metabolic acids, vomiting".

  • The list starting diarrhoea is metabolic acidosis.
  • The list starting anxiety hyperventilation is respiratory alkalosis: high pH from low PCO2, not high HCO3−.
Slides (2)

Reference values

L5LearningHigh yield
Within what range is arterial blood pH normally held, and what is the reference point?
  1. A. 7.35–7.45 (reference point 7.40)
  2. B. 7.40–7.50 (reference point 7.45)
  3. C. 7.25–7.35 (reference point 7.30)
AnswerA. 7.35–7.45 (reference point 7.40)
WhyNormal arterial pH is 7.35–7.45, with 7.40 as the reference point used to name a disorder.
Explanation
ValueRangeReference point
pH7.35–7.457.40
PCO233–44 mm Hg40
PO275–105 mm Hg
Na+135–145 mEq/L(avg 140)
HCO3−22–28 mEq/L24
Cl−98–106 mEq/L100
Anion gap8–16 mEq/L12
  • 7.40–7.50 is shifted to the alkaline side.
  • 7.25–7.35 is acidaemic throughout.
Slides (2)

Compensation

L6Learning
What is the general rule for how the body compensates an acid–base disorder?
  1. A. It pushes pH past 7.40 to the opposite side of normal
  2. B. It moves the other variable in the opposite direction to the primary change
  3. C. It moves the other variable in the same direction as the primary change
AnswerC. It moves the other variable in the same direction as the primary change
WhyCompensation changes the other variable in the same direction as the primary change, restoring the HCO3−/PCO2 ratio that sets pH.
Explanation

pH depends on the ratio [HCO3−]/(0.03 × PCO2), not on either value alone. If one term changes, pH is pulled back only by changing the other term the same way: a primary fall in HCO3− (metabolic acidosis) is offset by a fall in PCO2 (hyperventilation); a primary rise in PCO2 (respiratory acidosis) by a rise in HCO3− (renal retention).

  • Moving the other variable the opposite way would make the ratio worse, i.e., add a second disorder.
  • Compensation never pushes pH past 7.40; it only pulls it towards normal.

Tip: in a simple disorder PCO2 and HCO3− always move together, both up or both down.

Slides (2)
L7Learning
Why does a respiratory disorder have an acute phase and a chronic phase?
  1. A. Renal compensation takes a day or more → acute: small HCO3− change; chronic: larger
  2. B. Respiratory compensation takes a day or more → acute: small PCO2 change; chronic: larger
  3. C. Renal compensation is fastest at first → acute: large HCO3− change; chronic: smaller
AnswerA. Renal compensation takes a day or more → acute: small HCO3− change; chronic: larger
WhyThe kidney needs days to change HCO3−: an acute respiratory disorder shows only a small HCO3− change, a chronic one the full renal response.
Explanation

In the first hours HCO3− shifts only by chemical buffering: about 1–2 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg change in PCO2. Over days the kidney adds its response: 3–4 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg in chronic respiratory acidosis, 4–5 in chronic respiratory alkalosis. On the acid–base map each respiratory disorder therefore has two bands, acute and chronic.

  • The lungs do not compensate respiratory disorders; they compensate metabolic ones, and quickly.
  • The acute phase has the smaller HCO3− change, not the larger.

Metabolic disorders have no acute/chronic split because their respiratory compensation develops within hours.

Slides (3)
L8Learning
What is the expected compensation for a metabolic acidosis?
  1. A. Hyperventilation: PCO2 −0.6 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L fall in HCO3−
  2. B. Hyperventilation: PCO2 −1.2 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L fall in HCO3−
  3. C. Hyperventilation: PCO2 −3 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L fall in HCO3−
AnswerB. Hyperventilation: PCO2 −1.2 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L fall in HCO3−
WhyMetabolic acidosis: PCO2 falls about 1.2 mm Hg for every 1 mEq/L fall in HCO3−.
Explanation

Expected PCO2 = 40 − 1.2 × (24 − measured HCO3−). Diarrhoea case: HCO3− 16 (−8) → PCO2 ≈ 40 − 10 = 30; measured 31, so compensation is appropriate. Diabetic ketoacidosis case: HCO3− 8 (−16) → PCO2 ≈ 21; measured 19.

  • 0.6 mm Hg per mEq/L is the low end of the metabolic alkalosis factor (0.6–0.75).
  • 3 mm Hg per mEq/L is far more than the lungs achieve.

Winter's formula (PCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3− + 8 ± 2) gives nearly the same answer; the lecture uses the 1.2 rule.

Slides (2)
L9Learning
In what order do you interpret a blood gas?
  1. A. Anion gap → primary change (PCO2 or HCO3−) → is compensation the expected size? → in metabolic alkalosis, the pH
  2. B. pH → primary change (PCO2 or HCO3−) → is compensation the expected size? → in metabolic acidosis, the anion gap
  3. C. pH → primary change (PCO2 or HCO3−) → is compensation complete (pH 7.40)? → in metabolic alkalosis, the anion gap
AnswerB. pH → primary change (PCO2 or HCO3−) → is compensation the expected size? → in metabolic acidosis, the anion gap
WhypH gives the side, the variable that explains it is primary, the rules test compensation, and the anion gap splits metabolic acidosis.
Explanation

The lecture's worked cases all run this way:

  • pH: below 7.40 = acidosis, above = alkalosis.
  • Primary change: the variable that explains the pH (↑PCO2 or ↓HCO3− for acidosis; ↓PCO2 or ↑HCO3− for alkalosis).
  • Compensation: compare the other variable with its expected range; a mismatch means a second disorder.
  • Anion gap: in metabolic acidosis, normal gap = base lost, high gap = acid gained. The vignette adds: calculate it even when the gas looks normal.

The gap does not name the primary disorder, it is the tool for metabolic acidosis, and compensation never brings pH back to 7.40.

Slides (1)

Worked blood gases

L10LearningHigh yield
A woman with COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) has had epigastric pain for 3 hours: pH 7.37, PCO2 52, HCO3− 29. What fits?
  1. A. Respiratory acidosis without renal compensation
  2. B. Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
  3. C. Respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
AnswerC. Respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
WhypH just below 7.40 with high PCO2 = respiratory acidosis; HCO3− up 5 for a 12 mm Hg rise = chronic renal compensation of long-standing COPD.
Explanation

The 3-hour pain is a distraction: COPD retains CO2 for years. PCO2 52 (+12) with pH below 7.40 makes respiratory acidosis primary. The chronic rule predicts HCO3− + 3.6–4.8 ≈ 28–29; the measured 29 matches, which is why pH (7.37) is almost normal.

  • Without renal compensation, HCO3− would be ≈ 25–26 and pH ≈ 7.30.
  • Metabolic alkalosis would put pH above 7.40; with pH below 7.40, the high HCO3− is the compensation, not the cause.
Slides (2)

Anion gap

L11LearningHigh yield
What is the anion gap formula?
  1. A. [Na+] − ([Cl−] + [HCO3−])
  2. B. ([Cl−] + [HCO3−]) − [Na+]
  3. C. [Na+] − ([Cl−] − [HCO3−])
AnswerA. [Na+] − ([Cl−] + [HCO3−])
WhyAnion gap = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−): the main measured cation minus the two main measured anions.
Explanation

Plasma is electrically neutral, but a routine panel measures only Na+, Cl− and HCO3−. Subtracting the measured anions from Na+ leaves a "gap" that stands for the unmeasured anions (minus the unmeasured cations). K+ is left out of the course's formula.

  • Cl− minus HCO3− inside the bracket subtracts one anion from the other; both must be added.
  • (Cl− + HCO3−) − Na+ reverses the sign and gives a negative number.

Tip: if a stem gives K+, Ca2+ or glucose, leave them out.

Slides (2)
L12LearningHigh yield
Which disorder does the anion gap split in two, and what question does it answer?
  1. A. Metabolic acidosis — was acid gained or base lost?
  2. B. Metabolic alkalosis — was acid lost or base gained?
  3. C. Respiratory acidosis — is it acute or chronic?
AnswerA. Metabolic acidosis — was acid gained or base lost?
WhyThe gap splits metabolic acidosis: high gap = acid gained (organic anion added); normal gap = bicarbonate lost (replaced by Cl−).
Explanation

HCO3− falls either because an acid titrates it (lactate, ketones, toxins) or because it is lost from the gut or kidney. The primary use of the gap is to tell these apart; it also exposes unmeasured anions when the blood gas looks normal.

  • Acute vs chronic respiratory disorders are separated by the size of the HCO3− change, not by the gap.
  • The gap is not the tool for metabolic alkalosis in this course.
Slides (3)
L13Learning
What causes a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis?
  1. A. COPD, opioid overdose, myasthenia gravis
    Asthma, malignant hyperthermia
  2. B. Diarrhoea, renal HCO3− loss
    Vomiting, diuretics, NaHCO3 infusion
  3. C. Ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure
    Methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate
AnswerC. Ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure
Methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate
WhyHigh gap = acid gained with an unmeasured anion: ketones, lactate, acids retained in renal failure, and toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate).
Explanation

Each adds an anion: β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate (ketoacidosis), lactate (shock, hypoxia), sulfate and phosphate (renal failure: the kidney cannot excrete them), formate (methanol), glycolate (ethylene glycol), salicylate plus lactate and ketones (aspirin).

  • Diarrhoea and renal HCO3− loss give a normal-gap acidosis; vomiting, diuretics and bicarbonate infusion cause metabolic alkalosis.
  • COPD, opioids, myasthenia gravis, asthma, malignant hyperthermia cause respiratory acidosis.
Slides (3)

Hidden and mixed disorders

L14LearningHigh yield
Should you calculate the anion gap when pH, PCO2 and HCO3− are all normal?
  1. A. No — the gap is needed only when pH is low
  2. B. No — a normal blood gas rules out an acid–base disorder
  3. C. Yes — a normal blood gas can hide two opposing disorders
AnswerC. Yes — a normal blood gas can hide two opposing disorders
WhyCheck the anion gap even if the blood gas is normal: a high gap reveals a metabolic acidosis cancelled by an opposing disorder.
Explanation

An acidosis and an alkalosis of similar size can leave pH, PCO2 and HCO3− at their reference points. The gap does not depend on that balance: it rises whenever unmeasured anions accumulate. That is how the vignette's 16-year-old, with a perfect blood gas, was found to have a hidden metabolic acidosis.

  • Limiting the gap to a low pH would miss exactly these mixed cases.
  • A normal gas does not rule out disease: compensation never produces a perfect gas, but two opposing disorders can.
Slides (2)

Aspirin vs ethylene glycol

L15LearningHigh yield
What acid–base disorders does aspirin (salicylate) poisoning cause?
  1. A. Respiratory alkalosis + metabolic alkalosis
  2. B. Respiratory acidosis + normal-gap metabolic acidosis
  3. C. Respiratory alkalosis + high-gap metabolic acidosis
AnswerC. Respiratory alkalosis + high-gap metabolic acidosis
WhySalicylate stimulates the respiratory centre (respiratory alkalosis) and adds organic acids (high-gap metabolic acidosis): two primary disorders.
Explanation

The respiratory alkalosis dominates early (the lecture's 17-year-old: pH 7.57, PCO2 25). As salicylic acid, lactic acid and ketoacids accumulate, a high-gap metabolic acidosis develops. Both are primary processes, so PCO2 is lower than the acidosis alone would predict. (Some review slides call the later acidosis "compensation"; it is a separate disorder.)

  • Respiratory acidosis is not the salicylate picture, and its acidosis has a high gap, not a normal one.
  • Metabolic alkalosis is not caused by salicylate itself; vomiting can add one, as in the vignette.
Slides (2)
L16Learning
How is ethylene glycol metabolised?
  1. A. Alcohol dehydrogenase → glycolaldehyde → glycolic → glyoxylic → oxalic acid
  2. B. Alcohol dehydrogenase → acetaldehyde → acetic acid → acetyl-CoA
  3. C. Aldehyde dehydrogenase → glycolaldehyde → oxalic → glyoxylic → glycolic acid
AnswerA. Alcohol dehydrogenase → glycolaldehyde → glycolic → glyoxylic → oxalic acid
WhyAlcohol dehydrogenase in the liver starts it: ethylene glycol → glycolaldehyde → glycolic → glyoxylic → oxalic acid.
Explanation

Ethylene glycol itself is not very toxic; its acid metabolites are. Alcohol dehydrogenase oxidises it to glycolaldehyde, aldehyde dehydrogenase to glycolic acid (the main cause of the acidosis), then glyoxylic acid and finally oxalic acid, which precipitates with calcium.

  • Starting at aldehyde dehydrogenase and running oxalic → glyoxylic → glycolic reverses the pathway.
  • Acetaldehyde → acetic acid → acetyl-CoA is ethanol's pathway.
Slides (3)
Tier 2The next layer across every concept+16 questions

Causes of each disorder

L17LearningHigh yield
Which list gives causes of respiratory alkalosis?
  1. A. Anxiety hyperventilation; drugs acting on the respiratory centre (analeptics, salicylates)
    Hypoxaemia (via peripheral chemoreceptors)
    Pulmonary emboli; excessive mechanical ventilation
  2. B. Vomiting, diuretics
    Sodium bicarbonate infusion
    Metabolism of ketoanions and other salts of metabolic acids
  3. C. Opioids and other respiratory-centre depressants
    Hypoxaemia (via central chemoreceptors)
    Myasthenia gravis; insufficient mechanical ventilation
AnswerA. Anxiety hyperventilation; drugs acting on the respiratory centre (analeptics, salicylates)
Hypoxaemia (via peripheral chemoreceptors)
Pulmonary emboli; excessive mechanical ventilation
WhyRespiratory alkalosis = ↑alveolar ventilation: central (anxiety, analeptics, propanidid, salicylates), hypoxaemia, pulmonary emboli or excessive controlled ventilation.
Explanation

The lecture groups the causes by where they act: central (direct action on the respiratory centre: analeptics, propanidid, salicylate intoxication; anxiety/panic hyperventilation); hypoxaemia via peripheral chemoreceptors (e.g., high altitude); pulmonary via intrapulmonary receptors (pulmonary emboli); iatrogenic (excessive controlled ventilation).

  • The list starting vomiting, diuretics is metabolic alkalosis.
  • The list starting opioids reduces ventilation (respiratory acidosis); hypoxaemia drives breathing through peripheral, not central, chemoreceptors.
Slides (3)
L18Learning
Why does vomiting cause a metabolic alkalosis while diarrhoea causes a metabolic acidosis?
  1. A. Vomit carries away HCO3− (base); diarrhoeal fluid carries away gastric HCl (acid)
  2. B. Vomit carries away gastric HCl (acid); diarrhoeal fluid carries away HCO3− (base)
  3. C. Both lose acid, but diarrhoea also triggers hyperventilation
AnswerB. Vomit carries away gastric HCl (acid); diarrhoeal fluid carries away HCO3− (base)
WhyVomiting loses stomach acid (HCl) → base left behind → alkalosis; diarrhoea loses bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid → acidosis (normal anion gap).
Explanation

The gut secretes acid at the top (stomach) and bicarbonate lower down (pancreatic and intestinal secretions). Whichever end loses fluid sets the disorder: upper GI loss (vomiting, bulimia) = metabolic alkalosis; lower GI loss (diarrhoea, cholera) = metabolic acidosis with a raised Cl− (hyperchloraemic, normal gap).

  • Vomit carries away HCO3− reverses the two fluids.
  • Both lose acid: diarrhoea loses base; any hyperventilation is compensation for the acidosis, not its cause.
Slides (2)

Reference values

L19Learning
The exam review says single reference points are to be used for only some blood values; all other values are judged against their reference ranges. Which values are judged against a reference point?
  1. A. Na+, Cl− and anion gap
  2. B. PO2, Na+ and Cl−
  3. C. pH, PCO2 and HCO3−
AnswerC. pH, PCO2 and HCO3−
WhyReference points apply only to pH (7.40), PCO2 (40) and HCO3− (24); Cl−, anion gap and the rest are read against their ranges.
Explanation

The exam-review clarification (the reference table also prints points for Na+, Cl− and the anion gap, but only three are to be used): because pH, PCO2 and HCO3− are compared with single points, even a small change in HCO3− from 24 counts as an attempt at compensation. Other values (Cl−, anion gap) are abnormal only outside their ranges; a change in anion gap that stays within 8–16 may be ignored.

  • Na+, Cl−, anion gap are judged by range (the slide names Cl− and the gap explicitly).
  • PO2 has a range only and plays no part in naming the disorder.
Slides (2)

Compensation

L20Learning
Does compensation bring pH all the way back to 7.40?
  1. A. Yes — for metabolic disorders, because the lungs act within minutes
  2. B. No — it pulls pH towards 7.40 but stops short of it
  3. C. Yes — once renal compensation is complete after several days
AnswerB. No — it pulls pH towards 7.40 but stops short of it
WhyCompensation never fully normalises pH while the cause persists, so the side of 7.40 the pH is on still shows the primary disorder.
Explanation

Compensation is driven by the pH error itself: as pH approaches normal, the stimulus to keep hyperventilating, or to keep retaining bicarbonate, fades. pH therefore stays on the side of the primary disorder until the cause is removed (the lecture's V-shaped curve: 7.4 → 7.1 → back towards, but not to, 7.4).

  • Metabolic disorders are compensated quickly by the lungs, but still incompletely.
  • Even chronic renal compensation of a respiratory disorder stops short of 7.40.

Exam use: pH below 7.40 with both PCO2 and HCO3− abnormal → the acidosis is primary. A perfectly normal pH with abnormal PCO2 and HCO3−, or a normal blood gas with a high anion gap, suggests two disorders.

Slides (2)
L21Learning
What is the expected compensation for a respiratory acidosis?
  1. A. HCO3− up: acute +5–6, chronic +8–10 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in PCO2
  2. B. HCO3− up: acute +3–4, chronic +1–2 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in PCO2
  3. C. HCO3− up: acute +1–2, chronic +3–4 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in PCO2
AnswerC. HCO3− up: acute +1–2, chronic +3–4 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in PCO2
WhyRespiratory acidosis: HCO3− rises 1–2 mEq/L (acute) or 3–4 mEq/L (chronic) per 10 mm Hg rise in PCO2.
Explanation

These are the lecture's expected-compensation numbers. Example: PCO2 rises from 40 to 60 (+20). Acute: HCO3− ≈ 24 + 2–4 = 26–28. Chronic: HCO3− ≈ 24 + 6–8 = 30–32. A measured HCO3− outside the band that fits the history points to a second, metabolic disorder.

  • +3–4 acute, +1–2 chronic swaps the phases: renal compensation makes the chronic change larger.
  • +5–6 / +8–10 is far more than compensation achieves; HCO3− that high means a coexisting metabolic alkalosis.

Note: the worked case slides round the acute figure to 2 per 10 mm Hg.

Slides (2)
L22Learning
What is the expected compensation for a metabolic alkalosis?
  1. A. Hypoventilation: PCO2 +1.2 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3−; rarely above 80 mm Hg
  2. B. Hypoventilation: PCO2 +2–3 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3−; no upper limit
  3. C. Hypoventilation: PCO2 +0.6–0.75 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3−; rarely above 55 mm Hg
AnswerC. Hypoventilation: PCO2 +0.6–0.75 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3−; rarely above 55 mm Hg
WhyMetabolic alkalosis: PCO2 rises 0.6–0.75 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3−, and compensation should not take PCO2 above 55 mm Hg.
Explanation

Expected PCO2 = 40 + 0.6–0.75 × (measured HCO3− − 24). Bulimia case: HCO3− 39 (+15) → PCO2 ≈ 49–51; measured 49. The ceiling exists because hypoventilation also lowers PO2, and hypoxaemia then drives breathing again; a PCO2 above 55 in a metabolic alkalosis means a coexisting respiratory acidosis.

  • 1.2 mm Hg per mEq/L is the metabolic acidosis factor.
  • 2–3 mm Hg with no limit overstates the weakest of the four compensations.
Slides (2)
L23Learning
Using the rule that fits the history (acute or chronic), compensation is clearly outside the expected range. What does that mean?
  1. A. A second, independent acid–base disorder is present
  2. B. Compensation is complete and pH is back at 7.40
  3. C. Compensation has overshot, pushing pH past 7.40
AnswerA. A second, independent acid–base disorder is present
WhyCompensation follows predictable rules; a PCO2 or HCO3− well outside the expected range means a second primary disorder (a mixed disorder).
Explanation

For each simple disorder the lecture gives an expected range. Compare the measured value with it:

  • Metabolic acidosis with PCO2 higher than expected → a coexisting respiratory acidosis (the lungs are not keeping up).
  • Metabolic acidosis with PCO2 lower than expected → a coexisting respiratory alkalosis (classic in salicylate poisoning).
  • For a respiratory disorder, first pick the acute or chronic rule from the history; a change beyond that band means a metabolic disorder too.

Compensation is never complete and never overshoots, so neither of the other choices can explain a mismatch.

Slides (2)

Worked blood gases

L24LearningHigh yield
A 65-year-old with emphysema has had shortness of breath for 3 hours: pH 7.18, PCO2 58, HCO3− 26. Diagnosis?
  1. A. Acute respiratory acidosis, little renal compensation yet
  2. B. Chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
  3. C. Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
AnswerA. Acute respiratory acidosis, little renal compensation yet
WhyLow pH with high PCO2 = respiratory acidosis; HCO3− up only 2 for an 18 mm Hg rise after 3 hours = acute, before renal compensation.
Explanation

Step through it: pH 7.18 → acidosis. PCO2 58 (+18) explains the low pH → primary respiratory acidosis. HCO3− 26 (+2) fits the acute rule (1–2 per 10 mm Hg) and is well below the chronic expectation (+5–7, ≈ 29–31). The lecture's conclusion: acute respiratory acidosis without full renal compensation.

  • Chronic compensation would have raised HCO3− to about 30 and brought pH much nearer 7.40.
  • Metabolic acidosis needs a low HCO3− and a low PCO2; here both are high.
Slides (3)
L25LearningHigh yield
What acid–base disorder does hyperventilation syndrome (anxiety or panic) cause, and what are its symptoms?
  1. A. Respiratory alkalosis; dizziness, tingling of lips and fingertips
  2. B. Metabolic acidosis; deep, sighing Kussmaul breathing
  3. C. Respiratory acidosis; drowsiness, headache, flushed warm skin
AnswerA. Respiratory alkalosis; dizziness, tingling of lips and fingertips
WhyOverbreathing blows off CO2 → respiratory alkalosis; the alkalaemia lowers ionised calcium, causing tingling and numbness, plus dizziness.
Explanation

Hyperventilation syndrome is a non-medical cause of shortness of breath. A low PCO2 raises pH; in alkalaemia plasma proteins bind more Ca2+, so ionised calcium falls and nerves fire easily (tingling of lips and fingertips, carpopedal spasm). A low PCO2 also constricts cerebral vessels, causing dizziness.

  • Respiratory acidosis follows hypoventilation (CO2 retention), the opposite of overbreathing.
  • Kussmaul breathing is the lungs' compensation for a metabolic acidosis such as diabetic ketoacidosis.
Slides (2)

Anion gap

L26Learning
Why does adding an acid such as lactic acid or ketoacids widen the anion gap?
  1. A. Its H+ uses up HCO3−, and Cl− rises to take HCO3−'s place
  2. B. Its H+ uses up HCO3−, and its unmeasured anion takes HCO3−'s place
  3. C. Its anion is counted with Cl−, so the measured anions rise
AnswerB. Its H+ uses up HCO3−, and its unmeasured anion takes HCO3−'s place
WhyH+ from the acid titrates HCO3−; the acid's own unmeasured anion replaces it, so Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−) rises.
Explanation

HA + HCO3− → A− + H2O + CO2 (exhaled). For each HCO3− lost, one A− appears. Cl− is unchanged, so the measured anions fall and the gap widens by about as much as HCO3− fell: high-gap acidosis is normochloraemic. Example: diabetic ketoacidosis, Na+ 136, Cl− 101, HCO3− 8 → gap 27.

  • A rise in Cl− replacing HCO3− is the normal-gap pattern of bicarbonate loss.
  • Organic anions are not counted as Cl−; the analyser measures chloride specifically.
Slides (2)
L27Learning
After a large myocardial infarction a patient is in shock with a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. What is the acid, and which test measures it?
  1. A. Ketoacids from increased fatty-acid breakdown; urine ketones
  2. B. Lactic acid from anaerobic glycolysis in hypoxic tissue; serum lactate
  3. C. Bicarbonate lost through the kidney; serum Cl−
AnswerB. Lactic acid from anaerobic glycolysis in hypoxic tissue; serum lactate
WhyPoor perfusion → tissue hypoxia → anaerobic glycolysis makes lactic acid; lactate is the unmeasured anion, and serum lactate tracks severity.
Explanation

Without O2, pyruvate cannot be oxidised in mitochondria and is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD+. The H+ consumes HCO3− and the lactate anion widens the gap (the "L" of GOLD MARK and MUDPILES). Myocardial infarction, haemorrhage and other shock states are typical causes.

  • Ketoacids come from fatty-acid oxidation in insulin deficiency or starvation, not from shock.
  • Bicarbonate loss with a raised Cl− gives a normal gap, which contradicts this patient's high gap.
Slides (1)
L28Learning
What does GOLD MARK stand for (high-gap causes)?
  1. A. Glycols (ethylene, propylene)
    5-Oxoproline
    L-lactate
    D-lactate
    Metformin
    Acetazolamide
    Respiratory failure
    Ketoacidosis
  2. B. Glycols (ethylene, propylene)
    5-Oxoproline
    L-lactate
    D-lactate
    Methanol
    Aspirin
    Renal failure
    Ketoacidosis
  3. C. Glycols (ethylene, propylene)
    Opioids
    Lithium
    D-lactate
    Methanol
    Ammonium chloride
    Renal tubular acidosis
    Ketoacidosis
AnswerB. Glycols (ethylene, propylene)
5-Oxoproline
L-lactate
D-lactate
Methanol
Aspirin
Renal failure
Ketoacidosis
WhyGOLD MARK: Glycols, 5-Oxoproline, L-lactate, D-lactate, Methanol, Aspirin, Renal failure, Ketoacidosis.
Explanation

The newer mnemonic for high-gap metabolic acidosis, recommended to replace MUDPILES. It drops paraldehyde (now very rare) and iron/isoniazid (they act through lactic acidosis, which "L" covers), and adds three newly recognised acids: D-lactate, 5-oxoproline and propylene glycol.

  • The version with Metformin, Acetazolamide, Respiratory failure is wrong: respiratory failure causes a respiratory acidosis, and the M and A are Methanol and Aspirin.
  • The version with Opioids, Lithium, Ammonium chloride is wrong: opioids cause respiratory acidosis, and none of these is in the mnemonic.
Slides (2)

Hidden and mixed disorders

L29LearningHigh yield
A 16-year-old who vomited three times after a suspected ingestion has pH 7.40 but an anion gap of 20. How can her pH be normal?
  1. A. The acidosis is too mild to change the pH
  2. B. Hyperventilation fully compensated the acidosis
  3. C. Vomiting added a metabolic alkalosis that offsets it
AnswerC. Vomiting added a metabolic alkalosis that offsets it
WhyVomiting removed stomach acid, adding a metabolic alkalosis that cancels the high-gap acidosis: two primary disorders, not compensation.
Explanation

Loss of HCl raised HCO3− by about as much as the ingested acid lowered it, so HCO3− sits at 24 and pH at 7.40. Compensation cannot explain this: it would lower PCO2 (hers is 40), and it never returns pH fully to 7.40.

  • Hyperventilation would show as a PCO2 below 40.
  • A gap of 20 means about 8 mEq/L of extra acid anion; without the alkalosis HCO3− would have fallen to about 16, hardly "too mild".
Slides (2)

Aspirin vs ethylene glycol

L30Learning
Why does alkalinising the urine speed salicylate excretion?
  1. A. Salicylate, a weak acid, is ionised (A−) in alkaline urine and cannot diffuse back into blood
  2. B. Bicarbonate binds salicylate in plasma, so more of it is filtered
  3. C. Salicylate is protonated (HA) in alkaline urine, and the uncharged form is excreted faster
AnswerA. Salicylate, a weak acid, is ionised (A−) in alkaline urine and cannot diffuse back into blood
WhyIn alkaline urine weak-acid salicylate is mostly ionised (A−); charged molecules cannot cross the tubule wall back into blood, so salicylate is trapped and excreted.
Explanation

Henderson–Hasselbalch: when pH is above the pKa, the deprotonated A− form dominates, and each pH unit raises the A−/HA ratio tenfold. Membranes let uncharged HA through but not A−. Salicylate (pKa ≈ 3) is already mostly ionised in urine, but raising urine pH from about 6 to 8 cuts the uncharged, reabsorbable HA form roughly a hundredfold, so far more stays trapped as A−: "ion trapping".

  • Protonation to HA happens in acid urine, and HA is the form that is reabsorbed.
  • Bicarbonate does not bind salicylate; the effect is on the urine, not on filtration.
Slides (1)
L31Learning
How is ethylene glycol poisoning treated?
  1. A. Fomepizole, which inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase
  2. B. Fomepizole, which inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase
  3. C. Disulfiram, which inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase
AnswerA. Fomepizole, which inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase
WhyFomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, stopping ethylene glycol's conversion to toxic acids; ethanol, which competes for the enzyme, was used before it.
Explanation

Blocking the first step leaves the parent glycol, which is far less toxic and is cleared unchanged. Ethanol works the same way by competing for the enzyme but intoxicates, so fomepizole is preferred.

  • Aldehyde dehydrogenase is the second step; blocking it would not stop glycolaldehyde forming.
  • Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, not alcohol dehydrogenase, and is not the antidote.
Slides (2)
L32Learning
A patient will not say whether she took aspirin or ethylene glycol. Which tests tell them apart?
  1. A. Serum potassium, serum glucose, urine ketones
  2. B. Arterial PCO2, serum chloride, anion gap
  3. C. Serum salicylate, serum calcium, urine oxalate crystals
AnswerC. Serum salicylate, serum calcium, urine oxalate crystals
WhyHigh serum salicylate → aspirin; low serum Ca2+ and urine calcium oxalate crystals → ethylene glycol.
Explanation

Both poisons cause a high-gap metabolic acidosis, so the gap alone cannot separate them. When the patient cannot or will not say what was taken, these three tests can.

  • Potassium, glucose, urine ketones do not separate them; salicylate itself can produce ketones.
  • PCO2, chloride, anion gap: both raise the gap with a normal chloride, and PCO2 varies with compensation.
Slides (2)
Tier 3The rest of the section+14 questions

Naming the four disorders

L33Learning
What is the basic problem in metabolic acidosis?
  1. A. CO2 retained because ventilation is reduced
  2. B. Acid lost or base (bicarbonate) gained
  3. C. Acid gained or base (bicarbonate) lost by a non-respiratory process
AnswerC. Acid gained or base (bicarbonate) lost by a non-respiratory process
WhyMetabolic acidosis: excess acid produced (or ingested, or not excreted) and/or HCO3− lost, by a non-respiratory process; plasma HCO3− falls.
Explanation

Either way the numerator of the HH equation (HCO3−) falls: added acid uses up HCO3− in buffering (H+ + HCO3− → CO2 + H2O), or HCO3− is lost directly (gut or kidney). Lecture criteria: arterial pH < 7.40 and plasma HCO3− lower than expected. The anion gap later splits it into gain of acid (high gap) versus loss of base (normal gap).

  • CO2 retained is respiratory acidosis.
  • Acid lost or base gained is metabolic alkalosis.
Slides (1)

Causes of each disorder

L34Learning
Which cause of respiratory acidosis works by raising CO2 production rather than by reducing ventilation?
  1. A. Myasthenia gravis
  2. B. Opioid overdose
  3. C. Malignant hyperthermia
AnswerC. Malignant hyperthermia
WhyMalignant hyperthermia is a hypercatabolic state: muscle metabolism produces CO2 faster than ventilation can remove it, so PCO2 rises.
Explanation

PCO2 depends on the balance between CO2 production and alveolar ventilation. Most causes reduce ventilation; malignant hyperthermia (a drug-triggered runaway of skeletal-muscle metabolism, for example after some anaesthetics) instead floods the blood with CO2.

  • Myasthenia gravis weakens respiratory muscles: a nerve/muscle cause of reduced ventilation.
  • Opioid overdose depresses the respiratory centre: a central cause of reduced ventilation.
Slides (2)
L35Learning
A patient receives a large infusion of sodium lactate (a salt of a metabolic acid). Once the lactate is metabolised, which disorder tends to develop?
  1. A. Metabolic acidosis
  2. B. Metabolic alkalosis
  3. C. Respiratory acidosis
AnswerB. Metabolic alkalosis
WhyMetabolising the lactate anion consumes H+ (equivalent to generating HCO3−), so the salt acts as a base: metabolic alkalosis.
Explanation

Sodium lactate (or citrate, acetate, ketoanions) brings in the conjugate base without its proton. When the liver oxidises lactate− it takes up an H+ from body fluids, leaving HCO3− behind. That is why the lecture lists "administration of salts of metabolic acids" and "metabolism of ketoanions" under metabolic alkalosis.

  • Metabolic acidosis comes from lactic acid (lactate plus H+), as in tissue hypoxia, not from lactate given as a sodium salt.
  • Respiratory acidosis is a CO2-retention problem.
Slides (2)

Reference values

L36Learning
A blood gas shows pH 7.42, PCO2 30 mm Hg, HCO3− 19 mEq/L. Using the course’s reference points, how is it read?
  1. A. Respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
  2. B. No acid–base disorder, since the pH is in range
  3. C. Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
AnswerA. Respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
WhypH 7.42 is above the 7.40 reference point, so the primary process is an alkalosis: low PCO2 (respiratory alkalosis), with low HCO3− as renal compensation.
Explanation

Name the disorder from which side of 7.40 the pH lies, then find the variable that explains that side. A low PCO2 raises pH (fits); a low HCO3− lowers pH (does not fit, so it is compensation). A pH inside 7.35–7.45 with clearly abnormal PCO2 and HCO3− is a compensated disorder, not health. These values fit a chronic respiratory alkalosis (e.g., days at altitude).

  • No disorder: PCO2 30 and HCO3− 19 are both off their reference points.
  • Metabolic acidosis has the same direction of PCO2 and HCO3− but would put the pH below 7.40.
Slides (2)

Compensation

L37Learning
Which compensation is fast and which is slow?
  1. A. Renal: fast, minutes
    Respiratory (breathing): slow, a day or more
  2. B. Respiratory (breathing): fast, seconds
    Renal: fast, minutes
  3. C. Respiratory (breathing): fast, minutes
    Renal: slow, a day or more
AnswerC. Respiratory (breathing): fast, minutes
Renal: slow, a day or more
WhyBreathing changes PCO2 within minutes; the kidneys need a day or more to retain or excrete enough HCO3−.
Explanation

The respiratory centre responds to blood pH at once, so a metabolic disorder gets fast respiratory compensation. The kidneys must change H+ secretion, NH4+ excretion and new-bicarbonate production, which takes days, so a respiratory disorder is compensated slowly.

  • Making the kidney the fast system reverses the two.
  • The kidney never compensates within minutes; that is why an acute respiratory disorder looks almost uncompensated.

Hook: respiratory problem → renal fix (slow); metabolic problem → lung fix (fast).

Slides (2)
L38Learning
What is the expected compensation for a respiratory alkalosis?
  1. A. HCO3− down: acute −4–5, chronic −1–2 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg fall in PCO2
  2. B. HCO3− down: acute −1–2, chronic −4–5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg fall in PCO2
  3. C. HCO3− down: acute −1–2, chronic −3–4 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg fall in PCO2
AnswerB. HCO3− down: acute −1–2, chronic −4–5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg fall in PCO2
WhyRespiratory alkalosis: HCO3− falls 1–2 mEq/L (acute) or 4–5 mEq/L (chronic) per 10 mm Hg fall in PCO2.
Explanation

Example: PCO2 falls from 40 to 20 (−20). Acute: HCO3− ≈ 24 − 2–4 = 20–22. Chronic (e.g., a month on a ventilator): HCO3− ≈ 24 − 8–10 = 14–16. The chronic change is bigger than in respiratory acidosis (4–5 vs 3–4).

  • −1–2 / −3–4 borrows the chronic figure of respiratory acidosis.
  • −4–5 acute, −1–2 chronic swaps the phases.

Hook: acid 1–2 then 3–4; alkali 1–2 then 4–5.

Slides (2)

Worked blood gases

L39LearningHigh yield
A 17-year-old took a large dose of aspirin 3 hours ago; her breathing is full and rapid: pH 7.57, PCO2 25, HCO3− 23. Diagnosis?
  1. A. Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
  2. B. Acute respiratory alkalosis
  3. C. Chronic respiratory alkalosis
AnswerB. Acute respiratory alkalosis
WhyHigh pH with low PCO2 = respiratory alkalosis; HCO3− down only 1 for a 15 mm Hg fall = acute. Salicylate stimulates the respiratory centre directly.
Explanation

pH 7.57 → alkalosis. PCO2 25 (−15) explains it → primary respiratory alkalosis. The acute rule predicts HCO3− to fall 1.5–3 (the case slide uses 2 per 10 → −3); the measured −1 shows the kidney has barely started. Early salicylate poisoning looks like this; the high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis appears later as salicylic, lactic and keto-acids build up.

  • Chronic compensation would have lowered HCO3− by 6–7.5, to about 17.
  • Metabolic alkalosis needs a high HCO3− and would raise, not lower, PCO2.
Slides (2)
L40LearningHigh yield
A 24-year-old with suspected bulimia, BP 90/60: pH 7.52, PCO2 49, HCO3− 39, K+ 2.6. Diagnosis?
  1. A. Respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
  2. B. Metabolic alkalosis with partial respiratory compensation
  3. C. Metabolic alkalosis with complete respiratory compensation
AnswerB. Metabolic alkalosis with partial respiratory compensation
WhyHigh pH with high HCO3− = metabolic alkalosis from lost stomach acid; PCO2 rose 9 by hypoventilation, but pH is still 7.52: partial compensation.
Explanation

Vomiting removes HCl, and the stomach cells that made the H+ add HCO3− to the blood. pH 7.52 → alkalosis; HCO3− 39 (+15) explains it → primary metabolic alkalosis. PCO2 49 (+9) is compensatory hypoventilation. The lecture predicts +12 for full compensation and calls this partial; the table factor (0.6–0.75 per mEq/L) gives +9–11, so 49 sits at its low end. Low K+ and low BP fit loss of fluid and potassium.

  • Complete compensation does not happen; pH 7.52 is clearly alkalaemic.
  • Respiratory acidosis would give a pH below 7.40.
Slides (3)

Anion gap

L41Learning
What does the anion gap actually represent?
  1. A. Unmeasured cations minus unmeasured anions
  2. B. Unmeasured anions minus unmeasured cations
  3. C. Total anions minus total cations
AnswerB. Unmeasured anions minus unmeasured cations
WhyBecause plasma is neutral, Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−) equals the unmeasured anions minus the unmeasured cations.
Explanation

Electroneutrality: Na+ + unmeasured cations = Cl− + HCO3− + unmeasured anions. Rearranged: Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−) = unmeasured anions − unmeasured cations. So the gap is both "measured cation minus measured anions" and "unmeasured anions minus unmeasured cations", and it rises when unmeasured anions (lactate, ketoanions, toxins) accumulate.

  • Cations minus anions has the wrong sign.
  • Total anions minus total cations is zero in a neutral solution.
Slides (3)
L42Learning
Why does losing bicarbonate in diarrhoea leave the anion gap normal?
  1. A. Cl− rises to replace the lost HCO3−
  2. B. Lactate rises to replace the lost HCO3−
  3. C. K+ rises to replace the lost HCO3−
AnswerA. Cl− rises to replace the lost HCO3−
WhyAs HCO3− is lost, Cl− rises in its place, so Cl− + HCO3− stays about constant and the gap stays normal (hyperchloraemic acidosis).
Explanation

Intestinal fluid is rich in HCO3−. As it is lost, Cl− rises reciprocally, the sum Cl− + HCO3− hardly changes and the gap stays within 8–16. Hence "hyperchloraemic" or "normal-gap" metabolic acidosis. Example: Na+ 137, Cl− 118, HCO3− 5 → gap 14.

  • Lactate rising would add an unmeasured anion and widen the gap.
  • K+ falls in diarrhoea (it is lost in stool) and is not in the formula anyway.
Slides (3)
L43Learning
In GOLD MARK, what causes 5-oxoproline and D-lactate acidosis?
  1. A. 5-Oxoproline: short bowel syndrome
    D-lactate: chronic acetaminophen use
  2. B. 5-Oxoproline: chronic aspirin use
    D-lactate: liver failure
  3. C. 5-Oxoproline: chronic acetaminophen use
    D-lactate: short bowel syndrome
AnswerC. 5-Oxoproline: chronic acetaminophen use
D-lactate: short bowel syndrome
Why5-Oxoproline (pyroglutamic acid) builds up with chronic acetaminophen use, often in malnourished women; D-lactate arises in short bowel syndrome.
Explanation

In short bowel syndrome unabsorbed carbohydrate reaches the colon, where bacteria ferment it to D-lactic acid; routine lactate assays measure only L-lactate, so it can be missed. 5-Oxoproline accumulates when acetaminophen use depletes glutathione in poorly nourished patients.

  • The swapped pairing puts each cause on the other acid.
  • Aspirin is the "A" of GOLD MARK in its own right, and liver failure raises L-lactate, not D-lactate.
Slides (2)
L44LearningHigh yield
A man with 3 days of diarrhoea and poor skin turgor: pH 7.31, PCO2 31, HCO3− 16, Na+ 134, Cl− 110. Gap and diagnosis?
  1. A. Gap 8 → normal-gap metabolic acidosis with expected respiratory compensation
  2. B. Gap 8 → normal-gap metabolic acidosis with a coexisting respiratory acidosis
  3. C. Gap 18 → high-gap metabolic acidosis with expected respiratory compensation
AnswerA. Gap 8 → normal-gap metabolic acidosis with expected respiratory compensation
WhyGap = 134 − (110 + 16) = 8: normal, hyperchloraemic; expected PCO2 ≈ 40 − 1.2 × 8 ≈ 30, measured 31: appropriate compensation.
Explanation

pH 7.31 → acidosis; HCO3− 16 (−8) explains it → metabolic acidosis. Cl− 110 is above 106 and the gap is 8, so bicarbonate was lost, in the stool. The lecture's conclusion: normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

  • Gap 18 is a miscalculation: 134 − 126 = 8.
  • A coexisting respiratory acidosis would leave PCO2 well above the expected ≈ 30.
Slides (3)

Aspirin vs ethylene glycol

L45Learning
What three acids create the high anion gap in salicylate poisoning?
  1. A. Salicylic acid
    Lactic acid (uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation → anaerobic metabolism)
    Ketones (more fatty-acid breakdown)
  2. B. Acetic acid
    Lactic acid (stimulated oxidative phosphorylation → aerobic metabolism)
    Formic acid (more methanol breakdown)
  3. C. Salicylic acid
    Pyruvic acid (uncoupled glycolysis → aerobic metabolism)
    Glycolic acid (more glycol breakdown)
AnswerA. Salicylic acid
Lactic acid (uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation → anaerobic metabolism)
Ketones (more fatty-acid breakdown)
WhySalicylic acid itself, lactic acid (uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation → anaerobic metabolism) and ketones (more fatty-acid metabolism) widen the gap.
Explanation

Salicylate uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, so cells lean on anaerobic glycolysis and make lactate. Fatty-acid metabolism also increases, producing ketone bodies. With the salicylate anion, these unmeasured anions produce the high gap.

  • Glycolic acid comes from ethylene glycol, and uncoupling pushes metabolism towards anaerobic, not aerobic, pathways.
  • Formic acid is the methanol metabolite; acetic acid comes from ethanol.
Slides (2)
L46Learning
Alcohol dehydrogenase oxidises ethylene glycol to glycolaldehyde in the liver. What happens to its cofactor in this step?
  1. A. NADH is oxidised to NAD+
  2. B. FAD is reduced to FADH2
  3. C. NAD+ is reduced to NADH + H+
AnswerC. NAD+ is reduced to NADH + H+
WhyAlcohol dehydrogenase removes hydrogen from the alcohol and hands it to NAD+, which is reduced to NADH + H+.
Explanation

A dehydrogenase oxidises its substrate by removing two hydrogens (a hydride plus a proton). For alcohol dehydrogenase the acceptor is NAD+: ethylene glycol + NAD+ → glycolaldehyde + NADH + H+, the same reaction the enzyme performs on ethanol. This is the step that fomepizole (or, historically, competing ethanol) blocks. The next step, aldehyde dehydrogenase, is also NAD+-linked, so the pathway raises the NADH/NAD+ ratio, which also favours pyruvate → lactate.

  • NADH → NAD+ is the reverse direction: that would reduce a substrate, not oxidise it.
  • FAD → FADH2 belongs to other dehydrogenases, such as acyl-CoA dehydrogenase in β-oxidation; alcohol dehydrogenase uses NAD+.
Slides (1)

BIO-L24 Lipid digestion and absorption

Tier 1: 19 of 53
Learning questions 53
Tier 1Every concept once19 questions

Why fat needs special handling

L1Learning
Why is dietary fat hard to digest?
  1. A. Lipases are fat-soluble but the lumen is watery → the enzyme is trapped inside the droplets
  2. B. Lipases are water-soluble but fat is not → the enzyme can act only at the droplet surface
  3. C. Fat is water-soluble but lipases are not → the enzyme cannot reach the dissolved fat
AnswerB. Lipases are water-soluble but fat is not → the enzyme can act only at the droplet surface
WhyDigestive lipases are water-soluble while fat is not, so the enzyme meets its substrate only at the oil–water interface of each droplet.
Explanation

TAG is hydrophobic and clumps into large droplets in the watery gut lumen. Lipases are proteins dissolved in that water, so they can attack only the ester bonds of molecules at the droplet surface. One big droplet has very little surface for its volume, so digestion would be slow.

The body's answer is emulsification: bile salts and peristalsis break the fat into many tiny droplets, multiplying the surface on which pancreatic lipase can work.

  • Lipases are not fat-soluble; they never work inside a droplet.
  • Fat is not water-soluble; that is the whole problem.
Slides (2)
L2Learning
Which enzymes digest each dietary lipid class?
  1. A. TAG → phospholipases
    Phospholipids → lipases
    Cholesteryl esters → cholesterol esterase
  2. B. TAG → lipases
    Phospholipids → cholesterol esterase
    Cholesteryl esters → phospholipase A2
  3. C. TAG → lipases
    Phospholipids → phospholipases (A1, A2, C, D)
    Cholesteryl esters → cholesterol esterase
AnswerC. TAG → lipases
Phospholipids → phospholipases (A1, A2, C, D)
Cholesteryl esters → cholesterol esterase
WhyLipases split TAG, phospholipases (A1, A2, C, D) split phospholipids, and cholesterol esterase splits cholesteryl esters.
Explanation

Each enzyme family is named after its substrate. Lipases hydrolyse the glycerol–fatty acid ester bonds of TAG: lingual, gastric and pancreatic lipase in the gut, plus lipoprotein lipase and hormone-sensitive lipase in the body. Phospholipases are named by the bond they cut: A1 (fatty acid at C1), A2 (fatty acid at C2), C (glycerol–phosphate bond), D (phosphate–head group bond). Cholesterol esterase removes the fatty acid from cholesteryl ester.

  • The two wrong options swap enzymes between substrates; each enzyme is specific for its own bond.
Slides (2)

Mouth and stomach: the acid lipases

L3LearningHigh yield
Digestion of which dietary lipid starts in the mouth and continues in the stomach and duodenum?
  1. A. Cholesteryl ester
  2. B. Phospholipid
  3. C. Triacylglycerol
AnswerC. Triacylglycerol
WhyLingual lipase starts TAG digestion in the mouth, gastric lipase continues it in the stomach, and pancreatic lipase finishes it in the duodenum.
Explanation

TAG is the only dietary lipid with enzymes upstream of the duodenum. The two acid lipases (lingual, from glands on the back of the tongue, and gastric, from the stomach mucosa) begin cutting TAG, especially milk-type TAG with short and medium chains. The bulk of TAG is then digested by pancreatic lipase in the duodenum.

  • Cholesteryl ester is digested only in the small intestine, by pancreatic cholesterol esterase.
  • Phospholipid is digested only in the small intestine, by pancreatic phospholipase A2.

Note: the textbook summary figure at the end of the lecture shows lipids passing the mouth "unchanged"; the lecture's own slides and practice question key TAG digestion as starting in the mouth.

Slides (3)

Bile, emulsification and the gut hormones

L4LearningHigh yield
What does cholecystokinin (CCK) do?
  1. A. Gallbladder contracts → releases bile
    Pancreas releases digestive enzymes
  2. B. Gallbladder relaxes → stores bile
    Pancreas releases bicarbonate
  3. C. Gallbladder contracts → releases bile
    Stomach increases acid secretion
AnswerA. Gallbladder contracts → releases bile
Pancreas releases digestive enzymes
WhyCCK contracts the gallbladder (bile into the duodenum) and makes the pancreas release digestive enzymes, bringing both to the fat at once.
Explanation

CCK's name means "bile-sac mover". It contracts gallbladder smooth muscle and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, so stored bile (bile salts, phospholipid, cholesterol) enters the duodenum. It also stimulates pancreatic acinar cells to release lipase, colipase, phospholipase A2, cholesterol esterase and the proteases, and it slows gastric emptying so fat arrives at a manageable rate.

  • Gallbladder relaxation and bicarbonate: the opposite gallbladder action, and bicarbonate is secretin's main job.
  • More gastric acid is driven by gastrin; CCK does not stimulate acid secretion.
Slides (3)

Pancreatic enzymes: lipase, colipase, PLA2, esterase

L5LearningHigh yield
Which fatty acids does pancreatic lipase remove from TAG, and what is left?
  1. A. Positions 2 and 3 → 1-monoacylglycerol
  2. B. Position 2 only → 1,3-diacylglycerol
  3. C. Positions 1 and 3 → 2-monoacylglycerol
AnswerC. Positions 1 and 3 → 2-monoacylglycerol
WhyPancreatic lipase cuts the outer ester bonds (C1 and C3), releasing two fatty acids and leaving 2-monoacylglycerol (2-MAG).
Explanation

Pancreatic lipase is specific for the primary ester bonds at the ends of glycerol. It removes the fatty acid at C1 (giving a 2,3-diacylglycerol) and then the one at C3, leaving the fatty acid on the middle carbon: 2-monoacylglycerol. The 2-MAG and free fatty acids are what micelles carry to the enterocyte, which uses 2-MAG as the backbone to rebuild TAG.

  • Position 2 is exactly the bond pancreatic lipase leaves alone.
  • 1-monoacylglycerol arises only when an isomerase moves the C2 fatty acid to C1.
Slides (3)

Blocking fat digestion: orlistat and designer fats

L6LearningHigh yield
How does orlistat (Xenical) work?
  1. A. Blocks the cholesterol transporter of the brush border (also inhibits ACAT)
  2. B. Binds bile acids in the gut lumen (also blocks their ileal reabsorption)
  3. C. Binds irreversibly to the active site of pancreatic lipase (also inhibits gastric lipase)
AnswerC. Binds irreversibly to the active site of pancreatic lipase (also inhibits gastric lipase)
WhyOrlistat binds the open, active form of pancreatic lipase and irreversibly blocks its active site; it also inhibits gastric lipase.
Explanation

Pancreatic lipase has a lid over its active site that opens at the oil–water interface. Orlistat binds this open-lid conformation and attaches irreversibly to the active site, so TAG is not hydrolysed. Undigested TAG cannot enter micelles or enterocytes and is lost in the stool, which cuts calorie absorption; oily, loose stools are the main side effect.

  • Blocking the brush-border cholesterol transporter describes ezetimibe, which lowers cholesterol absorption, not fat calories.
  • Binding bile acids in the gut describes cholestyramine, a cholesterol-lowering resin.
Slides (2)

Bile: composition and bile acids

L7LearningHigh yield
From what, and where, are bile acids made?
  1. A. From cholesterol, in the intestine by gut bacteria
  2. B. From bilirubin, in the liver
  3. C. From cholesterol, in the liver
AnswerC. From cholesterol, in the liver
WhyBile acids are made from cholesterol in the liver, then conjugated with glycine or taurine before secretion.
Explanation

Hepatocytes convert cholesterol into the primary bile acids, cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid; the first, rate-limiting step (7α-hydroxylation) is feedback-inhibited by bile acids returning from the gut. Making bile acids is the body's main way of disposing of cholesterol, because the steroid ring cannot be broken down.

  • Gut bacteria modify primary bile acids into secondary ones; they do not make bile acids from cholesterol.
  • Bilirubin comes from haem and is a bile pigment, not a bile acid precursor.
Slides (2)
L8Learning
What are the four functions of bile salts and bile acids?
  1. A. Excrete excess cholesterol
    Keep cholesterol dissolved in bile
    Hydrolyse dietary TAG
    Help absorb fat-soluble vitamins
  2. B. Excrete excess cholesterol
    Keep cholesterol dissolved in bile
    Emulsify dietary TAG
    Help absorb fat-soluble vitamins
  3. C. Excrete excess cholesterol
    Keep cholesterol dissolved in bile
    Emulsify dietary TAG
    Help absorb water-soluble vitamins
AnswerB. Excrete excess cholesterol
Keep cholesterol dissolved in bile
Emulsify dietary TAG
Help absorb fat-soluble vitamins
WhyBile salts excrete cholesterol, keep biliary cholesterol in solution (with phospholipid), emulsify TAG for lipase, and enable fat-soluble vitamin absorption.
Explanation

Two functions concern cholesterol: making bile acids is the main route for disposing of excess cholesterol, and bile acids plus phospholipids hold biliary cholesterol in solution so it does not precipitate as gallstones. Two concern dietary fat: bile salts emulsify TAG so pancreatic lipase can reach it, and they form the mixed micelles that carry lipids and vitamins A, D, E and K to the brush border.

  • Bile salts hydrolyse nothing; that is lipase's job.
  • Water-soluble vitamins dissolve in the lumen and need no micelles.
Slides (1)

Enterohepatic circulation and cholestyramine

L9LearningHigh yield
What fraction of secreted bile salts is reabsorbed, where, and how?
  1. A. 50–60%; jejunum; Na+-coupled cotransporter
  2. B. 95–98%; terminal ileum; Na+-coupled cotransporter
  3. C. 95–98%; duodenum; passive diffusion
AnswerB. 95–98%; terminal ileum; Na+-coupled cotransporter
WhyAbout 95–98% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum by a Na+-dependent cotransporter; only about 2–5% is lost in stool.
Explanation

The ileal enterocyte has an apical Na+–bile salt cotransporter that uses the Na+ gradient to take up conjugated bile salts actively. Placing this uptake at the end of the small intestine keeps bile salts in the lumen through the duodenum and jejunum, where fat digestion and absorption need them. The lecture gives 98% recycling and about 5% of bile salts lost in feces.

  • Uptake in the duodenum would remove bile salts before they had done their job, and ionised conjugated bile salts cross membranes poorly by diffusion.
  • 50–60% recycling would force the liver to replace half the pool every cycle.
Slides (2)
L10Learning
How does cholestyramine lower serum LDL cholesterol?
  1. A. Less bile acid returns → liver turns more bile acid into cholesterol → more hepatic cholesterol → more LDL receptors → serum LDL falls
  2. B. Less bile acid returns → liver turns more cholesterol into bile acid → less hepatic cholesterol → more LDL receptors → serum LDL falls
  3. C. Less bile acid returns → liver turns more cholesterol into bile acid → less hepatic cholesterol → fewer LDL receptors → serum LDL falls
AnswerB. Less bile acid returns → liver turns more cholesterol into bile acid → less hepatic cholesterol → more LDL receptors → serum LDL falls
WhyLosing bile acids lifts feedback inhibition, so the liver converts more cholesterol into bile acids; low hepatic cholesterol up-regulates LDL receptors, pulling LDL out of the blood.
Explanation

Returning bile acids normally feedback-inhibit their own synthesis from cholesterol. With the resin removing them, that brake is released and the liver diverts its cholesterol into new bile acids. The hepatocyte's own cholesterol falls, so it makes more LDL (low-density lipoprotein) receptors and takes up more LDL from plasma. Serum LDL falls, which is why cholestyramine treats hypercholesterolaemia.

  • Fewer LDL receptors would raise serum LDL, not lower it.
  • The liver cannot turn bile acid back into cholesterol; the conversion is one-way.
Slides (2)

Gallstones (cholelithiasis)

L11LearningHigh yield
Why do cholesterol gallstones form?
  1. A. More bile salts enter bile than cholesterol + phospholipid can keep dissolved
  2. B. More phospholipid enters bile than bile salts + cholesterol can keep dissolved
  3. C. More cholesterol enters bile than bile salts + phospholipid can keep dissolved
AnswerC. More cholesterol enters bile than bile salts + phospholipid can keep dissolved
WhyBile is the route for excreting cholesterol; when more cholesterol enters it than bile salts and phospholipid can solubilise, cholesterol crystallises into stones.
Explanation

Cholesterol is almost insoluble in water; in bile it is held in mixed micelles and vesicles of bile salts and lecithin. The balance can tip two ways: too little bile acid (ileal disease, biliary obstruction, liver disease, excessive feedback inhibition) or too much cholesterol (obesity, oestrogens and pregnancy, diabetes, fibrates). Supersaturated bile precipitates cholesterol crystals in the gallbladder, which grow into stones.

  • Bile salts and phospholipid are the solvents for cholesterol; more of them prevents stones rather than causing them.
Slides (2)
L12Learning
What is the preferred treatment for symptomatic gallstones, and what is its consequence?
  1. A. Cholecystectomy; bile is no longer released in timed pulses → fatty food is tolerated less well
  2. B. Ursodeoxycholic acid; dissolves all stone types → no long-term effects
  3. C. Cholecystectomy; bile is no longer made by the liver → fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
AnswerA. Cholecystectomy; bile is no longer released in timed pulses → fatty food is tolerated less well
WhyAfter cholecystectomy the liver still makes bile and it still reaches the gut, but its timed release with meals is lost, limiting tolerance for fatty food.
Explanation

Removing the gallbladder is the preferred treatment. Bile then flows continuously from the liver into the duodenum, so cholesterol absorption is only mildly affected; what is lost is the store of concentrated bile delivered on CCK's signal. A large fatty meal may not be fully emulsified, so patients tolerate fatty foods less well.

  • The liver, not the gallbladder, makes bile, so bile production continues.
  • Ursodeoxycholic acid dissolves mainly cholesterol stones, slowly, and causes diarrhoea; it is second-line.
Slides (2)

Micelles and absorption

L13Learning
What goes into mixed micelles?
  1. A. Free fatty acids, 2-monoacylglycerol, lysophospholipid, cholesterol
    + colipase + water-soluble vitamins
  2. B. Free fatty acids, glycerol, chylomicrons, cholesterol
    + bile salts + fat-soluble vitamins
  3. C. Free fatty acids, 2-monoacylglycerol, lysophospholipid, cholesterol
    + bile salts + fat-soluble vitamins
AnswerC. Free fatty acids, 2-monoacylglycerol, lysophospholipid, cholesterol
+ bile salts + fat-soluble vitamins
WhyMixed micelles combine the products of digestion (fatty acids, 2-MAG, lysophospholipid, cholesterol) with bile salts and fat-soluble vitamins.
Explanation

In the jejunal lumen, the amphipathic digestion products and bile salts assemble into tiny mixed micelles (far smaller than the emulsion droplets), with vitamins A, D, E and K dissolved in their core.

  • Glycerol is water-soluble and needs no micelle, and chylomicrons are made later, inside the enterocyte.
  • Colipase is lipase's protein partner, and water-soluble vitamins dissolve in the lumen without micelles.
Slides (2)
L14Learning
How are short- and medium-chain fatty acids absorbed?
  1. A. Without micelles → straight into portal blood → liver (no chylomicrons)
  2. B. In micelles → re-esterified → portal blood → liver (in VLDL)
  3. C. Without micelles → into lymph → thoracic duct → blood (in chylomicrons)
AnswerA. Without micelles → straight into portal blood → liver (no chylomicrons)
WhyShort- and medium-chain fatty acids enter enterocytes without micelles and pass directly into portal blood to the liver, not into chylomicrons.
Explanation

Fatty acids under about 12 carbons dissolve in water, cross the enterocyte without being re-esterified, and leave into the portal capillaries bound to albumin. This route bypasses bile salts, re-esterification and chylomicrons.

  • Lymph and chylomicrons are the route for long-chain fatty acids.
  • They need no micelles, and VLDL is made by the liver, not the gut.

One lecture slide says "lymphatic–portal circulation to the liver"; another lecture slide and standard texts say they go directly into the bloodstream (portal vein), which is correct.

Slides (2)

Re-esterification and chylomicrons

L15LearningHigh yield
Into which particle is re-esterified dietary fat packaged, and what is its defining apolipoprotein?
  1. A. Chylomicron; apo B-100
  2. B. VLDL; apo B-100
  3. C. Chylomicron; apo B-48
AnswerC. Chylomicron; apo B-48
WhyThe enterocyte packs TAG, cholesteryl ester and phospholipid with apo B-48 into the nascent chylomicron; apo B-48 is unique to chylomicrons.
Explanation

Apo B-48 is made by enterocytes and is required to assemble and secrete chylomicrons. It comes from the same gene as apo B-100 but is a shorter version (48% of its length), made only in the intestine.

  • Apo B-100 is the full-length protein made by the liver; chylomicrons never carry it.
  • VLDL with apo B-100 is the liver's particle, carrying TAG the liver has made, not dietary fat.
Slides (3)
L16Learning
Which enzyme releases fatty acids from chylomicron TAG for the tissues?
  1. A. Hormone-sensitive lipase
  2. B. Pancreatic lipase
  3. C. Lipoprotein lipase
AnswerC. Lipoprotein lipase
WhyLipoprotein lipase (LPL) on capillary walls hydrolyses chylomicron TAG, releasing fatty acids for the tissues.
Explanation

As chylomicrons pass through capillaries of muscle and adipose tissue, LPL (activated by apo C-II) strips fatty acids from their TAG. The particle shrinks into a cholesterol-rich chylomicron remnant that the liver takes up.

  • Hormone-sensitive lipase works inside adipocytes, releasing fatty acids from stored TAG in fasting.
  • Pancreatic lipase acts in the intestinal lumen during digestion.
Slides (2)
L17Learning
What is the correct order of long-chain lipid absorption?
  1. A. Micelles → chylomicrons → fatty acids and monoacylglycerols enter the enterocyte → lymph vessels
  2. B. Micelles → fatty acids and monoacylglycerols enter the enterocyte → chylomicrons → lymph vessels
  3. C. Fatty acids and monoacylglycerols enter the enterocyte → micelles → chylomicrons → lymph vessels
AnswerB. Micelles → fatty acids and monoacylglycerols enter the enterocyte → chylomicrons → lymph vessels
WhyMicelles deliver fatty acids and 2-MAG to the brush border; inside the cell they are rebuilt into TAG and packed into chylomicrons, which leave via lymph.
Explanation

Lumen → cell → lymph: (1) digestion products and bile salts form mixed micelles in the lumen; (2) the lipids leave the micelle and enter the enterocyte; (3) in the ER they are re-esterified and packaged with apo B-48 as chylomicrons; (4) chylomicrons enter the lacteals and travel via the thoracic duct to the blood.

  • Micelles form in the lumen, before uptake, not inside the cell.
  • Chylomicrons are made inside the enterocyte, after uptake.
Slides (2)

Steatorrhoea and malabsorption

L18LearningHigh yield
Which vitamins are lost when fat absorption fails, and why?
  1. A. B12, C and folate; they are absorbed with dietary fat in micelles
  2. B. A, D, E and K; they are absorbed with dietary fat in micelles
  3. C. B1, B6 and C; bile salts bind them and carry them into the stool
AnswerB. A, D, E and K; they are absorbed with dietary fat in micelles
WhyVitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble: they are absorbed inside micelles with dietary fat, so any steatorrhoea carries them out in the stool.
Explanation

Fat-soluble vitamins have no separate carrier route; they dissolve in the micelle core, enter the enterocyte with the lipids and leave in chylomicrons. Maldigestion (no bile, no lipase) and malabsorption (diseased mucosa) both cause deficiency: night blindness (A), osteomalacia with low calcium (D), neuropathy and haemolysis (E), easy bruising and bleeding (K).

  • B12, C, folate, B1 and B6 are water-soluble and absorbed by their own carriers, not in micelles; bile salts do not bind them.
Slides (2)
L19Learning
What causes maldigestion steatorrhoea, and which fat appears in the stool?
  1. A. Too little bile (liver disease, blocked flow) or pancreatic insufficiency; triacylglycerol
  2. B. Bacterial or parasitic infection, Crohn’s or coeliac disease; triacylglycerol
  3. C. Too little bile (liver disease, blocked flow) or pancreatic insufficiency; fatty acids
AnswerA. Too little bile (liver disease, blocked flow) or pancreatic insufficiency; triacylglycerol
WhyMaldigestion means fat is not broken down (no bile to emulsify it, no pancreatic lipase), so the stool contains undigested TAG.
Explanation

In maldigestion the mucosa is healthy but the lumen lacks what digestion needs: bile (liver disease, biliary obstruction, poor emulsification) or pancreatic enzymes (pancreatic insufficiency, e.g., cystic fibrosis or chronic pancreatitis). TAG is never hydrolysed and passes into the stool as TAG.

  • Fatty acids in stool mean digestion worked and absorption failed (malabsorption).
  • Infection, Crohn's and coeliac disease damage the mucosa: they cause malabsorption.

Hook: maldigestion = undigested TAG.

Slides (2)
Tier 2The next layer across every concept+19 questions

Why fat needs special handling

L20Learning
How much energy does fat yield per gram, and what share of the body's stored energy is fat?
  1. A. 4.1 kcal/g; about 84% of stored energy
  2. B. 9.3 kcal/g; about 15% of stored energy
  3. C. 9.3 kcal/g; about 84% of stored energy
AnswerC. 9.3 kcal/g; about 84% of stored energy
WhyFat yields 9.3 kcal/g, more than twice carbohydrate or protein, and holds about 84% of the body's stored energy.
Explanation

Fat is the body's main energy store because it is a concentrated, anhydrous fuel: TAG is highly reduced and is stored without water, so each gram yields about 9.3 kcal and takes up little space. Adipose TAG therefore holds roughly 84% of stored body energy.

  • 4.1 kcal/g is the value for carbohydrate and protein, which are more oxidised and (as glycogen) stored with water.
  • About 15% is close to protein's share of stored energy; glycogen holds under 1%.
Slides (1)

Mouth and stomach: the acid lipases

L21Learning
Which TAG do the acid lipases prefer?
  1. A. TAG with long-chain saturated fatty acids (16–18 C), as in lard and beef fat
  2. B. Cholesteryl esters with short-chain fatty acids (<12 C), as in milk and butter
  3. C. TAG with short- and medium-chain fatty acids (<12 C), as in milk, butter, coconut oil
AnswerC. TAG with short- and medium-chain fatty acids (<12 C), as in milk, butter, coconut oil
WhyAcid lipases prefer TAG with short- and medium-chain fatty acids (<12 C), abundant in milk fat, butter and coconut oil.
Explanation

Short- and medium-chain fatty acids (fewer than 12 carbons) are typical of milk fat, butter and coconut oil. The acid lipases hydrolyse these TAGs best (they can also remove a long unsaturated fatty acid from position 3), which is why they matter so much for a milk-fed newborn.

  • Long-chain saturated TAG (lard, beef fat) is the substrate of pancreatic lipase in the duodenum.
  • Cholesteryl esters are not touched by the acid lipases; cholesterol esterase in the small intestine handles them.
Slides (3)

Bile, emulsification and the gut hormones

L22LearningHigh yield
How do bile salts act on dietary fat?
  1. A. As detergents → fuse many small droplets into one large one (coalescence)
  2. B. As enzymes → hydrolyse the ester bonds of TAG into fatty acids
  3. C. As detergents → break large droplets into many tiny ones (emulsification)
AnswerC. As detergents → break large droplets into many tiny ones (emulsification)
WhyBile salts are amphipathic detergents: they coat fat droplets and break them into many tiny, stable droplets (emulsification).
Explanation

A bile salt has a hydrophobic face (the steroid rings) and a hydrophilic face (hydroxyl groups and the charged glycine or taurine side chain). It lies at the oil–water interface with its greasy face in the fat and its polar face in the water. Coated droplets repel each other, so fat sheared by peristalsis stays as small, stable droplets and is prevented from coalescing.

  • Bile salts are not enzymes; they cut no bonds. Hydrolysis is pancreatic lipase's job.
  • Coalescence is exactly what bile salts prevent.
Slides (2)
L23Learning
What is the correct order of events after a fatty meal reaches the small intestine?
  1. A. I cells release CCK → fat enters duodenum → gallbladder contracts, sphincter of Oddi relaxes → bile emulsifies fat
  2. B. Fat enters duodenum → I cells release CCK → gallbladder contracts, sphincter of Oddi relaxes → bile emulsifies fat
  3. C. Fat enters duodenum → bile emulsifies fat → I cells release CCK → gallbladder contracts, sphincter of Oddi relaxes
AnswerB. Fat enters duodenum → I cells release CCK → gallbladder contracts, sphincter of Oddi relaxes → bile emulsifies fat
WhyFat in the duodenum is the stimulus for CCK; CCK then empties the gallbladder, and only once bile arrives can emulsification begin.
Explanation

The chain runs stimulus → hormone → effector → effect. Fat (and peptides) touching the duodenal and jejunal mucosa makes I cells secrete CCK into the blood. CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, so a pulse of concentrated bile enters the duodenum. Bile salts and peristalsis then emulsify the fat for pancreatic lipase.

  • CCK release before the fat arrives has no stimulus.
  • Emulsification before CCK lacks most of the bile: between meals it is held in the gallbladder.
Slides (1)
L24LearningHigh yield
What does secretin do?
  1. A. Makes the pancreas and liver release a bicarbonate-rich fluid
  2. B. Makes the pancreas release an enzyme-rich fluid
  3. C. Makes the gallbladder contract and release bile
AnswerA. Makes the pancreas and liver release a bicarbonate-rich fluid
WhySecretin makes the pancreas and liver secrete a bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralises acid chyme.
Explanation

Secretin acts on pancreatic duct cells and bile duct cells to secrete HCO3−. Together with bile (pH slightly above 7) this neutralises the acid chyme. That matters for fat digestion: pancreatic lipase is inactivated by acid, and bile salts work best ionised at near-neutral pH.

  • An enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion (from acinar cells) is CCK's action.
  • Gallbladder contraction is also CCK's action.

Hook: Secretin = soda (bicarbonate); CCK = enzymes + bile.

Slides (3)

Pancreatic enzymes: lipase, colipase, PLA2, esterase

L25Learning
According to the lecture, what does colipase do for pancreatic lipase?
  1. A. Keeps the pH optimal and prevents lipase from denaturing
  2. B. Emulsifies the fat droplet in place of bile salts
  3. C. Hydrolyses the fatty acid at position 2 of TAG
AnswerA. Keeps the pH optimal and prevents lipase from denaturing
WhyThe lecture says colipase maintains the optimum pH for pancreatic lipase and prevents its denaturation.
Explanation

Colipase is a helper protein, not an enzyme or an emulsifier. Textbooks describe its role mechanically: bile salts coat the emulsified droplet and would push lipase off it; colipase binds both lipase and the interface, anchoring lipase where its substrate is. The lecture summarises the job as keeping conditions right for lipase (optimum pH, no denaturation); use that wording on the exam.

  • Pancreatic lipase leaves the C2 fatty acid of TAG in place, and colipase cuts no bonds at all.
  • Emulsification needs bile salts plus peristalsis; colipase cannot replace bile.
Slides (2)
L26LearningHigh yield
What does pancreatic phospholipase A2 do, and what activates it?
  1. A. Removes the fatty acid at C2 → lysophospholipid; activated by trypsin
  2. B. Removes the fatty acid at C1 → lysophospholipid; activated by trypsin
  3. C. Cuts the glycerol–phosphate bond → diacylglycerol; activated by trypsin
AnswerA. Removes the fatty acid at C2 → lysophospholipid; activated by trypsin
WhyPhospholipase A2 removes the fatty acid from C2, leaving a lysophospholipid; it is secreted as a proenzyme and activated by trypsin.
Explanation

Dietary and biliary phospholipids (mostly phosphatidylcholine) are digested mainly by pancreatic phospholipase A2. Cutting the C2 ester releases one fatty acid and a lysophospholipid (a phospholipid with a single fatty acid, at C1); both go into mixed micelles. The family is named by bond: A1 = C1 fatty acid, A2 = C2 fatty acid, C = glycerol–phosphate bond, D = phosphate–head group bond.

  • The C1 fatty acid is phospholipase A1's bond.
  • Glycerol–phosphate bond → diacylglycerol is phospholipase C's reaction.
Slides (2)

Bile: composition and bile acids

L27Learning
Which cells secrete bile, and how much does the gallbladder concentrate it?
  1. A. Gallbladder epithelium; the liver concentrates it 10–20-fold
  2. B. Hepatocytes; the gallbladder concentrates it 2–3-fold
  3. C. Hepatocytes; the gallbladder concentrates it 10–20-fold
AnswerC. Hepatocytes; the gallbladder concentrates it 10–20-fold
WhyBile is formed and secreted by hepatocytes; the gallbladder stores it and concentrates it 10–20× by absorbing water and electrolytes.
Explanation

Hepatocytes secrete bile into the bile canaliculi between them, and it drains through the bile ducts. Between meals it is diverted into the gallbladder, whose epithelium absorbs Na+, Cl− and HCO3− with water following, concentrating the bile salts, cholesterol and phospholipid 10–20-fold. A small gallbladder can therefore deliver a large dose of bile salts with each meal.

  • The gallbladder does not secrete bile, and the liver does not concentrate it.
  • 2–3-fold greatly underestimates the gallbladder's concentrating power.
Slides (1)
L28LearningHigh yield
Why are conjugated bile salts better emulsifiers than unconjugated bile acids?
  1. A. Conjugation lowers the pKa → they stay ionised at intestinal pH → more amphipathic
  2. B. Conjugation raises the pKa → they stay protonated at intestinal pH → more hydrophobic
  3. C. Conjugation adds a fatty acid tail → they dissolve better inside fat droplets
AnswerA. Conjugation lowers the pKa → they stay ionised at intestinal pH → more amphipathic
WhyGlycine or taurine lowers the pKa, so bile salts stay ionised in the gut; a charged face opposite a hydrophobic ring makes them more amphipathic, better detergents.
Explanation

A good emulsifier needs two clearly separated faces. The conjugated side chain (pKa about 4 with glycine, about 2 with taurine) stays ionised at intestinal pH, giving a strongly hydrophilic face opposite the hydrophobic steroid rings. Unconjugated bile acids (pKa about 5–6) are partly protonated and neutral in the upper intestine, which makes them less soluble and lets them diffuse out of the lumen early.

  • Raising the pKa and staying protonated is the reverse of what conjugation does.
  • Conjugation adds an amino acid, not a fatty acid, and bile salts sit at the droplet surface rather than dissolving inside it.
Slides (1)

Enterohepatic circulation and cholestyramine

L29LearningHigh yield
A man has his terminal ileum resected after an accident. What fat-related problem should he be warned about?
  1. A. CCK is no longer secreted → the gallbladder cannot empty → bile stasis
  2. B. Bile salts are reabsorbed in the jejunum instead → no change in fat absorption
  3. C. Bile salts escape into the colon → the bile salt pool shrinks → fat malabsorption (steatorrhoea)
AnswerC. Bile salts escape into the colon → the bile salt pool shrinks → fat malabsorption (steatorrhoea)
WhyThe terminal ileum reabsorbs bile salts; without it they are lost in stool, the pool shrinks, and fat is poorly emulsified and absorbed (steatorrhoea).
Explanation

With the ileum gone, the enterohepatic loop is broken. The liver can raise synthesis only so far, so the bile salt pool and the duodenal bile salt concentration fall below what fat emulsification and micelle formation need. Long-chain fat and vitamins A, D, E and K are malabsorbed; extra bile acids reaching the colon also cause diarrhoea. Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum does the same. (The ileum also absorbs vitamin B12, a separate problem.)

  • The jejunum has no active bile salt transporter, so it cannot take over.
  • CCK comes from the duodenum and jejunum, which are intact.
Slides (1)

Gallstones (cholelithiasis)

L30Learning
What are pigment gallstones made of, and what is their main risk factor?
  1. A. Bile salts + some cholesterol and phospholipid; obesity
  2. B. Bile pigments + some cholesterol and calcium salts; chronic haemolysis
  3. C. Bile pigments + some cholesterol and calcium salts; oral contraceptives
AnswerB. Bile pigments + some cholesterol and calcium salts; chronic haemolysis
WhyPigment stones are mostly bile pigment (bilirubin) with some cholesterol and calcium salts; the key risk is chronic haemolysis, which floods bile with bilirubin.
Explanation

Chronic haemolysis (e.g., sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis) breaks down large amounts of haemoglobin; haem becomes bilirubin, which the liver excretes into bile. Excess bilirubin precipitates with calcium as calcium bilirubinate, forming pigment stones.

  • Oral contraceptives raise biliary cholesterol and favour cholesterol stones.
  • Bile salts and phospholipid dissolve cholesterol rather than forming stones, and obesity is a cholesterol-stone risk.
Slides (1)
L31Learning
Which oral drugs can dissolve gallstones, for which stones, and with what side effect?
  1. A. Cholestyramine or colestipol; mainly cholesterol stones; diarrhoea
  2. B. Chenodeoxycholic or ursodeoxycholic acid; mainly pigment stones; jaundice
  3. C. Chenodeoxycholic or ursodeoxycholic acid; mainly cholesterol stones; diarrhoea
AnswerC. Chenodeoxycholic or ursodeoxycholic acid; mainly cholesterol stones; diarrhoea
WhyOral chenodeoxycholic or ursodeoxycholic acid enrich bile with bile acid and slowly dissolve cholesterol stones; the side effect is diarrhoea.
Explanation

Swallowed bile acids join the enterohepatic pool and are secreted into bile, raising the bile acid-to-cholesterol ratio so cholesterol is drawn back into solution.
