This works only when stones are mainly cholesterol and takes months; extra bile acids reaching the colon cause diarrhoea, so cholecystectomy is preferred. (Dried bear bile, rich in ursodeoxycholic acid, was a traditional Chinese remedy.)

  • Pigment stones are bilirubin–calcium salts that bile acids cannot dissolve.
  • Cholestyramine and colestipol bind and remove bile acids, which would make bile more stone-forming, not less.
Slides (2)

Micelles and absorption

L32Learning
What job do micelles do?
  1. A. Package digestion products into chylomicrons inside the enterocyte
  2. B. Ferry digestion products through the watery layer to the brush border membrane
  3. C. Carry intact TAG through the enterocyte into the lacteals
AnswerB. Ferry digestion products through the watery layer to the brush border membrane
WhyMicelles shuttle hydrophobic digestion products through the watery layer to the brush border, the primary site of lipid absorption.
Explanation

A thin unstirred water layer covers the microvilli, and hydrophobic fatty acids and 2-MAG barely dissolve in it. Their hydrophilic surface lets micelles cross this water to the brush border, where the lipids leave the micelle and enter the enterocyte. The bile salts stay behind in the lumen to make more micelles.

  • Chylomicrons are assembled in the enterocyte's ER after absorption; micelles never enter the cell.
  • Micelles carry digestion products, not intact TAG, and never reach the lacteals.
Slides (2)
L33Learning
How well is cholesterol absorbed, and which drug reduces its absorption?
  1. A. Poorly, even from micelles; orlistat
  2. B. Well, mostly without micelles; ezetimibe
  3. C. Poorly, even from micelles; ezetimibe
AnswerC. Poorly, even from micelles; ezetimibe
WhyEnterocytes absorb cholesterol poorly even from micelles, and ezetimibe retards cholesterol absorption further.
Explanation

Only part of the free cholesterol in micelles is taken up by the brush-border transporter, and some is pumped back out into the lumen. Ezetimibe blocks this uptake, lowering absorption of both dietary and biliary cholesterol and hence plasma LDL.

  • Orlistat inhibits lipases, reducing TAG digestion; it does not target cholesterol uptake.
  • Cholesterol is hydrophobic and needs micelles; it is neither well absorbed nor absorbed without them.
Slides (1)

Re-esterification and chylomicrons

L34Learning
How is TAG rebuilt from 2-monoacylglycerol in the enterocyte?
  1. A. 2-MAG + 2 fatty acyl-CoA → TAG
  2. B. 2-MAG + 3 fatty acyl-CoA → TAG
  3. C. 2-MAG + 1 fatty acyl-CoA → TAG
AnswerA. 2-MAG + 2 fatty acyl-CoA → TAG
WhyTwo acyltransferases add two fatty acyl-CoAs to 2-MAG (first to DAG, then to TAG): monoacylglycerol + 2 acyl-CoA → TAG.
Explanation

2-MAG already carries a fatty acid on C2, leaving the C1 and C3 hydroxyls free. Acyl-CoA:monoacylglycerol acyltransferase adds one fatty acyl group to give DAG, and acyl-CoA:diacylglycerol acyltransferase adds the second to give TAG. This monoacylglycerol pathway is why the 2-MAG left by pancreatic lipase is so useful.

  • One acyl-CoA would give only DAG.
  • Glycerol has three carbons; with one already acylated there is room for just two more.
Slides (2)
L35Learning
By what route do chylomicrons reach the bloodstream?
  1. A. Lacteals → portal vein → liver → hepatic veins
  2. B. Lacteals → intestinal lymphatics → right lymphatic duct → right subclavian vein
  3. C. Lacteals → intestinal lymphatics → thoracic duct → left subclavian vein
AnswerC. Lacteals → intestinal lymphatics → thoracic duct → left subclavian vein
WhyChylomicrons travel from the lacteals through the intestinal lymphatics to the thoracic duct, which empties into the left subclavian vein.
Explanation

Because they travel in lymph, dietary long-chain fats bypass the liver on their first pass and reach peripheral tissues first. The milky lymph draining the gut after a fatty meal is called chyle.

  • The portal vein carries water-soluble nutrients and short- and medium-chain fatty acids, not chylomicrons.
  • The right lymphatic duct drains the right upper body; intestinal lymph goes to the thoracic duct.
Slides (1)
L36Learning
Which apolipoproteins does a nascent chylomicron acquire in the blood to become a mature chylomicron?
  1. A. Apo B-100 and apo C-II
  2. B. Apo C-II and apo E
  3. C. Apo B-48 and apo B-100
AnswerB. Apo C-II and apo E
WhyIn the blood the nascent chylomicron gains apo C-II and apo E (from HDL), becoming a mature chylomicron.
Explanation

Nascent chylomicrons leave the enterocyte carrying apo B-48. In the blood, HDL transfers apo C-II and apo E to them. Apo C-II activates lipoprotein lipase so the TAG can be unloaded; apo E later lets the liver recognise and take up the chylomicron remnant.

  • Apo B-48 is already present from the enterocyte; it is not gained in the blood.
  • Apo B-100 belongs to the liver's VLDL and LDL; chylomicrons never carry it.
Slides (2)

Steatorrhoea and malabsorption

L37Learning
What is steatorrhoea?
  1. A. Frothy, foul-smelling, floating stool with excess fat (normal fecal fat <6%)
  2. B. Black, tarry, sticky stool from digested blood (normal fecal fat <6%)
  3. C. Pale, hard, sinking stool with too little fat (normal fecal fat >6%)
AnswerA. Frothy, foul-smelling, floating stool with excess fat (normal fecal fat <6%)
WhySteatorrhoea is fatty stool, frothy, foul-smelling and floating, from excess lipid when fat digestion or absorption fails (normal fecal fat <6%).
Explanation

When fat is not digested or not absorbed it reaches the colon, where bacteria act on it; the stool becomes bulky, greasy, pale and malodorous, and floats because of its fat and gas content. Fat-soluble vitamins are lost with it. The lecture gives normal fecal fat as under 6%.

  • Stool with too little fat is not a disease entity.
  • Black, tarry stool is melaena, from upper GI bleeding.
Slides (2)
L38Learning
What happens to dietary fat when bile flow is blocked, e.g., by a gallstone?
  1. A. Poorly emulsified → absorbed directly into portal blood → fatty liver
  2. B. Poorly emulsified and poorly absorbed → steatorrhoea
  3. C. Emulsified normally by colipase → absorbed as chylomicrons → normal stool
AnswerB. Poorly emulsified and poorly absorbed → steatorrhoea
WhyWithout bile salts, fat is poorly emulsified and cannot form micelles, so it is poorly digested and absorbed and appears in the stool: steatorrhoea.
Explanation

Bile salts are needed twice: for emulsification (surface for lipase) and for micelles (transport to the brush border). Blocked bile flow (cholestasis) removes both, so long-chain fat and fat-soluble vitamins pass into the stool. The stool is also pale (no bilirubin), and bilirubin backing up into the blood causes jaundice.

  • Colipase is not an emulsifier and cannot replace bile.
  • Long-chain fat cannot reach portal blood without bile; only short- and medium-chain fatty acids go that way.
Slides (2)
Tier 3The rest of the section+15 questions

Mouth and stomach: the acid lipases

L39Learning
What do lingual and gastric lipase produce from TAG?
  1. A. Lysophospholipid + one fatty acid
  2. B. Diacylglycerol + one fatty acid
  3. C. Glycerol + three fatty acids
AnswerB. Diacylglycerol + one fatty acid
WhyThe acid lipases cut one ester bond, turning TAG into diacylglycerol (DAG) + one fatty acid.
Explanation

The acid lipases remove a single fatty acid (preferentially from position 3), leaving a 1,2-diacylglycerol. Chyme leaving the stomach therefore contains free fatty acids, 1,2-DAG and a lot of still-intact TAG, cholesteryl ester and phospholipid.

  • Lysophospholipid + fatty acid is what phospholipase A2 makes from a phospholipid.
  • Glycerol + three fatty acids is complete hydrolysis, which the acid lipases do not achieve; even pancreatic lipase stops mostly at 2-monoacylglycerol.
Slides (2)
L40Learning
In which patients does digestion by the acid lipases matter most?
  1. A. Elderly adults (low stomach acid)
    Cystic fibrosis (bile salts lacking)
  2. B. Newborns (milk fat)
    Cystic fibrosis (pancreatic lipase lacking)
  3. C. Adults on high-fat diets
    Gallstones (bile flow blocked)
AnswerB. Newborns (milk fat)
Cystic fibrosis (pancreatic lipase lacking)
WhyAcid lipases matter most in newborns, whose fat is milk fat, and in cystic fibrosis, where pancreatic lipase cannot reach the gut.
Explanation

In a healthy adult the acid lipases digest only a small share of TAG, because pancreatic lipase does most of the work. They become important when the substrate suits them, as in a newborn whose main fat is milk fat rich in short- and medium-chain fatty acids, and when pancreatic lipase is missing, as in cystic fibrosis, where thick secretions block the pancreatic ducts (these patients may also lack fat-soluble vitamins).

  • Low stomach acid would not make acid lipases more important, and the cystic fibrosis defect is pancreatic enzyme delivery, not bile salts.
  • In gallstone obstruction the problem is missing bile; acid lipases cannot handle the long-chain TAG of an adult diet.
Slides (1)

Pancreatic enzymes: lipase, colipase, PLA2, esterase

L41Learning
How is colipase activated?
  1. A. Secreted active; activated further by bile salts
  2. B. Secreted as procolipase; activated by pepsin in the stomach
  3. C. Secreted as procolipase; activated by trypsin in the intestine
AnswerC. Secreted as procolipase; activated by trypsin in the intestine
WhyColipase is secreted as the zymogen procolipase and is activated by trypsin in the intestinal lumen.
Explanation

Like the pancreatic proteases, colipase is made as an inactive precursor so it cannot act inside the pancreas. In the duodenum, enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen to trypsin, and trypsin then cleaves procolipase to colipase (and pro-phospholipase A2 to phospholipase A2). In acute pancreatitis, where trypsin is activated too early, colipase is activated inside the gland as well.

  • Pepsin is the gastric protease; procolipase only meets the chyme in the duodenum.
  • Colipase is not secreted active, and bile salts do not activate it.
Slides (2)
L42Learning
What does cholesterol esterase do, and where?
  1. A. Cholesteryl ester → cholesterol + fatty acid, in the small intestine
  2. B. Cholesteryl ester → cholesterol + fatty acid, in the stomach
  3. C. Cholesterol + fatty acid → cholesteryl ester, in the small intestine
AnswerA. Cholesteryl ester → cholesterol + fatty acid, in the small intestine
WhyPancreatic cholesterol esterase hydrolyses cholesteryl ester into free cholesterol + a fatty acid in the small intestine.
Explanation

Only free cholesterol can be taken up from micelles, so dietary cholesteryl ester must first be hydrolysed. Cholesterol esterase (cholesteryl ester hydrolase) is secreted by the pancreas into the duodenum and needs bile salts for full activity.

  • Cholesterol + fatty acid → ester is the reverse reaction; inside the enterocyte it is done by ACAT (acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase), not by the digestive esterase.
  • There is no cholesterol esterase activity in the stomach; cholesteryl ester digestion happens in the small intestine.
Slides (2)

Blocking fat digestion: orlistat and designer fats

L43Learning
What is olestra, and why does it provide no calories?
  1. A. 3 fatty acids on glycerol; cannot be absorbed by enterocytes
  2. B. 6–8 fatty acids on sucrose; cannot be hydrolysed by lipases
  3. C. 6–8 fatty acids on glucose; absorbed but not oxidised
AnswerB. 6–8 fatty acids on sucrose; cannot be hydrolysed by lipases
WhyOlestra is sucrose carrying 6–8 fatty acids; lipases cannot hydrolyse it, so it passes through the gut unabsorbed.
Explanation

Olestra (Olean) is a fat substitute that tastes and cooks like fat. Pancreatic lipase is built for a glycerol backbone; the crowded sucrose core with 6–8 ester-linked fatty acids does not fit, so no fatty acids or monoacylglycerols are released and nothing is absorbed. Like any unabsorbed fat it can carry fat-soluble vitamins out in the stool.

  • 3 fatty acids on glycerol is ordinary TAG, which is digested and absorbed normally.
  • The backbone is sucrose, not glucose, and olestra is never absorbed in the first place.
Slides (2)

Bile: composition and bile acids

L44Learning
According to the lecture, what is the lipid composition of bile?
  1. A. 85% bile salts
    10% free cholesterol
    5% phospholipid (mainly lecithin)
  2. B. 50% bile salts
    40% free cholesterol
    10% phospholipid (mainly lecithin)
  3. C. 85% free cholesterol
    10% bile salts
    5% phospholipid (mainly lecithin)
AnswerA. 85% bile salts
10% free cholesterol
5% phospholipid (mainly lecithin)
WhyPer the lecture, bile is 85% bile salts, 10% free cholesterol and 5% phospholipid, mainly lecithin (phosphatidylcholine).
Explanation

These figures describe bile's organic lipids (bile is mostly water and electrolytes, with bilirubin as its pigment). Bile salts dominate because they do the work: emulsifying fat, forming micelles and keeping cholesterol in solution. Cholesterol is there because bile is the body's route for excreting it, and lecithin helps bile salts hold it in solution.

  • Bile with 85% or even 40% cholesterol could not keep it dissolved: gallstones form when the cholesterol share rises only modestly.

Physiology texts give a somewhat different split (more phospholipid, less cholesterol), but bile salts are always the largest component; use the lecture's 85/10/5 on the exam.

Slides (1)
L45LearningHigh yield
What are the secondary bile acids, and how are they formed?
  1. A. Glycocholic and taurocholic acid; the liver conjugates primary bile acids with amino acids
  2. B. Deoxycholic and lithocholic acid; gut bacteria deconjugate and 7α-dehydroxylate primary bile acids
  3. C. Deoxycholic and lithocholic acid; the liver adds hydroxyl groups to primary bile acids
AnswerB. Deoxycholic and lithocholic acid; gut bacteria deconjugate and 7α-dehydroxylate primary bile acids
WhyIn the intestine, bacteria deconjugate primary bile salts and remove the 7α-hydroxyl, forming deoxycholic (from cholic) and lithocholic (from chenodeoxycholic) acid.
Explanation

Bile salts that reach the lower ileum and colon meet the gut flora. Bacterial enzymes first split off glycine or taurine (deconjugation), then remove the 7α-hydroxyl group: cholic acid becomes deoxycholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid becomes lithocholic acid. Some are reabsorbed, returned to the liver and re-conjugated; the bile acids lost in stool are mostly these deconjugated secondary acids.

  • Secondary bile acids form when bacteria remove a hydroxyl, not when the liver adds one.
  • Glycocholic and taurocholic acid are conjugated primary bile acids, made in the liver.
Slides (1)

Enterohepatic circulation and cholestyramine

L46LearningHigh yield
What is cholestyramine?
  1. A. A positively charged, unabsorbed resin that binds pancreatic lipase in the gut → it is inactivated
  2. B. A positively charged, unabsorbed resin that binds bile acids in the gut → they are excreted
  3. C. A negatively charged, absorbed resin that binds cholesterol in the blood → it is excreted
AnswerB. A positively charged, unabsorbed resin that binds bile acids in the gut → they are excreted
WhyCholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant: an insoluble, unabsorbed, positively charged anion-exchange resin that binds negatively charged bile acids in the gut.
Explanation

Cholestyramine stays in the gut lumen: it is water-insoluble, resistant to digestive enzymes and not absorbed. Its fixed positive charges trade chloride for the negatively charged bile acids, holding them so they cannot be reabsorbed in the ileum. The bound bile acids leave in the stool, breaking the enterohepatic circulation.

  • No resin binds lipase; inhibiting lipase is orlistat's action.
  • Cholestyramine is never absorbed and works only in the lumen; a negatively charged resin would repel bile acid anions.
Slides (2)

Gallstones (cholelithiasis)

L47LearningHigh yield
What are the “5 F's” of the classic gallstone patient, as given in the lecture?
  1. A. Fat, forty, fasting, flatulent, female
  2. B. Fat, fifty, fertile, febrile, female
  3. C. Fat, forty, fertile, flatulent, female
AnswerC. Fat, forty, fertile, flatulent, female
WhyThe lecture's 5 F's are fat, forty, fertile, flatulent, female; many lists use fair instead of flatulent.
Explanation

The mnemonic captures the cholesterol-stone risk factors: obesity (more biliary cholesterol), age around 40 and older, pregnancy and multiparity (oestrogen and progesterone), and female sex. "Flatulent" reflects the bloating many patients report; TA reviews often use fair (Caucasian) instead.

  • Fifty and febrile are not in the mnemonic; fever suggests a complication such as cholecystitis.
  • Fasting is not one of the 5 F's.
Slides (1)
L48Learning
Why are gallstones more common in women?
  1. A. Oestrogen increases bile salt secretion; progesterone speeds gallbladder emptying
  2. B. Progesterone increases cholesterol secretion into bile; oestrogen causes bile stasis
  3. C. Oestrogen increases cholesterol secretion into bile; progesterone causes bile stasis
AnswerC. Oestrogen increases cholesterol secretion into bile; progesterone causes bile stasis
WhyOestrogen raises biliary cholesterol secretion and progesterone relaxes the gallbladder, causing bile stasis.
Explanation

Both female hormones push towards stones. Oestrogen increases hepatic cholesterol uptake and secretion into bile, supersaturating it. Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, so the gallbladder empties less completely and bile sits longer, giving crystals time to form. That is why pregnancy, multiparity and oral contraceptives are risk factors.

  • The swapped pair reverses the hormones' roles.
  • Progesterone slows gallbladder emptying; faster emptying would protect against stones.
Slides (2)

Micelles and absorption

L49Learning
What happens to the bile salts of a micelle once its lipids have entered the enterocyte?
  1. A. They stay in the lumen, form new micelles, and are reabsorbed later in the terminal ileum
  2. B. They enter the enterocyte with the lipids and are packed into chylomicrons
  3. C. They enter the jejunal enterocyte and return to the liver in portal blood
AnswerA. They stay in the lumen, form new micelles, and are reabsorbed later in the terminal ileum
WhyMicelles are not absorbed whole: the lipids enter the jejunal enterocyte, while the bile salts stay in the lumen and are reabsorbed later in the terminal ileum.
Explanation

Only the lipid cargo crosses the brush border in the jejunum. The bile salts are reused to pick up more products as they move down the gut, and are finally taken up by the Na+–bile salt cotransporter of the terminal ileum and returned to the liver. This separation lets a small bile salt pool serve a whole meal.

  • Bile salts are not part of chylomicrons, which carry TAG, cholesteryl ester, phospholipid and apo B-48.
  • The jejunum has no active bile salt uptake; the ileum does that.
Slides (2)

Re-esterification and chylomicrons

L50Learning
Which enzyme esterifies cholesterol inside the enterocyte?
  1. A. Lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT)
  2. B. Acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT)
  3. C. Cholesterol esterase
AnswerB. Acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT)
WhyACAT transfers a fatty acyl group from fatty acyl-CoA to cholesterol, forming cholesteryl ester for the chylomicron core.
Explanation

Absorbed free cholesterol is re-esterified so it can be stored in the hydrophobic core of the chylomicron. ACAT is an intracellular ER enzyme that uses fatty acyl-CoA as the acyl donor.

  • Cholesterol esterase does the reverse (hydrolysis) in the intestinal lumen.
  • LCAT esterifies cholesterol in plasma, on HDL, using a fatty acid from lecithin.
Slides (2)
L51Learning
Why do chylomicrons enter lymph (the lacteals) rather than blood capillaries?
  1. A. They are too large to pass through blood capillary walls
  2. B. Lymph contains the lipoprotein lipase they need
  3. C. Blood capillaries lack receptors for apo B-48
AnswerA. They are too large to pass through blood capillary walls
WhyChylomicrons are too large to cross the walls of blood capillaries, but they pass easily through the wide gaps of the lacteals.
Explanation

Chylomicrons are the largest lipoproteins, up to about 1 µm across. They leave the enterocyte by exocytosis into the lamina propria, where the lymphatic capillary of the villus (the lacteal) has loose endothelial junctions they can slip through; blood capillary endothelium with its basement membrane keeps them out.

  • Entry into vessels does not depend on apo B-48 receptors.
  • Lipoprotein lipase sits on the blood capillaries of muscle and adipose tissue, not in lymph.
Slides (2)
L52Learning
Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses chylomicron TAG in adipose and muscle capillaries. What happens to the products?
  1. A. Both are repacked into new chylomicrons by the capillary endothelium
  2. B. Fatty acids go to the liver; glycerol enters muscle and adipose cells
  3. C. Fatty acids enter muscle and adipose cells; glycerol goes to the liver
AnswerC. Fatty acids enter muscle and adipose cells; glycerol goes to the liver
WhyFatty acids released by LPL are taken up by muscle (oxidation) and adipose (storage); glycerol travels to the liver, which can phosphorylate it.
Explanation

Fatty acids released at the capillary wall enter the nearby cells: muscle burns them and adipocytes re-esterify them into stored TAG. Glycerol is water-soluble and is carried in blood to the liver, which has glycerol kinase to use it (for gluconeogenesis or TAG synthesis).

  • The swapped option fails because adipocytes lack glycerol kinase and cannot use glycerol well.
  • Only enterocytes make chylomicrons, from absorbed dietary fat; the endothelium does not.
Slides (1)

Steatorrhoea and malabsorption

L53LearningHigh yield
How does cystic fibrosis cause steatorrhoea?
  1. A. Thick secretions block the pancreatic ducts → pancreatic lipase cannot reach the duodenum
  2. B. Enterocytes cannot make apo B-48 → absorbed fat cannot be packed into chylomicrons
  3. C. Autoimmune damage to the intestinal mucosa → digested fat cannot be absorbed
AnswerA. Thick secretions block the pancreatic ducts → pancreatic lipase cannot reach the duodenum
WhyIn cystic fibrosis, thick secretions plug the pancreatic ducts, so pancreatic enzymes (lipase, colipase) do not reach the duodenum: a maldigestion steatorrhoea.
Explanation

The defective chloride channel (CFTR) dehydrates secretions. In the pancreas, viscous mucus blocks the ducts, so lipase, colipase and the proteases cannot reach the small intestine (bile flow can be reduced too). Fat and protein are maldigested, stools are bulky, foul and fatty (TAG in stool), and fat-soluble vitamins are lost. The acid lipases become relatively important, and treatment includes oral pancreatic enzymes.

  • Autoimmune mucosal damage is coeliac disease (malabsorption).
  • Failure to pack fat into chylomicrons (no apo B-48 particles) is the enterocyte defect of abetalipoproteinaemia; in cystic fibrosis enterocytes package fat normally.
Slides (2)

BIO-L25 Fatty acid & triacylglycerol synthesis

Tier 1: 17 of 50
Learning questions 50
Tier 1Every concept once17 questions

Fat synthesis: the setting

L1LearningHigh yield
In what metabolic state, and under which hormone, does fatty acid synthesis run?
  1. A. Fasting state; high glucagon
  2. B. Fed state; high glucagon
  3. C. Fed state; high insulin
AnswerC. Fed state; high insulin
WhyFatty acid synthesis stores surplus fuel, so it runs in the well-fed state, when insulin and ATP are high (anabolism).
Explanation

After a meal, glucose and ATP are plentiful and the surplus is turned into fat for storage (de novo lipogenesis, DNL). Insulin is the signal: it dephosphorylates and activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, induces the lipogenic enzymes and drives glucose into cells. Knowing that this is a fed, high-insulin pathway predicts most of its regulation.

  • Fasting with high glucagon is the opposite state: fat is broken down (lipolysis, β-oxidation, ketogenesis), not made.
  • Fed state with high glucagon is a mismatched pair: glucagon falls after a carbohydrate meal, and glucagon switches acetyl-CoA carboxylase off.
Slides (2)
L2LearningHigh yield
What are the three phases of fatty acid synthesis, in order?
  1. A. Acetyl-CoA reaches the cytosol (as citrate) → acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA → fatty acid synthase builds palmitate
  2. B. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA reaches the cytosol (as citrate) → fatty acid synthase builds palmitate
  3. C. Acetyl-CoA reaches the cytosol (as citrate) → fatty acid synthase builds palmitate → acetyl-CoA carboxylase lengthens it
AnswerA. Acetyl-CoA reaches the cytosol (as citrate) → acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA → fatty acid synthase builds palmitate
WhyPhase I exports acetyl-CoA as citrate; Phase II carboxylates it to malonyl-CoA (ACC); Phase III builds palmitate on fatty acid synthase.
Explanation
  • Phase I, cytosolic entry of acetyl-CoA: citrate synthase (matrix) → citrate exported → ATP-citrate lyase (cytosol) → acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate.
  • Phase II, activated 2-carbon units: acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC, biotin, ATP, CO2) → malonyl-CoA. This is the committed, rate-limiting step.
  • Phase III, chain building: fatty acid synthase (FAS) joins one acetyl and seven malonyl units → palmitate (16:0).

Malonyl-CoA is made in the cytosol, so it never needs exporting. ACC only carboxylates acetyl-CoA; lengthening beyond 16 carbons is done by elongases.

Slides (2)

Phase I: getting acetyl-CoA out as citrate

L3LearningHigh yield
How is acetyl-CoA moved from the mitochondrion to the cytosol for fat synthesis?
  1. A. Citrate synthase (acetyl-CoA + OAA → citrate) → citrate exported → ATP-citrate lyase splits it back to acetyl-CoA + OAA
  2. B. Citrate lyase (citrate → acetyl-CoA + OAA) → acetyl-CoA exported → ATP-citrate synthase rejoins it to citrate
  3. C. Citrate synthase (acetyl-CoA + OAA → citrate) → citrate exported → aconitase splits it back to acetyl-CoA + OAA
AnswerA. Citrate synthase (acetyl-CoA + OAA → citrate) → citrate exported → ATP-citrate lyase splits it back to acetyl-CoA + OAA
WhyIn the matrix citrate synthase joins acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate (OAA); citrate is exported; in the cytosol ATP-citrate lyase splits it back.
Explanation

This is the citrate shuttle. When ATP and NADH are high, citrate builds up in the matrix, leaves on the tricarboxylate carrier, and ATP-citrate lyase cleaves it (spending ATP) into cytosolic acetyl-CoA, the substrate of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and OAA, which is recycled through malate and malic enzyme.

  • The route that exports acetyl-CoA and rejoins it by "ATP-citrate synthase" reverses the compartments: acetyl-CoA itself cannot be exported, and no such enzyme exists.
  • Aconitase isomerises citrate to isocitrate; it does not split it.
Slides (2)

Supplying NADPH

L4LearningHigh yield
What is the chief source of NADPH for fatty acid synthesis?
  1. A. Malate–aspartate shuttle
  2. B. Pentose phosphate pathway
  3. C. Citric acid cycle
AnswerB. Pentose phosphate pathway
WhyThe pentose phosphate pathway (hexose monophosphate shunt) is the chief NADPH source; malic enzyme supplies much of the rest.
Explanation

The oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway (HMP shunt) makes NADPH at glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase. It runs in the cytosol, next to fatty acid synthase, and is active in lipogenic tissues (liver, lactating breast, adipose). Insulin increases glucose flow into it. A block at glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase would therefore starve fat synthesis of reducing power.

  • The malate–aspartate shuttle moves NADH reducing equivalents into the mitochondrion; it makes no NADPH.
  • The citric acid cycle makes NADH and FADH2 in the matrix, for ATP.

The lecture calls the pentose phosphate pathway the chief source and credits malic enzyme with about half.

Slides (2)

Phase II: acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the committed step

L5LearningHigh yield
Which vitamin-derived prosthetic group does acetyl-CoA carboxylase need?
  1. A. Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5)
  2. B. Thiamine pyrophosphate (vitamin B1)
  3. C. Biotin (vitamin B7)
AnswerC. Biotin (vitamin B7)
WhyAcetyl-CoA carboxylase is biotin-dependent: biotin (vitamin B7), covalently bound to the enzyme, carries the CO2 that is added to acetyl-CoA.
Explanation

Biotin is a water-soluble B vitamin attached to a lysine of every biotin carboxylase (enzyme biotinylation). It acts as a CO2 carrier: it is carboxylated, then hands the carboxyl group to the substrate. The same cofactor serves pyruvate carboxylase and propionyl-CoA carboxylase.

  • Pantothenic acid (B5) forms coenzyme A and the 4′-phosphopantetheine arm of fatty acid synthase's acyl carrier protein: same pathway, different enzyme.
  • Thiamine pyrophosphate (B1) serves decarboxylations (pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase), not carboxylations.
Slides (2)
L6LearningHigh yield
What two jobs make malonyl-CoA the hinge of fat metabolism?
  1. A. Donor of 2-carbon units to fatty acid synthase
    Activates carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
  2. B. Donor of 2-carbon units to ketone body synthesis
    Inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
  3. C. Donor of 2-carbon units to fatty acid synthase
    Inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
AnswerC. Donor of 2-carbon units to fatty acid synthase
Inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
WhyMalonyl-CoA is the building block of fatty acid synthesis and inhibits CPT-I, the gate for fatty acids entering mitochondria: "store, don't burn".
Explanation

Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I), on the outer mitochondrial membrane, is the rate-limiting step of β-oxidation. When acetyl-CoA carboxylase is active (fed, high insulin), the malonyl-CoA it makes both feeds fatty acid synthase and blocks CPT-I, so newly made fatty acids are not immediately burned. In fasting, AMPK and glucagon switch ACC off, malonyl-CoA falls, CPT-I opens and β-oxidation runs.

  • Malonyl-CoA inhibits, not activates, CPT-I.
  • Ketone bodies are made from acetyl-CoA (via HMG-CoA) in fasting, not from malonyl-CoA.
Slides (2)

Phase III: fatty acid synthase builds palmitate

L7Learning
Which list gives the seven enzyme activities of fatty acid synthase?
  1. A. Acetyl transacylase
    Malonyl transacylase
    3-Ketoacyl synthase
    3-Ketoacyl reductase
    Dehydratase
    Enoyl reductase
    Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
  2. B. Acetyl transacylase
    Malonyl transacylase
    3-Ketoacyl synthase
    3-Ketoacyl reductase
    Dehydratase
    Enoyl reductase
    Thioesterase
  3. C. Acetyl transacylase
    Malonyl transacylase
    3-Ketoacyl synthase
    3-Ketoacyl reductase
    Isomerase
    Δ9 desaturase
    Thioesterase
AnswerB. Acetyl transacylase
Malonyl transacylase
3-Ketoacyl synthase
3-Ketoacyl reductase
Dehydratase
Enoyl reductase
Thioesterase
WhyLoad (acetyl and malonyl transacylase), condense (ketoacyl synthase), reduce–dehydrate–reduce (ketoacyl reductase, dehydratase, enoyl reductase), release (thioesterase).
Explanation

Follow one cycle: the two transacylases load acetyl (onto the synthase's cysteine) and malonyl (onto ACP); 3-ketoacyl synthase condenses them, releasing CO2; 3-ketoacyl reductase (NADPH), dehydratase and enoyl reductase (NADPH) turn the keto group into a saturated CH2; after seven cycles thioesterase cuts off palmitate.

  • Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is a separate enzyme that makes malonyl-CoA before FAS acts.
  • An isomerase belongs to β-oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids, and the Δ9 desaturase is an ER enzyme; FAS makes only saturated chains.
Slides (1)
L8Learning
What is the overall equation for palmitate synthesis?
  1. A. Acetyl-CoA + 7 malonyl-CoA + 14 NADPH + 14 H+ → palmitate + 7 CO2 + 6 H2O + 8 CoA + 14 NADP+
  2. B. Acetyl-CoA + 7 malonyl-CoA + 7 NADPH + 7 H+ → palmitate + 7 CO2 + 6 H2O + 8 CoA + 7 NADP+
  3. C. Acetyl-CoA + 8 malonyl-CoA + 14 NADH + 14 H+ → palmitate + 8 CO2 + 7 H2O + 9 CoA + 14 NAD+
AnswerA. Acetyl-CoA + 7 malonyl-CoA + 14 NADPH + 14 H+ → palmitate + 7 CO2 + 6 H2O + 8 CoA + 14 NADP+
WhyOne acetyl primer + 7 malonyl-CoA, reduced by 14 NADPH (two per cycle), give palmitate, 7 CO2 (one per malonyl), 6 H2O and 8 CoA.
Explanation

Build it from the cycle: 7 cycles × (1 malonyl in, 1 CO2 out, 2 NADPH used, 1 H2O from the dehydration). The last water is used when thioesterase hydrolyses palmitate off the enzyme, so 7 − 1 = 6 H2O net. CoA: 1 from acetyl-CoA + 7 from malonyl-CoA = 8.

  • 7 NADPH counts only one reduction per cycle; there are two.
  • 8 malonyl-CoA and NADH are both wrong: 8 would give 18 carbons, and FAS uses NADPH.
Slides (2)

Regulating acetyl-CoA carboxylase: minute to minute

L9LearningHigh yield
Two hours after eating half a pound of Halloween candy, which process is most active?
  1. A. Hormone-sensitive lipase, activated by cAMP (and adrenaline)
  2. B. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase, activated by palmitoyl-CoA (and glucagon)
  3. C. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase, activated by citrate (and insulin)
AnswerC. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase, activated by citrate (and insulin)
WhyA big sugar load means high insulin and plenty of citrate: the liver turns the surplus into fat, so acetyl-CoA carboxylase is switched on.
Explanation

Two hours after a carbohydrate meal the person is in the fed (absorptive) state: insulin high, glucagon low. Glucose floods glycolysis, citrate accumulates and is exported, and acetyl-CoA carboxylase is activated allosterically by citrate and by insulin-driven dephosphorylation. Glucagon, adrenaline, AMP (through AMPK), palmitoyl-CoA and PUFA would all switch it off.

  • Hormone-sensitive lipase breaks down stored fat in fasting and stress (cAMP, adrenaline); insulin inhibits it.
  • Palmitoyl-CoA and glucagon both inhibit ACC.
Slides (1)
L10LearningHigh yield
How does insulin reactivate phosphorylated acetyl-CoA carboxylase?
  1. A. Raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A → dephosphorylation
  2. B. Raises citrate and inhibits a protein phosphatase → polymerisation
  3. C. Lowers cAMP and activates a protein phosphatase → dephosphorylation
AnswerC. Lowers cAMP and activates a protein phosphatase → dephosphorylation
WhyInsulin lowers cAMP and activates protein phosphatase, which removes the phosphate from acetyl-CoA carboxylase (and other rate-limiting enzymes), making it active.
Explanation

This is insulin's general rule in the fed state: high insulin, low glucagon, dephosphorylated enzymes. The phosphatase activates glycogen synthase, pyruvate kinase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase together, so glucose is stored as glycogen and fat.

  • Insulin lowers cAMP, and a kinase adds phosphate; it cannot dephosphorylate.
  • Inhibiting the phosphatase would keep ACC phosphorylated and inactive.
Slides (2)

Long-term control and insulin's wider effects

L11Learning
At which three enzymes is fatty acid synthesis regulated?
  1. A. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase, fatty acid synthase, thioesterase
  2. B. ATP-citrate lyase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, fatty acid synthase
  3. C. Citrate synthase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, thioesterase
AnswerB. ATP-citrate lyase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, fatty acid synthase
WhyThe three control points are ATP-citrate lyase (induced by glucose and insulin), acetyl-CoA carboxylase (short and long term) and fatty acid synthase (gene expression).
Explanation
  • ATP-citrate lyase: induced by glucose and insulin.
  • Acetyl-CoA carboxylase: short-term allosteric control (citrate +, long-chain fatty acyl-CoA −) and covalent control (insulin +, glucagon −); long-term induction by a high-carbohydrate, low-fat diet and repression by fasting or a high-fat diet.
  • Fatty acid synthase: gene expression, ↑ by insulin and feeding, ↓ by PUFA and fasting.

Thioesterase and citrate synthase are not regulatory points of this pathway.

Slides (1)

Elongation, desaturation and the essential ω families

L12Learning
At which positions can human desaturases insert double bonds?
  1. A. Δ4, Δ5, Δ6, Δ9, Δ12; never beyond C12 toward the ω-end
  2. B. Δ4, Δ5, Δ6, Δ9; never beyond C9 toward the ω-end
  3. C. Δ9, Δ12, Δ15; never below C9 toward the carboxyl end
AnswerB. Δ4, Δ5, Δ6, Δ9; never beyond C9 toward the ω-end
WhyHumans have Δ4, Δ5, Δ6 and Δ9 desaturases only, so they can add double bonds between C9 and the carboxyl end but never beyond C9 (C10 to the ω-end).
Explanation

All the human desaturases work on the carboxyl side of C9. Double bonds beyond C9 (Δ12, Δ15) must already be present in the fatty acid the diet supplies. This one rule explains why linoleic (Δ9,12) and α-linolenic (Δ9,12,15) acids are essential, while oleic acid (Δ9 only) is not.

  • A human Δ12 desaturase would make linoleic acid non-essential.
  • Δ12 and Δ15 desaturases are plant enzymes; human desaturases work on the carboxyl side, not the ω side.
Slides (1)
L13Learning
How is arachidonic acid made from linoleic acid?
  1. A. Linoleic → (Δ6 desaturase) γ-linolenic → (elongase) 20:3 → (Δ5 desaturase) arachidonic acid (20:4Δ5,8,11,14)
  2. B. Linoleic → (Δ6 desaturase) α-linolenic → (elongase) 20:3 → (Δ5 desaturase) arachidonic acid (20:4Δ5,8,11,14)
  3. C. Linoleic → (Δ5 desaturase) γ-linolenic → (elongase) 20:3 → (Δ6 desaturase) arachidonic acid (20:4Δ5,8,11,14)
AnswerA. Linoleic → (Δ6 desaturase) γ-linolenic → (elongase) 20:3 → (Δ5 desaturase) arachidonic acid (20:4Δ5,8,11,14)
Whyω-6 pathway: linoleic (18:2) → Δ6 desaturase → γ-linolenic (18:3) → elongase → 20:3 → Δ5 desaturase → arachidonic (20:4).
Explanation

Desaturase, elongase, desaturase: Δ6 adds a bond near the carboxyl end, elongation pushes all bonds 2 places up (Δ6,9,12 → Δ8,11,14), then Δ5 adds the fourth bond. Every step stays on the carboxyl side, so the ω-6 identity is kept. The slide shows the ω-6 and ω-3 pathways under "in plants and fish", but humans run these steps too once the 18-carbon parent comes from the diet.

  • α-Linolenic acid is the ω-3 parent; it cannot be made from linoleic acid (that would need a Δ15 desaturase).
  • Putting Δ5 desaturase first and Δ6 last swaps the order of the two desaturases.
Slides (1)

Triacylglycerol: building, storing and moving it

L14Learning
In adipose tissue after a meal, how does insulin act on lipoprotein lipase (LPL) and hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL)?
  1. A. Activates LPL
    Inhibits HSL
  2. B. Inhibits LPL
    Activates HSL
  3. C. Activates LPL
    Activates HSL
AnswerA. Activates LPL
Inhibits HSL
WhyInsulin activates LPL (pulling fatty acids out of chylomicrons and VLDL into adipocytes) and inhibits HSL (stopping stored TAG being broken down): net fat storage.
Explanation

In the fed state adipose tissue shows ↑ GLUT4 glucose uptake (for glycerol 3-phosphate), ↑ LPL (for fatty acids) and ↓ HSL, so TAG accumulates. In fasting the pattern flips: insulin falls, adrenaline, glucagon and cortisol activate HSL, and fatty acids are released bound to albumin.

  • Inhibits LPL, activates HSL is the fasting pattern, the opposite of insulin's action.
  • Activating both lipases would make adipose take up and release fatty acids at once, a futile cycle.
Slides (1)

Glycerol 3-phosphate: liver versus adipose tissue

L15Learning
Why does adipose tissue store little TAG when glucose or insulin is low?
  1. A. No glycerol kinase → glycerol 3-P only from DHAP → needs insulin-driven glucose entry via GLUT4
  2. B. No glycerol 3-P dehydrogenase → glycerol 3-P only from free glycerol → needs glycerol kinase
  3. C. No lipoprotein lipase → fatty acids only from own synthesis → needs insulin-driven ACC
AnswerA. No glycerol kinase → glycerol 3-P only from DHAP → needs insulin-driven glucose entry via GLUT4
WhyWithout glycerol kinase, adipose depends on DHAP from glucose; glucose entry is insulin-mediated (GLUT4), so low glucose or insulin limits glycerol 3-phosphate and TAG.
Explanation

The chain runs: low insulin → little GLUT4 at the membrane → little glucose → little DHAP → little glycerol 3-phosphate → fatty acids cannot be esterified → little TAG. In fasting or uncontrolled diabetes, adipose tissue therefore releases more fatty acids than it stores, and plasma free fatty acids rise.

  • Adipose has glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase; it lacks glycerol kinase.
  • Adipose has lipoprotein lipase; that is its main fatty acid source.
Slides (2)

Acylation enzymes and clinical links

L16Learning
What is the sequence of TAG synthesis from glycerol 3-phosphate, with its enzymes?
  1. A. Glycerol 3-P → (GPAT) lysophosphatidic acid → (AGPAT) phosphatidic acid → (phosphatase) diacylglycerol → (DGAT) TAG
  2. B. Glycerol 3-P → (AGPAT) lysophosphatidic acid → (GPAT) phosphatidic acid → (phosphatase) diacylglycerol → (DGAT) TAG
  3. C. Glycerol 3-P → (GPAT) phosphatidic acid → (AGPAT) lysophosphatidic acid → (phosphatase) diacylglycerol → (DGAT) TAG
AnswerA. Glycerol 3-P → (GPAT) lysophosphatidic acid → (AGPAT) phosphatidic acid → (phosphatase) diacylglycerol → (DGAT) TAG
WhyGPAT adds acyl 1 (lysophosphatidic acid), AGPAT adds acyl 2 (phosphatidic acid), a phosphatase removes the phosphate (DAG), and DGAT adds acyl 3 (TAG).
Explanation

GPAT = glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase; AGPAT = acylglycerol-phosphate acyltransferase; DGAT = diacylglycerol acyltransferase. Lyso- means one acyl chain; phosphatidic acid (DAG phosphate) has two and is also the branch point for phospholipid synthesis. In the intestine, 2-monoacylglycerol is re-esterified by MGAT (monoacylglycerol acyltransferase) and then DGAT.

  • Putting AGPAT first and GPAT second swaps the two acyltransferases.
  • Putting phosphatidic acid before lysophosphatidic acid swaps the intermediates: lysophosphatidic acid (one chain) must come before phosphatidic acid (two chains).

The lecture diagram labels the first step "MGAT"; the enzyme that acylates glycerol 3-phosphate is GPAT.

Slides (2)
L17LearningHigh yield
What happens when the liver makes TAG faster than it can export it, and what is the lecture's clinical example?
  1. A. Fatty liver; alcoholic fatty liver (alcohol increases VLDL export)
  2. B. Fatty liver; familial hypercholesterolaemia (LDL receptor defect)
  3. C. Fatty liver; alcoholic fatty liver (alcohol impairs VLDL export)
AnswerC. Fatty liver; alcoholic fatty liver (alcohol impairs VLDL export)
WhyTAG that cannot leave as VLDL accumulates in hepatocytes: fatty liver (steatosis). Alcohol both raises TAG synthesis and impairs VLDL export.
Explanation

Hepatic steatosis occurs whenever TAG synthesis outpaces VLDL secretion: alcohol use, obesity, insulin resistance and diabetes (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease). It presents with an enlarged, sometimes tender liver and is the early, reversible stage of alcohol-related liver disease.

  • Alcohol decreases VLDL export; increased export would protect the liver.
  • Familial hypercholesterolaemia is a defect in LDL clearance that raises plasma cholesterol; it does not cause TAG build-up in the liver.
Slides (2)
Tier 2The next layer across every concept+18 questions

Fat synthesis: the setting

L18Learning
In which tissues does fatty acid synthesis mainly occur?
  1. A. Adipose tissue and red blood cells (less in liver)
  2. B. Liver and lactating mammary gland (less in adipose tissue)
  3. C. Skeletal muscle and heart muscle (less in liver)
AnswerB. Liver and lactating mammary gland (less in adipose tissue)
WhyThe liver and the lactating mammary gland are the main sites of de novo fatty acid synthesis; adipose tissue makes less.
Explanation

The liver turns surplus dietary carbohydrate into fatty acids and exports them as VLDL triacylglycerol; adipose tissue mostly stores fat made elsewhere (its own synthesis is minor). The lactating breast makes milk fat, including the medium-chain fatty acids released by thioesterase II. Kidney, brain and lung also have the pathway.

  • Red cells have no mitochondria, so they cannot make citrate to supply cytosolic acetyl-CoA.
  • Skeletal muscle and heart are fat-burning tissues: they take up fatty acids for β-oxidation.

The summary table lists adipose tissue beside liver; the detailed slide ranks it as the lesser site.

Slides (2)

Phase I: getting acetyl-CoA out as citrate

L19Learning
Citrate links a sugary meal to fat synthesis in two ways. Which pair is right?
  1. A. Carries acetyl units out of the mitochondrion
    Allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase
  2. B. Carries acetyl units out of the mitochondrion
    Allosterically inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
  3. C. Carries acetyl units into the mitochondrion
    Allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase
AnswerA. Carries acetyl units out of the mitochondrion
Allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase
WhyCitrate is both the carrier of acetyl units to the cytosol and the allosteric activator of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the committed step: why sugar is fattening.
Explanation

When glucose is abundant, citrate accumulates in the matrix and is exported. In the cytosol, ATP-citrate lyase releases its acetyl-CoA (the substrate), while citrate itself polymerises acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) into its active filament form (the switch). Substrate supply and enzyme activation rise together.

  • Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I) is inhibited by malonyl-CoA, the product of ACC, not by citrate.
  • The direction is out of the mitochondrion: synthesis is cytosolic.
Slides (1)

Supplying NADPH

L20Learning
How is the oxaloacetate left by ATP-citrate lyase recycled while making NADPH?
  1. A. OAA → PEP + CO2 (PEP carboxykinase, makes NADPH) → pyruvate (pyruvate kinase, makes ATP)
  2. B. OAA → malate (malic enzyme, makes NADPH) → pyruvate + CO2 (cytosolic malate dehydrogenase, uses NADH)
  3. C. OAA → malate (cytosolic malate dehydrogenase, uses NADH) → pyruvate + CO2 (malic enzyme, makes NADPH)
AnswerC. OAA → malate (cytosolic malate dehydrogenase, uses NADH) → pyruvate + CO2 (malic enzyme, makes NADPH)
WhyCytosolic malate dehydrogenase reduces OAA to malate (using NADH); malic enzyme then turns malate into pyruvate + CO2, making NADPH.
Explanation

Oxaloacetate cannot re-enter the mitochondrion directly. It is reduced to malate by the NADH-dependent malate dehydrogenase (the NADH comes from glycolysis), then malic enzyme decarboxylates malate to pyruvate, making NADPH. Pyruvate goes back into the mitochondrion, where pyruvate carboxylase can regenerate OAA. Net effect: glycolytic NADH is converted into NADPH for fatty acid synthase.

  • PEP carboxykinase uses GTP and makes no NADPH; it belongs to gluconeogenesis.
  • The route giving OAA → malate by malic enzyme swaps the two enzymes: malic enzyme acts on malate (making NADPH), and malate dehydrogenase reduces OAA (using NADH).
Slides (2)

Phase II: acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the committed step

L21LearningHigh yield
What is the rate-limiting, committed step of fatty acid synthesis?
  1. A. Acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA, by acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)
  2. B. Malonyl-CoA → palmitate, by fatty acid synthase
  3. C. Acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA, by malonyl transacylase
AnswerA. Acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA, by acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)
WhyAcetyl-CoA carboxylase carboxylates acetyl-CoA (2C) to malonyl-CoA (3C): the committed, rate-limiting and most regulated step.
Explanation

Committed means that once malonyl-CoA is made, its only fate is fatty acid synthesis; rate-limiting means this slowest step sets the flux. Hence ACC is where insulin, glucagon, adrenaline (epinephrine), citrate, palmitoyl-CoA and AMP all act.

  • Fatty acid synthase builds palmitate from malonyl-CoA, but it is regulated mainly by the amount of enzyme (induction), not minute-to-minute.
  • Malonyl transacylase is one activity of fatty acid synthase: it loads an existing malonyl group onto the acyl carrier protein. It does not make malonyl-CoA.
Slides (2)
L22Learning
Which two other biotin-dependent carboxylases are worth remembering?
  1. A. PEP carboxykinase
    α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
  2. B. Pyruvate carboxylase
    Propionyl-CoA carboxylase
  3. C. Pyruvate carboxylase
    Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
AnswerB. Pyruvate carboxylase
Propionyl-CoA carboxylase
WhyBiotin carries CO2 for acetyl-CoA carboxylase, pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate → oxaloacetate) and propionyl-CoA carboxylase (propionyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA).
Explanation

All three are carboxylases that add CO2 to a carbon next to a carbonyl group. Pyruvate carboxylase starts gluconeogenesis and refills oxaloacetate; propionyl-CoA carboxylase handles the 3-carbon end of odd-chain fatty acids and some amino acids.

  • PEP carboxykinase uses GTP and no biotin; α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase uses thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoate, FAD and NAD+.
  • Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is the next step after propionyl-CoA carboxylase, but it needs vitamin B12 (cobalamin), not biotin.
Slides (2)

Phase III: fatty acid synthase builds palmitate

L23LearningHigh yield
What is the product of fatty acid synthase?
  1. A. Myristate (14:0)
  2. B. Palmitate (16:0)
  3. C. Stearate (18:0)
AnswerB. Palmitate (16:0)
WhyFatty acid synthase stops at palmitate, the saturated 16-carbon fatty acid (16:0); all other fatty acids are made from it.
Explanation

Palmitic acid is the immediate product of de novo lipogenesis. When the chain on the acyl carrier protein reaches 16 carbons, the enzyme's own thioesterase I releases it. Palmitate is then activated to palmitoyl-CoA and lengthened by elongases or desaturated in the ER.

  • Myristate (14:0) is one cycle short; FAS does not normally release it (the lactating breast's thioesterase II releases shorter 8–12C chains).
  • Stearate (18:0) is made by elongating palmitate (smooth ER or mitochondria), not by FAS.
Slides (2)
L24Learning
Which reduced cofactor does fatty acid synthase use?
  1. A. NADH
  2. B. FADH2
  3. C. NADPH
AnswerC. NADPH
WhyFatty acid synthase reduces each new 2-carbon unit with NADPH, the cytosolic reductant for biosynthesis (2 per cycle, 14 per palmitate).
Explanation

Anabolic (reductive) pathways use NADPH; catabolic (oxidative) pathways use NAD+/FAD and produce NADH and FADH2. Fatty acid synthesis is the reverse of β-oxidation in chemistry, but it uses a separate cofactor so that the two can be controlled independently. Its NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway and malic enzyme.

  • NADH is the oxidative carrier that feeds the electron transport chain; it is the reductant made, not used, by β-oxidation.
  • FADH2 is produced by the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase step of β-oxidation.
Slides (2)
L25Learning
Why is only the fatty acid synthase dimer active?
  1. A. Each cycle needs the ACP of one chain and the ketoacyl synthase cysteine of the other
  2. B. The two chains must swap NADPH between their reductase sites
  3. C. Each cycle needs the biotin of one chain and the thioesterase of the other
AnswerA. Each cycle needs the ACP of one chain and the ketoacyl synthase cysteine of the other
WhyCondensation needs two thiols: the ACP phosphopantetheine SH of one monomer and the ketoacyl synthase cysteine SH of the other, which only face each other in the head-to-tail dimer.
Explanation

The growing acyl chain sits on the cysteine of 3-ketoacyl synthase while the incoming malonyl group sits on the ACP arm. These two thiols come from different monomers, so a single chain cannot condense; the dimer therefore has two functional halves working at once.

  • NADPH binds each reductase from solution; it is not passed between chains.
  • FAS contains no biotin: biotin belongs to acetyl-CoA carboxylase.
Slides (2)
L26Learning
When fatty acid synthase condenses an acetyl unit with a malonyl unit, what happens to the CO2 that acetyl-CoA carboxylase added?
  1. A. It is kept as the carboxyl group at the α-end of the chain
  2. B. It is released, driving the condensation and leaving a 4-carbon unit
  3. C. It is handed back to biotin for the next carboxylation
AnswerB. It is released, driving the condensation and leaving a 4-carbon unit
WhyThe condensation releases the CO2 that ACC attached; decarboxylation pulls the reaction forward, so 2C + 3C − CO2 gives a 4-carbon unit.
Explanation

FAS binds one acetyl and one malonyl unit, and a 2-carbon unit from malonyl joins the acetyl to make a 4-carbon (acetoacetyl) unit, which is then reduced. The slide words it as transfer from malonyl to acetyl; textbooks describe the acetyl group being added onto malonyl-ACP. It is the same condensation, and either way the free CO2 is the one ACC added. Carboxylating and then decarboxylating spends ATP to make the condensation favourable.

  • The α-end carboxyl of palmitate comes from the thioester carbon of the last malonyl unit, not from retained CO2.
  • The CO2 leaves as free gas or bicarbonate; it is not returned to biotin.
Slides (1)

Regulating acetyl-CoA carboxylase: minute to minute

L27Learning
In poorly controlled type 1 diabetes (insulin low, glucagon high), what state is hepatic acetyl-CoA carboxylase in?
  1. A. Phosphorylated (AMPK) → depolymerised → inactive
  2. B. Dephosphorylated (protein phosphatase) → polymerised → active
  3. C. Phosphorylated (AMPK) → polymerised → active
AnswerA. Phosphorylated (AMPK) → depolymerised → inactive
WhyWithout insulin and with glucagon high, ACC is phosphorylated via AMPK, depolymerised and inactive: malonyl-CoA falls and the liver oxidises fat.
Explanation

Insulin normally keeps ACC dephosphorylated through protein phosphatase. In insulin deficiency, glucagon (through AMPK kinases) and AMP drive phosphorylation, which increases depolymerisation. Low malonyl-CoA then releases CPT-I, so fatty acids pour into β-oxidation and ketogenesis, which is part of how diabetic ketoacidosis develops.

  • The dephosphorylated, active state needs insulin.
  • Phosphorylation causes depolymerisation, not polymerisation; the two never go together in this model.
Slides (2)

Long-term control and insulin's wider effects

L28LearningHigh yield
Through which signalling pathway does insulin bring GLUT4 to the cell membrane in muscle and fat?
  1. A. PI3-kinase → protein kinase B (Akt)
  2. B. Adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A
  3. C. MAP kinase → gene induction
AnswerA. PI3-kinase → protein kinase B (Akt)
WhyInsulin's receptor tyrosine kinase activates PI3-kinase → protein kinase B (Akt), which moves GLUT4 vesicles to the membrane of skeletal muscle and adipose cells.
Explanation

GLUT4 is the insulin-dependent glucose transporter of skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. Without insulin it sits in intracellular vesicles; PI3-kinase → Akt signalling translocates it to the plasma membrane, so glucose enters the cells. In adipocytes that glucose provides the DHAP needed for glycerol 3-phosphate. Impaired PI3-kinase signalling (insulin resistance) therefore reduces glucose uptake into muscle.

  • cAMP–PKA is the glucagon and adrenaline pathway; insulin lowers cAMP.
  • Insulin's MAP kinase arm gives growth-factor-like effects and enzyme induction (glucokinase), not GLUT4 translocation.
Slides (2)

Elongation, desaturation and the essential ω families

L29LearningHigh yield
Where does fatty acid elongation occur, and what is the two-carbon donor at each site?
  1. A. Rough ER: propionyl-CoA
    Peroxisomes: acetyl-CoA
  2. B. Smooth ER: acetyl-CoA
    Mitochondria: malonyl-CoA
  3. C. Smooth ER: malonyl-CoA
    Mitochondria: acetyl-CoA
AnswerC. Smooth ER: malonyl-CoA
Mitochondria: acetyl-CoA
WhyElongases add two carbons in the smooth ER (donor malonyl-CoA) and in mitochondria (donor acetyl-CoA), using NADPH, much as fatty acid synthase does.
Explanation

The ER system is the main one and works like fatty acid synthase (condense, reduce, dehydrate, reduce) on CoA esters, with malonyl-CoA as donor and NADPH as reductant. The mitochondrial system adds acetyl-CoA units. Both add two carbons at the carboxyl end, which is how palmitate becomes stearate and longer chains.

  • Elongation is in the smooth, not rough, ER, and propionyl-CoA (3C) is never the donor.
  • Smooth ER: acetyl-CoA; mitochondria: malonyl-CoA swaps the donors between the two sites.
Slides (1)
L30LearningHigh yield
Which are the two essential fatty acids, and to which ω family does each belong?
  1. A. Linoleic acid: ω-6
    α-Linolenic acid: ω-3
  2. B. Linoleic acid: ω-6
    Arachidonic acid: ω-6
  3. C. Linoleic acid: ω-3
    α-Linolenic acid: ω-6
AnswerA. Linoleic acid: ω-6
α-Linolenic acid: ω-3
WhyLinoleic acid (18:2Δ9,12, ω-6) and α-linolenic acid (18:3Δ9,12,15, ω-3) must come from the diet.
Explanation

The ω number is the position of the double bond nearest the methyl (ω) end, counted from that end. Linoleic acid's last bond is at Δ12 of 18 carbons: 18 − 12 = 6 → ω-6. α-Linolenic acid's last bond is at Δ15: 18 − 15 = 3 → ω-3. Both come from plant oils (and α-linolenic also from flaxseed, walnuts), and fish supply the longer ω-3s.

  • Arachidonic acid (ω-6) is made from linoleic acid, so it is essential only if linoleic acid is lacking.
  • Linoleic ω-3, α-linolenic ω-6 swaps the families.
Slides (2)
L31Learning
Which ω-3 fatty acids, concentrated in oily fish, are used clinically to lower plasma triacylglycerol?
  1. A. Linoleic and arachidonic acid
  2. B. EPA and DHA
  3. C. Oleic and palmitoleic acid
AnswerB. EPA and DHA
WhyThe marine ω-3 fatty acids EPA (20:5) and DHA (22:6) lower plasma triacylglycerol and are anti-thrombotic and anti-inflammatory.
Explanation

EPA and DHA reduce the liver's output of VLDL triacylglycerol, reduce platelet aggregation and improve endothelial function; this is the clinical importance of ω-3 fatty acids named in the lecture objectives (the slides show EPA and DHA highlighted on the ω-3 pathway). Typical modern diets have a high ω-6 : ω-3 ratio, and moving it toward ω-3 is considered cardioprotective.

  • Linoleic and arachidonic acid are ω-6 fatty acids; arachidonic acid is the precursor of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids.
  • Oleic and palmitoleic acid are monounsaturated fatty acids humans make themselves (ω-9, ω-7), not ω-3.
Slides (1)

Triacylglycerol: building, storing and moving it

L32Learning
Which organ is the primary site of triacylglycerol synthesis, and which is the main store?
  1. A. Synthesis: adipose tissue
    Storage: liver
  2. B. Synthesis: liver
    Storage: adipose tissue
  3. C. Synthesis: skeletal muscle
    Storage: adipose tissue
AnswerB. Synthesis: liver
Storage: adipose tissue
WhyThe liver is the primary site of TAG synthesis (it exports it as VLDL); adipose tissue is the main store (depot fat).
Explanation

The liver has everything for TAG synthesis: major de novo lipogenesis, glycerol 3-phosphate from both DHAP and glycerol (glycerol kinase), and free GLUT2 glucose entry. It keeps little TAG and packages it into VLDL, which delivers it to adipose tissue and muscle. Adipose tissue re-esterifies the delivered fatty acids and stores them.

  • The liver is not the main store; large liver TAG stores mean fatty liver.
  • Skeletal muscle mainly oxidises fatty acids and stores only small amounts of TAG.
Slides (2)

Glycerol 3-phosphate: liver versus adipose tissue

L33Learning
A 2-year-old has fasting hypoglycaemia and very high plasma and urine glycerol. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
  1. A. Glycerol kinase
  2. B. Glycerol 3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT)
  3. C. Hormone-sensitive lipase
AnswerA. Glycerol kinase
WhyThe liver's glycerol kinase phosphorylates the glycerol released by lipolysis; without it glycerol accumulates in blood and urine and is lost as a fasting gluconeogenic substrate.
Explanation

In fasting, hormone-sensitive lipase releases fatty acids and glycerol from adipose TAG. Adipose tissue cannot use the glycerol (no glycerol kinase), so it goes to the liver, where glycerol kinase makes glycerol 3-phosphate for gluconeogenesis (via DHAP) or TAG synthesis. A deficiency leaves glycerol unused: hyperglycerolaemia and glyceroluria, and less glucose made during fasting.

  • GPAT acts downstream on glycerol 3-phosphate; its loss would not raise free glycerol.
  • Hormone-sensitive lipase deficiency would lower glycerol release from fat.
Slides (1)

Acylation enzymes and clinical links

L34Learning
What does AGPAT deficiency cause?
  1. A. Familial hypertriglyceridaemia: excess adipose tissue + high VLDL
  2. B. Congenital generalised lipodystrophy: no adipose tissue + fatty liver
  3. C. Congenital generalised lipodystrophy: excess adipose tissue + normal liver
AnswerB. Congenital generalised lipodystrophy: no adipose tissue + fatty liver
WhyWithout AGPAT, adipocytes cannot make phosphatidic acid and TAG: congenital generalised lipodystrophy, with absent adipose tissue and fatty liver.
Explanation

If fat cannot be stored in adipose tissue, the fatty acids end up in the liver (and muscle), causing fatty liver and insulin resistance. AGPAT (acylglycerol-phosphate acyltransferase) adds the second acyl group, turning lysophosphatidic acid into phosphatidic acid.

  • Familial hypertriglyceridaemia is a lipoprotein disorder with normal or excess fat stores, not an AGPAT defect.
  • Lipodystrophy means loss of adipose tissue, and the liver is fatty, not normal.
Slides (1)
L35Learning
How does the high NADH/NAD+ ratio of chronic alcohol use push the liver toward fatty liver?
  1. A. ↓ Glycerol 3-phosphate (its oxidation to DHAP is speeded) and ↑ fatty acid oxidation → TAG broken down faster
  2. B. ↑ Glycerol kinase and ↑ VLDL export → TAG moved out of the liver faster
  3. C. ↑ Glycerol 3-phosphate (its oxidation to DHAP is blocked) and ↓ fatty acid oxidation → more TAG made and kept
AnswerC. ↑ Glycerol 3-phosphate (its oxidation to DHAP is blocked) and ↓ fatty acid oxidation → more TAG made and kept
WhyExcess NADH from ethanol oxidation blocks NAD+-requiring steps: glycerol 3-phosphate accumulates and β-oxidation slows, so fatty acyl-CoA is esterified into TAG that VLDL cannot clear.
Explanation

Alcohol and acetaldehyde dehydrogenases reduce NAD+ to NADH. With little NAD+, glycerol 3-phosphate cannot be oxidised to DHAP (so it piles up, phosphate-trapped in the hepatocyte), and β-oxidation slows (so fatty acyl-CoA piles up). The slide marks this block at "fatty acyl-CoA DH"; strictly, acyl-CoA dehydrogenase uses FAD, and the NAD+-requiring step that high NADH slows is 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase. The two substrates combine into TAG, while VLDL export is impaired. The same NAD+ shortage blocks gluconeogenesis from glycerol, adding hypoglycaemia.

  • High NADH slows NAD+-dependent oxidations; it does not speed them.
  • Alcohol impairs VLDL export.
Slides (2)
Tier 3The rest of the section+15 questions

Fat synthesis: the setting

L36Learning
Besides fatty acids, what can acetyl-CoA become?
  1. A. Citric acid cycle fuel
    Glucose (→ glycogen, ribose, lactose)
    Cholesterol (when glucagon is high)
  2. B. Glycine
    Cholesterol (→ bile acids, vitamin D, steroid hormones)
    Ketone bodies (when insulin is high)
  3. C. Citric acid cycle fuel
    Cholesterol (→ bile acids, vitamin D, steroid hormones)
    Ketone bodies (when insulin is low)
AnswerC. Citric acid cycle fuel
Cholesterol (→ bile acids, vitamin D, steroid hormones)
Ketone bodies (when insulin is low)
WhyAcetyl-CoA can be burned in the citric acid cycle, built into cholesterol and its products, or, when insulin is low, made into ketone bodies in the liver.
Explanation

Acetyl-CoA is the hub of fuel metabolism. In the fed state it goes to fatty acids (then triacylglycerol and membrane lipids) and cholesterol (then bile acids, vitamin D and steroid hormones). With low insulin, the liver turns the flood of acetyl-CoA from β-oxidation into ketone bodies.

  • Acetyl-CoA can make no net glucose: pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible, and the two carbons that enter the citric acid cycle leave as CO2.
  • It is not a source of glycine, and ketogenesis needs low, not high, insulin.
Slides (1)

Phase I: getting acetyl-CoA out as citrate

L37Learning
Why does citrate leave the mitochondrion only when the cell is well fuelled?
  1. A. High ATP and NADH activate isocitrate dehydrogenase → cycle speeds up → excess citrate leaks out
  2. B. High ATP and NADH inhibit isocitrate dehydrogenase → cycle backs up → citrate accumulates and leaks out
  3. C. Low ATP and NADH inhibit citrate synthase → cycle stalls → citrate accumulates and leaks out
AnswerB. High ATP and NADH inhibit isocitrate dehydrogenase → cycle backs up → citrate accumulates and leaks out
WhyWhen energy is high, ATP and NADH inhibit isocitrate dehydrogenase; the cycle backs up, citrate accumulates and is exported for fat synthesis.
Explanation

Isocitrate dehydrogenase is the cycle's rate-limiting step and is inhibited by ATP and NADH (a high NADH/NAD+ ratio). Isocitrate and citrate pile up, citrate leaves the matrix, and in the cytosol it both supplies acetyl-CoA and activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase. So the surplus that the cell cannot burn is diverted into storage.

  • High ATP and NADH slow, not speed up, the cycle.
  • Low ATP and NADH means the cell needs energy; the cycle runs fast and citrate is consumed, not exported.
Slides (2)
L38Learning
How does insulin speed the supply of citrate for fat synthesis in the liver?
  1. A. Activates fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase → ↑ fructose 6-phosphate → activates PFK-1 → faster glycolysis
  2. B. Inhibits PFK-2 → ↓ fructose 2,6-bisphosphate → releases PFK-1 → faster glycolysis
  3. C. Activates PFK-2 → ↑ fructose 2,6-bisphosphate → activates PFK-1 → faster glycolysis
AnswerC. Activates PFK-2 → ↑ fructose 2,6-bisphosphate → activates PFK-1 → faster glycolysis
WhyInsulin activates hepatic PFK-2; its product fructose 2,6-bisphosphate activates PFK-1, so glycolysis makes more pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → citrate.
Explanation

Phosphofructokinase-2 (PFK-2) is a bifunctional enzyme. In liver, insulin keeps it dephosphorylated, so its kinase is active and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6BP) rises. F2,6BP is the strongest activator of PFK-1, the rate-limiting step of glycolysis, and inhibits fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase. More glycolysis means more pyruvate for pyruvate dehydrogenase, and so more acetyl-CoA and citrate.

  • Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase is a gluconeogenic enzyme; insulin suppresses it.
  • Inhibiting PFK-2 lowers F2,6BP and slows glycolysis. That is what glucagon does.
Slides (2)

Supplying NADPH

L39Learning
Besides fatty acid synthesis, what else uses NADPH?
  1. A. β-Oxidation
    Cytochrome P450 system
    Detoxifying reactive oxygen species
  2. B. Steroid synthesis
    Cytochrome P450 system
    Detoxifying reactive oxygen species
  3. C. Steroid synthesis
    Glycolysis
    Detoxifying reactive oxygen species
AnswerB. Steroid synthesis
Cytochrome P450 system
Detoxifying reactive oxygen species
WhyNADPH is the reductant for biosynthesis (fatty acids, steroids, sterols), the cytochrome P450 system and antioxidant defence (glutathione).
Explanation

NADPH is kept highly reduced in the cytosol, so it is the electron donor for reductive synthesis (fatty acids, cholesterol and steroid hormones), for cytochrome P450 hydroxylations (drug metabolism, steroid synthesis) and for regenerating reduced glutathione, which detoxifies reactive oxygen species.

  • β-Oxidation is oxidative: it uses FAD and NAD+ and makes FADH2 and NADH.
  • Glycolysis uses NAD+ (at glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase), not NADPH.
Slides (2)

Phase III: fatty acid synthase builds palmitate

L40LearningHigh yield
In which direction is the palmitate chain built?
  1. A. From the carboxyl (α) end toward the ω-end
  2. B. From the ω-end toward the carboxyl (α) end
  3. C. From both ends toward the middle
AnswerB. From the ω-end toward the carboxyl (α) end
WhyThe acetyl primer becomes the ω-end (C15–16); each new unit is added at the thioester (carboxyl) end, so synthesis runs ω → α.
Explanation

The growing chain is always attached to the enzyme through its carboxyl carbon (as a thioester). New malonyl units are added at that end, so the first carbons laid down (the acetyl primer) end up at the methyl (ω) end and the last ones form the carboxyl group (C1, the α-end). Carbons are numbered from that carboxyl end.

  • Carboxyl → ω would require adding units at the methyl end, which has no activating group.
  • FAS has only one growing end; nothing is built from both ends.
Slides (1)
L41LearningHigh yield
What does thioesterase II do in the lactating breast?
  1. A. Releases shorter 8–12-carbon fatty acids, easier for infants to digest
  2. B. Adds double bonds to 16-carbon chains, making them easier for infants to digest
  3. C. Releases longer 20–22-carbon fatty acids, essential for infant brain growth
AnswerA. Releases shorter 8–12-carbon fatty acids, easier for infants to digest
WhyIn lactating mammary epithelium, thioesterase II (a separate cytosolic protein) cuts chains off FAS early, giving medium-chain (8–12C) fatty acids for milk.
Explanation

Medium-chain fatty acids in breast milk are easier for the infant to digest and absorb: they need less bile and pancreatic lipase and can enter the portal blood directly. Thioesterase II acts on the growing chain before FAS reaches 16 carbons.

  • Thioesterases hydrolyse thioester bonds; they do not add double bonds (that is the desaturases' job in the ER).
  • Longer 20–22-carbon fatty acids come from elongation and desaturation (or the diet), not from a thioesterase.
Slides (2)

Regulating acetyl-CoA carboxylase: minute to minute

L42Learning
Besides glucagon, adrenaline and palmitoyl-CoA, which two signals inhibit acetyl-CoA carboxylase?
  1. A. High NADPH (high energy)
    Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA)
  2. B. High ATP (high energy)
    Insulin
  3. C. High AMP (low energy)
    Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA)
AnswerC. High AMP (low energy)
Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA)
WhyHigh AMP (low energy, via AMPK) and dietary polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) both inhibit acetyl-CoA carboxylase.
Explanation

A rise in AMP (a low ATP/ADP ratio) means the cell is short of energy, so it should not spend ATP on fat synthesis; AMP inhibits ACC directly and by activating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which phosphorylates it. PUFA signal that dietary fat is abundant, so new synthesis is unnecessary (they also repress fatty acid synthase).

  • NADPH is a substrate of fatty acid synthase, not an inhibitor of ACC.
  • ATP favours the active polymer, and insulin activates ACC.
Slides (2)
L43Learning
How does citrate activate acetyl-CoA carboxylase structurally?
  1. A. Phosphorylates protomers into active dimers
  2. B. Polymerises protomers into active filaments
  3. C. Depolymerises filaments into active protomers
AnswerB. Polymerises protomers into active filaments
WhyCitrate increases polymerisation: inactive protomers link into long, active filaments, which form in the fed state.
Explanation

Citrate is an allosteric activator, so it acts by binding, not by covalent change. Its binding shifts the balance from free protomers to the filamentous polymer, the active enzyme. Palmitoyl-CoA, AMP and phosphorylation shift it back.

  • Citrate is a metabolite, not a kinase, so it phosphorylates nothing; phosphorylation (by AMPK) actually inactivates ACC.
  • Depolymerisation inactivates; that is what palmitoyl-CoA does.
Slides (2)

Elongation, desaturation and the essential ω families

L44LearningHigh yield
Where does the first double bond almost always go, and which enzyme places it?
  1. A. Δ12 (between C12 and C13); Δ12 desaturase
  2. B. Δ9 (between C9 and C10); stearoyl-CoA (Δ9) desaturase
  3. C. Δ9 (between C9 and C10); fatty acid synthase dehydratase
AnswerB. Δ9 (between C9 and C10); stearoyl-CoA (Δ9) desaturase
WhyStearoyl-CoA desaturase (Δ9 desaturase) places the initial double bond between C9 and C10; further double bonds are added after that.
Explanation

Δ numbers count from the carboxyl carbon (C1). The first double bond in a saturated fatty acid is nearly always at Δ9, made by the ER Δ9 desaturase; for example stearic 18:0 → oleic 18:1Δ9 and palmitic 16:0 → palmitoleic 16:1Δ9. Humans then add bonds only between C9 and the carboxyl end.

  • Humans have no Δ12 desaturase, which is exactly why linoleic acid (Δ9,12) is essential.
  • The FAS dehydratase forms a transient double bond inside each cycle that is reduced at once; it does not make unsaturated fatty acids.
Slides (1)
L45Learning
γ-Linolenic acid (18:3Δ6,9,12) is elongated by two carbons. What is the product?
  1. A. 20:3Δ6,9,12
  2. B. 20:3Δ4,7,10
  3. C. 20:3Δ8,11,14
AnswerC. 20:3Δ8,11,14
WhyElongases add two carbons at the carboxyl end (C1), so every existing double bond moves two numbers up: Δ6,9,12 → Δ8,11,14.
Explanation

Δ numbers count from the carboxyl carbon. Adding C1 and C2 at that end pushes each double bond two places further away, while its distance from the ω-end does not change (still ω-6). Δ5 desaturase then adds a bond at Δ5, giving arachidonic acid, 20:4Δ5,8,11,14, exactly the sequence on the ω-6 pathway.

  • Δ6,9,12 would be right only if carbons were added at the ω-end.
  • Δ4,7,10 moves the bonds the wrong way, as if counting from the ω-end.
Slides (1)
L46LearningHigh yield
A teenager eats a strictly fat-free diet for several weeks. Which fatty acid can he no longer make in normal amounts?
  1. A. Arachidonic acid (20:4)
  2. B. Palmitic acid (16:0)
  3. C. Oleic acid (18:1)
AnswerA. Arachidonic acid (20:4)
WhyArachidonic acid is made only from dietary linoleic acid; without dietary fat its supply (and that of the prostaglandins made from it) falls.
Explanation

Fatty acid synthesis from carbohydrate gives palmitic acid, elongation gives stearic acid, and Δ9 desaturase gives oleic acid, so the ω-9 and saturated fatty acids, triacylglycerol, phospholipids and cholesterol can all still be made. The ω-6 line (linoleic → γ-linolenic → arachidonic) cannot start without the essential precursor. Exam versions ask which lipid is most deficient: prostaglandins, which come from arachidonic acid.

  • Palmitic acid is the direct product of fatty acid synthase from carbohydrate.
  • Oleic acid is made by Δ9 desaturase from stearic acid.

Arachidonic acid is therefore not strictly essential when linoleic acid is adequate.

Slides (1)

Triacylglycerol: building, storing and moving it

L47Learning
What is a triacylglycerol (TAG) built from?
  1. A. Two fatty acyl-CoA and one phosphocholine added to a glycerol 3-phosphate backbone
  2. B. Three fatty acyl-CoA added one at a time to a glycerol 3-phosphate backbone
  3. C. Three free fatty acids added all at once to a free glycerol backbone
AnswerB. Three fatty acyl-CoA added one at a time to a glycerol 3-phosphate backbone
WhyTAG is glycerol esterified with three fatty acids, added one at a time from fatty acyl-CoA onto glycerol 3-phosphate.
Explanation

Each fatty acid is joined by an ester bond at its –COOH, which removes its negative charge, so TAG is a "neutral fat". The acyl groups go on in sequence: monoacylglycerol-level (lysophosphatidic acid) → phosphatidic acid → diacylglycerol → TAG. The fatty acids must be activated to acyl-CoA first; the backbone is glycerol 3-phosphate, not free glycerol.

  • Two acyl groups plus a phosphocholine head group is a phospholipid (phosphatidylcholine), not TAG.
  • Free fatty acids and free glycerol are not substrates: both must be activated (acyl-CoA; glycerol 3-phosphate).
Slides (2)
L48Learning
Which fatty acids typically sit on C1, C2 and C3 of stored TAG?
  1. A. C1 unsaturated
    C2 saturated
    C3 variable
  2. B. C1 variable
    C2 saturated
    C3 unsaturated
  3. C. C1 saturated
    C2 unsaturated
    C3 variable
AnswerC. C1 saturated
C2 unsaturated
C3 variable
WhyStored TAG usually has a saturated fatty acid on C1, an unsaturated one on C2 and a variable one on C3.
Explanation

The acyltransferases have positional preferences: GPAT tends to put a saturated acyl group on C1 of glycerol 3-phosphate, and AGPAT puts an unsaturated one on C2. C3 is filled last by DGAT with whatever acyl-CoA is available. The middle unsaturated chain is also what pancreatic lipase leaves behind as 2-monoacylglycerol.

  • C1 unsaturated, C2 saturated swaps the rule for C1 and C2; C1 variable, C2 saturated, C3 unsaturated misplaces all three (the variable position is C3, and C2 carries the unsaturated chain).

Memory hook: "saturated first, unsaturated in the middle".

Slides (1)
L49LearningHigh yield
Where do adipose tissue and muscle get most of the fatty acids for their TAG?
  1. A. Plasma: FFA on LDL, or TAG of VLDL (after a meal) and chylomicrons (post-absorptive, 6–12 h later)
  2. B. Plasma: FFA on albumin, or TAG of chylomicrons (after a meal) and VLDL (post-absorptive, 6–12 h later)
  3. C. Plasma: FFA on transferrin, or TAG of HDL (after a meal) and LDL (post-absorptive, 6–12 h later)
AnswerB. Plasma: FFA on albumin, or TAG of chylomicrons (after a meal) and VLDL (post-absorptive, 6–12 h later)
WhyFrom plasma: non-esterified fatty acids on albumin, or TAG in chylomicrons after a meal and VLDL in the post-absorptive state.
Explanation

Post-prandial means during and for several hours after a meal: chylomicrons bring dietary fat. Post-absorptive means 6–12 hours after a meal: VLDL brings liver-made fat. In both cases lipoprotein lipase must first hydrolyse the lipoprotein TAG. Adipocytes make relatively little fatty acid themselves.

  • The LDL / VLDL-after-a-meal choice swaps the timing of chylomicrons and VLDL, and free fatty acids ride on albumin, not LDL.
  • Transferrin carries iron; HDL and LDL are cholesterol carriers, not the main TAG sources.
Slides (2)

Glycerol 3-phosphate: liver versus adipose tissue

L50Learning
Where does each tissue get most of the fatty acids for its TAG: liver versus adipose tissue?
  1. A. Liver: its own synthesis (major)
    Adipose: lipoproteins via LPL (little made there)
  2. B. Liver: lipoproteins via LPL (major)
    Adipose: its own synthesis (major)
  3. C. Liver: chylomicron remnants via LPL (major)
    Adipose: albumin-bound FFA (little made there)
AnswerA. Liver: its own synthesis (major)
Adipose: lipoproteins via LPL (little made there)
WhyThe liver makes most of its own fatty acids (major de novo lipogenesis); adipose makes few and takes them from chylomicrons and VLDL via LPL.
Explanation
LiverAdipose
Glucose entryGLUT2GLUT4, insulin-dependent
Glycerol 3-P fromDHAP + free glycerolDHAP only
Fatty acids fromown synthesis (major)lipoproteins via LPL
TAGexported as VLDLstored
  • Liver from lipoproteins, adipose from its own synthesis reverses the tissues.
  • LPL acts on the capillaries of adipose tissue and muscle, not on the liver's main supply, and albumin-bound FFA is a lesser source for adipose.

BIO-L26 Degradation of triacylglycerols & fatty acids; ketone bodies (+ CV FA metabolic defect / MCAD)

Tier 1: 25 of 71
Learning questions 71
Tier 1Every concept once25 questions

Fasting: releasing stored fat

L1LearningHigh yield
Which adipose-tissue enzyme releases fatty acids from stored triacylglycerol (TAG) during fasting?
  1. A. Lipoprotein lipase (LPL)
  2. B. Acyl-CoA synthetase
  3. C. Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL)
AnswerC. Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL)
WhyHormone-sensitive lipase inside the adipocyte hydrolyses stored TAG to fatty acids and glycerol when insulin is low.
Explanation

Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) is the intracellular lipase of the fat cell. Its activity is set by hormones (hence the name): switched on by glucagon and adrenaline, switched off by insulin. It splits stored triacylglycerol so that fatty acids and glycerol leave the adipocyte.
