  • Lipoprotein lipase is the sister enzyme on the capillary wall. It is activated by insulin in the fed state and frees fatty acids from circulating chylomicrons and VLDL so adipose tissue can store them.
  • Acyl-CoA synthetase activates a free fatty acid inside the cell that will burn or store it; it does not release fat.

Hook: LPL loads the adipocyte (fed), HSL empties it (fasting).

Slides (3)
L2Learning
During a fast, how does hepatic fat breakdown support gluconeogenesis?
  1. A. Fatty acids supply carbon; acetyl-CoA is converted to pyruvate; glycerol supplies ATP
  2. B. Fatty acid oxidation supplies ATP; acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase; glycerol supplies carbon
  3. C. Fatty acid oxidation supplies ATP; acetyl-CoA inhibits pyruvate carboxylase; glycerol supplies carbon
AnswerB. Fatty acid oxidation supplies ATP; acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase; glycerol supplies carbon
Whyβ-Oxidation provides the ATP and the acetyl-CoA (obligatory activator of pyruvate carboxylase) that gluconeogenesis needs; glycerol provides the carbon.
Explanation

Gluconeogenesis is energetically expensive and starts with pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate → oxaloacetate), which is inactive without its allosteric activator acetyl-CoA. During fasting, hepatic β-oxidation of fatty acids from adipose tissue supplies both: ATP (and NADH) to drive the pathway, and acetyl-CoA to switch on pyruvate carboxylase (acetyl-CoA also inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase, so pyruvate is not burned). The carbon skeletons come from lactate, amino acids and glycerol.

  • Acetyl-CoA → pyruvate cannot happen: pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible, so fatty acids give no net glucose carbon.
  • Acetyl-CoA inhibiting pyruvate carboxylase is the reversal of its real effect.

This is why fatty acid oxidation defects (e.g. MCAD deficiency) cause fasting hypoglycaemia.

Slides (2)

Activation and the carnitine shuttle

L3Learning
What does activating a fatty acid to acyl-CoA cost, and why that much?
  1. A. 2 ATP equivalents: two ATP are each split to ADP + Pi
  2. B. 1 ATP equivalent: one ATP is split to ADP + Pi
  3. C. 2 ATP equivalents: ATP is split to AMP + PPi, and PPi is hydrolysed
AnswerC. 2 ATP equivalents: ATP is split to AMP + PPi, and PPi is hydrolysed
WhyAcyl-CoA synthetase splits ATP to AMP + PPi; pyrophosphatase then hydrolyses PPi, so two high-energy bonds are spent.
Explanation

Fatty acid + CoA + ATP → fatty acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi. Pyrophosphatase immediately hydrolyses PPi to 2 Pi, pulling the reaction forward. Two phosphoanhydride bonds are used, and regenerating ATP from AMP takes two phosphorylations, so the cost is counted as 2 ATP. That is the '−2' in the palmitate yield (131 − 2 = 129), paid once per fatty acid, however long the chain.

  • Two ATP to ADP gives the right count by the wrong chemistry: only one ATP molecule is used.
  • One ATP to ADP undercounts: the AMP-forming reaction costs two bonds.
Slides (2)
L4Learning
What are the three steps of the carnitine shuttle, in order?
  1. A. CPT-II (outer membrane): acyl-CoA → acylcarnitine
    CACT: carries acylcarnitine in, free carnitine out
    CPT-I (inner membrane): acylcarnitine → acyl-CoA in the matrix
  2. B. CPT-I (inner membrane): acylcarnitine → acyl-CoA
    CACT: carries acylcarnitine out, free carnitine in
    CPT-II (outer membrane): acyl-CoA → acylcarnitine in the cytosol
  3. C. CPT-I (outer membrane): acyl-CoA → acylcarnitine
    CACT: carries acylcarnitine in, free carnitine out
    CPT-II (inner membrane): acylcarnitine → acyl-CoA in the matrix
AnswerC. CPT-I (outer membrane): acyl-CoA → acylcarnitine
CACT: carries acylcarnitine in, free carnitine out
CPT-II (inner membrane): acylcarnitine → acyl-CoA in the matrix
WhyCPT-I on the outer membrane makes acylcarnitine, CACT swaps it across the inner membrane for free carnitine, and CPT-II rebuilds acyl-CoA in the matrix.
Explanation

CPT = carnitine palmitoyltransferase (also called carnitine acyltransferase); CACT = carnitine–acylcarnitine translocase.

  • CPT-I, outer membrane: acyl group moves from CoA to carnitine (forward reaction). This is the rate-limiting, malonyl-CoA-sensitive step.
  • CACT, inner membrane: antiporter, acylcarnitine in, free carnitine out.
  • CPT-II, inner face of inner membrane: acyl group moves back from carnitine to matrix CoA (reverse reaction); the acyl-CoA enters β-oxidation and carnitine recycles.

The swapped choice puts CPT-II outside; the reversed choice runs the shuttle backwards. Hook: CPT-I is the first enzyme the fatty acid meets (outer membrane); CPT-II is the second (inner membrane).

Slides (3)

Control: malonyl-CoA and CPT-I

L5LearningHigh yield
What is the rate-limiting step of fatty acid oxidation, and what inhibits it?
  1. A. CPT-I; citrate
  2. B. CPT-II; malonyl-CoA
  3. C. CPT-I; malonyl-CoA
AnswerC. CPT-I; malonyl-CoA
WhyCarnitine palmitoyltransferase I controls the entry of long chains into mitochondria and is inhibited by malonyl-CoA.
Explanation

CPT-I on the outer mitochondrial membrane is the gate of fatty acid oxidation: once a long-chain acyl group is inside the matrix it is committed to β-oxidation. Malonyl-CoA, the first intermediate of fatty acid synthesis, binds CPT-I and inhibits it, so the gate shuts whenever the cell is making fat.

  • Citrate is the activator of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (fat synthesis); it does not act on CPT-I.
  • CPT-II works on the inner membrane after the decision has been made; it is not malonyl-CoA-sensitive and not rate-limiting.
Slides (2)
L6Learning
What is the end product of fatty acid synthesis vs breakdown?
  1. A. Synthesis: stearate
    Breakdown: malonyl-CoA
  2. B. Synthesis: acetyl-CoA
    Breakdown: palmitate
  3. C. Synthesis: palmitate
    Breakdown: acetyl-CoA
AnswerC. Synthesis: palmitate
Breakdown: acetyl-CoA
WhyFatty acid synthase releases palmitate (16:0); β-oxidation cuts a fatty acid into acetyl-CoA units.
Explanation

Fatty acid synthase stops at 16 carbons, releasing palmitate; longer chains need elongases in the ER. β-Oxidation ends with acetyl-CoA (plus propionyl-CoA for odd chains), which goes to the citric acid cycle or, in the fasting liver, to ketone bodies.

SynthesisBreakdown
Whenfedstarved
Whereliver cytosolmuscle/liver mitochondria
Carriercitratecarnitine
CoenzymeNADPHNAD+, FAD
ControlACCCPT-I
Productpalmitateacetyl-CoA

Stearate is an elongation product; malonyl-CoA is a synthesis intermediate.

Slides (1)

Beta-oxidation and ATP yield

L7LearningHigh yield
What are the four reaction types of one β-oxidation cycle, in order?
  1. A. Oxidation → hydration → oxidation → thiolysis
  2. B. Oxidation → oxidation → hydration → thiolysis
  3. C. Hydration → oxidation → oxidation → thiolysis
AnswerA. Oxidation → hydration → oxidation → thiolysis
WhyDehydrogenation (FAD) → hydration → dehydrogenation (NAD+) → thiolysis: the four-step cycle of β-oxidation.
Explanation
  • Oxidation 1: acyl-CoA dehydrogenase removes 2 H (→ FADH2) to make a trans double bond.
  • Hydration: enoyl-CoA hydratase adds water across it → 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA.
  • Oxidation 2: 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase oxidises the OH to a ketone (→ NADH).
  • Thiolysis: thiolase uses CoA to cut off acetyl-CoA.

The hydration must sit between the two oxidations: a double bond cannot be oxidised again until water has made it an alcohol. Synthesis runs the mirror sequence: condensation → reduction → dehydration → reduction.

Slides (2)
L8LearningHigh yield
How many ATP does complete oxidation of one palmitate (16:0) yield, compared with one glucose (lecture values)?
  1. A. Palmitate 129; glucose 36–38
  2. B. Palmitate 131; glucose 36–38
  3. C. Palmitate 106; glucose 36–38
AnswerA. Palmitate 129; glucose 36–38
WhyPalmitate gives 129 ATP (131 made − 2 for activation) versus 36–38 for glucose, using the older P/O values the lecture uses.
Explanation

With NADH = 3, FADH2 = 2 and acetyl-CoA = 12 ATP, palmitate's 7 FADH2 + 7 NADH + 8 acetyl-CoA give 14 + 21 + 96 = 131, minus the 2 ATP equivalents spent on activation = 129. A glucose molecule gives 36–38 on the same scale.

  • 131 is the gross figure, before the activation cost is subtracted.
  • 106 is the modern figure (NADH 2.5, FADH2 1.5); it does not belong with the lecture's 36–38 for glucose (modern glucose ≈ 30–32).
Slides (2)

Peroxisomes, α- and ω-oxidation

L9LearningHigh yield
Where does each minor fatty acid oxidation pathway run?
  1. A. ω-oxidation: peroxisome
    α-oxidation: ER
    VLCFA β-oxidation: mitochondria
  2. B. ω-oxidation: ER
    α-oxidation: peroxisome
    VLCFA β-oxidation: peroxisome
  3. C. ω-oxidation: mitochondria
    α-oxidation: peroxisome
    VLCFA β-oxidation: ER
AnswerB. ω-oxidation: ER
α-oxidation: peroxisome
VLCFA β-oxidation: peroxisome
Whyω-oxidation is in the endoplasmic reticulum; α-oxidation and β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA) are both in peroxisomes.
Explanation

Only ordinary β-oxidation is mitochondrial. The awkward substrates go elsewhere:

  • ω-oxidation uses cytochrome P450 of the smooth ER to oxidise the methyl (ω) end.
  • α-oxidation of branched phytanic acid is peroxisomal (defect: adult Refsum disease).
  • VLCFA (>C20) are shortened by peroxisomal β-oxidation (defects: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, Zellweger).

The wrong choices scramble these organelles; VLCFA cannot start in mitochondria, and the ER does no β-oxidation. Hook: the two 'P' pathways (phytanic, very long) are Peroxisomal.

Slides (2)

Odd-chain and unsaturated fatty acids

L10Learning
How is propionyl-CoA converted to succinyl-CoA?
  1. A. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin, ATP) → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → racemase → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12) → succinyl-CoA
  2. B. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (B12, ATP) → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → racemase → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (biotin) → succinyl-CoA
  3. C. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin, ATP) → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → racemase → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12) → succinyl-CoA
AnswerA. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin, ATP) → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → racemase → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12) → succinyl-CoA
WhyCarboxylase (biotin, ATP) → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → racemase → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → mutase (vitamin B12) → succinyl-CoA.
Explanation
  • Propionyl-CoA carboxylase adds CO2 using ATP and biotin (the same chemistry as pyruvate and acetyl-CoA carboxylases) → D-methylmalonyl-CoA.
  • Methylmalonyl-CoA racemase (epimerase) converts D → L.
  • Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, with deoxyadenosylcobalamin (B12), rearranges the carbon skeleton → succinyl-CoA.

Succinyl-CoA enters the citric acid cycle and can go on to glucose. The wrong choices swap the two vitamins or the D/L order. Hook: carboxylases use biotin; the mutase uses B12.

Slides (3)
L11Learning
Which two extra enzymes does β-oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids need?
  1. A. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase
    Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
  2. B. Enoyl-CoA hydratase
    FAD-dependent acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
  3. C. Enoyl-CoA isomerase
    NADPH-dependent 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase
AnswerC. Enoyl-CoA isomerase
NADPH-dependent 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase
WhyNatural cis double bonds sit in the wrong place for the cycle; enoyl-CoA isomerase and NADPH-dependent (2,4-dienoyl-CoA) reductase reposition or remove them.
Explanation

The cycle's hydratase only accepts a trans-Δ2 double bond. Dietary unsaturated fatty acids have cis bonds at odd or even positions.

  • A cis-Δ3 bond (odd position) is moved to trans-Δ2 by enoyl-CoA isomerase; the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase step is skipped.
  • A double bond at an even position creates a 2,4-dienoyl-CoA, which 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase reduces with NADPH before the isomerase finishes the job.

Wrong choices: hydratase and acyl-CoA dehydrogenase are the standard enzymes of every cycle; propionyl-CoA carboxylase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase are the extras for odd-chain fatty acids, the other awkward case.

Slides (2)

Ketone bodies: why and how the liver makes them

L12LearningHigh yield
When does the liver make ketone bodies in large amounts?
  1. A. When fat is burned faster than the citric acid cycle can use the acetyl-CoA (prolonged fasting, uncontrolled diabetes)
  2. B. When protein is broken down faster than the urea cycle can clear the ammonia (prolonged fasting, liver failure)
  3. C. When glucose is burned faster than the citric acid cycle can use the pyruvate (exercise, hyperglycaemia)
AnswerA. When fat is burned faster than the citric acid cycle can use the acetyl-CoA (prolonged fasting, uncontrolled diabetes)
WhyLow insulin floods the liver with fatty acids; β-oxidation makes more acetyl-CoA than the citric acid cycle can take, and the surplus becomes ketone bodies.
Explanation

Ketogenesis is the liver's overflow route for acetyl-CoA. In fasting or type 1 diabetes insulin is low and glucagon high, so hormone-sensitive lipase releases fatty acids that pour into the liver. Their β-oxidation makes acetyl-CoA faster than the citric acid cycle can burn it, because oxaloacetate is being drawn off into gluconeogenesis and the high NADH from β-oxidation slows the cycle. The excess acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria is condensed into ketone bodies and exported as a water-soluble fuel.

  • Protein breakdown beyond urea-cycle capacity raises ammonia, not ketones.
  • Glucose oxidation is low in these states; carbohydrate does not feed ketogenesis.
Slides (3)
L13Learning
What are the four steps of ketone body synthesis?
  1. A. Thiolase: 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA
    HMG-CoA synthase: + acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA
    HMG-CoA lyase: → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA
    3-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (NADH): → β-hydroxybutyrate
  2. B. HMG-CoA synthase: 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA
    Thiolase: + acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA
    HMG-CoA lyase: → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA
    3-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (NAD+): → β-hydroxybutyrate
  3. C. Thiolase: 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA
    HMG-CoA lyase: + acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA
    HMG-CoA synthase: → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA
    3-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (NADH): → β-hydroxybutyrate
AnswerA. Thiolase: 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA
HMG-CoA synthase: + acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA
HMG-CoA lyase: → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA
3-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (NADH): → β-hydroxybutyrate
WhyThiolase joins 2 acetyl-CoA, HMG-CoA synthase adds a third, HMG-CoA lyase releases acetoacetate, and 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase reduces it with NADH.
Explanation

All four steps run in liver mitochondria:

  • Thiolase: 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA (the last step of β-oxidation run backwards).
  • HMG-CoA synthase: acetoacetyl-CoA + a third acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA). This is the regulated step.
  • HMG-CoA lyase: HMG-CoA → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA.
  • 3-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase: acetoacetate + NADH → β-hydroxybutyrate + NAD+.

The wrong options swap synthase with thiolase or with lyase, or give the reduction NAD+ instead of NADH. Net: three acetyl-CoA go in, one comes back out, and one four-carbon acetoacetate leaves.

Slides (3)

Ketone bodies: fuel for a long fast

L14LearningHigh yield
Why can't the liver use the ketone bodies it makes?
  1. A. It lacks thiolase
  2. B. It lacks HMG-CoA synthase
  3. C. It lacks thiophorase
AnswerC. It lacks thiophorase
WhyThe liver has no thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase), so it cannot reactivate acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA; it makes ketones but must export them.
Explanation

This is what makes ketone bodies a fuel for other organs. The liver builds them, but without thiophorase it cannot turn acetoacetate back into acetoacetyl-CoA, so the ketones are released to the blood instead of being burned where they are made. The liver's own energy in fasting comes from β-oxidation of fatty acids.

  • Liver has plenty of thiolase: it uses it in β-oxidation and in the first step of ketogenesis.
  • Liver is rich in mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase: that is how it makes ketones.

Exam phrasing: "which tissue cannot use ketone bodies?" → liver (and red cells, which lack mitochondria).

Slides (3)
L15Learning
What is the main survival benefit of ketone production in a prolonged fast?
  1. A. It fuels the liver, so less fat must be released from adipose tissue
  2. B. It fuels the brain, so less muscle protein is broken down for gluconeogenesis
  3. C. It fuels red cells, so less lactate returns to the liver
AnswerB. It fuels the brain, so less muscle protein is broken down for gluconeogenesis
WhyKetones let the brain run largely on fat-derived fuel, so the body needs far less glucose from muscle protein and can survive weeks without food.
Explanation

Fatty acids cannot be turned into glucose (acetyl-CoA gives no net oxaloacetate), and the brain cannot oxidise fatty acids. Early in a fast the brain's glucose therefore comes from gluconeogenesis, largely from amino acids released by muscle protein breakdown. Once ketones rise, the brain burns them instead, glucose demand falls and proteolysis slows: protein is spared and survival is extended.

  • The liver cannot use ketones.
  • Red cells cannot use ketones (no mitochondria); they keep using glucose and return lactate to the liver (Cori cycle).
Slides (1)

Diabetic ketoacidosis

L16Learning
What hormone pattern drives diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?
  1. A. Little insulin, little glucagon: the fasting programme switched off
  2. B. Little insulin, much glucagon: the fasting programme running unchecked
  3. C. Much insulin, much glucagon: the fed and fasting programmes both on
AnswerB. Little insulin, much glucagon: the fasting programme running unchecked
WhyUncontrolled (usually type 1) diabetes gives ↓ insulin and ↑ glucagon: the liver behaves as if starving even though blood glucose is high.
Explanation

In ordinary fasting a little insulin is still secreted and restrains lipolysis and ketogenesis, so ketones settle at a level the buffers can handle. In type 1 diabetes without insulin there is no brake: glucagon acts unopposed, so lipolysis, β-oxidation, ketogenesis and gluconeogenesis all run flat out. Ketones are made far faster than tissues can use them, and the acids overwhelm the bicarbonate buffer.

  • Low glucagon would switch fat mobilisation off, not on.
  • High insulin blocks hormone-sensitive lipase and activates ACC, so ketogenesis would stop.
Slides (2)

MCAD deficiency: the defect

L17LearningHigh yield
Which pathway is most directly affected by medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency?
  1. A. Peroxisomal α-oxidation of C14–C18 fatty acids
  2. B. Mitochondrial β-oxidation of C6–C12 fatty acids
  3. C. Peroxisomal β-oxidation of fatty acids over C20
AnswerB. Mitochondrial β-oxidation of C6–C12 fatty acids
WhyMCAD catalyses the first step of each mitochondrial β-oxidation turn for C6–C12 acyl-CoAs; SCAD (<C6), LCAD (C14–C18) and VLCAD (>C20) cover the other lengths.
Explanation

β-Oxidation uses a family of chain-length-specific acyl-CoA dehydrogenases. A long fatty acid such as palmitate (C16) starts on LCAD, but once it is shortened to C12 and below it needs MCAD. In MCAD deficiency every chain therefore stalls at medium length (C6–C10), so even long-chain fat cannot be fully oxidised. It is the commonest inherited defect of fatty acid oxidation.

  • α-Oxidation is the peroxisomal route for branched phytanic acid (defective in adult Refsum disease).
  • Peroxisomal β-oxidation shortens very-long-chain fatty acids (>C20); it is defective in Zellweger syndrome and X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.
Slides (2)
L18LearningHigh yield
Individuals with MCAD deficiency have reduced gluconeogenesis because of…
  1. A. Low ATP and high acetyl-CoA
  2. B. High ATP and low acetyl-CoA
  3. C. Low ATP and low acetyl-CoA
AnswerC. Low ATP and low acetyl-CoA
WhyWithout β-oxidation the fasting liver lacks ATP to power gluconeogenesis and acetyl-CoA, the obligatory activator of pyruvate carboxylase.
Explanation

Gluconeogenesis is expensive (about 6 ATP equivalents per glucose), and in the fasting liver that energy comes from β-oxidation. β-Oxidation also supplies the acetyl-CoA that allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase, the first step from pyruvate to oxaloacetate. With MCAD blocked both fall together, so gluconeogenesis stalls just when glycogen has run out.

  • Acetyl-CoA is low, not high: it comes from the oxidation that is blocked (which is also why ketones are low).
  • ATP is low, not high, for the same reason.
Slides (2)

Helga's case: MCAD deficiency in practice

L19Learning
Why is Helga's plasma anion gap 20 (normal 8–16)?
  1. A. Ketone bodies (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate) have accumulated
  2. B. Medium-chain monocarboxylic and dicarboxylic acids have accumulated
  3. C. Bicarbonate has been lost in three days of vomiting
AnswerB. Medium-chain monocarboxylic and dicarboxylic acids have accumulated
WhyThe unmeasured anions are the medium-chain mono- and dicarboxylic acids that escape the MCAD block, not ketones, which are only a trace.
Explanation

The anion gap rises when an acid adds unmeasured anions to plasma while its H+ uses up bicarbonate. In Helga those acids are octanoate, hexanoate and the ω-oxidation products (adipic, suberic, sebacic acids), each with one or two carboxyl groups. Her acidosis is the mirror image of DKA's: a high gap without ketones.

  • Ketone bodies are a trace (hypoketosis), so they cannot explain the gap.
  • Vomiting loses gastric acid (HCl), which pushes toward metabolic alkalosis; and bicarbonate loss would give a normal-gap acidosis anyway.
Slides (2)
L20Learning
Which list is the case's differential diagnosis for hypoketotic hypoglycaemia?
  1. A. Carnitine deficiency
    CPT deficiency
    LCAD deficiency
    MCAD deficiency
    Type 1 diabetes
  2. B. Carnitine deficiency
    CPT deficiency
    LCAD deficiency
    MCAD deficiency
    Congenital hyperinsulinism
  3. C. Carnitine excess
    CPT deficiency
    Thiophorase deficiency
    MCAD deficiency
    Congenital hyperinsulinism
AnswerB. Carnitine deficiency
CPT deficiency
LCAD deficiency
MCAD deficiency
Congenital hyperinsulinism
WhyLow ketones with low glucose mean either fat cannot be oxidised (carnitine, CPT, LCAD, MCAD defects) or insulin is blocking lipolysis (congenital hyperinsulinism).
Explanation

Two mechanisms produce hypoketotic hypoglycaemia:

  • A block in fatty acid oxidation: no carnitine (carnitine deficiency), no shuttle (CPT deficiency), or no dehydrogenase for long (LCAD) or medium (MCAD) chains. Fat is released but cannot be burned.
  • Too much insulin (congenital hyperinsulinism): lipolysis and ketogenesis are suppressed, so fat is never released.

Type 1 diabetes gives hyperglycaemia with high ketones. Thiophorase deficiency causes ketoacidosis (ketones made but not used), and carnitine excess is not a disease.

Slides (2)
L21LearningHigh yield
What dietary advice is given for an infant with MCAD deficiency?
  1. A. Never fast: feeds every 3–4 h with high fat; prefer medium-chain-TAG formula
  2. B. Never fast: feeds every 3–4 h with adequate complex carbohydrate; avoid medium-chain-TAG formula
  3. C. Fast overnight: feeds every 8–10 h with simple sugars; avoid medium-chain-TAG formula
AnswerB. Never fast: feeds every 3–4 h with adequate complex carbohydrate; avoid medium-chain-TAG formula
WhyPrevention is avoiding fasting: frequent (every 3–4 h) feeds with enough complex carbohydrate, and no formula based on medium-chain triacylglycerol.
Explanation

The child's only problem is that medium-chain fat cannot be burned once glycogen runs out, so management keeps the glucose supply continuous: feeds every 3–4 hours, adequate calories from slowly digested complex carbohydrate, extra carbohydrate during illness, and no long fasts. Formulas whose main fat is medium-chain triacylglycerol (MCT) are avoided because those are the very chains MCAD must oxidise.

  • High-fat and MCT-rich feeding loads the blocked pathway.
  • Long overnight fasts are exactly what triggers a crisis.
Slides (2)

Carnitine-shuttle defects and ackee poisoning

L22Learning
What causes primary carnitine deficiency, and how does it present (as taught)?
  1. A. Too little carnitine (vegan diet; transporter, liver synthesis or renal reabsorption defects); peripheral neuropathy and ataxia
  2. B. Too much carnitine (meat-rich diet; overactive transporter or reabsorption); hypoglycaemia with ketosis
  3. C. Too little carnitine (vegan diet; transporter, liver synthesis or renal reabsorption defects); muscle cramps and weakness
AnswerC. Too little carnitine (vegan diet; transporter, liver synthesis or renal reabsorption defects); muscle cramps and weakness
WhyPrimary carnitine deficiency is low cellular carnitine from poor intake, a defective carnitine transporter, poor liver synthesis or renal loss; it causes muscle cramps and weakness.
Explanation

Without carnitine, long-chain fatty acids cannot be carried into mitochondria, so the tissues that live on fat suffer most. Heart and skeletal muscle cannot make carnitine and depend on uptake through a high-affinity plasma-membrane transporter, so a transporter defect starves them: mild to severe cramps and weakness (clinically also cardiomyopathy and fasting hypoketotic hypoglycaemia). Strict vegans can become deficient because carnitine comes mainly from meat.

  • Neuropathy and ataxia belong to adult Refsum disease.
  • Carnitine excess is not a disease, and ketosis needs working fat oxidation.
Slides (2)
L23Learning
How does hypoglycin A block β-oxidation?
  1. A. Its metabolites inhibit HMG-CoA synthase
  2. B. It raises malonyl-CoA, which blocks CPT-I
  3. C. Its metabolites sequester carnitine and CoA
AnswerC. Its metabolites sequester carnitine and CoA
WhyHypoglycin A's metabolites trap carnitine and CoA, so fatty acids can be neither activated nor shuttled, and β-oxidation stops.
Explanation

Hypoglycin A is converted to methylenecyclopropylacetyl-CoA (MCPA-CoA), which forms dead-end esters that tie up the cell's CoA and carnitine (and also directly inhibits short- and medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenases). Without free CoA and carnitine, fatty acids cannot be oxidised, so the liver loses the ATP and acetyl-CoA it needs for gluconeogenesis: severe hypoglycaemia, by the same logic as MCAD deficiency.

  • Blocking HMG-CoA synthase would stop ketogenesis but not β-oxidation itself.
  • Malonyl-CoA rises in the fed state; hypoglycin does not act through it.
Slides (1)
L24Learning
On the fasting fuel map, which fat-oxidation defects are drawn in the liver, and which in muscle?
  1. A. Liver: MCAD deficiency, CPT-II deficiency, Jamaican vomiting sickness
    Muscle: CPT-I deficiency
  2. B. Liver: MCAD deficiency, CPT-I deficiency, Jamaican vomiting sickness
    Muscle: CPT-II deficiency
  3. C. Liver: CPT-I deficiency, CPT-II deficiency
    Muscle: MCAD deficiency, Jamaican vomiting sickness
AnswerB. Liver: MCAD deficiency, CPT-I deficiency, Jamaican vomiting sickness
Muscle: CPT-II deficiency
WhyLiver blocks (MCAD, CPT-I, ackee poisoning) cut off ketones and gluconeogenesis → hypoketotic hypoglycaemia; muscle CPT-II deficiency starves working muscle of ATP.
Explanation

The map follows fatty acids released by hormone-sensitive lipase to their two main users. In the liver, β-oxidation supplies the acetyl-CoA for ketone bodies, plus the ATP and acetyl-CoA (the pyruvate carboxylase activator) that drive gluconeogenesis. A hepatic block (MCAD deficiency, liver CPT-I deficiency, or hypoglycin A from unripe ackee in Jamaican vomiting sickness) therefore shows up as fasting hypoketotic hypoglycaemia. In muscle, β-oxidation feeds the citric acid cycle for ATP; the muscle form of CPT-II deficiency causes weakness and rhabdomyolysis during exercise or fasting.

  • CPT-II is the defect drawn in muscle, not liver; CPT-I (liver isoform) is the hepatic one.
  • MCAD deficiency and ackee poisoning present as hypoglycaemic crises, not muscle breakdown.

MCAD is present in all tissues, and CPT-II deficiency also has rare severe infantile forms; the map shows where each classically presents.

Slides (3)

Peroxisomal disorders

L25Learning
An infant has hypotonia, seizures and raised phytanic, pristanic and very-long-chain fatty acids from a peroxisome biogenesis defect. What distinguishes this from adult Refsum disease?
  1. A. One α-oxidation enzyme is missing, whereas adult Refsum lacks whole peroxisomes
  2. B. VLCFA import into peroxisomes fails, whereas adult Refsum lacks whole peroxisomes
  3. C. Whole peroxisomes fail to form, whereas adult Refsum lacks one enzyme in normal peroxisomes
AnswerC. Whole peroxisomes fail to form, whereas adult Refsum lacks one enzyme in normal peroxisomes
WhyZellweger-spectrum disease is a biogenesis defect that knocks out all peroxisomal pathways; adult Refsum is a single enzyme (phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase) loss.
Explanation

What accumulates tells you the level of the defect:

  • Zellweger spectrum (peroxins): VLCFA and phytanic/pristanic acids accumulate, because peroxisomal β-oxidation and α-oxidation are both lost.
  • X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1): only VLCFA accumulate; the transporter imports VLCFA-CoA, while phytanic acid is still handled.
  • Adult Refsum disease (phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase): only phytanic acid accumulates; VLCFA are normal.

The two wrong options reverse which disease is the whole-organelle defect.

Slides (2)
Tier 2The next layer across every concept+24 questions

Fasting: releasing stored fat

L26Learning
How does insulin switch hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) off?
  1. A. Activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates HSL into its inactive form
  2. B. Binds HSL directly as an allosteric inhibitor inside the adipocyte
  3. C. Activates a phosphatase (removes HSL's phosphate) and a phosphodiesterase (lowers cAMP)
AnswerC. Activates a phosphatase (removes HSL's phosphate) and a phosphodiesterase (lowers cAMP)
WhyInsulin dephosphorylates HSL through a protein phosphatase and lowers cAMP through a phosphodiesterase, so HSL returns to its inactive, unphosphorylated form.
Explanation

HSL is active when phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase A. Insulin attacks both halves of that signal: it activates phosphodiesterase, which breaks down cAMP so PKA falls silent, and a protein phosphatase, which strips the phosphate off HSL. Dephospho-HSL is inactive, so lipolysis stops after a meal.

  • Protein kinase A phosphorylating HSL is what glucagon and adrenaline do, and phosphorylation activates HSL.
  • Direct allosteric binding: insulin is a peptide hormone acting through its membrane receptor; it never binds HSL.

Hook: on this enzyme, phosphate = fasting = on.

Slides (2)
L27LearningHigh yield
Why can't adipocytes reuse the glycerol released by lipolysis?
  1. A. They lack hormone-sensitive lipase
  2. B. They lack glycerol kinase
  3. C. They lack glucose 6-phosphatase
AnswerB. They lack glycerol kinase
WhyAdipocytes have no glycerol kinase, so they cannot phosphorylate glycerol; it leaves the cell and goes to the liver.
Explanation

To be reused, glycerol must first be phosphorylated to glycerol 3-phosphate by glycerol kinase (ATP → ADP). Adipocytes lack this enzyme, so the glycerol freed by lipolysis diffuses into the blood and travels to the liver, which has glycerol kinase and uses it for gluconeogenesis. Adipocytes make the glycerol 3-phosphate they need for TAG synthesis from glucose instead (glucose → DHAP → glycerol 3-phosphate), which is why fat storage needs insulin-stimulated glucose uptake.

  • Hormone-sensitive lipase is present in adipocytes; it is what releases the glycerol.
  • Glucose 6-phosphatase is the last enzyme of gluconeogenesis in liver and kidney; it has nothing to do with glycerol uptake.
Slides (1)

Activation and the carnitine shuttle

L28LearningHigh yield
Which tissues cannot use fatty acids as fuel?
  1. A. Brain and mature red cells
  2. B. Heart and mature red cells
  3. C. Brain and skeletal muscle
AnswerA. Brain and mature red cells
WhyThe brain does not oxidise fatty acids, and mature red cells have no mitochondria, so neither can burn fat.
Explanation

β-Oxidation needs mitochondria, so cells without them (mature erythrocytes) cannot use fatty acids and depend on glycolysis. The brain has mitochondria but does not oxidise fatty acids to any useful extent (albumin-bound fatty acids barely cross the blood–brain barrier); in prolonged fasting it switches to ketone bodies instead.

  • Heart is the opposite: fatty acids are its preferred fuel at rest.
  • Skeletal muscle cannot make carnitine, but it imports it with a high-affinity transporter and burns fat avidly.
Slides (3)
L29Learning
Which vitamin is coenzyme A made from?
  1. A. Niacin (vitamin B3)
  2. B. Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5)
  3. C. Riboflavin (vitamin B2)
AnswerB. Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5)
WhyCoenzyme A is built from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), so every fatty acid activation depends on B5.
Explanation

Coenzyme A contains pantothenate, a thiol (from cysteamine) and an ADP. Its –SH forms the high-energy thioester in fatty acyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA. The same pantetheine arm forms the acyl carrier protein domain of fatty acid synthase.

  • Niacin (B3) is the precursor of NAD+ and NADP+, used by 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase.
  • Riboflavin (B2) is the precursor of FAD, used by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.

So one turn of activation plus β-oxidation needs B5, B2 and B3.

Slides (3)
L30Learning
Which fatty acids need the carnitine shuttle to enter the mitochondrial matrix?
  1. A. Short chains (medium and long chains cross the inner membrane on their own)
  2. B. Long chains (short and medium chains cross the inner membrane on their own)
  3. C. Medium chains (short and long chains cross the inner membrane on their own)
AnswerB. Long chains (short and medium chains cross the inner membrane on their own)
WhyLong-chain acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane and needs carnitine; short and medium chains enter without it.
Explanation

The inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to CoA and to long-chain acyl-CoA. Long chains (over about 12 carbons) are therefore handed to carnitine and carried in as acylcarnitine. Short- and medium-chain fatty acids cross the inner membrane as free acids and are activated inside the matrix, so they do not depend on carnitine, CPT-I or the translocase.

  • The other two choices invert the rule: it is the long chains, the main dietary and stored fatty acids such as palmitate and oleate, that are carnitine-dependent.

Clinical use: medium-chain triacylglycerol supplies fuel when the carnitine shuttle is defective.

Slides (2)

Control: malonyl-CoA and CPT-I

L31Learning
How do hormones switch acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) on and off?
  1. A. Insulin dephosphorylates it (on); glucagon and adrenaline phosphorylate it (off)
  2. B. Insulin phosphorylates it (on); glucagon and adrenaline dephosphorylate it (off)
  3. C. Insulin dephosphorylates it (off); glucagon and adrenaline phosphorylate it (on)
AnswerA. Insulin dephosphorylates it (on); glucagon and adrenaline phosphorylate it (off)
WhyDephosphorylated ACC is active (insulin); phosphorylated ACC is inactive (glucagon, adrenaline via protein kinase A, and AMP-kinase).
Explanation

ACC is covalently regulated, the mirror image of hormone-sensitive lipase:

  • Insulin activates a phosphatase → dephospho-ACC → active → malonyl-CoA ↑ (synthesis on, oxidation off).
  • Glucagon (glucagon receptor) and adrenaline (β-receptors) → cAMP → protein kinase A → phospho-ACC → inactive. AMP-kinase phosphorylates the same way when energy is low.
  • Citrate activates ACC allosterically; long-chain acyl-CoA inhibits it.

The wrong choices invert either the chemistry (insulin does not phosphorylate ACC) or the outcome (phosphorylation inactivates ACC). Hook: in the fasting state phosphate switches the fat-releasing enzyme (HSL) on and the fat-making enzyme (ACC) off.

Slides (2)

Beta-oxidation and ATP yield

L32Learning
What does acyl-CoA dehydrogenase do in β-oxidation, and what does it produce?
  1. A. Forms a trans double bond between the α- and β-carbons; FADH2
  2. B. Forms a trans double bond between the α- and β-carbons; NADH
  3. C. Forms a cis double bond between the β- and γ-carbons; NADH
AnswerA. Forms a trans double bond between the α- and β-carbons; FADH2
WhyAcyl-CoA dehydrogenase (FAD-dependent) removes hydrogens from C2 (α) and C3 (β) to make trans-Δ2-enoyl-CoA and FADH2.
Explanation

The α-carbon is C2 (next to the thioester carbonyl, C1); the β-carbon is C3, the one that will be oxidised (hence 'β-oxidation'). Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase passes the electrons to its bound FAD; FADH2 hands them via electron-transferring flavoprotein to coenzyme Q, bypassing complex I (so it is worth fewer ATP than NADH). There is a family of chain-length-specific isozymes: SCAD, MCAD, LCAD, VLCAD.

  • NADH is made by the second oxidation (3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase).
  • Cis double bonds at β–γ occur in natural unsaturated fatty acids and need an isomerase; the cycle makes trans α–β bonds.
Slides (3)
L33LearningHigh yield
Why is fat the main fuel of prolonged fasting?
  1. A. It holds ~1.5× the energy of the same mass of carbohydrate or protein
  2. B. It holds ~2.5× the energy of the same mass of carbohydrate or protein
  3. C. It holds ~4× the energy of the same mass of carbohydrate or protein
AnswerB. It holds ~2.5× the energy of the same mass of carbohydrate or protein
WhyFat is the body's most concentrated fuel: about 2.5× the energy per gram of carbohydrate or protein.
Explanation

Fatty acids are highly reduced (mostly CH2) and stored without water, so each gram yields far more ATP when oxidised than glycogen or protein (roughly 9 vs 4 kcal/g). Adipose tissue therefore stores weeks of energy, while liver glycogen lasts about a day. During a fast, fat is mobilised from adipose tissue and burned in liver and muscle.

  • 1.5× and 4× are the neighbouring wrong values; the lecture states 2.5×.

The per-molecule version of the same point: one palmitate gives 129 ATP, one glucose 36–38.

Slides (2)
L34Learning
How many turns of β-oxidation does palmitate (16:0) need, and what do they yield?
  1. A. 7 turns → 7 FADH2, 7 NADH, 8 acetyl-CoA
  2. B. 7 turns → 7 FADH2, 7 NADH, 7 acetyl-CoA
  3. C. 8 turns → 8 FADH2, 8 NADH, 8 acetyl-CoA
AnswerA. 7 turns → 7 FADH2, 7 NADH, 8 acetyl-CoA
WhyA 16-carbon chain needs 7 cuts to give 8 two-carbon units: 7 FADH2, 7 NADH and 8 acetyl-CoA.
Explanation

Each turn makes one cut. Cutting a 16-carbon chain into 8 pieces takes n/2 − 1 = 7 cuts, and each cut yields one FADH2 and one NADH. The last turn acts on a 4-carbon chain (butyryl-CoA) and releases two acetyl-CoA, so there are 8 acetyl-CoA, one more than the number of turns.

  • 7 acetyl-CoA forgets that the final turn leaves two.
  • 8 turns would cut the last acetyl-CoA, which is not possible.

For any even chain of n carbons: n/2 − 1 turns, n/2 acetyl-CoA.

Slides (2)

Peroxisomes, α- and ω-oxidation

L35Learning
When does ω-oxidation rise above its normally minor role?
  1. A. When α-oxidation is defective, e.g. adult Refsum disease
  2. B. When β-oxidation is defective, e.g. MCAD deficiency
  3. C. When insulin is high, e.g. after a large meal
AnswerB. When β-oxidation is defective, e.g. MCAD deficiency
WhyWhen β-oxidation is blocked (classically MCAD deficiency), the trapped medium chains are diverted to ER ω-oxidation and appear as dicarboxylic acids.
Explanation

ω-Oxidation is a spill-over route. In medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, C6–C10 fatty acids cannot continue through β-oxidation; the ER oxidises their ω-end, producing medium-chain dicarboxylic acids (adipic, suberic, sebacic) and their glycine and carnitine conjugates (e.g. suberylglycine) in plasma and urine. Dicarboxylic aciduria with low ketones is a diagnostic clue.

  • Adult Refsum disease blocks α-oxidation; phytanic acid accumulates, but the hallmark is not dicarboxylic aciduria.
  • High insulin suppresses fatty acid oxidation altogether.
Slides (3)

Odd-chain and unsaturated fatty acids

L36LearningHigh yield
Which vitamin-derived coenzyme does methylmalonyl-CoA mutase need?
  1. A. Vitamin B12 (deoxyadenosylcobalamin)
  2. B. Folate (tetrahydrofolate)
  3. C. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate)
AnswerA. Vitamin B12 (deoxyadenosylcobalamin)
WhyMethylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses deoxyadenosylcobalamin, a coenzyme form of vitamin B12.
Explanation

The mutase rearranges L-methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA (a carbon-skeleton shift) by radical chemistry that only cobalamin can do. In B12 deficiency methylmalonyl-CoA builds up and is hydrolysed to methylmalonic acid, which appears in blood and urine. Raised methylmalonic acid therefore distinguishes B12 deficiency from folate deficiency (both raise homocysteine, but only B12 lack raises methylmalonic acid).

  • Folate carries one-carbon units; it is not needed by the mutase.
  • Vitamin B6 is the transaminase cofactor; the lecture text wrongly mentions it for this pathway.
Slides (3)

Ketone bodies: why and how the liver makes them

L37Learning
Why do acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate add acid to the blood?
  1. A. They are acids with pKa ≈ 3.5, so at blood pH they are almost fully dissociated and release H+
  2. B. They are acids with pKa ≈ 7.4, so at blood pH they are only half dissociated and release H+
  3. C. They are bases with pKa ≈ 9.5, so at blood pH they bind H+ and use up buffer
AnswerA. They are acids with pKa ≈ 3.5, so at blood pH they are almost fully dissociated and release H+
WhyWith a pKa of 3.5, acetoacetic and β-hydroxybutyric acids are almost completely ionised at pH 7.4, so each molecule made releases one H+.
Explanation

An acid is half dissociated when pH = pKa. At pH 7.4, about four units above a pKa of 3.5, the anion outnumbers the acid roughly 10,000 to 1, so virtually every molecule has given up its proton. When ketones are made faster than they are burned, the H+ uses up bicarbonate and the unmeasured ketoacid anions widen the anion gap: a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (ketoacidosis).

  • A pKa of 7.4 would mean only half dissociated at blood pH.
  • They are carboxylic acids, not bases; a base binding H+ would raise pH.

Acetone has no carboxyl group, so it adds no acid. (Textbook pKa values are about 3.6 for acetoacetic and 4.4 for β-hydroxybutyric acid; either way both are almost fully dissociated.)

Slides (2)
L38LearningHigh yield
How is acetone formed, and what happens to it?
  1. A. Spontaneous loss of CO2 from acetoacetate; excreted mainly by the kidney as an acid
  2. B. Enzymatic decarboxylation of HMG-CoA; converted back to acetyl-CoA in muscle
  3. C. Spontaneous loss of CO2 from acetoacetate; not a fuel, breathed out (fruity breath)
AnswerC. Spontaneous loss of CO2 from acetoacetate; not a fuel, breathed out (fruity breath)
WhyAcetoacetate decarboxylates spontaneously to acetone, a volatile dead end exhaled through the lungs, giving ketotic patients fruity breath.
Explanation

Acetone forms without an enzyme, simply by loss of CO2 from acetoacetate. It cannot be turned back into acetyl-CoA, so it is not a fuel. Being volatile, it leaves mainly through the lungs: the sweet, fruity odour on the breath is a bedside sign of ketoacidosis.

  • Acetone has no carboxyl group, so it is not an acid; the ketones found in urine are mainly acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate.
  • HMG-CoA is cleaved by lyase to acetoacetate, not decarboxylated to acetone, and acetone is never reused.

Trap: the fruity smell is acetone, not acetoacetate.

Slides (3)

Ketone bodies: fuel for a long fast

L39Learning
How do extrahepatic tissues turn acetoacetate back into acetyl-CoA?
  1. A. Thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase) → acetoacetyl-CoA → thiolase → 2 acetyl-CoA
  2. B. Thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase) → HMG-CoA → lyase → 2 acetyl-CoA
  3. C. Acyl-CoA synthetase (ATP) → acetoacetyl-CoA → thiolase → 1 acetyl-CoA + acetone
AnswerA. Thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase) → acetoacetyl-CoA → thiolase → 2 acetyl-CoA
WhyThiophorase moves CoA from succinyl-CoA onto acetoacetate; thiolase then splits acetoacetyl-CoA into two acetyl-CoA for the citric acid cycle.
Explanation

In the mitochondria of muscle, heart, kidney and (in starvation) brain:

  • β-hydroxybutyrate is first oxidised back to acetoacetate, making NADH;
  • succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase) transfers CoA from succinyl-CoA, giving acetoacetyl-CoA + succinate;
  • thiolase cleaves acetoacetyl-CoA with free CoA into 2 acetyl-CoA, which enter the citric acid cycle.

HMG-CoA is a synthesis intermediate made only in liver, not part of the breakdown route. Activation by acyl-CoA synthetase with ATP is how fatty acids are activated, and no acetone is made on the way to acetyl-CoA.

Slides (3)
L40Learning
How do blood glucose and β-hydroxybutyrate change over 40 days of fasting?
  1. A. Glucose dips in the first days, then holds steady; β-hydroxybutyrate climbs for about three weeks, then plateaus
  2. B. Glucose falls steadily for weeks; β-hydroxybutyrate rises in the first days, then holds steady
  3. C. Glucose climbs for weeks; β-hydroxybutyrate rises for a few days, then falls back
AnswerA. Glucose dips in the first days, then holds steady; β-hydroxybutyrate climbs for about three weeks, then plateaus
WhyGluconeogenesis holds glucose near 3.6–3.8 mM after an early dip, while β-hydroxybutyrate keeps rising for ~3 weeks to ~6 mM, overtaking glucose.
Explanation

On the lecture graph, glucose drops from about 4.8 to 3.8 mM within 3 days and then stays flat for the rest of the fast, because the liver (and later the kidney) defends it by gluconeogenesis. β-Hydroxybutyrate starts near zero, passes glucose at about day 10 and plateaus near 5.5–6 mM after about 3 weeks. Free fatty acids and acetoacetate rise much less, to about 1.3–1.4 mM.

  • Glucose does not keep falling: it is held at a floor.
  • Glucose never climbs in a fast, and ketones do not peak and fall; they keep rising for weeks as the brain adapts.
Slides (1)

Diabetic ketoacidosis

L41Learning
A 20-year-old who stopped his insulin has pH 7.26, PCO2 19 mmHg, HCO3− 8, Na+ 136 and Cl− 101 mEq/L, with urine ketones 2+. What is his anion gap, and what fills it?
  1. A. 27 mEq/L; acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate anions
  2. B. 27 mEq/L; chloride retained in place of bicarbonate
  3. C. 17 mEq/L; acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate anions
AnswerA. 27 mEq/L; acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate anions
WhyAnion gap = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−) = 136 − (101 + 8) = 27; the missing anions are the ketoacid anions.
Explanation

The anion gap estimates unmeasured anions; normal is about 8–16 mEq/L. Here 136 − 109 = 27, clearly high. Each acetoacetic or β-hydroxybutyric acid molecule gives its H+ to bicarbonate (which leaves as CO2), and its anion takes bicarbonate's place in plasma, so HCO3− falls without any rise in Cl−. The low PCO2 (19 mmHg) is respiratory compensation.

  • When chloride replaces lost bicarbonate (diarrhoea, renal loss), the gap stays normal; here Cl− is normal.
  • 17 is an arithmetic slip: 136 − 101 − 8 = 27.
Slides (2)

MCAD deficiency: the defect

L42LearningHigh yield
Which laboratory combination is the fingerprint of MCAD deficiency during a fast?
  1. A. Hypoglycaemia with inappropriately low ketones
  2. B. Hyperglycaemia with inappropriately low ketones
  3. C. Hypoglycaemia with markedly raised ketones
AnswerA. Hypoglycaemia with inappropriately low ketones
WhyA fasting child should make ketones as glucose falls; in MCAD deficiency fat cannot be burned, so glucose falls and ketones stay low: hypoketotic hypoglycaemia.
Explanation

Normally, as fasting glucose falls, insulin falls and the liver switches to β-oxidation and ketogenesis, so hypoglycaemia comes with high ketones (ketotic hypoglycaemia). In a fatty acid oxidation defect the liver cannot make acetyl-CoA from fat: ketone production is low and gluconeogenesis fails too. Low glucose with low ketones therefore points to a block in fat oxidation (or to hyperinsulinism, which suppresses lipolysis).

  • Hyperglycaemia with low ketones is not a fasting picture.
  • Hypoglycaemia with high ketones is the normal response of a starving child.
Slides (2)
L43LearningHigh yield
A 6-month-old becomes lethargic and vomits after an overnight fast. Glucose and ketones are low; C8 acylcarnitine and urine dicarboxylic acids are high. Which deficiency is most likely?
  1. A. Primary carnitine deficiency
  2. B. MCAD deficiency
  3. C. CPT-I deficiency
AnswerB. MCAD deficiency
WhyHypoketotic hypoglycaemia + raised octanoylcarnitine (C8) + dicarboxylic aciduria = MCAD deficiency.
Explanation

All three cause fasting hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, so the acylcarnitine profile decides:

  • MCAD deficiency: chains get into mitochondria but stall at C6–C10, so C8/C10 acylcarnitines rise and ω-oxidation makes dicarboxylic acids.
  • Primary carnitine deficiency: free carnitine and acylcarnitines are low, because there is little carnitine to load acyl groups onto.
  • CPT-I deficiency: long-chain acyl groups are never put onto carnitine, so acylcarnitines are low while free carnitine is normal or high.
Slides (2)

Helga's case: MCAD deficiency in practice

L44LearningHigh yield
Why is Helga's plasma ammonia 100 µmol/L (normal under 20)?
  1. A. Octanoate (C8) uncouples liver mitochondria → less ATP → less urea made
  2. B. Excess ketone bodies inhibit the urea cycle enzymes → less urea made
  3. C. Raised insulin drives muscle protein breakdown → more ammonia released
AnswerA. Octanoate (C8) uncouples liver mitochondria → less ATP → less urea made
WhyAccumulated octanoic acid is a mitochondrial toxin that uncouples oxidative phosphorylation; the ATP-hungry urea cycle slows and ammonia builds up.
Explanation

The urea cycle costs 3 ATP (4 high-energy bonds) per urea and runs partly inside liver mitochondria. In MCAD deficiency the liver is fat-laden and works poorly, and medium-chain fatty acids, especially octanoate, act as uncouplers that dissipate the proton gradient. With less ATP, less ammonia is converted to urea. School answer: "decreased fatty acid oxidation and decreased urea synthesis".

  • Ketone bodies are only a trace in this child.
  • Insulin is low in a fasting infant, and insulin is anabolic: it restrains protein breakdown.
Slides (2)
L45Learning
How does congenital hyperinsulinism differ from MCAD deficiency?
  1. A. Presents at birth, often large for gestational age; free fatty acids and β-hydroxybutyrate both suppressed
  2. B. Presents at birth, often small for gestational age; free fatty acids markedly raised
  3. C. Presents in adolescence, often obese; ketones raised but free fatty acids suppressed
AnswerA. Presents at birth, often large for gestational age; free fatty acids and β-hydroxybutyrate both suppressed
WhyExcess insulin blocks lipolysis and ketogenesis, so free fatty acids and β-hydroxybutyrate are both low; insulin's growth effect in the womb makes the baby large.
Explanation

Both conditions give low ketones during hypoglycaemia, for different reasons. In MCAD deficiency fat is mobilised normally, so free fatty acids are high; it just cannot be oxidised past C12. In congenital hyperinsulinism insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, so free fatty acids are low too. Fetal hyperinsulinism also acts as a growth signal, so the baby is typically large for gestational age and hypoglycaemic from the first hours of life, whereas MCAD babies are well until a fast.

  • Small size with high free fatty acids is the opposite pattern.
  • Ketones cannot be raised while insulin is high.
Slides (1)

Carnitine-shuttle defects and ackee poisoning

L46Learning
What causes secondary carnitine deficiency?
  1. A. Acylcarnitines from CPT-I defects increase renal reabsorption of carnitine
  2. B. Free carnitine from MCAD defects blocks intestinal uptake of carnitine
  3. C. Acylcarnitines from CPT-II or CACT defects inhibit renal reabsorption of carnitine
AnswerC. Acylcarnitines from CPT-II or CACT defects inhibit renal reabsorption of carnitine
WhyIn CPT-II or CACT defects acylcarnitines accumulate and inhibit renal reabsorption of carnitine, so free carnitine is lost in the urine.
Explanation

"Secondary" means the carnitine shortage results from another defect. When acylcarnitines cannot be carried across the inner membrane (CACT) or unloaded in the matrix (CPT-II), they build up, spill into plasma and interfere with carnitine reabsorption in the kidney, so free carnitine is wasted in the urine. Blood acylcarnitines separate the two forms: raised in secondary deficiency, low in primary.

  • CPT-I is what makes acylcarnitines, so CPT-I defects produce few of them.
  • MCAD deficiency does not raise free carnitine, and the loss is renal, not intestinal.
Slides (1)
L47Learning
How are carnitine-shuttle defects treated?
  1. A. High-carbohydrate, low long-chain-fat diet
    Extra medium-chain fat
    Limited physical activity
    Carnitine supplements
  2. B. High-protein, low medium-chain-fat diet
    Extra long-chain fat
    Limited physical activity
    Biotin supplements
  3. C. High-carbohydrate, low long-chain-fat diet
    Avoid medium-chain fat
    Limited physical activity
    Carnitine restriction
AnswerA. High-carbohydrate, low long-chain-fat diet
Extra medium-chain fat
Limited physical activity
Carnitine supplements
WhyTreatment avoids the blocked long-chain route: high carbohydrate, low long-chain fat, extra medium-chain fat, less exercise, and carnitine supplements.
Explanation

Each part targets the defect:

  • High carbohydrate reduces the need for fat oxidation; low long-chain fat limits the substrate that needs the shuttle.
  • Medium-chain fat crosses the inner mitochondrial membrane without carnitine, giving a usable fat fuel.
  • Limited activity avoids the energy crises that trigger rhabdomyolysis.
  • Carnitine replaces what is lacking or lost in urine.

Extra long-chain fat loads the blocked shuttle, and biotin plays no part in it; avoiding medium-chain fat and restricting carnitine would remove the two measures that help. Contrast MCAD deficiency, where medium-chain fat must be avoided.

Slides (2)

Peroxisomal disorders

L48Learning
What is the defect in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD)?
  1. A. ABCD1, which carries VLCFA-CoA into peroxisomes
  2. B. PEX genes, which build the peroxisome
  3. C. CACT, which carries acylcarnitines into mitochondria
AnswerA. ABCD1, which carries VLCFA-CoA into peroxisomes
WhyX-ALD is an X-linked defect in ABCD1, the peroxisomal membrane transporter that imports VLCFA-CoA; VLCFA accumulate and damage myelin and the adrenal cortex.
Explanation

ABCD1 is an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter in the peroxisomal membrane. Without it, very-long-chain fatty acids (C24, C26) cannot reach peroxisomal β-oxidation and build up in plasma and tissues, especially brain white matter and the adrenal cortex. Being X-linked, it affects boys: progressive demyelination and adrenal insufficiency.

  • PEX (peroxin) defects cause the Zellweger spectrum, which loses all peroxisomal functions.
  • CACT is a mitochondrial carnitine-shuttle protein; VLCFA are not oxidised in mitochondria.
Slides (1)
L49Learning
Which set of features describes adult Refsum disease?
  1. A. Cerebellar ataxia
    Peripheral polyneuropathy
    Retinitis pigmentosa
    Adrenal insufficiency
  2. B. Cerebellar ataxia
    Peripheral polyneuropathy
    Retinitis pigmentosa
    Hearing loss
  3. C. Cardiomyopathy
    Peripheral polyneuropathy
    Retinitis pigmentosa
    Rhabdomyolysis
AnswerB. Cerebellar ataxia
Peripheral polyneuropathy
Retinitis pigmentosa
Hearing loss
WhyPhytanic acid build-up damages nerves, cerebellum, retina and inner ear: cerebellar ataxia, peripheral polyneuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa and hearing loss.
Explanation

The lecture's four features all come from phytanic acid accumulating in neural tissue and the retina. Retinitis pigmentosa shows first as night blindness. School vignettes sometimes add loss of smell, scaly skin (ichthyosis) or short metacarpals.

  • Adrenal insufficiency belongs to X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (VLCFA).
  • Cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis belong to muscle CPT-II deficiency.
Slides (2)
Tier 3The rest of the section+22 questions

Fasting: releasing stored fat

L50LearningHigh yield
What activates and what inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL)?
  1. A. Activated: insulin
    Inhibited: glucagon, adrenaline (and cortisol)
  2. B. Activated: glucagon, adrenaline (and cortisol)
    Inhibited: insulin
  3. C. Activated: glucagon, insulin
    Inhibited: adrenaline (and cortisol)
AnswerB. Activated: glucagon, adrenaline (and cortisol)
Inhibited: insulin
WhyGlucagon and adrenaline (helped by cortisol) switch HSL on to mobilise fat; insulin switches it off.
Explanation

HSL is the control point for fat mobilisation. The fasting and stress hormones turn it on: glucagon and adrenaline acutely through cAMP, cortisol more slowly by inducing the enzyme. Sympathetic activity (exercise, stress) therefore raises plasma fatty acids. Insulin, the fed-state hormone, inhibits HSL so stored fat is not released while fuel is plentiful.

  • Insulin activating HSL is the classic reversal: insulin promotes storage.
  • Insulin and glucagon together activating HSL pairs two hormones that always act in opposite directions, and adrenaline never inhibits HSL.
Slides (3)
L51LearningHigh yield
How are the free fatty acids released from adipose tissue carried in the blood?
  1. A. Packaged in VLDL
  2. B. Bound to serum albumin
  3. C. Dissolved free in plasma, unbound
AnswerB. Bound to serum albumin
WhyLong-chain fatty acids are insoluble in water, so they travel to liver and muscle bound to serum albumin.
Explanation

A long hydrocarbon tail makes fatty acids nearly insoluble in plasma. Albumin, the main plasma protein, has several hydrophobic pockets that bind them, so the 'free' fatty acids (free meaning not esterified) ride on albumin from adipose tissue to liver and muscle, where they are taken up and oxidised.

  • VLDL carries triacylglycerol that the liver has made and exports; it is not the vehicle for fatty acids leaving adipose tissue.
  • Unbound in plasma: only a tiny fraction is truly unbound; they would not dissolve in useful amounts.
Slides (2)
L52Learning
A chronic alcoholic becomes hypoglycaemic after a long fast. Lipolysis still delivers glycerol to the liver, yet little becomes glucose. Why?
  1. A. Ethanol directly inactivates liver glycerol kinase
  2. B. Hepatic ATP is too low to phosphorylate glycerol
  3. C. High NADH/NAD+ blocks oxidation of glycerol 3-phosphate to DHAP
AnswerC. High NADH/NAD+ blocks oxidation of glycerol 3-phosphate to DHAP
WhyEthanol oxidation floods the liver with NADH; glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase needs NAD+, so glycerol 3-phosphate is not oxidised to DHAP.
Explanation

Alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase both reduce NAD+ to NADH, so the hepatic NADH/NAD+ ratio soars. Glycerol entering gluconeogenesis must pass glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase, which uses NAD+; with NAD+ scarce the reaction is pushed back toward glycerol 3-phosphate, which is diverted into TAG synthesis (fatty liver, VLDL) instead of DHAP. The same redox shift turns pyruvate into lactate and oxaloacetate into malate, starving gluconeogenesis further.

  • Ethanol inactivating glycerol kinase: there is no such direct effect; phosphorylation still happens.
  • Too little ATP: the liver is not ATP-depleted; the block is redox, at the NAD+-dependent step.
Slides (2)

Activation and the carnitine shuttle

L53LearningHigh yield
Where does the body's carnitine come from?
  1. A. Mainly dietary vegetables; limited synthesis in liver from methionine and folate
  2. B. Mainly dietary meat; limited synthesis in liver and kidney from lysine and SAM
  3. C. Mainly synthesis in skeletal muscle from lysine and SAM; little from the diet
AnswerB. Mainly dietary meat; limited synthesis in liver and kidney from lysine and SAM
WhyCarnitine comes mainly from meat; liver and kidney can make a limited amount from lysine and S-adenosylmethionine (SAM).
Explanation

Carnitine (the name comes from Latin carnis, meat) is abundant in red meat and dairy. Endogenous synthesis uses lysine (the carbon backbone) and SAM (the three methyl groups) in liver and kidney, but it covers only part of the need. That is why strict vegans can develop nutritional (primary) carnitine deficiency.

  • Vegetables are poor sources; folate is not a carnitine precursor.
  • Skeletal muscle holds most of the body's carnitine but cannot make it: it imports it from plasma.
Slides (2)

Control: malonyl-CoA and CPT-I

L54Learning
How does a low-energy state (high AMP) speed up fatty acid oxidation?
  1. A. AMP-kinase activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase and promotes malonyl-CoA synthesis → CPT-I runs faster
  2. B. AMP-kinase inactivates acetyl-CoA carboxylase and promotes malonyl-CoA breakdown → CPT-I runs faster
  3. C. Protein kinase A inactivates CPT-I and promotes malonyl-CoA breakdown → CPT-II runs faster
AnswerB. AMP-kinase inactivates acetyl-CoA carboxylase and promotes malonyl-CoA breakdown → CPT-I runs faster
WhyHigh AMP activates AMP-activated protein kinase, which inactivates ACC and stimulates malonyl-CoA decarboxylase; malonyl-CoA falls and CPT-I opens.
Explanation

When ATP is used faster than it is made (e.g. exercising muscle), AMP rises and activates AMP-kinase (AMPK). AMPK does two things that lower malonyl-CoA: it phosphorylates and inactivates acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC-2 in muscle), so no new malonyl-CoA is made, and it activates malonyl-CoA decarboxylase, which converts existing malonyl-CoA back to acetyl-CoA. CPT-I is released and fat burning rises to restore ATP.

  • Activating ACC would raise malonyl-CoA and slow CPT-I.
  • Protein kinase A inactivating CPT-I: CPT-I is not regulated by phosphorylation, and CPT-II is not the control point.
Slides (2)
L55Learning
Which molecule carries acyl or acetyl groups across the mitochondrial membrane for fatty acid synthesis vs breakdown?
  1. A. Synthesis: citrate (out of mitochondria)
    Breakdown: carnitine (into mitochondria)
  2. B. Synthesis: carnitine (out of mitochondria)
    Breakdown: citrate (into mitochondria)
  3. C. Synthesis: citrate (into mitochondria)
    Breakdown: carnitine (out of mitochondria)
AnswerA. Synthesis: citrate (out of mitochondria)
Breakdown: carnitine (into mitochondria)
WhyCitrate exports acetyl units from mitochondria to the cytosol for synthesis; carnitine imports long acyl groups into mitochondria for breakdown.
Explanation

Acetyl-CoA is made in the mitochondria but fatty acids are built in the cytosol, so acetyl units leave as citrate (citrate shuttle; ATP-citrate lyase regenerates acetyl-CoA outside). Fatty acids for oxidation must go the other way, entering the matrix as acylcarnitine.

  • Carnitine for synthesis, citrate for breakdown swaps the carriers.
  • Citrate into, carnitine out of mitochondria keeps the carriers but reverses both directions.
Slides (1)
L56Learning
Which redox coenzymes do fatty acid synthesis and breakdown use?
  1. A. Synthesis: NADPH (reduction)
    Breakdown: NAD+, FAD (oxidation)
  2. B. Synthesis: NADH (reduction)
    Breakdown: NADP+, FAD (oxidation)
  3. C. Synthesis: NAD+, FAD (oxidation)
    Breakdown: NADPH (reduction)
AnswerA. Synthesis: NADPH (reduction)
Breakdown: NAD+, FAD (oxidation)
WhySynthesis is a reduction using NADPH; breakdown is an oxidation that reduces FAD and NAD+.
Explanation

Building a saturated chain means reducing carbonyl groups to CH2, which needs electrons from NADPH (from the pentose phosphate pathway and malic enzyme). β-Oxidation does the reverse and hands electrons to FAD (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase) and NAD+ (3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase), which then feed the electron transport chain.

  • NADH for synthesis / NADP+ for breakdown swaps the phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated forms: anabolic reductions use NADPH, catabolic oxidations use NAD+.
  • NAD+/FAD for synthesis, NADPH for breakdown reverses the pathways: synthesis is a reduction, breakdown an oxidation.
Slides (1)

Beta-oxidation and ATP yield

L57Learning
Which ATP values per NADH, FADH2 and acetyl-CoA does the lecture use?
  1. A. NADH 2
    FADH2 3
    Acetyl-CoA 12
  2. B. NADH 3
    FADH2 2
    Acetyl-CoA 10
  3. C. NADH 3
    FADH2 2
    Acetyl-CoA 12
AnswerC. NADH 3
FADH2 2
Acetyl-CoA 12
WhyOlder accounting: NADH = 3, FADH2 = 2, acetyl-CoA = 12 ATP (its cycle turn gives 3 NADH + 1 FADH2 + 1 GTP).
Explanation

NADH enters at complex I and drives three proton-pumping sites (3 ATP). FADH2 enters at coenzyme Q, skipping complex I (2 ATP). One acetyl-CoA in the citric acid cycle yields 3 NADH (9) + 1 FADH2 (2) + 1 GTP (1) = 12.

  • NADH 2, FADH2 3 swaps them: FADH2 always gives less because it skips complex I.
  • Acetyl-CoA 10 is the modern value, which goes with NADH 2.5 and FADH2 1.5, not with 3 and 2.
Slides (3)

Peroxisomes, α- and ω-oxidation

L58Learning
Why does peroxisomal β-oxidation make less ATP than mitochondrial β-oxidation?
  1. A. Its thiolase releases propionyl-CoA instead of acetyl-CoA, which cannot enter the citric acid cycle
  2. B. Its enoyl-CoA hydratase spends ATP to add water across the double bond
  3. C. Its first enzyme, acyl-CoA oxidase, passes electrons straight to O2 (→ H2O2) instead of the electron transport chain
AnswerC. Its first enzyme, acyl-CoA oxidase, passes electrons straight to O2 (→ H2O2) instead of the electron transport chain
WhyPeroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase hands its electrons straight to O2, making H2O2, so that step yields no ATP.
Explanation

In mitochondria, acyl-CoA dehydrogenase sends electrons from FADH2 to the electron transport chain (worth 2 ATP per turn in the lecture's values). In peroxisomes, acyl-CoA oxidase hands them directly to molecular oxygen, forming hydrogen peroxide, which catalase breaks down to water and O2. That energy is lost as heat. The rest of the cycle is similar; NADH and acetyl-CoA are exported, and the shortened acyl-CoA (<C20) goes to mitochondria.

  • Propionyl-CoA is the end product of odd-chain fatty acids, not the peroxisomal problem.
  • Hydratase uses no ATP in either organelle.
Slides (3)
L59Learning
Why can't phytanic acid enter β-oxidation directly?
  1. A. A double bond on its β-carbon blocks the cycle
  2. B. A methyl group on its α-carbon blocks the cycle
  3. C. A methyl group on its β-carbon blocks the cycle
AnswerC. A methyl group on its β-carbon blocks the cycle
WhyPhytanic acid (3,7,11,15-tetramethylhexadecanoic acid) carries a methyl branch on C3, the β-carbon, which cannot be oxidised to the β-keto group thiolase needs.
Explanation

β-Oxidation must turn the β-carbon into a ketone. In phytanic acid that carbon already holds a methyl group, so it cannot become a C=O and the cycle stalls. α-Oxidation removes the first carbon, which moves the methyl to the α-position (C2) of the new chain, pristanic acid, where it does not block β-oxidation.

  • Double bond on the β-carbon describes an unsaturated fatty acid; that is handled by an isomerase, not α-oxidation.
  • Methyl on the α-carbon is the situation after α-oxidation (pristanic acid), and it is β-oxidisable.
Slides (1)

Odd-chain and unsaturated fatty acids

L60Learning
Besides odd-chain fatty acids, which amino acids feed into propionyl-CoA?
  1. A. Leucine, lysine, phenylalanine, tyrosine
  2. B. Isoleucine, alanine, cysteine, tryptophan
  3. C. Valine, isoleucine, methionine, threonine
AnswerC. Valine, isoleucine, methionine, threonine
WhyValine, isoleucine, methionine and threonine (plus odd-chain fatty acids) are degraded to propionyl-CoA.
Explanation

Propionyl-CoA is a meeting point: odd-chain fatty acids, Met, Thr, Ile and Val all enter here and pass through methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. That is why a block in this pathway is worsened by protein intake. Mnemonic: VOMIT (Valine, Odd-chain fatty acids, Methionine, Isoleucine, Threonine).

  • Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic (acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate); phenylalanine and tyrosine go to fumarate and acetoacetate.
  • Alanine, cysteine, tryptophan go to pyruvate (and acetyl-CoA); only isoleucine of this set is right.
Slides (1)
L61LearningHigh yield
Which fatty acids can supply carbon for net glucose synthesis during a fast, and through which intermediate?
  1. A. Odd-chain fatty acids, via propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA
  2. B. Even-chain fatty acids, via acetyl-CoA → oxaloacetate
  3. C. Branched phytanic acid, via pristanic acid → pyruvate
AnswerA. Odd-chain fatty acids, via propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA
WhyThe final propionyl-CoA of an odd-chain fatty acid becomes succinyl-CoA, a citric acid cycle intermediate that can be drawn off to oxaloacetate and glucose.
Explanation

Succinyl-CoA → succinate → fumarate → malate leaves the mitochondrion and is converted to oxaloacetate → phosphoenolpyruvate → glucose. So the last three carbons of an odd-chain fatty acid are glucogenic, a small but real contribution to gluconeogenesis in fasting.

  • Even-chain fatty acids yield only acetyl-CoA; its two carbons are lost as CO2 in the citric acid cycle, so there is no net oxaloacetate and no net glucose.
  • Phytanic acid is α-oxidised to pristanic acid, which is β-oxidised to acetyl- and propionyl-CoA; it does not form pyruvate.
Slides (2)

Ketone bodies: why and how the liver makes them

L62Learning
Where are ketone bodies made?
  1. A. In liver and muscle mitochondria
  2. B. Only in liver mitochondria
  3. C. Only in liver cytosol
AnswerB. Only in liver mitochondria
WhyKetogenesis runs only in hepatic mitochondria, where β-oxidation releases its acetyl-CoA and where the mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase sits.
Explanation

The ketogenic enzymes (thiolase, mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase, HMG-CoA lyase, β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase) are in the matrix of liver mitochondria, right where β-oxidation dumps its acetyl-CoA. The liver then exports the ketone bodies to other tissues.

  • Muscle burns ketone bodies but does not make them in any meaningful amount.
  • The cytosol holds a different HMG-CoA synthase isozyme whose HMG-CoA goes to cholesterol synthesis. So HMG-CoA made in mitochondria → ketone bodies; HMG-CoA made in the cytosol → cholesterol.

Textbooks allow a small contribution from kidney; the lecture says liver only.

Slides (2)

Ketone bodies: fuel for a long fast

L63Learning
How many ATP (older values) do acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate each yield?
  1. A. Acetoacetate 24
    β-Hydroxybutyrate 24
  2. B. Acetoacetate 23
    β-Hydroxybutyrate 26
  3. C. Acetoacetate 26
    β-Hydroxybutyrate 23
AnswerB. Acetoacetate 23
β-Hydroxybutyrate 26
WhyAcetoacetate gives 2 acetyl-CoA (24 ATP) minus ~1 for activation = 23; β-hydroxybutyrate adds an NADH (+3) = 26.
Explanation

With the lecture's older conversion values (acetyl-CoA 12, NADH 3):

  • Acetoacetate → 2 acetyl-CoA = 24 ATP, minus 1 because thiophorase spends a succinyl-CoA that would otherwise have made a GTP → 23.
  • β-Hydroxybutyrate is first oxidised to acetoacetate, making 1 NADH (+3) → 26.

The equal-yield option ignores both the activation cost and the extra NADH; the swapped option reverses which ketone carries the extra reducing power. With modern values (NADH 2.5, acetyl-CoA 10) the figures are about 19 and 21.5; the exam uses 23 and 26.

Slides (2)
L64Learning
Very well fed vs starved for 5 weeks: acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate?
  1. A. Acetoacetate 0.04 → 6.0 mM
    β-Hydroxybutyrate 0.03 → 1.3 mM
  2. B. Acetoacetate 0.04 → 1.3 mM
    β-Hydroxybutyrate 0.03 → 6.0 mM
  3. C. Acetoacetate 0.4 → 1.3 mM
    β-Hydroxybutyrate 0.3 → 2.0 mM
AnswerB. Acetoacetate 0.04 → 1.3 mM
β-Hydroxybutyrate 0.03 → 6.0 mM
WhyBoth start near zero; after 5 weeks β-hydroxybutyrate reaches ~6 mM, about five times acetoacetate (1.3 mM).
Explanation

In the fed state ketones are barely detectable (0.03–0.04 mM). Five weeks of starvation raise β-hydroxybutyrate about 200-fold and acetoacetate about 30-fold. β-Hydroxybutyrate dominates because the fat-burning liver has a high NADH/NAD+ ratio, which drives 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase toward the reduced form.

  • The swapped option makes acetoacetate the main ketone, the reverse of the table.
  • The other option starts ten times too high: fed ketone levels are in the hundredths of a mM.
Slides (2)

Diabetic ketoacidosis

L65Learning
In poorly controlled type 1 diabetes, which insulin-stimulated proteins are less active than normal?
  1. A. Lipoprotein lipase
    Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
    Fatty acid synthase
    GLUT4
  2. B. Hormone-sensitive lipase
    Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
    Fatty acid synthase
    GLUT4
  3. C. Lipoprotein lipase
    Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
    HMG-CoA synthase
    GLUT1
AnswerA. Lipoprotein lipase
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Fatty acid synthase
GLUT4
WhyInsulin drives LPL, ACC, fatty acid synthase and GLUT4; without insulin all four fall, while hormone-sensitive lipase rises.
Explanation

Insulin is the storage hormone. It moves GLUT4 to the membrane of muscle and fat cells, induces lipoprotein lipase in adipose capillaries, and activates and induces acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase in the liver. In uncontrolled type 1 diabetes all four are low, which is why glucose stays in the blood and fat is not stored.

  • Hormone-sensitive lipase is inhibited by insulin, so it is more active.
  • Mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase is induced in fasting and diabetes, and GLUT1 is the insulin-independent basal transporter.
Slides (1)
L66Learning
A man with untreated type 1 diabetes and ketoacidosis is given insulin. Which value will rise as a result?
  1. A. Blood glucose
  2. B. Blood pH
  3. C. Blood ketone bodies
AnswerB. Blood pH
WhyInsulin switches off hormone-sensitive lipase and ketogenesis and lets tissues burn the ketones, so acid production stops and pH rises toward normal.
Explanation

Insulin reverses the DKA cascade: it inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase (less fatty acid reaches the liver) and activates ACC (malonyl-CoA rises and closes CPT-I), cutting the acetyl-CoA overflow into ketone bodies. Ketoacids already present are oxidised by muscle and other tissues, which regenerates bicarbonate, and the pH climbs.

  • Blood glucose falls: insulin moves glucose into muscle and fat through GLUT4 and stops hepatic glucose output.
  • Ketone bodies fall as production stops and use continues.

Clinical aside: insulin also drives K+ into cells, so serum potassium falls and must be watched.

Slides (1)

MCAD deficiency: the defect

L67Learning
What is the typical story of MCAD deficiency?
  1. A. Infant unwell while fed regularly; improves when fasting because fat burning then takes over
  2. B. Child well at rest; develops muscle cramps and dark urine only after hard exercise
  3. C. Infant well while fed regularly; decompensates when fasting (illness, missed feed) because it cannot switch to fat
AnswerC. Infant well while fed regularly; decompensates when fasting (illness, missed feed) because it cannot switch to fat
WhyInfants with MCAD deficiency are normal while fed; a fast (overnight, vomiting, infection) exposes the block, causing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, lethargy and coma.
Explanation

Between meals the body relies on fat for energy and for the acetyl-CoA and ATP that drive gluconeogenesis. A baby with MCAD deficiency copes as long as feeds come every few hours. When intake stops (a viral illness with vomiting, a long sleep), liver glycogen runs out within about 12 hours and the child becomes lethargic, then unrousable. Some die suddenly, and the death may be labelled a "Reye-like syndrome".

  • Fasting makes things worse, never better, because fat burning is the defective pathway.
  • Exercise-induced cramps and dark urine (myoglobinuria) is the story of muscle CPT-II deficiency.
Slides (2)
L68LearningHigh yield
In which form do stranded medium chains leave the mitochondria in MCAD deficiency?
  1. A. As C14–C18 acylcarnitines (C16 and C18 build up in blood and urine)
  2. B. As C6–C10 acyl-CoAs (C8 and C10 build up in blood and urine)
  3. C. As C6–C10 acylcarnitines (C8 and C10 build up in blood and urine)
AnswerC. As C6–C10 acylcarnitines (C8 and C10 build up in blood and urine)
WhyTrapped medium-chain acyl groups are transferred onto carnitine and leave as C6–C10 acylcarnitines; octanoylcarnitine (C8) is the hallmark marker.
Explanation

Behind the block, medium-chain acyl-CoAs accumulate in the matrix. Carnitine acyltransferases move the acyl groups onto carnitine, and the acylcarnitines (or free medium-chain fatty acids) leave the mitochondria and reach blood and urine. Helga's plasma hexanoyl- (C6) and octanoylcarnitine (C8) were 40–50 times normal. A raised C8 acylcarnitine is also how newborn screening picks up MCAD deficiency.

  • C14–C18 acylcarnitines build up in long-chain defects (LCAD, CPT-II), not in MCAD deficiency.
  • Acyl-CoAs cannot cross membranes; they must become acylcarnitines (or free acids) to leave.
Slides (1)

Helga's case: MCAD deficiency in practice

L69Learning
Why must infants with MCAD deficiency avoid formula based on medium-chain triacylglycerol (MCT)?
  1. A. Its fatty acids need carnitine, which they lack
  2. B. Its fatty acids raise malonyl-CoA and block CPT-I
  3. C. Its fatty acids are the very chains they cannot oxidise
AnswerC. Its fatty acids are the very chains they cannot oxidise
WhyMCT supplies C8–C10 fatty acids, exactly the substrates of the missing MCAD; they would only feed acylcarnitine, dicarboxylic acid and octanoate build-up.
Explanation

MCT formulas are used in carnitine-shuttle defects (carnitine deficiency, CPT-I, CACT, CPT-II) because medium chains enter mitochondria without carnitine and bypass the block. In MCAD deficiency the block is inside the mitochondrion at the medium-chain step, so MCT is harmful: the same treatment with the opposite effect.

  • Medium chains cross the inner mitochondrial membrane without carnitine.
  • Malonyl-CoA is made from acetyl-CoA during fatty acid synthesis, not from dietary medium chains.
Slides (2)

Carnitine-shuttle defects and ackee poisoning

L70LearningHigh yield
What causes Jamaican vomiting sickness?
  1. A. Hypoglycin A in ripe breadfruit
  2. B. Hypoglycin A in unripe ackee fruit
  3. C. Phytanic acid in dairy products
AnswerB. Hypoglycin A in unripe ackee fruit
WhyEating unripe ackee (native to West Africa, brought to Jamaica in 1776) delivers hypoglycin A, a toxic amino acid that blocks β-oxidation.
Explanation

Hypoglycin A is concentrated in the unripe fruit; properly ripened ackee that has opened naturally contains far less. It is metabolised to a toxic CoA derivative that stops fatty acid oxidation and causes severe hypoglycaemia.

  • Breadfruit is a different Caribbean staple with no hypoglycin.
  • Phytanic acid from dairy, fish and chlorophyll is the fatty acid that accumulates in adult Refsum disease.
Slides (1)

Peroxisomal disorders

L71LearningHigh yield
Which enzyme is deficient in adult Refsum disease?
  1. A. Pristanoyl-CoA oxidase (peroxisomal β-oxidation)
  2. B. Cytochrome P450 ω-hydroxylase (ω-oxidation)
  3. C. Phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase (peroxisomal α-oxidation)
AnswerC. Phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase (peroxisomal α-oxidation)
WhyAdult Refsum disease is a deficiency of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase, the first enzyme of peroxisomal α-oxidation, so phytanic acid accumulates.
Explanation

Phytanic acid (from chlorophyll; found in dairy products and some fish) has a methyl group on its β-carbon that blocks β-oxidation. α-Oxidation removes one carbon to give pristanic acid, which β-oxidation can then handle. Phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase starts α-oxidation; without it phytanic acid builds up in blood and nerve tissue. Treatment is dietary restriction of phytanic acid.

  • Pristanoyl-CoA is processed by β-oxidation after the α-oxidation step; that is not the Refsum defect.
  • ω-Oxidation in the ER handles medium chains when β-oxidation fails (MCAD deficiency).
Slides (2)
